Despite the EU catch prohibition, deep-sea sharks continue to be caught incidentally by hooks-and-lines fisheries in the Azores. However, information on the bycatch of these species in the region remains scarce. In this data-limited context, knowledge from local fishers can provide a valuable source of information.

In this study, we assessed the vulnerability of two deep-sea shark species (Deania profundorum and Deania calceus) to the bottom longline fishery in the Azores, using the EASI-Fish model. We compared the outcomes of this assessment before and after incorporating knowledge from fishers into key parameters describing the fishery. This local knowledge was obtained through a series of workshops and discussions with fishers and fisheries representatives across several islands in the Azores. The participants were asked to review assumptions regarding the depth range of the fishery and fishing season duration, as well as to provide feedback on the spatial distribution of fishing effort and predicted species distributions.

The incorporation of information from fishers resulted in substantial changes to key model inputs and corresponding differences in outputs, particularly for D. profundorum. This work highlights the potential contribution of fishers' knowledge to improving the representation of fisheries in quantitative assessments in data-limited settings.

59: In the oceanic archipelago of the Azores, deep-water elasmobranchs (DWEs) are frequently caught as bycatch in bottom longline fisheries, largely due to their spatial overlap with the distribution of commercially targeted species. This work aimed to examine this spatial overlap in order to identify trade-off areas that would minimising the bycatch of DWE species while optimising the catch of commercial species. To do so, probabilities of presence of both commercial and DWE were derived from existing species distribution models and combined using different weights as multiplication factors. Several weights combinations were tested to give priority to different management concern for both commercial and DWE species. The resulting outputs were maps with values ranging from -1 to 1, negative values indicating areas where fishing should be avoided to limit bycatch and positive values indicating favourable areas for fisheries. An analysis of how these areas impact each species distribution was also conducted. The results showed that such approach and methodology are effective tools to identify trade-off areas and advise fisheries. The use of weights combination enabled to propose and compare several scenarios, allowing to visualise the outputs from contrasting management priorities. This adjustment was further improved by analysing how trade-off areas impact species-specific species distribution.

60: Elasmobranchs are recognized bioindicators of marine metal contamination, yet tissue-specific accumulation patterns beyond liver and muscle remain poorly characterized. This study examined the distribution of 13 trace elements (Al, Cr, Mn, Fe, Ni, Cu, Zn, As, Se, Sr, Mo, Ba, Pb), quantified by ICP-MS, across four tissues — muscle, skin, heart, and brain — in twelve adult male Galeus melastomus (TL > 34 cm) collected during the 2025 MEDITS trawl survey in the Strait of Sicily. Despite its limited commercial value, G. melastomus is a common trawl bycatch species, making it a useful indicator of contaminant exposure across Mediterranean fishing grounds. Quantitative comparisons revealed clear tissue-specific patterns. Strontium and barium were markedly enriched in skin (mean Sr ~296 vs 4–13 µg/g in other tissues; Ba ~1.35 vs 0.05–0.10), reflecting the mineralized nature of dermal structures exposed to seawater. Iron peaked in heart tissue, consistent with its high metabolic and vascular demand, while arsenic was highest in muscle, matching the known affinity of organoarsenicals for muscular tissue. Notably, copper concentrations were higher in brain and heart than in muscle and skin, a pattern rarely reported for elasmobranchs and worth further investigation. These findings highlight strong tissue-dependent accumulation of trace elements in G. melastomus and support multi-tissue sampling for reliable biomonitoring of Mediterranean elasmobranch populations.
61: Across vertebrates, brain organisation continues to change during postnatal development, often in association with ontogenetic shifts in ecology, behaviour and sensory demands. In sharks, however, such developmental changes remain poorly documented, and virtually nothing is known about brain ontogeny in deep-water species. We examined whole-brain growth and the development of major brain regions (olfactory bulbs, telencephalon, diencephalon, optic tectum, cerebellum, medulla oblongata) across young-of-the-year, subadult and adult stages of the deep-water blackmouth catshark Galeus melastomus. Brain mass increased with body mass, but at a slower rate, and relative brain mass differed significantly among all three life stages. As sharks grew, the olfactory bulbs, medulla oblongata and cerebellum grew faster than the rest of the brain, the optic tectum at a similar rate, and the telencephalon and diencephalon more slowly. Overall, regional growth broadly matched patterns reported in other sharks, although the proportional growth of the optic tectum and the progressive changes in relative brain mass across life stages distinguished G. melastomus. These features may be associated with the timing of sensory pathway maturation and ecological transitions during growth. Our results provide an ontogenetic framework for understanding brain organisation in a deep-water shark.
62: Fisheries management measures relating to elasmobranchs have increased nationally and internationally since the mid-1990s. There has also been a concurrent increase in using nature conservation instruments to afford species-level protection, including Multilateral Environmental Agreements (MEAs; e.g. CITES and CMS). Proposals to list species in the Appendices of MEAs require reflection on defined criteria, yet adoption often aligns closely to IUCN Red List Assessment status. Under the IUCN criteria, species threat status can be based on observed, estimated, projected, inferred or suspected changes. Fisheries management generally differs in the population assessment methods, with more defined ways of interpreting information by data source(s), temporal/spatial scales of underlying data (and representativeness), potential impact of management on the underlying data, and other data quality issues. There are well-defined criteria for listing species in the Appendices of CITES, but the acceptance of listing proposals (2022–2025) reveals a growing contrast in approaches between nature conservation and fisheries science audiences. This paper examines the need for improved societal consideration on interpreting scientific recommendations in delivery of MEA mandates, whether from ‘honest brokers’ or ‘issue advocates’. This is particularly important for exploited aquatic resources, as listing on MEAs can potentially (a) not negate the underlying pressure(s) on the species; (b) impact fishing communities and food security; (c) divert resources away from species or taxa of greater concern; (d) impact the availability, representativeness and quality of datasets for monitoring stock status; and (e) undermine the scientific review and listing process if species not meeting the criteria are listed.

63: With extinction risk rising faster for chondrichthyans, reversing their decline demands action across a range of availalbe tools, ranging from fisheries management, spatial protection to cross-border data sharing and policy alignment. The Critically Endangered Angelshark (Squatina squatina), has vanished from most of its historical range, making coordinated international action essential for its recovery. The Convention on Migratory Species (CMS) provides an intergovernmental framework required to manage transboundary ecological challenges of this scale. CMS enables Range States to align conservation strategies across entire distributions, preventing jurisdictional discrepancies from undermining species protection. Central to this approach are Single Species Action Plans (SSAPs), which translate regional mandates into binding, cross-border strategies for priority species. In 2024, the Mediterranean Angelshark Population became subject to the first SSAP for a chondrichthyan under CMS, a proof of concept for similar plans for other species. Operationalizing this required a formal structure linking governments and scientists. An International Working Group was established for this purpose, and brings together government and expert representatives from Mediterranean Range States. The WG has mapped Angelshark occurrence against MPAs and has set measurable targets. With the Angel Shark Conservation Network, the WG is developing guides, protocols, and reporting tools.

64: Metropolitan France holds 106 chondrichthyans, with about 10% threatened following the IUCN and many others Data Deficient. Their legal framework is highly fragmented, spanning international conventions and RFMOs to EU and national regulations, across fisheries, trade and environmental policy, creating uncertainty and making it hard to assess whether current rules effectively protect threatened species. This study synthesizes the policy framework governing chondrichthyans in metropolitan France. We identify all applicable regulations, their content, binding force and scope, highlighting key strengths, gaps, and inconsistencies, and examine French administrative powers and how they implement and strengthen this framework. Most legal texts derive from international or EU law, with few from French legislation. Although French authorities have tools to regulate fisheries and protect marine biodiversity, these are rarely used for chondrichthyans, which fall outside the general species protection regime; existing regulations focus mainly on fisheries and cover only a fraction of species. Stronger measures are needed for threatened species remaining poorly protected. A key contribution is an up-to-date catalogue of regulations applicable to chondrichthyans in metropolitan France, including recent amendments and new regulations. This reduces uncertainty by identifying applicable regulations and coverage gaps per species, helping stakeholders implement and improve this framework.

65: Egypt has one of the largest fishing fleets in the southern Mediterranean, which commonly interacts with elasmobranch. A bycatch monitoring project was conducted in a collaborative effort between Banlastic Egypt and iSea across two main landing sites, "Alexandria and Damietta" with over 62 port visits between December 2025 and August 2026. A total of 3,228 individuals were recorded, comprising 35 elasmobranch species, weighing around 61,600 kg. The most common species were Common guitarfish (Rhinobatos rhinobatos), Common smooth-hound (Mustelus mustelus), Longnose spurdog (Squalus blainville), Blackchin guitarfish (Glaucostegus cemiculus), and Lusitanian cownose ray (Rhinoptera marginata). Alarmingly, 79% of recorded individuals belong to IUCN Red List threatened categories. Morphometric data were collected for multiple species, contributing baseline biological observations currently absent from the literature for this region. Field observations also indicated a clear social dimension: most fishers acknowledge legal restrictions yet continue landing threatened species due to limited economic alternatives. These findings, together with recent research, suggest Egypt's Mediterranean coast as a significant elasmobranch bycatch hotspot and underscore the need for community-engaged conservation strategies and strengthened regional monitoring. 66: Modern Western conservation stems from colonial practices. Coloniality describes the persistence of these philosophies and patterns that entrench Western, colonial-era narratives and power structures, at the expense of marginalised social groups. Colonial practices have negative impacts on conservation outcomes, but remain underexplored in shark conservation. This thesis used knowledge hierarchies and policy preferences as themes to explore how coloniality might be present in shark conservation. A thematic analysis was performed on in-depth and semi-structured expert interviews (n=4) with actors from the shark conservation field. Their perspectives were coded. This found that while knowledge and awareness on the subject are growing, knowledge hierarchies are still present through disregard for local needs, parachute science, non-meaningful and exploitative local involvement and seeing Western science as inherently objective. It was also found that there are one-size-fits-all policy preferences that devalue and miss local needs and capacities. Large NGOs and Western-based institutions control narratives, funds and opportunities. Lastly, shark conservation narratives push Western-centric ideals and values, and villainise local communities, especially fishers. This all promotes colonial-era power imbalances. Based on this research, six recommendations to decolonise shark conservation were formulated.

The Angel Shark Conservation Network (ASCN) was established in 2016 to empower action to restore and safeguard angel shark populations across their natural range. The ASCN encourages and supports organisations and individuals to deliver actions outlined within these planning documents, promoting a coordinated approach to angel shark recovery. 68: In the Southwest Atlantic, at least four angelshark species have been confirmed: Squatina argentina (Argentine Angelshark), S. guggenheim (Angular Angelshark), S. occulta (Hidden Angelshark), and S. varii (Vari's Angelshark). Argentina and Uruguay, conversely, have a joint-management agreement for elasmobranchs that issues fishing quotas instead of prohibitions, and there is evidence of exportation to Brazil. Despite this, research on Southwest Atlantic angelsharks remains scarce, especially molecular data, present mostly for S. guggenheim. 69: Shark fishing practices are causing serious animal and environmental harm globally. Currently, laws are ineffective in protecting sharks. Research shows that harmful shark fishing practices are growing on a global scale, despite the increasing number of protective laws. Consequently, this presentation will propose a solution which adopts a holistic approach to shark protections through biocentrism. It will argue that the law should not be viewed in isolation but as one element of the solution. The other elements which will be discussed are environmental ethics and culture. Under environmental ethics, shark protections that are grounded in anthropocentric (human-centred) ethics will be criticised because they morally justify exploiting animals for human gains. Instead, it will be argued that biocentric (life-centred) ethics should guide protections based on its values, including intrinsic value, moral consideration, and perceiving all lives as equal while providing each species with what they need to thrive. Subsequently, the importance of cultural relationships with sharks in coastal nations will be discussed to establish their significance to shark fishing practices. It will also look at the ways in which anthropocentric cultures can transition from harmful practices to biocentric conservation practices while protecting culture. The concluding argument will be that biocentrism should guide shark protections through law, ethics, and culture.
70: The first confirmed nursery habitat worldwide for a guitarfish species was recently identified in the Eastern Levantine Basin for the Critically Endangered blackchin guitarfish (Glaucostegus cemiculus) at Ma'agan Michael. Building on this, we expanded long-term monitoring 90 km south, of Evtach MPA and evaluated it as a second nursery habitat and conducted an analysis comparing the two confirmed nurseries. At Evtach, same-day paired surveys showed significantly higher neonate densities than at a nearby reference site (6.97 vs. 0.90 individuals/km; n = 10 pairs; Wilcoxon P = 0.014). Neonates occurred from August to November in all monitored years (2017-2018, 2023-2025). This shows that Evtach fulfills all three nursery habitat criteria and exhibits the same seasonal pattern reported at Ma'agan Michael. Size-adjusted disc morphology did not differ between nurseries (PERMANOVA, P = 0.574), and mass-length allometric scaling was conserved (Likelihood ratio test, P = 0.537). However, neonates from Evtach exhibited higher expected body mass at a given length (SMA elevation, P = 0.0096) and significantly better body condition than those from Ma'agan Michael (SMI: 112.5 ± 10.9 vs. 108.0 ± 13.9; Wilcoxon P = 0.011). Our findings reveal strong ecological similarity between nurseries while highlighting spatial variation in juvenile condition. Comparative nursery ecology can help identify and prioritize habitats essential for recruitment and persistence of this endangered batoid.

71: Fuvahmulah, Maldives, hosts one of the largest documented aggregations of tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier), with over 320 individuals identified through long-term photo-identification. This predictable food subsidy provides a unique opportunity to investigate how provisioning may influence tiger shark ecology. 72: For the last 10 years, the Angel Shark Project has monitored the largest known nursery area for the Critically Endangered angelshark (Squatina squatina), Las Teresitas, Tenerife, North-East Atlantic. Long-term monitoring of this area has contributed to a better understanding of the species’ biology and habitat use, which has been used to delineate an Important Shark and Ray Area (ISRA) and to develop targeted conservation measures at the local scale. Ray species have experienced significant population declines in recent decades and are highly vulnerable to anthropogenic impacts due to their slow life cycles, low fecundity, and susceptibility to bycatch. Despite their ecological importance, knowledge of the spatial ecology of rays in the northwestern Mediterranean remains limited and is based mainly on fishing records and occasional sampling. Understanding their spatial ecology is essential for designing effective conservation strategies. In this study, acoustic telemetry is used to assess movement patterns, site fidelity, habitat use, and connectivity in four ray’s species along the northwestern Mediterranean coast: Myliobatis aquila and Aetomylaeus bovinus (Myliobatidae), and Dasyatis pastinaca and Pteroplatytrygon violacea (Dasyatidae).

The study area includes a network of Marine Protected Areas (MPAs), allowing for the assessment of functional connectivity. Preliminary results reveal movement patterns and a preference for shallow sandy habitats associated with Cymodocea nodosa meadows, mostly outside existing MPAs. These habitats serve as both feeding grounds and movement corridors between neighbouring bays.

Our findings highlight gaps in current MPA coverage and the need to integrate critical habitats, movement routes, and species-specific requirements into conservation and fisheries management to improve batoid conservation.

74: Sharks and rays are key apex and meso-predators in coastal Caribbean ecosystems. However, researchers have not adequately characterized their community structure in nearshore waters of Saint Barthélemy, French West Indies despite the presence of established Marine Protected Areas (MPA). We deployed baited remote underwater video surveys (BRUVS) in relatively shallow (<8m depth) nearshore habitats (<250m from shoreline) to determine relative abundance of elasmobranchs within these areas. Additionally, across two years, we sampled single and replicated sites within and outside MPA to determine if abundance differed between these treatments. We systematically analyzed each video and recorded species identity, number of individuals, time in frame, approach behavior, feeding posture, and interactions with the bait cage. We used meancounts rather than MaxN or MaxIND to better estimate populations represented in these surveys. Analyses are ongoing to compare survey results between sites inside and outside the MPA and to evaluate associations with habitat characteristics, including coral and seagrass presence, human recreation, boating activity, island location, and current direction. Preliminary results from Season 1 revealed a significant difference between MPA and non-MPA sites. Our results improve understanding of MPA function and elasmobranch relative abundance within nearshore Caribbean habitats, while providing essential data to the local natural-resource management agency.
75: Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) are expanding under the global goal to protect 30% of the ocean by 2030. However, effective conservation depends on whether protection covers vulnerable species and key habitats. Chondrichthyans are among the most threatened marine vertebrates, mainly due to fishing. This study assessed how well Australia’s no-take MPAs, where fishing is prohibited, protect chondrichthyan distributions and Important Shark and Ray Areas (ISRAs). We also compared two spatial planning scenarios for expanding no-take protection to 30% of Australian waters: strengthening protection within existing MPAs, or also allowing new no-take areas outside them. Existing no-take areas poorly represented chondrichthyan biodiversity and ISRAs, with species richness highest in areas open to fishing and outside MPAs. Strengthening protection within existing MPAs improved representation but left many targets unmet. Allowing new no-take areas outside current boundaries more than doubled the number of targets achieved and reduced average target shortfall from 18.9±29.8% to 3.4±6.4%. Irreplaceable areas were concentrated on the continental shelf and slope, while most existing no-take MPAs occurred in the deep sea. These results show that area-based targets alone are insufficient: combining species distributions with ecologically important habitats can support more representative and strategically located protection for chondrichthyans.

76: Filfla (Malta, Central Mediterranean) is a tiny islet characterized by its offshore location, unique benthic topography and status as Malta’s first marine protected area (MPA). Despite recognition in oral histories as a key shark area, it has received little scientific attention outside ornithology, resulting in a very limited marine survey history. Regardless, historical and contemporary records continue to indicate that Filfla supports a diverse elasmobranch assemblage. Carcharodon carcharias was recorded at Filfla in 1956, the 1960s and 1987. Squatina spp. were seen in 2006 and 2022, and local fishers report a possible nursery around the islet. Galeus melastomus was photographed in a cavern in 2006. Sharklab-Malta's SCUBA surveys have added to this picture since 2012, with presence/absence records to 2015 detailing 8 batoid species, and a quantitative baseline snapshot in 2024 recorded 162 batoids across 3 species, Dasyatis pastinaca, Bathytoshia lata and Myliobatis aquila, including D. pastinaca courtship behaviour and a recorded mating attempt. At least 11 elasmobranch species are now known from the 1NM exclusion zone that marks the MPA boundary. However, a legacy fishing exemption from 1990 remains active within the MPA, and several of the species recorded remain without any national protection despite CMS/Barcelona Convention updates. We present this synthesis to argue for expanded, standardised survey efforts at Filfla and closure of its regulatory gaps.

78: Pelagic sharks range across expansive oceans, yet some biological requirements depend on localised reef habitats. Cleaning provides parasite removal and tissue maintenance, suggesting cleaning services may be important to wide-ranging species. 79: The Indo-Pacific leopard shark (Stegostoma tigrinum) has undergone severe declines across much of its range, with the Western Indian Ocean–Southeast Asian subpopulation listed as Critically Endangered. We used a 14-year dataset (2011–2025) of underwater surveys and photo-identification records to investigate the spatial ecology, site fidelity, and behaviour of leopard sharks in southern Mozambique. Across 9,219 surveys, 631 leopard shark sightings were recorded, representing 164 identified individuals. The population was strongly female-biased and dominated by adult and subadult sharks. Sightings were concentrated at a small cluster of reefs north of Tofo, highlighting these reefs as an important habitat for the species. Photo-identification records revealed long-term site fidelity, with 35% of sharks resighted at least once and 27% recorded across multiple years, including one individual documented over an 11-year period. Inter-regional movements were rare, with only three sharks recorded moving between Tofo and Morrungulo, approximately 60 km apart. Three courtship interactions were documented, representing the first records of courtship behaviour for S. tigrinum in the Western Indian Ocean. Observed behaviours included close pursuit and caudal fin grasping, consistent with pre-copulatory behaviour. Our findings support the need for targeted protection of key habitats and continued long-term monitoring to inform conservation management.

The Amvrakikos Gulf is a known nursery area for elasmobranchs, including Gymnura altavela and Aetomylaeus bovinus, while its role for Myliobatis aquila has remained unclear until recently. The specific distribution of early life stages and their fishery interactions were poorly understood. This study assessed the spatiotemporal distribution of early life stages and fishery interactions of these three threatened species across the Gulf.

Data from 1,298 fishing deployments were analysed using GIS and statistical analyses to examine differences in catch intensity by port, month, depth, and fishing métier.

Early life stages dominated catches of all three species. Estuarine conditions favoured early life stages, with catch rates peaking from late spring to early autumn. They occurred at shallower depths than mature individuals, though M. aquila was distributed deeper than the other two. Prawn fishery had the highest total catch due to greater fishing effort, while standardised catch rates were highest in métiers using larger mesh sizes, likely reflecting increased entanglement risk from the wider disc width.

These findings confirm the Gulf's nursery function for G. altavela and A. bovinus and support including M. aquila in the Gulf’s ISRA delineation. Management should engage local fishers through training in safe handling and release, and advocate for measures for these species in the area’s Natura2000 Management Plan and the revision of the National Park’s Presidential Decree.

The last known reproductive population of the Critically Endangered Common Guitarfish (Rhinobatos rhinobatos) was rediscovered in southeastern Spain after being presumed extinct in the Western Mediterranean for over three decades. Since 2024, the GuitarProtect Initiative has combined acoustic telemetry, underwater visual censuses, and community science to improve the understanding of its spatial ecology and inform conservation.

Acoustic telemetry has provided over two years of continuous monitoring (July 2024–August 2026), revealing high residency within known and newly identified hotspot areas for individuals up to a certain body size. However, larger individuals increasingly disappear from monitored shallow-water areas, with some subsequently returning while others remain undetected. This pattern raises questions about ontogenetic shifts in habitat use and potential fishing-related mortality, motivating the expansion of the acoustic array into deeper waters in September 2026. Initial deep-water BRUV and ROV surveys provide complementary information on habitat use, with early results presented here.

The programme is complemented by 96 underwater visual census transects and over 600 community science records of sharks and rays. Together with genetic and blood analyses, these approaches are improving our understanding of the spatial ecology and biological status of this highly threatened population, providing a solid evidence base for current conservation and management.

83: Emergent fungal pathogens have impacted numerous flora and fauna including bats, frogs, salamanders, snakes, turtles, crocodilians, coral, fish, chestnuts, elms, and various crops. Here, we focus on the fungal pathogen Ophidiomyces ophidiicola (Oo), an introduced pathogen that infects wild and captive snakes. An extreme generalist, this pathogen maintains a vast host range across North America and has been documented in Europe, Asia, and Australia. One of the primary problems with detecting Oo is the difficulty of synthetic swabs to effectively pull spores from infected snakes, resulting in high frequency of false negatives. To remedy this, it is recommended that several swabs be used across the length of the body to more effectively collect spores. In this study, we aim to assess the ability of alternative methods of collecting spores from infected hosts. Corn snakes, Pantherophis guttatus, will be experimentally infected in the lab. Following signs of infection, snakes will be sampled using dry swabs, swabs with solvent, two kinds of tape lifts, as well as water baths that will be filtered through nanopore filters. These methods have shown to be effective in other situations, such as lifting DNA from crime scenes (tape-lifts) or pulling zoospores of chytrid fungus from frogs (water baths). With this project we hope to reduce the rate of false negatives, reduce costs associated with detection of Oo (by eliminating the need for duplicate swabs), and increase the ability of wildlife biologists to detect Oo in wild populations. 84: Character displacement, in which species are more dissimilar in sympatry compared to allopatry, is a common outcome of competition and can manifest in ecological and/or morphological traits. Determining if and how character displacement manifests within given populations is important for understanding how species have evolved to reduce competition and coexist. Multiple species of Slimy Salamanders of the Plethodon glutinosus group occur sympatrically or allopatrically at sites across the Ouachita Mountains. We measured snout-vent length of adult Plethodon albagula (N=227), Plethodon ouachitae (N=323), and Plethodon kiamichi (N=86) from 215 sites throughout the Ouachita Mountains to test for character displacement in body size. We found that when in sympatry, Plethodon albagula were larger while Plethodon ouachitae were smaller compared to conspecifics in allopatric populations. By contrast, Plethodon kiamichi showed no significant difference in body size between allopatric and sympatric populations. Results for Plethodon albagula and Plethodon ouachitae supported character displacement in body size, but further research is needed to determine the drivers of this divergence as both exploitative and interference competition have been found to mediate interspecific interactions in Plethodon. Hirusha Algewattage
85: The cornified scales of squamates bear cutaneous mechanoreceptors (sensilla) to maintain tactile sensory function with the environment. Sensilla of various squamate species have been described previously, but their ecological significance is unclear. Therefore, a natural experiment was designed to correlate the sensillar morphology and distribution to environmental and behavioral factors by comparing two Iguanian species that differ in key aspects. The Green Anole (Anolis carolinensis) is a small arboreal species adapted to leaping among branches and the Green Iguana (Iguana iguana) is a large arboreal and semi-aquatic species. The type, size, density, distribution and surface structure of the sensilla were recorded for the entire body of preserved specimens using stereomicroscopy and SEM. In Anolis, the surfaces of the scales and bristled sensilla are micro-ornamented; in Iguana, the surfaces of the scales and lenticular sensilla are smooth. The higher sensillar density on cranial aspects of the head and trunk of both species reflects air flow-sensing by the Anole’s bristled sensilla and waterflow-sensing by the Iguana’s lenticular sensilla. Our results highlight mechanosensory adaptations in relation to differing ecological and locomotory demands and support the use of A. carolinensis as an extant functional-morphological model to test Homberger's theory which posits that avian flight evolved from small arboreal lizard-like ancestors that leaped among branches and that feathers evolved from bristled sensilla functioning as airflow sensors and micro-turbulators during aerial locomotion. Chloé M. Allen-Love
86: Little is known about deep-sea species of sharks due to technological limitations and difficulty exploring their habitats. Many are caught as bycatch from deep-sea fisheries, providing little to any information on population ecology, behavior, or reproduction. One way to effectively study reproduction in sharks is through reproductive endocrinology. Gonadal steroid hormone concentrations in blood plasma are frequently used to evaluate correlations between hormones and reproductive status of elasmobranchs. This study focused on analyzing hormone concentrations in Genie’s Dogfish, Squalus clarkae, a recently identified and poorly studied species of shark found in deep-sea sites of the southeast U.S. Gulf coast. Blood samples were collected from both male and female S. clarkae in a large toxicology study on the Deepwater Horizon Oil Spill between 2011 and 2015. The objective of this experiment was to analyze patterns between blood plasma hormone concentration levels and the reproductive condition of male and female S. clarkae. Concentration levels of estradiol (E2) and testosterone (T) were measured in blood plasma samples through chemiluminescence immunoassays (CLIAs) in males and females, respectively. Associations between plasma T and E2 concentrations with animal maturity and reproductive stage are presented. Yara Alshwairikh
87: Artificial light at night (ALAN) is an anthropogenic sensory pollutant which disrupts the natural light cycles organisms use to regulate physiological and behavioral processes. Such disruptions may have biological effects, and could interact with natural biotic stressors, like predation, in complex ways. We experimentally investigated the effects of ALAN and simulated predation risk on the reproductive behaviors of adult gray treefrogs (Hyla versicolor). We hypothesized that ALAN would disrupt reproductive behaviors, particularly if there was also a threat of predation. We established mesocosms which were exposed to the presence or absence of LED lights and the presence or absence of recordings of American bullfrog (Rana catesbeiana) advertisement calls. We assessed the effects of these treatments on adult reproductive behaviors, including habitat selection and oviposition site selection. Our initial results indicate that treatments did not significantly impact habitat selection, oviposition site selection, or call characteristics. However, we also conducted behavioral assays to test if frogs which had selected different environments differed in risk-taking or exploratory behavior in a standardized environment without artificial light. Frogs using mesocosms with ALAN took significantly longer to leave the shelter during our behavior assay if the mesocosm was not exposed to bullfrog recordings. These findings may be indicative of personality differences, such as boldness, where frogs using mesocosms with ALAN are less bold and thus take longer to leave. This suggests there are behavioral differences between frogs using different habitats, which may have further implications for reproductive success or predation risk in the presence of ALAN. Catherine Alton Catherine Alton; Catherine Hanks; Kelly Diamond; Lorin Neuman-Lee; Sarah Pepperman; Anne Sabol; Jennifer
88: Microplastics (MPs; <5 mm) are an emerging class of environmental pollutants that are now considered a global ecotoxicological concern due to their persistence, ubiquity, and potential for biological interaction. MPs are introduced into marine systems through anthropogenic sources, where they absorb hydrophobic contaminants and concentrate in the environment. Mounting evidence from laboratory models demonstrates that MPs can induce oxidative stress, inflammation, reproductive impairment, as well as altered behavior through physical obstruction, reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, and endocrine disruption. However, data on the biological effects of environmentally relevant MP concentrations in long-lived marine predators such as sharks is sparse. Coastal South Carolina estuaries represent MP hotspots, with particles documented in local sediments, plankton, fishes, and even bottlenose dolphins, but shark exposure remains uncharacterized. Because sharks occupy diverse trophic positions, and are uniquely exposed to and threatened by pollution through their ecology, they represent a population potentially at risk for adverse MP associated effects. To examine the trends regarding shark uptake and stress of MPs, we will be 1) performing plastic extraction from various tissues and comparative quantification both within tissues and across trophic guilds through chemical imaging and 2) correlating the comparative plastic load across species to known markers of toxicological stress like antioxidant enzymes and inflammatory biomarkers. We hypothesize that demersal feeders will exhibit higher MP burdens than pelagic species due to greater benthic contact and ingestion of sediment-associated prey, and that increasing MP load will correspond with elevated oxidative stress and inflammatory activation in liver and blood tissues. Jasmine Antonucci
89: Since 2018, fossilized teeth from White Sharks, Carcharodon carcharias (Linnaeus, 1758), have been discovered in increasing numbers along the Narragansett Bay in Narragansett, Rhode Island, USA. To date, 21 fossil White Shark teeth have been documented from this location. These teeth range in size from crown heights of 3.2 mm to 30.0 mm and include teeth from a range of positions in the dentition. After an effort to increase public awareness of these finds by the Atlantic Shark Institute, the number of teeth reported from this locale has continued to grow.  The variety of tooth crown and root coloration across specimens is consistent with teeth fossilizing in sediments with different age and mineralogical profiles. Whether the Narragansett Bay teeth were unearthed by erosion within the bay or transplanted via wave and tidal action remains to be seen. Here, we draw comparisons between Narragansett Bay and other known deposits of fossilized lamnid teeth on the East Coast of North America, identify next steps in the study of the Narragansett Bay teeth, and discuss our findings in the context of White Shark’s historic and prehistoric presence in southern New England. Jenna Aquino Jenna Marie Aquino; Jessica Flores; Jazmin Gallardo; Todd Clardy; Samantha Leigh; Misty Paig-Tran; Benjamin
90: The Dunes Sagebrush Lizard (Sceloporus arenicolus) is endemic to the Mescalero-Monahans Sand Dune Ecosystem of southeastern New Mexico and adjacent Texas in the United States. This species only occurs in Shinnery Oak-dominated sand dunes and faces ongoing threats from oil and gas development, habitat fragmentation. In July 2024, the species was listed as Federally Endangered under the Endangered Species Act. Despite the urgency for its conservation, there are very limited genomic resources for this and other Sceloporus species. Here, we present the first reference genome for S. arenicolus constructed from long read HiFi sequences and paired end HiC reads. This genome serves as an important tool for assessment of inbreeding, estimate of population size change, and identification of loci under location selection pressures. Furthermore, this reference genome expands representation across the Sceloporus phylogeny and will serve useful for comparative genomic students across phyrnosomatid lizards. Irvin Arroyo-Torres Irvin Arroyo-Torres; Sara Brant; Lisa Barrow; Grace Carmona-Yong; Layla Denee; Takuma Shiina; Ethan
91: The first documented megamouth shark (Megachasma pelagios) was caught in 1976 in Hawaiʻi and deposited at the Bernice Pauahi Bishop Museum. The discovery of a new species, genus, and family of large shark—characterized by exceptional morphology and behavior as a diel vertically migrating filter feeder—represents one of the most surprising ichthyological discoveries of the 20th century. In 2026, the Bishop Museum is commemorating the 50th anniversary of this discovery through a series of public programs and educational initiatives that highlight the biology of M. pelagios, the story of its discovery, and stewardship of the holotype. These efforts use the megamouth shark as a focal point to engage audiences in broader themes of ocean exploration, biodiversity, and taxonomy. In parallel with these activities, we are undertaking efforts to support long-term preservation of the holotype and its history, including preparations to replace the specimen’s aging storage container, and the compilation of historical documents, photographs, media coverage, and firsthand accounts from individuals involved in the original discovery.
92: Understanding how digestion influences metabolism in sharks is important for estimating energy use and the energetic costs associated with feeding. However, post-feeding metabolic data in ram-ventilating sharks remain limited. In this study, we measured oxygen consumption (MO₂) in a juvenile bonnethead shark (Sphyrna tiburo, n = 1) using a large closed respirometry system. Dissolved oxygen was recorded with a Hach handheld meter and DLO probe during sealed 30-minute trials. Oxygen consumption was calculated from the linear decline in dissolved oxygen and converted to mass-specific MO₂. Trials were conducted at baseline, immediately after feeding, and again three and six hours later. Preliminary data indicate baseline metabolic rates were 200 mg O₂ kg⁻¹ hr⁻¹. After feeding, metabolic rates increased to values between 300–400 mg O₂ kg⁻¹ hr⁻¹. Oxygen consumption varied across feeding states, highlighting dynamic metabolic responses in this active shark. Post-feeding increases in oxygen consumption are widely observed in fishes as metabolic energy is directed toward digestion and nutrient absorption. In active sharks, routine swimming already uses much of the available metabolic scope, which may limit how strongly metabolism increases after feeding. This makes feeding metabolism especially important when trying to interpret energy budgets and feeding ecology in this species. A next step would be to repeat these trials with additional juvenile bonnetheads while also improving measurement sensitivity by reducing chamber volume. It would also be useful to run trials sequentially on the same individual across feeding states to better track how metabolic rate changes following feeding. Angel L. Ayala-Leyva Angel Ayala-Leyva; Mariana Palencia-Martínez; Israel Solano-Zavaleta; Gonzalo Ramírez-Cruz; Stacey Weiss; A.
93: Black sea bass are an ecologically and economically important marine fish distributed along the Atlantic coast of the United States from the Gulf of Mexico to Maine. Their broad geographic range exposes populations to substantial thermal variation, making them an ideal model for examining how temperature influences vertebrate skeletal muscle performance. We tested the hypothesis that reduced temperatures significantly slow muscle contraction kinetics and thereby diminish overall contractile performance. Axial white muscle tissue was dissected from adult individuals collected in South Carolina and Connecticut to capture potential regional variation. Muscle preparations were maintained in vitro, electrically stimulated, and assessed under controlled temperature treatments representing ecologically relevant conditions. Contraction kinetics, including time to peak tension and relaxation time, were quantified at each temperature. Cold exposure significantly prolonged both contraction and relaxation times, demonstrating that lower temperatures impair muscle contractile speed and overall performance. These results support our hypothesis and suggest that temperature strongly modulates functional capacity in this species. Because muscle performance underlies swimming ability, foraging success, and predator avoidance, thermal sensitivity may have important ecological consequences. Furthermore, these findings have implications for mariculture, as temperate thermal conditions may optimize growth and production efficiency. Future work will examine performance across the species’ full thermal range to better define physiological limits and aquaculture potential.
94: Non-lethal assessment of embryos in utero is critical for understanding shark reproduction; yet, opportunities to quantify embryo morphometrics in free-ranging elasmobranchs remain rare. Ultrasonography has traditionally been used to assess reproductive state in sharks, and recent advances now allow more detailed measurements of embryo morphology in live-bearing species. We evaluated ultrasonography for estimating maximum neonate girth in blacktip reef sharks (Carcharhinus melanopterus) on the west coast of Mo’orea, French Polynesia. In October 2024, nine late-stage gravid females (127-149 cm TL) were scanned using an E.I. Medical EVO III ultrasonography unit, and embryo girths were measured post hoc using proprietary software. During the same parturition season, 49 unique neonates were captured from nursery sites located on the west coast using gill nets, of which 29 were assigned an age range of 0-12 days based on their umbilical wound class (UWC). Neonate girths ranged 18.6-24.2 cm (mean ± SD = 21.1 ± 1.5 cm; CV = 7.2 %), while in utero girths ranged 18.5-25.1 cm (mean ± SD = 20.5 ± 1.9 cm; CV = 9.2 %). The unpaired mean difference was 0.6 cm, showing strong agreement between ultrasound-derived estimates and observed neonate measurements. These findings demonstrate that ultrasonography can reliably estimate embryo size in utero under field conditions. This provides a practical, nonlethal approach for inferring developmental stage, estimating time of parturition, and assessing maternal investment in live-bearing sharks. These results highlight the value of ultrasound as a field-ready tool for studying reproduction and supporting conservation of K-selected elasmobranchs. Chuck Bangley
95: Trematode parasites are commonly found in amphibian systems, yet their transmission pathways and host associations are poorly understood. In California’s Central Coast, California Newts (Taricha torosa) have been observed with cysts caused by trematodes in the genus Euryhelmis, but the life cycle and host species involved in transmission remain unclear. Our project aims to identify the hosts contributing to the Euryhelmis life cycle and characterize parasite communities within these freshwater ecosystems. To address this, we combine field sampling and molecular approaches. We collect potential intermediate hosts, such as freshwater snails, from aquatic sites and screen these for parasite infections using both microscopy and molecular barcoding. Fecal samples from possible mammalian definitive hosts are also collected and examined for parasite presence. We identify parasite samples using DNA barcoding targeting the 28S rRNA and COI gene regions, allowing for comparison of parasite lineages across hosts. By linking parasite identities among multiple hosts, we will clarify transmission pathways and determine whether currently sampled snail species contribute to infection in the California Newt. This project will generate new data for Euryhelmis and other trematodes to clarify how parasite communities differ across hosts, and also assess potential ecological or conservation implications associated with parasite burdens in amphibian populations. Julia Laterza Barbosa
96: Augusta University’s Zoological Collections, which house a diverse array of vertebrate and invertebrate specimens, has gone under many years of disrepair and inadequate curation. With over 3,000 fluidpreserved specimens in addition to numerous skins and taxidermy mounts used regularly for educational purposes, restoration of the collection has become a major priority. Recent and ongoing efforts have focused on improving specimen care, organization, and documentation to elevate the collection to research-grade, museum-quality standards. Many of these specimens are undergoing the process of being digitized and added to data aggregators such as iDigBio and GBIF. In addition to restoration, the collection is also undergoing expansion. Fish sampling is conducted at least monthly across a range of habitats, including local freshwater systems and coastal regions of Georgia, contributing new material to the ichthyological collection. In addition to the voucher collections, Augusta University maintains a living collection through an on-site aquarium. These animals, in life, serve as educational resources and, upon natural death, are accessioned into the voucher collection along with their locality data. These live specimens serve as educational resources and, upon natural death, are preserved and incorporated into the permanent collection. Using these efforts in restoration, curation, and growth, Augusta University aims to continue contributing to scientific discourse and education through making specimens accessible and available for public use both now, and in the future. Ethan Barnes
97: Rivers in the Southern Great Plains (SGP) are hydrologically and environmentally dynamic, exhibiting strong seasonality with recurring periods of flooding and stream drying. In addition to this variability, this region currently faces stressors including flow alteration, habitat fragmentation, and changes in land use, consequently affecting native fish communities. We used survey data collected across 50 years including historical (1980 – 2002) and contemporary (2003 – 2025) time periods to examine temporal changes in fish assemblage composition and species occurrence within the upper Red River (RR), a system within the SGP in Texas. Across the 22 locations sampled in both study periods, overall site-level turnover included losses of 20 fish species (e.g., Chub Shiner, Mississippi Silvery Minnow) and gains of 4 taxa, including the invasive Gulf Killifish. Analysis revealed changes in species occurrence, largely driven by increases in generalists (e.g., Western Mosquitofish), while salttolerant taxa (e.g., Red River Pupfish) remained relatively stable, and species within the guild of pelagic-broadcast spawners (e.g., Macrhybopsis spp.) and those currently listed as species of conservation need within Texas declined. Areas with the greatest changes included the Pease River, a major tributary to the RR mainstem, where significant differences in species composition were identified, caused by declines in numerous Centrarchid (e.g., Bluegill, Longear Sunfish) and short-lived Leuciscid species. Future research will examine the regional (e.g., land cover, hydrology) factors driving these changes to help identify effective conservation plans to support the resilience and persistence of freshwater communities within the SGP. Daisy Barraza
98: The behavior of native species may change after the introduction of non-native congeners. Two species of freshwater fish, the Rainbow Darter (Etheostoma caeruleum) and Greenside Darter (E. blennioides), were recently introduced to the Potomac River in Maryland. Their introduction may affect the foraging behavior of the native Fantail Darter (E. flabellare) and Tessellated Darter (E. olmstedi). In this study, I sought to determine if native species exhibit a high degree of diet overlap with non-native congeners in streams where all four species are known to occur. If native species have similar diets without introduced species, using gastric lavage, we collected partially digested stomach content from multiple populations throughout the year to determine the degree of dietary niche overlap between native and introduced congeners. These samples are then compared to the available macroinvertebrate prey at each population. If the introduction generates competition, there is potential for the exclusion of native species. A greater understanding of dietary niche overlaps between introduced and native species can determine whether introduced congeners threaten native species.
99: Several distantly related species of the weakly electric fish genus Brachyhypopomus (Hypopomidae) occupy both normoxic and persistently hypoxic habitats, with populations in hypoxic systems exhibiting enlarged gill surface area. It remains unclear whether between-population differences in gill traits associated with respiratory surface area are fixed through development or become increasingly exaggerated with body size. We compared normoxic and hypoxic populations of three upper Amazon species using ANCOVA, MANCOVA, and PCA to evaluate gill metrics across body size. In Brachyhypopomus beebei, the hypoxic population exhibited greater mean filament length (MFL), mean hemibranch length (MHL), total filament length (TFL), and total hemibranch area (THA) relative to the normoxic population across all measured body sizes. Similar patterns were observed in B. walteri for MHL, THA, and total filament number (TFN). These observations are consistent either with phenotypic plasticity emerging early in development and persisting through growth or with locally adapted trait differences. By contrast, in B. walteri, two traits, MFL and TFL, became increasingly divergent through development, consistent with later-onset phenotypic plasticity. In B. brevirostris, differences in gill traits between normoxic and hypoxic populations were minor regardless of size, suggesting limited plasticity, ongoing gene flow, or alternative mechanisms of hypoxia tolerance such as anaerobic respiration. These contrasting patterns suggest that even among hypoxia-tolerant congeners, variation in respiratory traits may reflect multiple underlying processes, including phenotypic plasticity, developmental timing, and genetic differentiation. Resolving the mechanisms underlying these patterns will require integrated laboratory rearing experiments and population genetic analyses. Edmund W Basham Edmund Basham; Luke Larter; Patrick Champagne; Gregory Jongsma; Kelly Zamudio; David Cannatella; Douglas
100: Florida's Big Bend region is an important area for coastal elasmobranchs throughout their development. The Grubbs Lab at Florida State University Coastal and Marine Laboratory conducted a study from 2009 to 2021 in Florida’s Big Bend region, spanning a 300 km stretch of coastline from the St. Marks River to the Anclote River, Florida, using fishery-independent longline and gillnet surveys. Catch rate analyses are used to evaluate species abundance and distribution patterns. Prior work assessed Atlantic Sharpnose sharks (Rhizoprionodon terraenovae), a common species in this system and found population declines. This work evaluates other prevalent species like Sphyrna tiburo and Carcharhinus limbatus from the study to assess trends in abundance and distribution over time. Ashmika Behere
101: North American freshwater fishes display unequal biodiversity across biogeographic zones, yet the environmental and organismal processes driving this pattern remain unclear. Diversity may accumulate through a combination of ecological and evolutionary processes, operating over a range of spatiotemporal scales, shaped by environmental heterogeneity and the long-term persistence of lineages within habitats. Ecological factors driving the body-shape diversity include environmental factors that promote morphological diversification, and abiotic filters that constrain the persistence of viable phenotypes. Evolutionary factors include differential rates of speciation, extinction, and dispersal of clades with different phenotypes. Cypriniformes represent an excellent system for testing the effects of habitat diversity and abiotic filtering on morphological diversification across broad geographic zones. Two cypriniform clades, Leuciscidae and Catostomidae, exhibit high diversity and strong regional differences across the conterminous USA, with most diversity concentrated east of the Rocky Mountains, several geographically widespread genera (e.g., Catostomus, Rhinichthys), and a highly relictual fauna in the arid West. Here, we examine the geographic distribution of ecomorphological diversity in Cypriniformes across the conterminous USA. We quantify body shape disparity using 3D geometric morphometrics and PCA for a majority of Leuciscidae and Catostomidae and characterize habitat diversity by quantifying niche space from WorldCLIM abiotic environmental layers in ArcGIS. Together, these data reveal how the geographic distribution of habitat diversity corresponds to broad-scale patterns of body shape diversity across the conterminous USA’s biogeographic regions and demonstrate how fine-scale morphological and environmental data can illuminate ecomorphological trends across broad geographic scales. Michael F. Benard
102: There is an increasing interest in understanding how artificial, large marine infrastructure is impacting coastal habitats and ecosystems, especially marine life. This is particularly important given the recent expansion of marine infrastructure development, such as offshore wind farms and port terminals. In the central coast of Peru, a Liquefied Natural Gas port terminal was constructed in an undeveloped stretch of coastline. Long-term monitoring of the fish community in the surrounding area reports large numbers of elasmobranchs, especially stingrays. These elasmobranchs have been found to feed on fish and other marine life and could play a vital role in the coastal ecosystem surrounding the terminal. Further, among the elasmobranch species reported there are threatened species, including a species in critical danger of extinction. To determine their residency and movement patterns, elasmobranchs including five species (Hypanus dipterurus, Mustelus mento, Myliobatis chilensis, Myliobatis peruvianus, Pseudobatos planiceps) were tagged with acoustic transmitters via surgical implantation. Four acoustic receivers were deployed surrounding the infrastructure, to detect tagged animals. Detections were examined through time to understand residency patterns surrounding the infrastructure. Spatial patterns were also examined to determine if there were preferences for specific areas at the terminal. Preliminary results include several species displaying residency at the infrastructure (e.g., Hypanus dipterurus, Mustelus mento), as well as potential seasonal and individual movement patterns for some species. These results are discussed in the context of ecological drivers, including the potential for marine infrastructure to attract and concentrate elasmobranch prey populations. Kara Bensel
103: Atlantic spinner sharks (Carcharhinus brevipinna) are widespread coastal predators in the western Atlantic, yet their trophic ecology remains poorly understood, in part because they are frequently misidentified as Atlantic blacktip sharks (Carcharhinus limbatus). This study examines regional and seasonal variation in the feeding ecology of both species across the U.S. Atlantic coast. Sharks are sampled opportunistically during collaborative field efforts using standardized hook-and-line methods, and non-lethal biological samples including blood, muscle tissue biopsies, and stomach or cloacal swabs are collected following established handling protocols. Environmental conditions at capture locations, including temperature, salinity, and dissolved oxygen, are recorded to evaluate how habitat conditions relate to resource use. Stable isotope analysis of carbon and nitrogen from muscle tissue is used to estimate trophic position and prey-source reliance over longer time scales, while dietary DNA metabarcoding of stomach or cloacal samples provides finer-scale information on recently consumed prey. Together, these complementary approaches allow assessment of whether spinner sharks and blacktip sharks exhibit regional specialization, opportunistic feeding, or seasonal shifts in prey use. We expect to identify meaningful differences in diet composition and trophic position across regions and seasons and to clarify how environmental conditions influence feeding patterns. These results will improve understanding of predator-prey dynamics and strengthen the ecological foundation for ecosystem-based fisheries management and future species-specific assessment efforts. Leah Bergman
104: It is well known that among marine organisms the accumulation of toxic pollutants increases in top predators due to biomagnification. Many previous studies have demonstrated that sharks are amongst the top predators who often exhibit the highest concentrations of marine pollutants. Of these pollutants, the toxic, nonessential metal mercury (Hg) is of special concern because of its ability to cause detrimental effects on neurological function and reproduction. Within many shark species, elevated concentrations of Hg have been observed. However, when it comes to the accumulation of Hg in several commercially and recreationally important species on the U.S. East Coast not much is known. This study focused on sandbar sharks, Carcharhinus plumbeus, a species that is common along the U.S. east coast but remains relatively understudied when it comes to Hg accumulation. This study examined Hg accumulation in sandbar sharks from the Gulf coast of Florida. In addition to providing baseline data on Hg burden in Gulf sandbars, we also compared spatial differences between Hg levels in Gulf and Atlantic coast sandbar sharks in recent years. The data demonstrates that there is not a significant difference in Hg accumulation between the two locations. It also shows that there are still individual sandbar sharks from both regions that have Hg levels that remain above federal thresholds for human consumption.
105: Eastern box turtles (Terrapene carolina carolina) are experiencing population declines across their range due to habitat fragmentation, road mortality, and anthropogenic pressures, raising concerns about reduced genetic connectivity in urban environments. This study evaluates the suitability of published microsatellite markers and applies them to assess genetic diversity within an urban box turtle population. The Marian University Nina Mason Pulliam EcoLab in Indianapolis, Indiana, is a 75-acre urban forest located ~3 miles from downtown Indianapolis and bordered by roads to the north and east, the university to the south, and residential neighborhoods to the west. Potential habitat corridors exist between other nearby habitats, making this a valuable system for understanding connectivity in urban landscapes. Blood samples were collected from radio-tracked individuals (n ≈ 15) and preserved in EDTA at −80°C. Genomic DNA was extracted using Qiagen DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kits, and a panel of published microsatellite loci (8–12 markers) was screened for amplification success and polymorphisms. Successfully amplifying markers were used for preliminary genotyping, and genetic metrics including heterozygosity and allelic diversity were analyzed in R. Initial results indicate that several loci amplify consistently and exhibit detectable variation within the population, supporting their utility for population-level analyses. Preliminary patterns suggest measurable genetic diversity, though further analyses are ongoing to better resolve levels of connectivity and potential structuring within this urban system. These findings establish a foundation for future conservation genetic work in T. c. carolina and contribute to understanding how urbanization may influence genetic diversity and long-term population viability. Parker Binns
106: Urban heat is a major stressor impacting wildlife in urban areas. As ectotherms, herptiles’ body temperatures are closely related to environmental temperature, thus they may be more susceptible to the impacts of urban heat than other taxa. One potential mechanism enabling persistence under heat stress is behavioral modification to reduce exposure to high temperatures. In this study, we investigate the impacts of urban heat on the activity patterns of Puerto Rican Anolis lizards. We aim to: (1) investigate whether anoles exhibit divergent activity patterns between urban and forested habitats, and whether these changes are associated with exposure to urban heat, and (2) assess whether changes in activity in urban areas differ across ecological zones. We conducted hourly surveys of anole activity at paired urban-forest transects in four locations across three ecological zones in both the summer and winter seasons. Additionally, we measured ambient weather conditions each hour and surface temperatures on structures commonly used as lizard perches. Urban lizards were generally more active than forest lizards in the morning hours, although this pattern was mediated by regional differences in climate. We also found differences in summer and winter activity in the urban environments, but more consistent patterns across seasons in the forest. These findings suggest that urban lizards may be shifting their behavior to reduce thermal stress, particularly in warm and dry ecoregions. These behavioral shifts may shield lizards from the immediate stress of urban heat, but may also impede adaptation to warming conditions as urbanization and climate change intensify. Sonny Bleicher
107: Chemical ecology studies on squamates often focus on reproductive behavior and conspecific trailing, though we know comparatively little about how rattlesnakes use chemical signals in conspecific communication. This is surprising given that rattlesnakes exhibit social, aggregative behavior. In North American rattlesnake species, gravid females aggregate in communal birthing sites at hibernacula in early summer and give birth in late summer/early fall. We hypothesized that when presented with conspecific male or gravid female scent, gravid female prairie rattlesnakes (Crotalus viridis) would trail females to facilitate aggregation, therefore we designed a Y-maze study to assess this during early summer, a known time of aggregation in this species. We extracted lipids from males and gravid females from a single population in NW Colorado and presented these to gravid females (N=28) as defined, paired scent trails. Conspecific scent was a strong motivator of female behavior with success in 89% of scent trials and only in 41% of bias trials (no scent). Gravid females did not discriminate between trails based on choice data (10/23 chose the female scented arm). However, we found that specific behaviors were linked based on probabilities from sequence analysis (e.g., exploration behavior followed emergences [0.69] and pauses [0.72]). Importantly, there was a two-fold higher probability that gravid females would transition to following the male trail after encountering the female trail (0.1 vs. 0.05). Our results indicate that gravid females likely aggregate based on scent though other factors outside aggregation (e.g., relatedness, nutritional state) undoubtedly drive female behavior. Ashley Bobnar
108: <span lang="EN-US" style="mso-ascii-font-family: Aptos; msofareast-font-family: 'Times New Roman'; mso-hansi-font-family: Aptos; mso-bidi-font-family: 'Times New Roman'; color: black; mso-font-kerning: 0pt; mso-ligatures: none;">Global participation in research for elasmobranch rewilding initiatives is essential for their conservation. Animal welfare expectations differ among international regulations and independent institutions requiring the development of a uniform non-invasive sampling method that can assess population status, diversity, and relatedness for ex-situ and in-situ reproductive conservation. Mucus swabs have been used to successfully collect DNA and perform genetic analyses in a few elasmobranch studies, yet a standardized and validated protocol that consistently yields sufficient DNA across species has not been published. South-East Zoo Alliance for Reproduction and Conservation will partner with Jacksonville Zoo Botanical Gardens (2026-263-AM-SEZARC) to sample 14 cownose rays (Rhinoptera bonasus; 8 males and 6 females) every 2 – 3 weeks over a 12-week span comparing swab materials at three bilateral anatomical sites — gill slits, spiracles, and dorsal skin. Swab-derived DNA will be validated against paired whole blood samples via DNA extraction and microsatellite genotyping at the Field Museum. Genetic comparisons in DNA yield (ng), DNA concentration (ng/µL) will be made between collection methods using linear mixed-effects models and Bland-Altman analysis. Genotyping success at fifteen established loci will be evaluated using percent genotype concordance to assess agreement between methods. The validated protocol will be applied to test its applications in several species including Carcharhinus acronotus, <span lang="ENUS" style="mso-ascii-font-family: Aptos; mso-fareast-font-family: 'Times New Roman'; mso-hansi-font-family: Aptos; mso-bidi-font-family: 'Times New Roman'; color: black; mso-font-kerning: 0pt; mso-ligatures: none;">C. leucas, Pristis pectinata, Rhina ancylostoma<span lang="EN-US" style="mso-ascii-font-family: Aptos; mso-fareast-font-family: 'Times New Roman'; mso-hansi-font-family: Aptos; mso-bidi-font-family: 'Times New Roman'; color: black; mso-font-kerning: 0pt; mso-ligatures: none;">, and Carcharias taurus in collaboration with Minorities in Shark Science and other aquarium and field organizations. Mary E (Beth) Bowers
109: In our increasingly connected world, pathogens can spread globally before they are detected, creating detection lags that obscure the timing of invasions and their initial impacts on host populations. Here, we aim to reconstruct cryptic invasions of the amphibian chytrid fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) and investigate the long-term dynamics of amphibian resilience to this pathogen. To do so, we collected lake-bottom sediment cores from Pennsylvania and Ohio, two regions with unknown histories of Bd introduction and amphibian decline. These sediments preserve continuous temporal records of environmental DNA, which is shed by aquatic organisms and deposited in chronological layers, providing an untapped archive of amphibian-Bd interactions through time. We describe our protocol for sedimentary DNA extraction, SYBR-based qPCR pathogen screening, and present preliminary results from both modern surface sediments and historical sediment core samples. In future work, we will expand our sediment sampling and screening to other regions, apply Bd- and frog-specific target capture arrays to enrich DNA from bulk sediment extracts, and use sequenced read counts as proxies for Bd and frog abundance through time. This project stands to complement ongoing museum collections research with natural archives of sedDNA, unearthing centuries of hidden ecological history to reconstruct Bd invasions and amphibian declines otherwise lost to time. Reilly Boyt Reilly Boyt; Claire Goodfellow; Lauren Meyer; Chloe Roberts; Maddie English; Lisa Hillier; Aaron Carlisle; Dayv
110: The ghost knifefishes of the clade Apteronotini are among the most phenotypically diverse electric fishes, and their interrelationships have been the subject of longstanding study. Previous taxonomic work has focused mostly on external characteristics (meristics, morphometrics, pigmentation) to diagnose and differentiate taxa. Apteronotini is represented by 31 valid species in 4 nominal genera, of which we have osteological data for 18 species. Here we use micro-CT scans of over 100 specimens to study ontogenetic, static, geographic, and interspecific allometries using 3D geometric morphometric, principal component, phylogenetic, and biogeographic analyses. Our phylogeny partitions the species into 8 clades provisionally ranked at the genus level, of which 3 were previously recognized as Apteronotus sensu stricto. Of these clades, 4 have species in trans-Andean basins, suggesting clade ages greater than 11 Ma, 2 are in the Orinoco, 3 in the Guinanas, 4 in the Amazonian lowlands, 3 in the Brazilian Shield, and 4 in La Plata. Trans-Andean basins are the center of diversity with 12 species, and only 4 species are currently known from Amazonian lowlands. None of the multi-species clades are monophyletic in a major basin, and most species are restricted to a single basin, with the notable exception of A. albifrons. Craniofacial sexual dimorphism is widespread and may characterize Apteronotini as a whole. Traits previously proposed for the A. leptorhynchus group are estimated to be plesiomorphic, and characterize several clades.These results indicate the role of dispersal and vicariance in diversification, and of homoplasy and homology in mosaic evolution. Creed C. Branham
111: How species will respond to climate is important for guiding management actions to conserve species. For Plethodon in the southern Appalachian Mountains, there is concern for how high elevation species will respond to climate warming, as they will likely have to adapt to avoid decline or displacement. One method of increasing their adaptive capacity is through hybridization. There are broad hybrid zones throughout much of southern Appalachia which allow high-elevation endemics to access genes from low-elevation populations that are better suited for warmer environments, potentially increasing their ability to persist in the face of climate change. For example, recent research shows that there are genes migrating from low elevation P. teyahalee to high elevation endemic species such as P. jordani and P. shermani, allowing for wide adaptive variation in body size at maturity in response to hydroclimate. Larger body size corresponds to reduced rates of evaporative water loss—a beneficial trait for amphibians in hotter, drier climates. Meanwhile, nearby on Cheoah Bald, P. cheoah is morphologically indistinguishable from P. shermani yet does not hybridize with P. teyahalee, limiting their ability to access these beneficial alleles. This sympatry without hybridization is a phenomenon that allows for the comparison of adaptive capacity of closely related species with and without hybrid zones. Our work measures the variation in minimum body size at maturity along a climate gradient to determine whether species without hybridization show restricted adaptive variation compared to those within an active hybrid zone. Stephen Bredin
112: The diversity-stability theory proposes that more diverse biological communities have more stable interaction networks and are thus better able to maintain their functions and persist in the face of disturbance. With advances in sequencing and analytical tools, this theory has been increasingly extended to microbial communities interacting with vertebrate hosts. A recent study by members of our team indicated that threatened amphibian species from Brazil and Madagascar carry lower skin bacterial diversity than non-threatened congenerics. The consistency of these findings across continents suggests the broad scale at which low microbiome diversity may compromise host health in species already burdened with the threat of extinction. The goal of this research is to test whether bacterial interactions within diverse host-associated bacteriomes can also serve as reliable indicators of bacteriome stability and predictors of host endangerment. Using the original amphibian dataset, we will build bacterial co-occurrence networks and compare network metrics (e.g. modularity, nestedness) between threatened vs. non-threatened amphibian species. I hypothesize that bacteriome co-occurrence network metrics will better predict host endangerment in Brazilian and Malagasy amphibians than bacterial diversity alone. I predict that host species with skin bacteriomes exhibiting signatures of network stability will be less likely to be threatened than species with less stable networks. Identifying signatures of bacteriome networks that serve as proxies for host population health and risk of endangerment could provide valuable insights for both the theoretical ecology and the applied conservation of declining species.
113: Sharks play a key role in structuring marine ecosystems, yet global populations have declined by over 70% since the 1970s, mainly due to fishing, habitat degradation, and climate change. Globally, it is challenging to manage and conserve shark populations because there is a lack of historical baseline data. This study utilizes disarticulated shark dermal denticles preserved in the sediment of the blue hole near Middle Caicos, Turks and Caicos Island (TCI) to reconstruct shark communities from the last ~1500 years. Sediment cores that include both pre- and post-European colonization layers were sampled and processed to isolate denticles. The denticles were counted and grouped into morphotypes. To aid in identifying taxa to species or family based on morphology, we compared denticles common to species present in Caribbean reef and coastal environments, such as Bull Sharks (Carcharhinus leucas), Nurse Sharks (Ginglymostoma cirratum) and other reef-associated sharks. We find higher denticle abundance and diversity in pre-colonial settlement layers compared to post, suggesting greater shark presence before European colonization in TCI. These changes are likely driven by increased human impacts, including increased technological advancements in fishing, maritime trade, salt production, and environmental changes. This study expands our understanding of the local shark community prior to written records and modern survey data using denticles from TCI. This study also provides support for the efficacy of using dermal denticles from sediment cores to understand long-term shark decline, environmental shifts, and anthropogenic impacts globally, in addition to supporting improved conservation and marine management in the TCI region. Gracie Brown
114: The Yellowfin Goby (Acanthogobius flavimanus)–native to freshwater, brackish, and marine waters of Japan, Korea, and China–was first discovered in the lower San Joaquin River in California in 1963. Since then, this invasive species has spread both North and South. Yellowfin Goby were first identified within Humboldt Bay by citizen scientists in 2021, and larvae were found in 2023, 2024-25, and 2025-26 surveys. We compared current larval Yellowfin Goby populations within Humboldt Bay against surveys from previous years to identify changes in population size and potential trends in dispersal and development. We collected ichthyoplankton samples throughout Humboldt Bay using two methods: light traps were deployed once per month from 2024-25 in three constructed wetland ponds within Humboldt Bay, and plankton tows were conducted monthly in 5 sites across Humboldt Bay in 2025-26. The increasing abundance of A. flavimanus is concerning, as it shares habitat in Humboldt Bay with a core population of the endangered Northern Tidewater Goby (Eucyclogobius newberryi) and has been implicated in the decline of native species in San Francisco Bay. Dylan Bryant
