115: Emerging infectious diseases strongly contribute to the decline of wildlife globally. Specifically, Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) and Ranavirus (Rv) infections can result in morbidity and mortality events for amphibians. Despite documentation of infections in the genus Eurycea, few studies have examined infection dynamics in the cryptic Eurycea quadridigitata, the Coastal Plains Dwarf Salamander. Here, we sought to quantify the infection dynamics of the minimally studied E. quadridigitata present in Central Florida, a location where information on the species is particularly limited. We utilized a combination of leaf litter traps and coverboard arrays to sample salamanders, and measured body morphometrics, determined life stage, and collected tail tissue for pathogen analysis for each individual. We then extracted DNA from tail clips and used established qPCR protocols to detect and quantify Rv and Bd infection presence and intensity. In total, we sampled 79 unique E. quadridigitata, with 71 tail clip tissues utilized for pathogen analysis. Bd prevalence was 5.6% (4/71), and Rv prevalence was 30.9% (22/71), and there was one instance of coinfection in the population, 1.4% (1/71). Both Bd (p = 0.73) and Rv (p = 0.11) prevalence were not affected by month of capture. Bd prevalence did not differ by life stage (p = 0.18) , however, Rv prevalence did (p = 0.05), with advanced life stages more likely to harbor infection. This study represents the first documentation of Rv infection in E. quadridigitata, and assists in elucidating the disease dynamics of ephemeral forested wetland systems by uncovering another pathogen vector.
116: Smooth hammerhead sharks (Sphyrna zygaena) have not been reported in the Galapagos Marine Reserve for over two decades, with the last confirmed records consisting of two adults captured during experimental longline surveys carried out in the western region of the reserve in 2003. Further, juvenile stages of this species have never been documented in the archipelago. In 2024, multiple juvenile smooth hammerhead sharks were recorded in Tagus Cove, Isabela Island. Identification was confirmed through morphological characteristics and supported by molecular analysis using Cytochrome Oxidase I (COI) using a Maximum Likelihood approach. Across three consecutive annual expeditions (2024-2026), juveniles ranging from 76–138 cm total length were consistently observed. This represents the first record of juvenile smooth hammerhead sharks in the Galápagos Marine Reserve and suggests that Tagus Cove may function as a critical habitat for juveniles. The site is located within the western bioregion of the archipelago, characterized by cooler sea surface temperatures and aligns with this species known thermal preferences, which typically occupies cooler waters relative to other hammerhead species, such as the scalloped hammerhead shark (Sphyrna lewini). Notably, co-occurrence of these two species has not been observed, indicating potential spatial or thermal habitat partitioning. Identifying important habitats for juvenile smooth hammerhead sharks is essential given the significant fishing pressures faced by this species throughout the Eastern Tropical Pacific. These findings provide important baseline data to support future conservation and management efforts. Frank Burbrink
Maria Antonia Izurieta Burbano de Lara
117: Human-dominated landscapes present both challenges and opportunities for wildlife conservation. In California’s Central Valley, historically characterized by extensive wetlands and floodplains, agricultural development and water management have dramatically reshaped habitat and ecological dynamics. Despite these changes, snake species—including the federally threatened Giant Gartersnake (Thamnophis gigas) and invasive watersnakes (Nerodia sipedon and Nerodia fasciata)—continue to persist within these landscapes. Understanding the processes that influence their persistence and population dynamics is essential for effective conservation and management. My research examines how landscape context, management actions, and population processes interact to influence snake populations in altered ecosystems. Using field data and spatial analyses, I investigate three interconnected themes: (1) invasive snake population dynamics and demographic responses to removal and environmental variability, (2) the intersection of land use and snake occurrence, and (3) the potential for agricultural practices that balance snake conservation and agricultural productivity. This research aims to strengthen the scientific basis for managing snake populations in dynamic, human-dominated environments. More broadly, it contributes to understanding how conservation can succeed in working landscapes where wildlife and human activities are deeply intertwined. Andrea Burt
118: The hammerhead sharks (family Sphyrnidae) are an immediately recognizable group of sharks due to their unique head shape. Though there has long been an interest in hammerhead development, there are currently no explicit staging tables published for any members of the group. The Bonnethead shark Sphyrna tiburo is the smallest member of Sphyrnidae and is abundant in estuarine and nearshore waters in the Gulf of Mexico and Western North Atlantic Ocean. Due to their relative abundance, close proximity to shore, and brief gestation period, it has been possible to collect and document multiple embryonic specimens at progressive stages of development. This stage series covers a period of development from stages that match the vertebrate phylotypic period, from Stage 23, through stages of morphological divergence to complete development at birth—Stage 35). A variety of techniques were used to document crucial stages that lead to their extreme craniofacial diversity, resulting in the formation of one of the most distinctive characters of any shark species, the cephalofoil or hammer-like head. Documenting the development of hard-to-access vertebrates, like this viviparous shark species, offers important information about how new and diverse morphologies arise that otherwise may remain poorly studied. This work will serve as a platform for future comparative developmental research both within sharks and across the phylogeny of vertebrates, underpinning the extreme potential of craniofacial development and morphological diversity in vertebrate animals. Grace CadwalladerOlsker
119: Using new livestreaming technology to observe a "mega-den" of prairie rattlesnake (Crotalus viridis), we observed a previously undescribed behavior that appears to represent a novel form of communication. We observed rattlesnakes of all ages and sexes repeatedly perform a "head-twitching" behavior when they were together or when they approached one another. The motion is distinct from known courtship behaviors. In this study, we aimed to catalog all instances of the behavior recorded on a continuously running livestream in 2025 to unravel the purpose of this behavior. We asked community scientists to record (in the YouTube chat) and compile every instance of the behavior, and we then analyzed the behavior of the snakes before and after each twitching event. We also analyzed whether the behavior occurred more frequently at certain times of year, times of day, at certain temperatures, or after rain. We will present results in the context of hypotheses about the function(s) of the twitching behavior. Julien Campisi
120: Anuran tadpoles have complex mouthparts composed of keratinized jaw sheaths, several rows of keratinized toothlets called keratodonts, and sensory papillae. Interspecific variation of these mouthparts is well described; however, intraspecific variation has not been well documented among generalist species. In this study, tadpoles of the American Bullfrog (Rana catesbeiana) and Green Frog (Rana clamitans) were collected from nine localities in Dayton, Ohio. A total of 147 tadpoles spanning multiple developmental stages (Gosner Stages 26 to 41) were collected and imaged under a stereomicroscope. For each tadpole, total length was measured, the number of keratodonts in the second posterior labial tooth row was counted, and the width of the upper jaw sheath was recorded. These measurements were used to examine how oral morphology changes during development. Results indicate that in both species, the number of keratodonts and the size of the jaw sheath increases with total length and developmental stage, suggesting that oral structures scale with growth as tadpoles develop. No significant differences in oral morphology were observed between R. catesbeiana and R. clamitans, suggesting that these two species are not experiencing strong competitive pressure for the same food resources. These findings demonstrate that even within generalist tadpole species, oral morphology can vary during ontogeny and across populations. Overall, this study contributes to understanding developmental variation in tadpole oral morphology. Joseph Cannizzaro IV
121: The micronucleus (MN) assay is a commonly employed genotoxicity test used for detecting DNA damage resulting from exposure to chemical pollutants and other environmental stressors. MN are small, chromatincontaining round bodies visible in the cytoplasm of cells, which can represent chromosomal fragments resulting from un- or mis-repaired DNA strand breaks and/or small extrachromosomal bodies formed from genomic instability. The MN assay is routinely used in fish toxicity studies because it can be easily performed using peripheral blood smears due to the occurrence of nucleated erythrocytes in most non-mammals. DNA damage and mutations have been shown to accumulate more in different organs and systems of the individual; subsequently, this correlates with MN as well. MN has been found in higher frequencies in the gills, kidneys, and livers of teleosts when compared to the usual peripheral blood. However, to date, this idea has not been implemented for Elasmobranchs. The spleen is the origin site at which erythrocytes are produced and distributed throughout the body for Elasmobranchs. In this study, we examined Giemsa-stained blood smears to compare the average MN frequency from caudal venipuncture to that of MN frequency in spleen erythrocytes of various Elasmobranch species. We predict an increase in the average MN frequency of spleen erythrocytes compared to that of peripheral blood. Andrew Capitosti
122: Keratinized skin appendages of vertebrates are a diverse class of organs, including scales, feathers, and hair. These structures exhibit substantial diversity and develop using a shared, ancient appendage program. Unlike other tetrapods, keratinized appendages are reduced in amphibians, although some lineages possess true skin appendages such as keratinized claws, digging spades, and nuptial pads. In lieu of mineralized teeth, most tadpoles possess keratinized jaw sheaths and keratinized labial teeth (i.e., keratodonts) that function as an alternative feeding tool. The evolutionary origin and development of these novel tadpole structures are still poorly understood, despite their ecological and evolutionary importance. Recently, it was proposed that tadpole keratinized mouthparts originated by partially co-opting the developmental program that mediates mineralized tooth formation and are therefore derived from modified oral placodes adopting a keratinized fate. Alternatively, these structures may represent novel true skin appendages that became activated in the mouth. To evaluate these hypotheses, I tested the role of Hedgehog (Hh), Wingless (Wnt), Bone morphogenic (Bmp), and Fibroblast growth factor (Fgf) signaling during tadpole keratinized mouthpart development. If these structures are derived from modified oral placodes, the disruption of these pathways will impede keratinized mouthpart formation comparable to true teeth. Frog embryos were reared in the presence of small molecule inhibitors targeting each pathway; resulting phenotypes were assessed, and differences in gene expression patterns between treated and control embryos were determined by in situ hybridization assays. The results will help further understand the evolutionary origin of a novel epithelial appendage.
123: Many desert-dwelling animals have evolved remarkable adaptations to obtain water from their environment. Among snakes, several species of viperids exhibit rain-harvesting behavior, a set of movements that includes coiling and dorsoventral flattening their bodies that increases surface area for capturing and pooling rainfall. However, during brief summer storms, rainfall can be quite limited, resulting only in a moistening of the snake’s skin and no substantial pooling. Despite a lack of water accumulation, Prairie Rattlesnakes (Crotalus viridis) exhibited swallowing motions while pressing their snouts firmly against their skin, even levering the bodies upwards, opposite to where they were drinking. These behaviors suggest that water accumulated in sufficient quantities to make drinking possible. However, it remains unclear how such a small amount of rainwater is retained in the skin and how the snakes might access it. Based upon previous work in other rain-harvesting squamates (Moloch horridus, the Thorny Devil, and Phrynosoma cornutum, Texas Horned lizard), we hypothesize that rainwater accumulates within interscalar tissue in rattlesnakes providing a source of water the snakes may drink from. Using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and traditional histological techniques, we are characterizing the morphology of these interscalar regions within the skin of Prairie Rattlesnakes. Additionally, using macrovideography, we characterize the ability of the skin to absorb water by placing drops of water on the surface of the skin and tracking its movement. Our preliminary observations are consistent with studies on the Thorny Devil and the Texas Horned lizard that showed interscalar regions of those squamates function to capture rainwater. Eloise Cave
125: Fishes exhibit a range of life history strategies (LHS; opportunistic, periodic, equilibrium) that can inform species responses to gradients of environmental stability and resource predictability, especially in freshwater systems facing environmental changes. In this study, we described LHS of fishes inhabiting streams within the Neches and Sabine River basins in Texas. Fishes were collected at 60 stream sites over three seasons (summer, fall, and spring) from 2023-2024. In addition, we assessed the influence of local environmental variables on the relative proportions of LHS. Life history traits for each species were compiled from online databases and classified to their LHS affinity, defined by the life history continuum model proposed by Winemiller & Rose (1992). Across seasons and basins, intermediate and opportunistic dominated assemblages. Specific environmental variables influenced the proportions of LHS seasonally. In the summer, wider streams were positively associated with opportunistic strategists and negatively associated with equilibrium strategists. In fall and spring, greater woody debris were negatively associated with opportunistic strategists and positively associated with equilibrium strategists. Substrate grain size was important in spring with larger grain size being positively associated with opportunistic strategists and negatively associated with equilibrium strategists. The proportion of periodic strategists remained stable across seasons likely reflecting their adaptations to predictable changes in seasonal conditions across these streams, while the proportions of opportunistic and equilibrium strategists were explained by habitat structure and stream size, Our findings provide a framework for understanding LHS of our native fishes in East Texas and their potential vulnerability to increasing environmental changes. Olivia Chock
126: Gopher Tortoises (Gopherus polyphemus) are a keystone species that construct large burrows, providing crucial refugia for over 350 commensal species. However, populations of G. polyphemus have declined severely due to anthropogenic land-use changes, resulting in the reduction or loss of burrows in modified landscapes. Despite this, the effectiveness of these burrows in altered locations as an ecosystem service remains understudied. Here we sought to determine the impact of anthropogenic habitat alteration on the effectiveness of G. polyphemus burrows for commensal species. We deployed passive infrared wildlife cameras 45 burrows on the University of Central Florida’s main campus (27 in anthropogenically-altered locations and 18 in unaltered areas) to identify vertebrate utilization of the burrows. In total, we recorded 1,387 total trap days (1,099 days at altered locations and 288 days at unaltered locations), detecting 760 commensal observations across 30 species (267 burrow interactions and 69 burrow occupancies). Both habitat types supported regular commensal species, highlighting the importance of Gopher Tortoises even in altered habitats, but altered burrows exhibited lower commensal usage. Additionally, we observed higher detections of mesopredators in altered areas, suggesting a potential challenge for sustaining long-term survivability. Ultimately, this study enhances our understanding of G. polyphemus burrows in altered landscapes and highlights the importance of preserving this species even in non-ideal locations. Natalie Claunch Natalie Claunch; Mark Sandfoss; Amy Yackel Adams; Bailey Zohar; Eric Tillman; William Welsh; Christina Romagosa; Alex Nicely; Taylor Brotons; Rachel Keeffe; Dustin Siegel; Robert Aldridge; Bryan Kluever; Andrea
127: The Fenwick lab has been surveying and sampling Mediterranean geckos (Hemidactylus turcicus) on the University of Central Oklahoma (UCO) campus for over ten years, building on survey data since 2005. The site is interesting because there is known introduction history to a single building from a single source population that has been sampled. Slow dispersal of this species makes it easy to track the spread of a single colonization. This project continues to track ongoing spread by identifying new off-campus buildings with geckos. When found, we collect tail tips and genotype using 16 microsatellite loci for population genetic estimates. This year we added genotypes for over 100 individuals, including 18 buildings up to a mile away from campus. We use ARLEQUIN and STRUCTURE to evaluate genetic differences within the population. Data show low genetic variation and two genetic clusters ordered by increasing distance from Howell Hall. We have not yet found the edge of the range of this colonization and plan to continue sampling, as well as complete genotyping of already-collected samples using newly programmed liquid-handling robots. Maddy Cochrane
128: Understanding how aquatic organisms respond to contaminant exposure in fast-flowing streams can be a challenge in ecotoxicology, where a balance between experimental control and environmental realism is required to be predictive of natural conditions. We developed a scalable, low-cost design that integrates individual isolation and environmentally relevant pulse-dilution dosing that mimics natural runoff into streams. Utilizing stream salamander larvae as a case study, the system consists of gravity-fed recirculating channels housed within a temperature-controlled water bath. The design supports repeated behavioral observations and specimen identification through isolated, mesh-divided chambers. We structured chemical treatments to mimic storm-driven runoff by gradually adding a dose to reach the target concentration, then diluting and fully replacing the water to reproduce the dynamics of a high flow stream. In our case study, the system kept water parameters within target ranges, with survival stabilizing after acclimation and growth remaining consistent across trials. Individual isolation enabled consistent visualization of behavioral metrics and resource use, which can be difficult in traditional pooledgrouping designs. This novel design overcomes a common tradeoff between replication, behavioral accessibility, and realistic exposure regimes. This approach is adaptable across taxa and experimental questions, providing a practical framework for studying responses to environmentally relevant chemical pulses and improving connections between laboratory experiments and field conditions. Taryn Cornell
129: The Western Rattlesnake Complex – the Arizona Black Rattlesnake (Crotalus cerberus), the Prairie Rattlesnake (C. viridis), the Northern Pacific Rattlesnake (C. oreganus), and the Mojave Rattlesnake (C. scutulatus; MJR hereafter) – has been studied extensively for hybridization and gene flow across species boundaries. Despite being in sympatry in western Texas and southeastern New Mexico, MJR have not been confirmed genetically to hybridize in the wild with Western Diamond-backed Rattlesnakes (C. atrox; WDB hereafter), despite confirmed reproduction in a husbandry setting. In 2010, FHSM 14943 was collected as roadkill from Brewster Co., Texas – one of seven Texas counties where MJRs and WDBs co-occur. This specimen was initially identified in the catalog and tissue database as a WDB, thus was included in a study focused on WDB phylogeography. Genomic analyses indicated FHSM 14943 as an outlier specimen, but still nested within east-Cochise WDBs. Returning to this voucher, and using Klauber’s dichotomous key to rattlesnakes, we identified the specimen as a juvenile Mojave Rattlesnake (alternating tail rings with white bands larger than black bands, division between prefrontal and frontal scales, large and flat crescentic scale bordering supraocular). After these conflicting lines of evidence, we isolated mitochondrial bycatch for this specimen from whole genome resequencing data. Mitochondrial loci identified this specimen as a WDB as well. Given the conflicting data (morphological, genomic, mitochondrial) and the collection of this specimen in an area of sympatry, we infer that FHSM 14943 is the first confirmed wild hybrid between WDBs and MJRs using integrative lines of evidence. Matthew T. Craig
130: The littoral zone of freshwater lakes are often highly productive, with greater macrophyte growth relative to the limnetic zone. The littoral zone is also known to serve as spawning and nursery grounds for various species of fish. Lake Maurepas, an oligohaline lake in southeastern Louisiana, remains poorly studied, particularly regarding the structure and composition of its littoral-zone fish communities. Having been extensively logged between 1876 and 1956, the nearshore areas of Lake Maurepas are riddled with remnant stumps and logs, making sampling in these areas difficult. Since 2022, Southeastern Louisiana University has been involved in a comprehensive ecological monitoring program ahead of a potential carbon sequestration project in Lake Maurepas. The fish community in offshore and open-water areas of the lake are currently being monitored with trawling, gillnetting, boat electroshocking, and environmental DNA sampling. For this project, we seasonally sampled six sites along the southern shore of Lake Maurepas using a 30.5-m block seine to create an enclosed sample area along the shoreline. Within each sample area, we pulled a 6-m seine to collect fish. All fish collected were identified, enumerated, and archived in the Southeastern Louisiana Vertebrate Museum. Preliminary results from our spring and summer 2026 littoral zone sampling will be presented. Paul V. Cupp Jr
131: Mercury is a marine toxicant that enters marine environments, polluting habitats and posing risks to ecosystem health. Often, predators at the highest trophic level of ecosystems accumulate the highest levels of mercury in their organs and tissues. This is due to biomagnification, the process in which the amount of a toxicant accumulates as it is transferred up the food web. Mercury has been shown to cause adverse effects to the reproductive and the central nervous system. Therefore, it is important to monitor environmental concentrations and effects of Hg so we can take preventive measures. It’s especially critical to understand how sharks deal with mercury as they age. We sampled Carcharhinus plumbeus (sandbar shark), Rhizoprionodon terraenovae (Atlantic sharpnose shark), Carcharinus limbatus (blacktip shark), Sphyrna lewini (scalloped hammerhead) and Sphyrna tiburo (bonnethead), using hand deployed bottom longline, gillnet, and drumline fishing. Muscle biopsies were obtained from sharks and analyzed for total mercury using a DMA-80 Direct Mercury Analyzer. The mercury levels from these samples were then analyzed separately for species and gender. Lastly, the relationship between mercury accumulation and age sharks age was determined using published age-growth relationships to convert shark length data to estimated age. Ashley Mackenzie Dawdy
132: The gopher tortoise (Gopherus polyphemus), a keystone species within the longleaf pine ecosystem, experience widespread population declines due to anthropogenic alteration. In these impacted environments, G. polyphemus often exhibit increased physiological stress and a higher likelihood of infection and apparent disease. Specifically, G. polyphemus frequently suffers from Upper Respiratory Tract Disease (URTD) caused by the bacterium Mycoplasma spp., though the virus Ranavirus (Rv) can exhibit similar clinical signs in some individuals. Here, we examined the presence, prevalence, and intensity of Mycoplasma spp., and Rv in G. polyphemus populations across anthropogenically-impacted and relatively unimpacted sites on the University of Central Florida campus. To date, we sampled 33 tortoises across three field sites: UCF’s East Parcel (n = 9), a highly altered sand mound site (n = 8), and the Arboretum natural preserve (n = 16). Seven individuals exhibited clear signs of nasal erosion, with two confirmed positives of Mycoplasma testudineum present in these individuals. The presence of nasal erosion significantly differed by sex (p = 0.002), with both qPCR positives coming from 2 females. We observed no significant difference by site type; thus, we predict that larger regional-level influences may better explain differences in tortoise disease, not local habitat differences. Ultimately, this research will continue to inform land management at UCF and better our understanding of the complex interactions between urbanization and disease ecology. As UCF continues to expand, this work will provide burrow locations on the land scheduled for development. Lindsey DeHaan
133: Suction-feeding sharks lack the many skeletal linkages and coordinated movements that allow teleosts to functionally engage the trunk musculature to augment the muscle power needed for suction feeding. Instead, evidence suggests that most suction-feeding sharks rely solely on hypobranchial musculature during suction generation. These muscles should have a relatively small power output compared to the combination of head and trunk muscles used by teleosts, yet they are capable of the same or higher levels of performance. Here, we aim to describe and quantify muscle-tendon architecture and leverage in representatives of three divergent groups of suction-feeding sharks to reveal features that may facilitate high-powered suction feeding. We used DiceCT reconstructions to quantify muscle features and measure 3D moment arms of the hypobranchial muscles of Chiloscyllium plagiosum (high-powered suction feeder), Squalus acanthias (feeding generalist), and Mustelus canis (durophagous species). While the general morphology of the primary hyoid-depressing muscles is similar across species, moment arms differ significantly. In C. plagiosum, this moment arm starts at near-zero, a feature resulting from the alignment of the muscles with the articulations of the hyoid and drastically increases at early degrees of hyoid depression. This supports previously proposed catch mechanism hypotheses. The primary jaw-opening muscles exhibited an opposite relationship. Muscle moment arms were consistent, but the muscle architecture of C. plagiosum resulted in a higher potential for force output.
134: Sharks swim using lateral body undulations and amplitude increases toward the caudal fin, where thrust is primarily generated. Four carcharhiniform shark species have been shown to swim using a double oscillating system where the head frequency and amplitude differ from the tailbeat. While prior studies have described species-specific swimming kinematics, our study aims to characterize and quantify the presence of a double-oscillating swimming mechanism has not been quantified broadly among species with varying morphology and swimming styles. Video was collected in-situ using aerial drones, where individuals are categorized by social context (conspecific, heterospecific, or solitary) and behavioral state (steady swimming, turning, and hunting). Video frames were annotated using Computer Vision Annotation Tool (CVAT), and object detection You Only Live Once (YOLO) models that automate tracking of six anatomical landmarks along the body overtime for kinematic analysis. This approach enables detection and quantification of double-oscillatory patterns during in-situ observation and allows for comparison of oscillatory dynamics across different social contexts, behaviors, and among species. This data set includes video from five species (Sphyrnidae spp., Carcharhinus limbatus, Negaprion brevirostris, Ginglymostoma cirratum, and Pristis pectinata) encompassing examples varying in social context (N=39) and behavioral context (N=32), respectively. Results highlight early evidence of double-oscillating swimming across species and differences in oscillatory dynamics among behavioral and social contexts, including differences in turning frequency and time in social settings. This project integrates drone-based imaging and automated kinematics analysis in a scalable, non-invasive framework for studying marine vertebrates, supporting broader applications for ecological monitoring and ocean observation. Calum Devaney
135: The Rwenzori Mountains of Africa straddle the borders of Uganda and Democratic Republic of the Congo, and they are home to many endemic and threatened species. Among these species are three endemic skinks with a conflated taxonomic history that are known from very few specimens: Leptosiaphos meleagris, Panaspis burgeoni, and P. helleri. These taxa and other congeners in these two closely related skink genera have undergone numerous taxonomic revisions throughout the 20th century, creating confusion about the composition of each genus, especially the Panaspis species. To assess the taxonomic status of P. burgeoni and P. helleri, we examined the morphology and geographic distributions of all known specimens, and compared them among each other and to L. meleagris. We conclude that P. burgeoni and P. helleri are junior subjective synonyms of L. meleagris based on extensive overlap in geography, morphology, and coloration that indicate insufficient diagnostic traits. Diego Deville
136: Elasmobranch communities in the Upper Florida Keys remain comparatively understudied despite the ecological importance and intensive human use of the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary (FKNMS). We conducted a multi-method assessment of elasmobranch diversity, relative abundance, and community structure across inshore and offshore habitats near Key Largo, Florida, from January 2024 to August 2025. Surveys incorporated benthic longlines, drumlines, baited remote underwater video systems (BRUVs), and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to evaluate habitat- and method-specific detection patterns. Across all methods, a total of thirteen species were detected inshore and eight offshore. Multivariate analyses revealed that habitat type strongly structured inshore communities, with seagrass and hardbottom habitats supporting distinct assemblages, whereas offshore patch and bank reef communities overlapped substantially. Habitat explained more variation in community structure than survey method inshore, while offshore differences were comparatively weak. Nurse Sharks (Ginglymostoma cirratum) dominated seagrass habitats, whereas hardbottom shoals supported greater taxonomic richness and overall diversity. Offshore communities were characterized by reef-associated and wide-ranging predators, including Tiger Sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier) and Caribbean Reef Sharks (Carcharhinus perezi). No single survey method captured the full extent of community diversity; UAVs improved detection of shallow-water taxa, while drumlines improved detection of large, mobile predators. These findings highlight the ecological importance of nearshore habitat heterogeneity and demonstrate the value of complementary survey approaches for more comprehensively and perhaps more accurately characterizing elasmobranch assemblages. This study establishes a regional baseline for habitat-linked community structure and provides insights to inform ecosystem-based management within a heavily used marine sanctuary. Sneha Dharwadkar
137: The increased accessibility of Computed Tomography (CT) data provides an opportunity to assess the morphology of the skeletal labyrinth, which houses the membranous labyrinth of the ear, in one of the two primary clades of elasmobranchs: Squalomorphi. This study describes the morphology of the skeletal labyrinth of ten species of squalomorphs: Chlamydoselachus anguineus, Heptranchias perlo, Hexanchus griseus, Notorynchus cepedianus, Squatina californica, Centrophorus squamosus, Squaliolus laticaudus, Oxynotus centrina, Isistius brasiliensis, and Etmopterus bullisi. Hexanchiforms are found to have more robust skeletal labyrinth spaces housing the semicircular canals and ampullae, while squaliforms have more slender labyrinths that likely better reflect the shape of the membranous structures within. Prior studies in fishes and tetrapods have found a relationship between ear morphology, phylogenetic history, and ecological factors. Given the variety in diet and habitat across this sample of taxa, we advocate for broader taxonomic coverage and finer delineation of ecological categories in future assessments of the drivers of ear geometry. This work supported by the National Science Foundation award IOS 2402409 Holly Doerr
138: A major environmental problem today is the amount of plastics polluting natural ecosystems. Over time, these plastics break down into microplastics (plastics less than 5 mm), and nanoplastics (less than 1um). The effects of these microplastics on the environment and its inhabitants are still largely unknown, which is why there is a growing concern and need for researchers to focus on its impacts. Tadpoles and frogs are highly sensitive to environmental change, making them susceptible to micro- and nanoplastics. In this study, African Clawed Frog (Xenopus laevis) tadpoles were observed for feeding behavior changes after being either purposefully exposed to 50 ug/L of plastics that were 740 nm - 4990 nm in size or not being exposed to any plastics during their larval development. It was found that exposure to this size range of nano- and microplastics had a significant impact on how the tadpoles interacted with their food during a behavioral assay. These findings further indicate the importance of analyzing exactly how microplastic exposure manipulates behavioral and physiological function. Michael J. Dreslik
139: Damselfishes (Pomacentridae) are an exceptionally diverse group of soniferous fishes that occupy a range of ecological roles across shallow to rariphotic reefs. Many species are aggressive, defending nests using acoustic signals that consist of a single pulse. Some species also emit pulse trains, often referred to as “dips,” during social interactions. The mechanism underlying sound production has been investigated in a limited number of derived pomacentrids, such as clownfishes, and has been hypothesized to involve the oral jaw. Given the importance of acoustic signaling in territorial behavior, we tested the hypothesis that evolutionary relationships within this family are associated with variation in acoustic parameters and morphology. Paired small-aperture acoustic arrays and 360° video systems were deployed to collect data across eight Caribbean damselfish species that occur in shallow water (2 m) to the mesophotic (100 m). We quantified similarities and differences in individual pulse characteristics within and among species, compared these patterns with variation in jaw morphology, and predicted the mechanism by clustering sound characteristics and comparing to other families of fishes with known sound production mechanisms. Our results suggest that sound production is unlikely to be driven by oral jaw or stridulatory mechanisms, and instead is more consistent with sonic muscle-based processes. In addition, the variation in pulse characteristics among species aligns with phylogenetic relationships, highlighting the potential of acoustic traits as evolutionary synapomorphies. Our findings support the development of passive acoustic tools for species-specific detection, providing a scalable approach for conservation of this ecologically important reef fish family. David D. Duvernell
140: Marine protected areas (MPAs) are widely implemented to protect biodiversity, critical habitat, and ecosystem function. Despite their designation as ecosystem management tools, MPAs have received significant attention in the context of fisheries management. However, because traditional fisheries management tends to focus on single-species approaches, most metrics of MPA performance fail to capture community-level reserve effects on fish assemblages. This drawback severely limits our ability to quantify MPA contributions to key ecological functions and services. Here, we propose the use of functional diversity as a multi-species fisheries benchmark, which may better evaluate community-level MPA benefits. Our efforts leverage a multi-year, multi-method biomonitoring dataset collected by the California Collaborative Fisheries Research Program, one of California’s largest and longest running MPA monitoring initiatives. With the help of hundreds of volunteer recreational anglers, we paired standardized hook-and-line surveys with simultaneous eDNA sample collection to characterize fish biodiversity inside and outside of two San Diego marine reserves from 2023-2025. eDNA samples were processed and analyzed using metabarcode sequencing of the 12S rRNA MiFish marker gene locus to generate complementary information on fish community composition, frequently detecting taxa not captured by traditional hook-and-line surveys. We are now combining biodiversity data with species-specific trait information (e.g., trophic ecology, physiology, morphology, habitat use, sociality) to understand how MPAs mediate the functional and ecological structure of nearshore fish assemblages in California. Grace Emanuelson
141: The coastal waters of North Carolina host one of the most diverse assemblages of shark species along the U.S. Atlantic seaboard, shaped by the convergence of warm and cold currents and the region’s extensive network of estuaries, sounds, and barrier islands. Despite this ecological richness, sharks in North Carolina remain understudied compared to neighboring states, with limited opportunities for coordinated data collection, collaborative research, and long-term monitoring. The North Carolina Shark Conservancy (NCSC) was founded in 2025 to address this gap by developing a dedicated, inclusive platform for shark research, conservation, and education across the state. NCSC initiatives are driven by community collaboration and scientific accessibility, thus the development of the region’s first North Carolina Shark Stranding Network. This collaborative framework is designed to document, investigate, and archive stranding events to better understand mortality causes, seasonal trends, and species distribution along the coast while providing tissue and necropsy samples to regional and global databases. In parallel, we are developing multiple community-driven initiatives that enable the collection of observations and data documenting shark presence, behavior, and habitat use in nearshore environments. These datasets will serve as foundational baselines for future population studies and habitat assessments, while also contributing to collaborative research and conservation efforts. Roseline Ewa Roseline Ewa; Tobit Liyandja; Brian Sidlauskas
142: Energetic performance in estuarine predators is shaped by environmental gradients such as salinity and temperature, which influence activity, behavior, and habitat use. These factors modulate overall dynamic body acceleration (a proxy for energy expenditure), affecting foraging success and predator evasion. However, how environmental variability translates to energetic performance and habitat suitability in dynamic estuarine systems remains poorly understood. Juvenile bull sharks (Carcharhinus leucas), a Species of Greatest Conservation Need, depend on estuarine nurseries during early development and are uniquely capable of tolerating low salinities. This physiological plasticity, combined with variable estuarine conditions, provides an ideal system for examining links between environmental change and energetic performance. This study will use tri-axial accelerometer biologging to quantify activity in free-ranging juvenile bull sharks across spatial and temporal gradients. Machine learning algorithms will classify behavioral states from accelerometry data and generate performance curves relating energetic expenditure to environmental conditions, allowing the identification of environmental optima and thresholds that structure habitat use. These relationships will be incorporated into mechanistic habitat suitability models integrating environmental data and Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD) long-term fisheryindependent survey catch data. Forecasting habitat shifts under warming and increased salinity (drought) scenarios will provide actionable science into how climate change may alter critical nursery habitats. By linking species occurrence to energetically optimal conditions, these results will support TPWD management decisions on when and where estuarine habitats should be prioritized for conservation under increasing temperatures and drought-driven salinity change. Naomi Farbaugh Naomi Farabaugh; Gina Clementi; Kirk Gastrich; James Kilfoil; Jennifer Caselle; Eric Clua; Serge Planes; Michael
143: Strategies for camouflage in marine habitats include using cryptic coloration to blend in with the environment and/or to obscure an individual’s silhouette. The selective pressures associated with camouflage in the open ocean present a challenge for species living in an environment where there are few physical habitat structures, such as corals, which impact camouflage selective pressures for in-shore taxa. The ability to possess camouflage capabilities can play a vital role for cartilaginous fishes to obscure their position while they sneak up on prey or limit visibility from potential predators. Many pelagic sharks rely on camouflage associated with downwelling light from the sun or bioluminescent light produced by the shark. This selective pressure drives two primary forms of camouflage in pelagic sharks: countershading and bioluminescence. Both methods functionally produce a lighter ventral surface that can blend in with downwelling light, and a darker dorsal surface that can blend in with the dark water below when visualized from above. In this study we explore the evolution of camouflage patterns across all species of sharks, with a primary focus on investigating the camouflage patterns in pelagic species. Annmarie Fearing Annmarie Fearing; Kelcee Smith; Kevin Feldheim; Alec Moore; Patricia Charvet; Vanessa Cruz; Madalyn Cooper; Christy Davies; Alexis Gentry; Cat Gordon; Bryan Huerta-Beltrán; Corinne Kemper; Matthew McDavitt; Claudio
144: Macroecological patterns of biodiversity are often linked to regional differences in niche space, yet similar biomes do not necessarily present equivalent ecological conditions. As a result, similar biomes in different regions may differ in the amount of niche space available for diversification. Cypriniformes provide an excellent system for testing these ideas because they are widely distributed across the Northern Hemisphere and occupy a broad range of freshwater habitats, including benthic and pelagic environments in lakes and rivers, lowland floodplain systems in North America, and torrential high-mountain streams across Eurasia. Here, we examine how habitat diversity and body shape variation differ across broad geographic scales in North American and Eurasian Cypriniformes. We quantified fine-scale habitat data using the WorldClim v2 dataset in ArcGIS and quantified body shape variation using 3D geometric morphometrics. We then compared patterns of habitat diversity and ecomorphological variation across biogeographic regions that share similar biomes. Our results show that niche diversity varies across broad geographic scales and that ecomorphological variation also differs among regions within similar biomes. Together, these findings suggest that similar biomes do not represent equivalent niche space and that geographic differences in niche diversity may help explain large-scale patterns of morphological diversification. Jessé Figueiredo
145: Porotergus is a clade of seven valid species inhabiting large rivers of tropical South America, exhibiting a range of craniofacial phenotypes that reflect trophic and behavioral differences. Species vary from those with short to elongate snouts and gracile to robust oral jaws, few to many oral teeth, and some with pronounced secondary sexual dimorphism in oral jaw size. Porotergus gimbeli and P. duende from the Amazon basin present a short snout with gracile oral jaws; P. gymnotus from the Essequibo basin displays an intermediate phenotype; and four species - P. apurensis, P. bonapartii, P. paranaensis, and P. sp. "ringtail" from the Orinoco, Amazon, and La Plata basins - possess a long snout with robust oral jaws. This mosaic of snout and jaw phenotypes indicates high evolutionary potential in these traits. We used CT imaging of >100 specimens representing all valid species, landmark-based 3D geometric morphometrics, and multivariate statistics (PCA) to examine differences in skull morphology. We assessed ontogenetic allometry (variation with body size), static allometry (variation among adults of a single population), geographic allometry (variation among adults of different populations), and interspecific allometry. We hypothesize that Porotergus skull evolution reflects homoplastic and lineage-specific transitions dominated by heterocephaly expressed as snout elongation relative to the braincase, alongside pronounced differences in the structure of the branchial basket and Weberian ossicles. Broader patterns of skull evolution in Porotergus parallel those of other riverine electric fishes, characterized by allopatric speciation and functional homoplasy of the oral jaws associated with trophic and behavioral roles. Anet Filipova
146: The age and growth of the lemon shark, Negaprion brevirostris, in the Northwest Atlantic was last studied in 1988. Given the original study occurred over 25 years ago, a revised comprehensive study is necessary to reevaluate the growth of lemon sharks as their life history characteristics may have changed. Lemon shark vertebrae (N=360, Female=156, Male=188) were sampled from fishery-dependent and scientific surveys from 20092023 and processed using standard protocols. Band counts were independently determined by two readers assuming band pairs are formed annually following validated ages using oxytetracycline. Observed and back-calculated sizeat-age data were independently used to fit 5 growth models; the traditional von Bertalanffy, a 2- and 3-parameter von Bertalanffy growth model with a size-at-birth intercept (L0), and the Gompertz and logistic growth model. The Gompertz model using back-calculated size-at-age data was determined to be the most parsimonious model, with growth parameters predicted as L0=55.8 cm fork length, k=0.15 year−1 and G=0.143 (235 cm FL) for sexes combined. The oldest aged sharks were 21 and 23 yrs for males and females. This study suggests lemon shark growth rates are faster than previously determined and are among those species ranked as “medium-growing” among sharks. Sam Fisher
147: Morphological diversity among closely related species often reflects adaptations to differing ecological conditions. This project investigated the relationships between two phenotypic axes, body shape and skeletal ossification, and environmental gradients in Neotropical weakly electric ghost knifefishes of the family Apteronotidae. Focal species inhabit river systems across the Amazon and Orinoco basins that vary substantially in stream order (Strahler from headwater to mouth), water chemistry (conductivity, dissolved minerals), and predation intensity (number and abundances of piscivorous species). Body shape was quantified using two-dimensional geometric morphometrics (GMM) on landmarked photographs, while skeletal ossification was assessed as relative bone density (RBD) derived from Hounsfield unit (HU) intensities extracted from CT scans of craniofacial bones using 3D Slicer. We used Principal Component Analysis (PCA) with species scored to biogeographic and habitat categories to link environmental gradients with phenotypic differences. We found species with deeper bodies in the Amazon Basin, and also in white waters, as compared to the Orinoco Basin and black and clear waters. We also found more reticulated skeletons in fishes of large river channels and more laminar skeletons in fishes of small streams. These results indicate predation pressure, water chemistry, and stream order are important drivers of phenotypic diversity in these riverine electric fishes. Together, these analyses provide the first systematic, quantitative assessment of morphological-environmental correlations in this ecologically and evolutionarily important teleost clade. Kristina Fite
148: Ectothermic animals depend on environmental temperature, which can limit how well they perform. Some ectothermic species also use chemical defenses that affect neuromuscular function. Dendrobatid poison frogs are a special case because they store alkaloid defenses that can interfere with muscle and nerve function, while still relying on movement to escape predators, find food, and reproduce. Currently, little is known about how temperature and alkaloid exposure interact to shape motor function in dendrobatids. Our project investigates how different alkaloids and thermal conditions affect jumping performance in the dendrobatid frog, Epipedobates anthonyi. Specifically, we will examine the effects of decahydroquinoline and tricyclic alkaloids on locomotor performance across a range of temperatures (10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35 °C). Jumping distance, time, and speed will be quantified using a performance track that allows precise temperature regulation to ensure frogs maintain the experimental temperature during the trials. By experimentally manipulating both alkaloid exposure and environmental temperature, this study aims to identify the individual and interactive effects of these two factors on locomotor performance. Our results will provide insight into tradeoffs between chemical defense and motor function, with implications for understanding ectothermic performance under changing thermal environments. Amanda Fleming
149: Managing energetic costs is a key aspect to any living organism. In the core of this lies metabolism, an organism’s ability to turn nutrition into usable chemical energy. Poison frogs from the family Dendrobatidae exhibit a demanding physiological cost, with needs to forage, hide, display mating, territorial and parental care behaviors. Additionally, these frogs hold a remarkable ability to sequester alkaloids from their diet. These sequestered alkaloids are then deposited in glands on the frog’s skin and serve as a defense against predators and microbes. In organisms outside of those who have evolved to sequester these chemicals, the alkaloids take a major toll on an organism’s physiology. We hypothesized the sequestration of these alkaloids will have a metabolic cost for the frogs, with frogs sequestering alkaloids having higher metabolic rates. To test this hypothesis, we used three groups of captive-raised, alkaloid-free Epipedobates anthonyi, including a control group receiving an oral administration of saline solution and two treatment groups receiving 10 μg of decahydroquinoline (DHQ) and 10 μg tricyclic alkaloids (TRI). We used a Qubit low-range respirometer setup at a controlled temperature to measure oxygen consumption and production of carbon dioxide. We will be presenting comparisons of these treatment groups. If alkaloid sequestration results in a physiological cost, specifically increased metabolic activity, it would indicate that frogs sequestering alkaloids require more energy to sustain other functions such as foraging and reproduction. These frogs would also be more susceptible to climate change as temperature will also directly impact metabolism. Alex Sutton Flynt
150: Since the 1970s, shark populations have experienced dramatic declines due to various pressures, including anthropogenic, with nearly one-third of all elasmobranch species now threatened with extinction. While overfishing remains the primary threat to shark populations, evidence suggests trace element (TE) contamination is an overlooked factor in conservation planning. Although TE toxicity is rarely a direct cause of mortality in sharks, sub-lethal effects such as oxidative stress and reduced reproductive ability may hinder population recovery. Furthermore, the ability of TE to bioaccumulate within organisms and biomagnify through food webs amplifies their ecological impacts. In this study, 16 TEs (As, Cd, Co, Cr, Cu, Fe, Hg, Mg, Mn, Mo, Ni, Pb, Se, Sn, V, Zn) were quantified using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS), alongside two stable isotopes (δ13C & δ15N) analyzed via isotope ratio mass spectrometry (IRMS).  Dorsal fin tissues were collected between 2015 and 2025 from six shark species in southeastern Florida: nurse sharks (Ginglymostoma cirratum), sandbar sharks (Carcharhinus plumbeus), lemon sharks (Negaprion brevirostris), tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier), great hammerhead sharks (Sphyrna lewini), and bull sharks (Carcharhinus leucas). Stable isotope analysis revealed variation in dietary niche among species and sex, while TE accumulation patterns were primarily species-specific. Bayesian ellipses indicated substantial trophic niche overlap among species. Great hammerhead and sandbar sharks consistently elevated across ten and seven TEs, respectively, whereas lemon and nurse sharks showed lower concentrations in nine and six TEs.  These differences may be driven by habitat use, particularly between nearshore and offshore environments, influencing exposure to TE contamination.
151: Understanding the drivers of biodiversification is a fundamental objective in evolutionary biology, yet much remains unknown regarding the underlying mechanisms that create biodiversity. The cessation of gene flow between populations plays a causal role in this process, therefore identifying barriers between lineages is a viable approach to discover some of these drivers. The riverine barrier hypothesis, which was originally suggested by Alfred Russell Wallace in 1854, posits that rivers act as agents of speciation for terrestrial animals. The primary drainages of Mainland Southeast Asia, a biodiversity hotspot with remarkably high in situ biodiversification, correspond with lineage boundaries in several groups. Here we perform a meta analysis of publications where the evolution of river-proximal taxa was examined and assess the degree at which lineage barriers correspond with river drainages. Cameron Gabriel
152: Despite being a common year-round resident in Florida’s Indian River Lagoon (IRL) ecosystem, much is unknown about the movement ecology of the Bluntnose Stingray (Hypanus say). This project used passive acoustic telemetry (PAT) to describe the movements of H. say individuals in the IRL. Ten stingrays were tagged with V9 acoustic transmitters between July 2025 and December 2025, and the movements were compared with water quality and weather parameters. Supplemental fisheries independent monitoring (FIM) data was included to investigate the impact of seasonality and lunar phase on historical H. say presence. As of January 2026, eight of the ten tagged stingrays were detected across nine receivers in the southern IRL. Detected stingrays displayed a low average residency index (26%) and the ability to execute movements greater than 10 km in under a week. Preliminary results showed that water temperature and DO were found to impact movement and number of daily detections in this species. Additional factors that were found to influence historical presence of H. say in the southern IRL included seasons and lunar phases. This study is the first known description of H. say movement, and the environmental factors that drive movement in this species. Jennifer Gardner
153: Natural history collections serve as critical repositories of biodiversity data, offering a window into the evolutionary history of species and global patterns of change. However, their utility in research may be constrained by long-term effects of fluid preservation and sub-optimal maintenance. Without proper maintenance of fluid balance, wet specimens can become dehydrated, potentially causing irreversible damage to tissues. Rehydration methods using water vapor and graded ethanol reintroduction have been successful in desiccated fish, mammals, and invertebrates. Here, I assess the efficacy of these rehydration methods in dried-out snake specimens. In addition to gross morphology, I use computed tomography scans to measure skeletal features and draw comparisons before and after rehydration. These rehydrated specimens will be compared to well-maintained representative specimens using phylogenetic paired t-tests to determine if these methods successfully restored the specimens’ physical condition. By determining if rehydrated specimens can provide high-quality morphological data, this project aims to extend the value of neglected historical collections. The results will provide evidence-based guidance for museums and researchers to make maximal use of damaged specimens in both research and educational contexts. This research reinforces the enduring value of specimen-based research, ensuring that rare and historic specimens continue to contribute to our understanding of vertebrate functional morphology and evolution. Jim Gelsleichter
154: Dendrobatid poison frogs are widely studied for their aposematic coloration and alkaloid-based defenses. Several recent studies have started to examine how traits like boldness and exploration relate to these physical defenses, with evidence suggesting that such risk-taking behaviors are correlated with aposematic coloration. However, while physical defenses and risky behaviors are well documented, defensive behaviors in dendrobatids have not been as well studied. As part of a larger study, we will further examine the recently described body-raising behavior in Costa Rican populations of Dendrobates auratus and how it relates to physical defenses and risky behaviors. Body-raising is a defensive behavior that appears to emphasize warning coloration to potential predators. Prior studies indicate that the intensity and frequency of the behavior vary across D. auratus populations and are correlated with dorsal coloration. Our study will quantify body-raising and bold behavior in two populations of D. auratus that differ in alkaloid defenses and dorsal aposematic coloration. We will use a Threat Stimulus Test with a moving bird model as a simulated predator to measure bold behavior and defensive responses. We will quantify frog alkaloid defenses at each population using a Transcutaneous Amphibian Skin Stimulator (TAS) and Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (GC-MS), and will also measure frog dorsal conspicuousness and pattern using standardized digital images. Our research will provide valuable insight into the defensive behaviors of a dendrobatid poison frog and further establish links between physical defenses, risky behavioral characteristics, and defensive behaviors. April George
155: The genus Bavayia (Gekkota: Diplodactylidae) is a diverse group of micro-endemic, insular gecko lizards from New Caledonia, characterized by a non-adaptive radiation that has resulted in numerous cryptic species. Due to their subtle diagnostic features, species within this genus are particularly difficult to identify based on morphology alone, a challenge that is compounded when these animals enter the international pet trade. In many cases, specimens are traded under incorrect or overly broad taxonomic labels, which complicates conservation efforts and responsible captive management. We here use mitochondrial (ND2) sequence data and a recently published comprehensive taxonomic revision of the genus to evaluate the species identity of nearly all known Bavayia ‘species’ currently found in the pet trade. This research highlights the importance of integrating modern molecular techniques with updated taxonomic literature to monitor biodiversity within the commercial trade and ensure the accurate identification of specialized herpetofauna. Elizabeth Gerbi
156: Nonnative species have large and varied impacts on ecosystems they invade. Understanding critical biological traits of a species can help predict invasion potential and inform management strategies. Environmental temperature contributes to species distribution since it affects many physiological mechanisms, particularly for ectotherms. Ectotherms native to tropical regions have narrower thermal tolerance limits than temperate organisms, hindering their rapid expansion into colder climates. In analyses of global patterns of nonnative species diversity, South Florida is identified as a hotspot of high established nonnative species richness across taxonomic groups. Typhlonectes natans, an aquatic caecilian native to Colombia and Venezuela, was discovered in the urban canal system of Miami-Dade and has since become established. While these caecilians experience stable temperatures in their native range, they can encounter more variable temperatures in South Florida canals. To understand the biological characteristics contributing to the potential invasiveness of T. natans, I assessed their thermal tolerance. Individuals were captured from the canals and acclimated to 25 °C. Trials were conducted to determine critical thermal minima (CTmin) and maxima (CTmax), defined as the temperature at which an individual shows a loss of righting response for >10 s. Water temperatures were decreased or increased at a rate of 0.15 °C/min. Preliminary results showed a mean CTmin of 13.00 ± 0.29 °C and mean CTmax of 39.48 ± 0.34 °C. These data may provide insight into the potential northern nonnative range of T. natans. Haley Gipson
157: Biofluorescence occurs when molecules absorb photons at one wavelength (excitation), transition briefly to an excited state, then re-emit new photons at a longer wavelength (emission), which produces a visible glow that varies in color and intensity under different excitation wavelengths. Amphibian biofluorescence is newly documented and appears to vary among species and between sexes. This natural history survey examines how amphibian fluorescence responds to ultraviolet (UV) (365 nm) and blue light (450 nm) wavelengths; two wavelengths that can reveal different fluorophores and anatomical patterns in vertebrate skin. The objective of this study is to survey amphibian species in northeastern Pennsylvania and determine (1) whether specific wavelengths produce distinct biofluorescent reactions, (2) whether fluorescence varies within a species, (3) whether amount or presence is sexually dimorphic, and (4) where biofluorescence is anatomically located. It is expected that new biofluorescence patterns will be catalogued in local species. Documenting these patterns in regional amphibians contributes to a broader understanding of biofluorescence and supports the development of standardized procedures for future comparative and functional studies. Brad Glorioso
158: Gobies (Gobiidae; ca. 2,000 species) exhibit repeated convergent losses of vision, yet the genomic mechanisms of eye degeneration in this group remain unexplored. We inferred a time-calibrated phylogeny of Gobiaria from 1,081 exon loci (1,071 nuclear + 10 mitochondrial) sampled across 509 species under both Maximum Likelihood (IQ-TREE, RAxML-NG) and multispecies coalescent (ASTRAL) approaches. Phylogenetic comparative methods (Pagel's correlation, stochastic character mapping, hidden-rates Markov models) reveal correlated evolution between eye state and habitat across the gobioid radiation. To investigate the genomic basis of one such transition, we focused on Typhlogobius californiensis (Oxudercidae), a blind, unpigmented species whose two closest sighted relatives (Gillichthys mirabilis and Quietula y-cauda) diverged ca. 10 Ma, providing a natural comparative framework. We generated chromosome-level, phased genome assemblies for all three species using PacBio HiFi long reads and Hi-C data. Assemblies range from 771 Mb to 870 Mb per haplotype, with contig N50 values exceeding 5 Mb (range: 5.7 - 34.1 Mb). Annotation of the phototransduction pathway (KEGG map04744) reveals that T. californiensis has lost SAG (S-arrestin; K19627), which terminates phototransduction by binding phosphorylated rhodopsin, while both sighted relatives retain the full complement of 18 pathway orthologs. These results add a marine counterpart to the well-studied Astyanax cavefish system and suggest that the genomic signatures of vision loss may follow similar pathways across independent freshwater and marine origins. Viktor Cárdenas González
159: Crocodylian nests are important indicators of reproductive activity, but traditional surveys can be limited by cost, access, and observer safety. Thermal unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) may provide a useful alternative for characterizing nest surface temperatures under field conditions. We evaluated how flight altitude and time of day influenced the thermal characteristics of known American alligator (Alligator mississippiensis) nests in Texas coastal marsh habitat. Using field-confirmed nests, we conducted 66 UAV flights across three altitudes (12.19 m, 30.48 m, and 60.96 m) and multiple diel periods. Imagery was processed into orthomosaics and evaluated using temperature-based metrics and image characteristics. Thermal metrics differed significantly across altitudes for maximum temperature (H = 13.57, P = 0.0011), temperature range (H = 19.39, P < 0.0001), and pixel count (H = 25.76, P < 0.0001). Lower-altitude flights yielded higher maximum temperature estimates, a larger spread between minimum and maximum temperature estimates, and greater pixel representation of nests than higher-altitude flights. Minimum and mean temperatures also differed by diel period, with morning flights recording lower values than afternoon flights (minimum temperature: F = 18.51, P < 0.001; mean temperature: F = 13.98, P = 0.0004), suggesting that cooler morning conditions may have enhanced temperature differences between nesting material and surrounding habitat. Overall, low-altitude morning flights provided the clearest thermal characterization of known nests, whereas flights at 30.48 m offered a practical balance between image detail and survey coverage. R. Dean Grubbs
160: The Short-tailed Kingsnake (Lampropeltis extenuata) is a slender colubrid endemic to the sandhills and scrub habitats of north-central Florida. Morphologically, L. extenuata represents a distinctive form within the genus Lampropeltis; until 2009, it was regarded as the sole extant member of the genus Stilosoma. Due to the fossorial nature and rarity of this species, many aspects of its biology are unstudied, and its cranial anatomy has not previously been described. Here, we present the first description of the cranial osteology of L. extenuata and compare its cranial elements with those of Lampropeltis getula (Eastern Kingsnake; closest relative) and Atractaspis irregularis (Mole Viper; a well-studied stenotopically fossorial taxon). Our results indicate that the skull of L. extenuata exhibits greater specialization for a stenotopically fossorial lifestyle (e.g., miniaturization of skull, paedomorphism, spatulate premaxilla) than is seen in morphologically typical members of Lampropeltis. Additionally, we video recorded four instances of L. extenuata engaging in proficient head-first burrowing behavior in the wild. We also reassessed the taxonomic validity of Stilosoma vetustum, an extinct species described from a single fossil vertebra. After a comparative anatomical analysis to modern Lampropeltis vertebrae, we do not find this vertebra to be diagnostic enough to warrant taxonomic action and recognize S. vetustum as a nomen dubium. More broadly, we developed a classification system to characterize differing degrees and forms of head-first burrowing (HFB) within Serpentes, as the term “fossorial” has historically been applied flexibly to a wide range of lifestyles. Sydney Haas
161: Neotropical freshwater fishes represent the most species-rich vertebrate fauna on Earth, with approximately 6,700 valid species, yet many groups remain poorly understood due to unclear species boundaries and a lack of reliable diagnostic characters, particularly among cryptic and pseudocryptic lineages. Rhamphichthyinae (Gymnotiformes), the sand-snout knifefishes, exemplify these challenges. This clade has a complex taxonomic history marked by repeated species descriptions and subsequent synonymizations. Three genera are currently recognized: Gymnorhamphichthys (five species), Rhamphichthys (seven), and the monotypic Iracema, totaling 13 species. While Rhamphichthys has been recently revised and Iracema is known only from the type specimens, Gymnorhamphichthys lacks modern taxonomic reassessment. This study used integrated taxonomy to resolve species boundaries and interrelationships within Gymnorhamphichthys to evaluate the current classification and biogeographic ranges of the nominal species. I apply an integrative framework combining micro-computed tomography (CT scanning), 3D geometric morphometrics, and DNA barcoding. A time-calibrated, total-evidence phylogenetic tree for Rhamphichthyinae is being developed to infer evolutionary relationships. Integrating phylogenetic and geographic data will allow reconstruction of ancestral geographic ranges and diversification patterns. Preliminary analysis of 337 museum lots, 62 CT scans, and genetic data 49 specimens (plus GenBank sequences) indicate at least two undescribed species within populations assigned to G. cf. rondoni in the Essequibo basin which differ in meristic traits (e.g., pectoral fin rays), and the Araguaia basin, which are distinguished by differences in COI sequences. This research clarifies species diversity, stabilizes taxonomy, and provides a comprehensive evolutionary framework for Rhamphichthyinae, improving understanding of Neotropical fish diversification. Samantha Haggard
162: Mercury (Hg) is known to have negative consequences on vertebrate physiology, including reproductive health. For example, high levels of Hg have been shown to impair reproduction in male vertebrates through various mechanisms that can lead to spermatotoxicity. Like other top marine predators, sharks and their relatives have been shown to accumulate significant quantities of Hg, placing them at risk from the possible effects of this toxic metal. However, to the best of our knowledge, no studies to date have explored Hg concentrations in shark semen to evaluate possible Hg-related risks to male reproduction. Therefore, in this study, we explored Hg concentrations in semen of male sharks and rays to address this gap in scientific knowledge. Semen concentrations of Hg were examined using a Milestone DMA-80 Direct Mercury Analyzer and compared with Hg levels observed in other tissues. Angela M. Haggard
163: Anthropogenic infrastructure often dramatically reshapes aquatic ecosystems, posing challenges for numerous organisms including freshwater turtles, which remain one of the most imperiled groups of vertebrates globally. Specifically, these habitat alterations and the presence of infectious diseases compound to increase the likelihood of mortality events and subsequent decline in turtle species. In Florida, stormwater retention pond habitat quality varies dramatically due to inconsistent monitoring practices and can outnumber natural wetlands, restricting turtles to these stormwater retention basins. Here we sought to determine the community composition within these stormwater retention wetlands and how residing within these wetlands altered Ranavirus (Rv) infection status and body condition of aquatic turtles. We utilized a combination of trapping methods and standardized visual encounter surveys to study freshwater turtle communities across 9 wetlands (6 stormwater basins and 3 natural) at The University of Central Florida, in Orlando, Florida, USA. We determined the species, collected morphometric data to determine body condition, individually marked, and swabbed each individual following established protocols. We then utilized an Rv specific qPCR assay to determine the presence and infection intensity within each individual. To date, we have captured 80 unique individuals, representing six different species. Additionally, 11/53 individuals tested positive for Rv, though all exhibited low infection intensity, and none showed clinical signs of infection, indicating that Rv likely does not impact this system, even in urbanized locations. This study helps to answer critical questions and provides a baseline to better understand the disease dynamics of Rv in common aquatic turtle species moving forward. Pamela Hart Matthew Niemiller; Jonathan Armbruster; Michael Sandel; Eric Maxwell; Orran Bierstein; C. Anderson; Jacob
164: The sawfishes are considered one of the most threatened groups of fish on the planet. While they were once in abundance in nearly 90 countries, their populations have been severely depleted, with local extinctions in many countries. Their elongated rostra lined with tooth-like projections increases their chances of entanglement in fishing gears, and their highly valued rostra and fins and has led to high mortalities in fisheries. Coupled with their late sexual maturity and low reproductive output, this makes them slow to recover from population declines. The Smalltooth Sawfish (Pristis pectinata) has dwindled down to roughly 20% of their historic range. They are currently only found in viable numbers in southwestern Florida, although there are sporadic records of P. pectinata across the northern Gulf of Mexico in more recent years. The use of environmental DNA (eDNA) technology has become favored as an early-detection tool for rare species owing to its ability to efficiently detect traces of target DNA in environmental samples. This provides a reliable and non-invasive method of studying P. pectinata in an area where presence is unknown. Here, 32 x 3-L water samples were collected in Saint Andrew Bay, Saint Joseph Bay, and Saint Vincent Sound, Florida in the summer of 2023. Water samples were filtered, DNA extracted, and a Droplet Digital PCR assay was used to screen for P. pectinata DNA. The results of this study are instrumental to our understanding of the presence and habitat use of P. pectinata in the northern Gulf of Mexico. Delson Hays
165: The toothed rostrum of sawfish is their most distinctive feature, yet the growth and structure of rostral teeth is not well described in the literature. In many fish species hard structures that grow throughout life are used to quantify growth and age, however, sawfish rostral teeth do not show visible banding that would make this possible. Size-at-age models in sawfish exhibit high variation for larger age classes due to low sample sizes, and the only reliable method for age estimation is vertebral aging, which is only possible with dead fish. In species as critically endangered as sawfish there is a need to constrain size-at-age models using new methods that can be applied to living fish, or reconstructed from archived samples. In this study we used Micro-CT to image the internal structure of Largetooth Sawfish (Pristis pristis) rostral teeth of a range of archived samples from embryos to large adult fish from the Brazilian Amazon coast and Venezuela. The internal structure of these rostral teeth is highly organized, with internal structures increasing steadily in complexity through time. Although banding is not visible, internal structures increase predictably with fish size and scale with other morphological measurements. The results indicate that sawfish rostral teeth may provide morphological data that could constrain size-at-age models, especially if archived samples of large fish can be used to increase sample sizes. Vital Heim
166: The cloacae of squamate reptiles are multifunctional structures, responsible for facilitating parturition, defecation, urination, and copulation. The vaginal pouch is the part of the cloacal region that directly interacts with the hemipenes during copulation and its study can provide insight into the coevolutionary patterns of squamate genitalia. Recent work in snakes has found a high degree of morphological variation in the vaginal pouch within and between species, and some have described a vestigial ‘pouch’ in males. Lizards are closely related to snakes and are also known to have elaborate genitalia, yet have not been studied in such depth, especially the anatomy of females. Here, we aim to quantify the 3D morphological diversity of the vaginal pouches and male ‘pouches’ of the Argentine Giant Tegu (Salvator merianae), a large species of teiid lizard known to have morphologically complex hemipenes. Our sample includes 40 adult tegu lizards collected from the Everglades National Park, FL, where they are invasive. We quantify 3D shape variation using silicone endocasts of the vaginal pouches, automatic landmarking techniques, and geometric morphometrics. We compare the morphological variation and allometry of these structures to that of tegu hemipenes as well as to squamates more broadly. This work will enable us to compare patterns of evolution in snakes versus lizards and develop a better understanding of the evolution of genitalia of squamate reptiles. Victoria Hemingway
167: Environmental DNA (eDNA) shedding rates vary with organismal physiology and behavior. In oligotrophic cave environments where resources are scarce, food availability and trophic interactions can strongly modulate activity, potentially altering eDNA release. Little is known about how these ecological pressures influence eDNA shedding in subterranean species, creating uncertainty in the reliability of current monitoring approaches.
