This study aims to advance eDNA technologies for detecting the rare Southern Cavefish (Typhlichthys subterraneus) and the Southern Cave Crayfish (Orconectes australis) within resource-limited cave systems. To evaluate how ecological drivers shape eDNA production and release, we conducted controlled laboratory experiments simulating predator-prey interactions to quantify species-specific shedding rates. The resulting shedding parameters will support modeling of eDNA detectability in subterranean environments, ultimately informing more efficient, reliable, and non-invasive sampling strategies for cave fauna. Initial laboratory work confirmed recovery of suspended eDNA from experimental samples, and DNA extraction and gel electrophoresis verified that the material was suitable for digital droplet PCR (ddPCR). Field validation will pair eDNA sampling in a cave known to support these species with a concurrent visual encounter survey. Preliminary results from laboratory and field efforts will be presented, highlighting progress toward a more robust framework for noninvasive monitoring of aquatic cave species and broader conservation applications in carefully balanced subterranean ecosystems. Eric J. Hilton
168: The lemon shark (Negaprion brevirostris) is a widely distributed coastal species in the northwestern Atlantic Ocean, yet its reproductive biology remains poorly described. Existing studies are limited and largely rely on genetic approaches. Reproductive tracts (N = 283) were collected from fishery-dependent and scientific surveys, including 136 females and 147 males. Results indicate a seasonal reproductive cycle, with females exhibiting a biennial ovarian cycle. Median length (L50) and age at maturity were estimated using logistic models as 196 cm fork length (FL) and 11.9 years for females, and 183 cm FL and 11.4 years for males. Mean litter size was 12.0 individuals with no significant difference between uteri (p = 0.556) and no relationship with maternal length or age (p > 0.17). Male reproductive structures were positively correlated with fork length (Spearman’s p > 0.51, p < 0.001), following a staggered sigmoidal progression; claspers reached L50 at 169.4 cm, followed by testes (180.4cm) and the epididymis (183.2 cm). Female reproductive structures showed similar patterns (p > 0.37, p < 0.001), with oviduncal gland development beginning at 183.1 cm, follicle maturation at 191.9 cm and uterine expansion at 205.5 cm. This study provides the first comprehensive assessment of lemon shark reproduction based on direct examination, refining key life history parameters for the northwestern Atlantic population. Natasha Hinojosa Natasha Hinojosa; Laura Lardinois; Andrew Sellers; Rebecca Bridge; Javiera Mora; Heraclio Sanjur; Kevin Gomez; Helio Quintero; Rodnyel Arosemena; Jon Cybulski; Matthieu Leray; Giacomo Bernardi; Rita Mehta; Hannah
169: Understanding how environmental conditions influence detection probability is essential for accurately estimating occupancy. The Blacksburg salamander (Plethodon jacksoni) is an endemic salamander with a narrow range in southwestern Virginia and northwestern North Carolina. However, factors influencing its detection probability remain poorly understood. We conducted repeated visual encounter surveys at three sites in Blacksburg, Virginia from 2025 to 2026. We evaluated how environmental and climatic conditions influence detection probability. Surveys were conducted every two weeks, during which site covariates (e.g., elevation, slope, and aspect) and sampling covariates (e.g., temperature, humidity, and ground temperature) were recorded. Detection probability was analyzed using a single-season occupancy model. We hypothesized that detection probability may vary across our sampling period due changes in activity with season. We also predicted that species occupancy will be associated with site characteristics such as rock type. Our results can inform seasonal activity and habitat preferences of this species as well as assessments of conservation threats. Ultimately, we aim to develop a long-term survey and monitoring approach to guide the implementation of conservation actions for this rare salamander. Ethan Holladay
170: The Atlantic stingray, Hypanus sabinus, is an abundant coastal and euryhaline batoid species frequently captured as bycatch in the Gulf of Mexico. Despite this abundance, Atlantic stingrays are considered a data-poor species as limited information exists on their life history. Updated age and growth information for Atlantic stingrays is needed to help fill knowledge gaps that can be used for conservation and fishery management implications. The objective of this study is to use vertebral centra from approximately 400 Atlantic stingrays collected between 2016 and 2017 in the northern Gulf of Mexico to estimate size-at-age relationships. Size-at-age data will be compared between sexes and evaluated using multiple growth models, including the three-parameter von Bertalanffy growth function (VBGF), the modified two-parameter VBGF, Gompertz, and logistic models. Results from this study will provide critical insights into Atlantic stingray growth dynamics for improved conservation strategies and fill any crucial data gaps towards this species' life history. R.C. Hoover
171: The evolution of body shape can be influenced by habitat characteristics, such as association with the benthos in fishes. Ecological shifts between benthic and pelagic habitats in fishes have been previously shown to affect rates of morphological evolution due to inhabiting a new niche. One fish family that shifted between benthic and pelagic habitats is minnows (Leuciscidae). Previous research demonstrated that pelagic species evolve more slowly in trophic traits than benthic species, despite a higher rate of speciation. However, how habitat preference drives other aspects of fish morphological evolution was not studied. We developed a novel unbending method for mitigating non-biological shape variation due to preservation artifacts affecting posture. This was tested against the unbending method in the R package LOST that uses a similar method to TPSutil. Our approach was similar to LOST in accuracy, with much greater computing speed, and greater flexibility in the types of curves that can be fit. We then quantified shape for 2,684 specimens across 274 species of North American Leuciscidae. With mouth angle as a proxy for benthic association, we tested how mouth angle correlated with evolutionary rates of body shape by dividing species into quartiles by mouth angle. We found no significant difference in rates of body shape evolution among mouth angle quartiles using compare.evol.rates (geomorph). Ongoing MuSSCRat analysis in RevBayes to account for background evolution are being performed. These findings will provide further insight into the role of ecological shifts in driving functional trait evolution in diverse clades. Kenzie Horton
172: American Bullfrogs (Lithobates catesbeianus) are an important game species across most of their native range. Revenue from licenses to hunt bullfrogs can fund conservation efforts, including habitat restoration and other benefits to wildlife. Recent reports suggest that certain bullfrog populations in Arkansas might be declining. To address this concern, we surveyed bullfrog populations at 10 parcels of state-owned lands in northeastern Arkansas. We conducted both auditory and time-constrained visual surveys. Collected specimens were screened for the presence of limb deformities, skin lesions, and oropharyngeal parasites. Of the sites we sampled, bullfrogs were absent from fewer than 35% as detected using either visual or audible cues. We captured 46.9% of all bullfrogs observed during visual surveys, none of which presented signs of limb deformities or oropharyngeal parasites. We discuss our findings with respect to site-specific habitat characteristics, as well as the natural and anthropogenic factors that could be potential contributors to bullfrog population dynamics in Arkansas. Asmaul Husna
173: African Small Barbs (Enteromius, Clypeobarbus, Cheilobarbus, Barboides, etc.) are a group of small cyprinids that include more than 261 species in 10 genera. Among them, Enteromius alone includes 227 species, making it one of the largest vertebrate genera. Although these species constitute a significant component of the African freshwater fish fauna, they remain among the most enduring taxonomic challenges in African ichthyology. Once assumed to be monophyletic, Enteromius is now considered non-monophyletic, and recent studies have identified four clades within this genus and its relatives. Clear convergence in form and structure has been identified between distantly related members of the clade, including characters such as the presence/absence of lateral lines and dorsal spines, as well as body shape. To address these issues, the present study uses comparative phylogenetic analyses of geometric morphometrics on the phylogenetic tree constructed by Ren and Mayden (2016) to examine the role of convergence in body shape evolution and to determine whether there is morphological differentiation among the four clades of Enteromius identified to date. Lameace Hussain (They/She) Lameace Hussain; Sean McKnight; Daniel Haro; Christina Romagosa; Nia Morales
174: The Bimini Biological Field Station Foundation (Bimini Shark Lab) is a marine science non-profit organization operating in Florida and The Bahamas. The three missions of the Bimini Shark Lab are Education, Conservation, and Research, and through these a major priority of the Shark Lab is to provide field-based opportunities to the next generation of marine scientists. Access to career skill building opportunities can be challenging for some students and early career individuals. The Shark Lab provides several scholarship-based programs to assist students with their career development. The internship program aims to provide individuals with an immersive experience encompassing a diverse range of activities related to the marine science field, including science communication, operation of a field station, field-based research activities, and assisting with the running of visiting courses. Teacher and Educator Workshops are designed to assist educators in the development of educational materials about sharks and the marine ecosystems. The Early Career Scientist Workshop aims to provide entry level scientists with mentoring, networking, discussion platforms, and field activities geared towards preparation for a career in marine science. The Bimini Shark Lab also collaborates internationally with fellow researchers and students to provide data and access to ongoing research projects. This poster will highlight the various programs of the Bimini Shark Lab in an effort to further accessibility to opportunities for students and early career individuals, and to support the network of marine scientists and conservationists. Kevin Hutcheson
175: Mercury (Hg) is a heavy metal environmental pollutant released mainly through anthropogenic sources such as coal burning and ferrous metals production. Once Hg is emitted, it will eventually undergo deposition and make its way into aquatic ecosystems. Following this, Hg can then be converted from its inorganic, less bioavailable, forms into an organic form, methylmercury (MeHg), by methylating bacteria. Bioaccumulation over time and the biomagnification of Hg can cause long-lived and high trophic level predators like sharks to accumulate large amounts of Hg within their tissues. This has led to health concerns for humans when diets include species with high Hg loads as well as concerns for these Hg-burdened animals. Hg is known to cause a variety of negative health effects including reduced reproductive capacity, altered neurological function, impaired immune function, and more. Recent preliminary analyses of total Hg (THg) distribution among a large array of tissues within Atlantic sharpnose sharks (Rhizoprionodon terraenovae) and finetooth sharks (Carcharhinus isodon) have revealed elevated accumulation among critical immune related organs. The purpose of this study is to build on these early observations and explore Hg distribution in shark tissues and organs to determine if immune organs are targets for Hg accumulation. The information gathered from this distribution analysis will be used as a launching point for focused research on organ specific effects of Hg in sharks through in vitro Hg exposure studies. Emma Jackson
176: Larval smelts (Family Osmeridae) are difficult to identify to species solely through morphological characters. However, species-level identification is crucial for monitoring populations of threatened taxa such as Longfin Smelt (Spirinchus thaleichthys), whose northernmost California population is found in Humboldt Bay. Despite this, monitoring efforts of larval Longfin Smelt are infrequent in this location, with this survey of Humboldt Bay larvae being one of just two in the last ten years. Additionally, there are few studies describing morphological characters for use in larval identification of osmerids, resulting in a heavy reliance on costly genetic methods in past surveys. To strengthen the application of morphological identification in larval osmerids, this study used morphology supported by DNA barcodes to assess occurrences of Longfin Smelt in Humboldt Bay. This was done through the identification of four morphotypes which were primarily used to differentiate Surf Smelt (Hypomesus pretiosus) from Longfin Smelt. Morphotypes consisted of a variety of morphometric characters, such as pigment spots and myomere counts, and included individuals in the yolk-sac and pre-flexion phases. Collected genetic information should produce DNA barcodes that support the application of these morphotypes in larval osmerid identification. Through this, it was possible to determine the abundance of larval Longfin Smelt collected from larval fish surveys during 2025-26. Comparison of these data against historic data from 2016-17 show changes in abundance of Longfin Smelt in Humboldt Bay, and highlight the need for regular monitoring of this at-risk species locally. Deja Johnston
177: Accurate estimations of abundance and distribution of managed species are essential for effective fisheries management and ecosystem conservation, yet these estimates can be biased by imperfect detection methods. In fisheries-independent surveys, the fishing gear used can strongly influence which species are detected, potentially leading to misrepresentations of stock robustness, community composition, and habitat occupancy. Despite this, few studies have incorporated gear bias when investigating elasmobranch presence and abundance in South Florida. This study addresses this gap by applying a Bayesian multi-method occupancy modeling framework to evaluate gear-specific detection probabilities for coastal shark species in and around Biscayne Bay, Florida. Using 2024 and 2025 data collected by the University of Miami Shark Research and Conservation Program, which includes drumline and longline replicate sampling events and environmental and operational covariates, we test the hypothesis that detection probability of target species differs significantly between gear types, and is further moderated by environmental variables. Expected outcomes include species-specific detection probabilities across gear types and identification of potential environmental drivers affecting detectability, with the goal of improving understanding of shark species composition across ecosystems. These results will provide insight into how survey methods shape ecological inference and support more reliable conservation and management decisions for shark populations. Julia Joos
178: Glucocorticoids are energy mobilizing hormones that have long been known to be labeled as stress hormones due to their increasing concentration with increasing stress on an organism (Munck & Guyre, 1986). However, glucocorticoid levels can also fluctuate based on ecology and energetic demands of an organism. The objective of this study is to examine the effects of home range size and movement rate on baseline glucocorticoid levels of timber rattlesnakes (Crotalus horridus). We hypothesized that movement rates and home range sizes would be positively correlated with glucocorticoid levels due to their nature as energy mobilizing steroid hormones. We used surgically implanted radio transmitters to determine home range sizes and movement rates for timber rattlesnakes located in northeast Pennsylvania. We collected blood samples at differing times of the year that correlate with varying timber rattlesnake activity levels. Preliminary data show that individuals that maintain larger home ranges and/or increased movement rates maintain elevated baseline glucocorticoid levels. Our data suggests that if you are studying stress in a wild animal, you should consider the animal's ecology. Michael C. Kardos
179: Olfaction is a vital sense in elasmobranchs (sharks and rays), necessary for localizing predators, prey, and conspecifics and navigating the environment. Importantly, elasmobranchs can experience indeterminate growth and lifelong neurogenesis, meaning their nervous system continuously grows throughout life, with a high degree of cellular proliferation in the olfactory system. As a result, marked anatomical changes can occur throughout ontogeny, often correlating with shifts in ecology. However, little is known about intraspecific variability in the olfactory system, particularly in threatened species, which can provide insights into their biology. The speartooth shark (Glyphis glyphis) is a vulnerable species, distributed in macrotidal river systems of northern Australia and southern Papua New Guinea. Juveniles occupy tidal waters, either migrating downstream and upstream with the tide daily, or migrating downstream into estuaries at the first major rain of the wet season; however, migration at adulthood is not well understood. This project aims to quantify intraspecific variation in the olfactory rosette (oR) of G. glyphis throughout early ontogeny. The left oR was removed from immature (n=7) and subadult (n=2) G. glyphis, and oR size, fineness ratio, interlamellar distance, and lamellar number was quantified. Individual lamellae were imaged using scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Olfactory rosette complexity, including sensory and nonsensory epithelial surface area and presence of apical knobs, was compared between individuals and maturity stages, and shows changes throughout early ontogeny. While not a functional study, understanding changes to the oR may allow us to make predictions about variation in sensory capacity throughout ontogeny in G. glyphis. Claudia G Kern
180: Adult phenotypes result from interactions among developmental stability mechanisms and developmental instability. In the realm of stability mechanisms, modularity has been identified as a primary evolutionary developmental component that facilitates the evolvability of complex systems. Among the various definitions of modularity, a module is a network of interacting elements that behave as quasi-independent units or as semi-autonomous sets of highly correlated traits within larger units. Here, we have explored the modular organization of the Weberian apparatus across key cypriniform taxa. This complex system consists of a series of anterior centra, neural arches, supraneurals, and pleural ribs that form a mechanical linkage that transmits the movement of the swim bladder to the inner ear. For this study we employed micro-CT technology and 3-D geometric morphometrics to test the modularity of the anterior vertebrae relative to more posterior vertebral regions. We also investigated covariation among elements within the Weberian apparatus. Results of this study demonstrate that the modularity of the Weberian apparatus can be related to species-specific differences in morphology, as well as to possible coincident evolution driven by environmental conditions. Through testing several modularity hypotheses, different groupings of Weberian elements have been identified that account for variation across taxonomic groups. Results from this study are presented in a phylomorphospace for the evolutionary history of Weberian apparatus morphology. Gavin Kerr
181: Successful treefrog reproduction depends on suitable environmental conditions at calling sites, which influence their ability to attract mates. Human-driven habitat changes can disrupt these reproductive cues, potentially altering mating success. This project examined whether invasive tree species influence calling behavior and habitat use of native treefrogs in East Texas wetlands in urbanized and natural sites. We focused on two widespread invasive trees: Chinese Privet and Chinese Tallow, and three native treefrog species: Green, Gray, and Cope’s Gray. We combined recordings of calling behavior with detailed measurements of calling sites (tree species identity, structure, and temperature) and frog characteristics (mass, length, and temperature). By comparing tree availability with observed calling locations across multiple breeding ponds, we assessed whether frogs preferentially selected or avoided invasive tree species. We found that treefrog and tree species varied by call sites, with natural sites having more variability than urban sites where invasive trees were more abundant. In natural sites, we found that treefrogs avoided invasive tree species, while in the urban sites, where only Cope’s Gray Treefrogs were observed, we found that they readily used invasive trees for calling behavior. This research addresses a critical link between urbanization, plant invasions, and treefrog reproductive behavior. Understanding how invasive vegetation alters breeding habitat quality, and affects frog species presence, can improve wetland management and restoration strategies aimed at conserving treefrog populations. Our findings help us better understand whether invasive trees merely coexist with native frogs or actively shape the reproductive landscape on which they depend Asher Kolden
182: Hypothesized associations between biodiversity and pathogen risk have long been debated. However, how biodiversity across multiple biological scales affects wildlife health remains to be explored. The waterborne fungal pathogen Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) has caused global declines in amphibian species. Habitat complexity, amphibian community diversity, and the amphibian skin-associated microbial community (skin microbiome) diversity can affect Bd dynamics in amphibian communities. At the macroscopic scale, diverse life history strategies (e.g., reproductive modes) and microhabitat specializations influence pathogen exposure and disease dynamics. At the microscopic scale, the amphibian skin microbiome can have complex and sometimes inhibitory interactions with Bd. Not only can habitat complexity shape amphibian species diversity and composition through available microhabitats, but habitat complexity (e.g., plant diversity) may also impact the environmental microbial pool available for recruitment to the skin microbiome. Our objective is to test whether biodiversity effects at one of these ecological scales (habitat, host, and microbiome) amplify or dampen diversity at other scales, and if these cross-scale interactions increase or reduce Bd prevalence in amphibian communities in the Atlantic Forest in Brazil. We expect habitat complexity to indirectly reduce disease prevalence in amphibian communities by enhancing both host species diversity and skin microbiome diversity. Preliminary analyses using Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs), accounting for the effects of season and sampling campaign, indicate that amphibian skin microbiome richness is linked to reduced Bd prevalence. Our results will provide insights into the relationships between multiscale biodiversity effects on host-pathogen interactions in wildlife. Kevin Kotyk
183: Dendrobatid poison frogs are well known for their conspicuous coloration and chemical defenses, the latter consisting of a diverse array of alkaloids that are sequestered from dietary arthropods. While these alkaloids are primarily recognized for deterring predators, recent work suggests that some alkaloids may protect against bacterial and fungal infection. However, with more than 28 different structural classes of alkaloids present in dendrobatids, the role individual alkaloids play in microbial inhibition remains poorly understood. Herein, we present the first study to investigate whether tricyclic alkaloids, one of the most common structural classes present in dendrobatid poison frogs, possess antimicrobial properties. To test this hypothesis, tricyclic alkaloids were extracted and quantified from ladybug beetles, Hippodamia convergens. Extracted alkaloids were tested against two bacterial species, Escherichia coli and Bacillus subtilis, and one fungal species, Candida albicans, using the Kirby-Bauer disc diffusion protocol. Diffusion assays demonstrated that the tricyclic alkaloids significantly inhibited the growth of E. coli and B. subtilis, while there was no significant difference in inhibition for C. albicans, suggesting that inhibition may be dependent on microbial type. Our results provide a new understanding of chemical defenses present in dendrobatids with evidence of antimicrobial activity in a widespread and ecologically relevant class of alkaloid. Elizabeth Kramer
184: Among teleost fishes, linkages between the gas bladder and perilymphatic space of the inner ear, which increase sensitivity and extend frequency bandwidth, have evolved multiple times. Some cichlid species within the subfamilies Etroplinae and Ptychochrominae exhibit structural modifications of the anterior gas bladder and posterior neurocranium that create a direct (otophysic) mechanical linkage between the gas bladder and inner ear, yet gas bladder morphology has not been broadly characterized across the family. Here, we characterize anterior gas bladder, exoccipital, and otolith morphologies across 53 cichlid genera using MRI and micro-CT scans of museum specimens and use ancestral state reconstruction to test whether these specializations evolved independently. Ancestral state reconstruction analysis predicts that the common ancestor of Cichlidae possessed an anteriorly bifurcate gas bladder that did not directly contact the neurocranium but did have enlarged exoccipital foramina, suggesting some capacity for enhanced hearing prior to the evolution of a direct otophysic connection. Both Etroplinae and Ptychochrominae independently evolved extensive diverticula that penetrate the posterior neurocranium. There are 11 instances of reversal to a gas bladder with a single chamber without anterior extensions and three independent instances of gas bladder reduction, while exoccipital foramina were lost independently in Cichlinae and Pseudocrenilabrinae. Auditory electrophysiology reveals hearing abilities spanning from the relatively unmodified Katria katria to specialized Paretroplus species, consistent with the morphological specializations observed. These results provide a foundation for understanding how gas bladder modifications linked to hearing enhancement have evolved within cichlids and teleost fishes more broadly. Hyejung Kwon
185: The rapid expansion of genomic data has led to the development of advanced computational tools for studying molecular evolution. HyPhy (Hypothesis testing using PHYlogenies) is a widely used software package for codon-based branch-site and gene-wide selection analyses using a suite of different evolutionary models. HyPhy offers both a web-based platform and a local command-line interface, each with distinct operational characteristics. The web-based platform provides an interactive interface for analysis, including automatically generated phylogenetic trees and manual branch labelling, but is limited by server availability and is less customizable. In contrast, the local command-line interface enables analyses to be performed independently of server resources, but requires manual data preparation that results in a high barrier to entry and can cause variability across analyses due to human error. To address these limitations, we developed HYphlow, a graphical interface that enables local HyPhy analyses, but with automated, reproducible data handling and execution. HYphlow automates data preparation steps, including species name validation against the NCBI taxonomy database, input file reconciliation across trait data, sequence alignments, and phylogenetic tree files, and integrates parsimony-guided branch labelling for consistency and reproducibility. Furthermore, HYphlow provides an optimized execution environment for HyPhy-based selection analyses by implementing asynchronous task execution with multiprocessing across allocated CPU cores, enabling efficient parallel execution and reducing computational time for multi-gene datasets. Using previously published datasets, we demonstrate that HYphlow produces results consistent with those obtained using manual workflows in a standardized and automated environment in considerably less time, supporting reproducible and large-scale evolutionary analyses. Chase Lambeth
186: Damselfishes (Pomacentridae) are a widespread group of primarily marine fishes that are part of the major acanthomorph assemblage, Ovalentaria (Teleostei). Although relationships within the family Pomacentridae are relatively well-established, the family’s relationship to other families within Ovalentaria is poorly understood. The members of Ovalentaria form a very large and diverse group containing over 6,000 species found in estuarine, freshwater, and marine habitats worldwide. This lineage represents more than a third of all percomorphs and over 15% of ray-finned fishes (Actinopterygii). It includes several orders (e.g., Atheriniformes, Cyprinodontiformes, Gobiesociformes) and more than 40 families, including well-known ones like Anablepidae, Cichlidae, Exocoetidae, Poeciliidae, and Pomacentridae. Due to their diversity, the evolutionary relationships within this group remain unclear, particularly for the placement of families like Pomacentridae as well as several other families (e.g., Embiotocidae, Plesiopidae, Pseudochromidae, and Grammatidae). Sequence data from mitochondrial (12S, 16S, ATPase 8/6, cytochrome b, cytochrome c oxidase I, and d-loop) and nuclear (histone 3, recombination activating gene 1, and Tmo-4c4) genes will be collected and analyzed via maximum likelihood. The phylogenetic relationships will be presented and discussed. Karl Larsen
187: The Atlantic Shark Institute is a 503(c)(3), fully volunteer non-profit focused on supporting shark research in Rhode Island and beyond. Since 2021, the organization has deployed a yearly 22 receiver acoustic telemetry array, and, with the help of fishermen volunteers, tagged >50 juvenile white sharks and 17 juvenile sand tigers. Now, we are presenting our preliminary assessment of space use across this array for these two species to see how much, if any, habitat overlap occurs between juveniles in southern New England. Curtis Lawrence
188: Animals utilize chemosensation to locate resources including shelter, food, and reproductive partners. For temperate taxa, finding overwintering sites is crucial for survival. Many organisms, such as snakes, demonstrate fidelity to their overwintering sites; however, it has not been determined how snakes initially locate these sites. The ability of some snake species, particularly pitvipers, to follow terrestrial maternal pheromonal trails has been noted in anecdotal reports, but specific studies examining general neonate trailing ability are lacking. We examined the ability of three species, across two phylogenetic families with varying overwintering ecologies, to follow terrestrial and airborne pheromonal emissions from maternal, non-maternal conspecific, and sympatric heterospecific individuals using modified Y-mazes. Neonate Armenian vipers (Montivipera raddei) and Wagner’s vipers (M. wagneri) successfully trailed both maternal and conspecific terrestrial and airborne cues, but did not successfully trail cues from a heterospecific sympatric species. Neonate northern water snakes (Nerodia sipedon) did not demonstrate any significant trailing ability across all trials of either pheromone modalities. Though all three neonates are temperate ovoviviparous species, the Montivipera are terrestrial and den communally, whereas Nerodia are semiaquatic and hibernate individually. Our results suggest that vipers — and potentially communally denning species — may have a greater innate ability to follow conspecific cues than those that do not. Additional study is needed to assess the trailing ability of neonates in tropical climates, oviparous species, and other habitat types such as arboreal, fossorial, and aquatic. Moreover, following cues from conspecifics may aid in gene dispersal. Elibardo Leal
189: Timber rattlesnakes (Crotalus horridus) show substantial geographic variation in how they overwinter and reproduce across their range, but populations in lowland Texas remain poorly understood. In upland areas, these snakes often gather in large communal hibernacula and return to the same sites year after year, likely because those locations offer stable temperatures and specific structural features. In contrast, lowland populations may use more scattered refuges due to milder winters. Maternal rookery sites have received far less attention, despite their importance for reproductive success. This study examines and compares overwintering hibernacula (both communal and single occupancy) and maternal rookery sites used by C. horridus in east Texas. Fieldwork takes place at a focal site in Montgomery County, Texas, an isolated population near the southwestern edge of the species’ range, where individuals are tracked using radiotelemetry and refugia are characterized using structural surveys and thermal monitoring. Preliminary surveys conducted from January–December 2025 have identified candidate hibernacula and maternal rookery sites within the study area, including sites consistent with communal denning. Communal hibernacula are expected to be more structurally complex and thermally stable than single-occupancy sites, while maternal rookeries are predicted to show intermediate conditions. Movement within refugia is predicted to increase during thermal extremes, with stronger site fidelity to more stable habitats. This work improves understanding of habitat use in a lowland population and provides insight into how environmental variation shapes refuge use at the edge of the species’ range, informing conservation in fragmented landscapes. Justin Lee
190: The Great Plains region contains habitats typified by remnant and restored prairies, fallowed fields, and agricultural land. These ecosystems experience both natural and anthropogenic disturbances such as fire, drought, and agricultural land-use. Many taxa have home ranges constrained to these habitats including a variety of herpetofaunal species. Due to their cryptic nature, snake diversity, abundance, and range can be difficult to detect, especially in habitats that experience frequent disturbances. Coverboards, however, can create optimal microhabitats attractive to some snake species which facilitate their detection and capture. We investigated the effects of two land management practices (burning and haying) on the detection rate of snakes on a restored prairie in Sedgwick County, KS. As part of a long-term monitoring effort at Wichita State University’s Ninnescah Biological Reserve, we collected data from four sites with varied land management practices. Each site contained a set of 10 coverboard pairs (1.2 m x 1.2 m plywood; 0.9 m x 1.2 m tin) placed 1 m apart every 20 m along two 100 m transects. Initial results from 5 years of data suggest that combined land management practices (sites both burned and hayed) have little effect on detection of snake species overall. However, we observed that Coluber constrictor and Pantherophis obsoletus detections increased post-disturbance at ~500 days and ~1500 days, respectively. When the two management types were isolated, prescribed burns had a marginal effect on overall snake detection rates, while haying had a more significant effect where detection rates peaked at ~500 and ~1500 days. Luke J. Linhoff
191: Ocean warming poses an ongoing threat to many marine species, with the larval stage often being especially vulnerable to changing temperatures. Temperature can affect both the organ development of larvae and their somatic growth, though these two processes are rarely examined together in detail. Allometric scaling – the rate at which a focal trait scales with body size – can provide a measure of organ development and may yield insight into the nuanced effects temperature can have on larvae. We measured mass, feeding rate, and various morphometric traits of larval California grunion reared under temperatures ranging from 14°C to 26°C. By analyzing images of individual larvae, we calculated the sizes of eyes, stomachs, and snouts relative to overall body size. Our results suggest that larvae raised at warmer temperatures had eyes, stomachs, and snouts that developed faster relative to their standard length than larvae raised at colder temperatures. These larvae also exhibited a higher feeding rate and attained a larger size at warmer temperatures. Accelerated organ development at high temperatures may increase a larva’s ability to obtain and digest food and may thus help larvae cope with high temperatures and greater metabolic demands. This mechanism may buffer grunion populations somewhat from the effects of ocean warming, though more evaluation is necessary as these buffering effects may not be sustained at temperature extremes. By analyzing morphological traits, we can disentangle size and developmental patterns – providing a more nuanced understanding of larval dynamics. Taylor Lunningham Taylor Lunningham; Katelyn Sewcharran; Jules Johnson; Julia Sutton; Elizabeth Fairchild; Jessica Robinson; Stacy
192: A complete understanding of habitat use at specific life stages is required to develop management strategies for marine species. Although there is an increasing body of knowledge regarding juvenile shark habitat use in the southeastern US, quantitative assessment of community distribution in Georgia’s inshore waters remains limited. This includes information regarding presence, abundance, and habitat usage of several managed and protected species. To address knowledge gaps in these areas, stratified random longline sampling has been used to target immature sharks in the region. To compare regional dispersal and environmental predictors of species distributions, two major systems were selected for analyses: the Altamaha River estuaries and the exclusively tidally influenced waters of St. Catherines Sound. Four major habitats were identified for these systems, which include beachfront surf, beachfront tidal creeks, large inshore channels (>300-m width) and smaller inshore tidal tributaries (<300-m width). Salinity, temperature, depth, and tide stage were documented at all sampling sites during each set to allow for environmental predictor assessments in best fit models at the species level. All sharks were documented, measured (weight and length), sexed, and tagged prior to release. Preliminary results have identified habitat preferences vary at the species level. In some cases, such as Lemon Sharks (Negaprion brevirostris), species may have strong preference for conditions like those offered in the more shallow beachfront habitat, while others such as Sandbar Sharks (Carcharhinus plumbeus) have demonstrated preference for more inland deep channeled habitat. These observations highlight a need to understand the elasmobranch community as individual species. Kady Lyons
193: The batfish genus Dibranchus (Family Ogcocephalidae) includes 13 nominal species found in the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans. Two species occur in the Atlantic Ocean: Dibranchus atlanticus Peters, 1876 and Dibranchus tremendus Bradbury, 1999. Both species have broad ranges, inhabiting the eastern and western Atlantic Ocean. However, D. atlanticus from the eastern and western Atlantic have been noted to have anatomical differences, such as pectoral fin ray counts and body colouration. We compared specimens from the eastern and western Atlantic using morphological characters and new genetic data and evaluated the monophyly of the linage. Additionally, we examined the history of the Atlantic Ocean species of Dibranchus, and how the legacy of materials collected by NOAA and predecessor agencies and deposited in the Smithsonian Institution shape our understanding of these fish today. John Maerz
194: Maintaining buoyancy is essential for many aquatic species to regulate their vertical position in the water column. While most pelagic fishes have a swim bladder that can be adjusted to regulate buoyancy, sharks lack such a gas-filled organ. Most species are negatively buoyant and only rely on their large lipid-rich liver and active locomotion to generate lift. Carcharias taurus, a large shark distributed in coastal waters worldwide, is the only shark species known to gulp atmospheric air to hold in their stomachs. Although this behavior has been speculated to provide buoyancy control, the underlying drivers and implications of this behavior have not been investigated. Our study assessed the prevalence of air gulping in Carcharias taurus and the energetic and behavioral consequences of this behavior, especially regarding buoyancy control. To this end, eleven C. taurus individuals were fitted with highresolution acceleration data loggers in Delaware, USA, for periods of 1-4 days. Body posture and relative energetic expenditure were estimated from the acceleration data and used to assess buoyancy dynamics following the 63 gulping events recorded. Movement metrics such as tailbeat period and path tortuosity were derived and used to classify discrete behavioral phases to investigate the behavioral implications of gulping. Preliminary data revealed a steep increase in buoyancy following gulping events, and that C. taurus can retain gulped air in their stomach for at least 10 hours. These results support our hypothesis that air gulping by C. taurus is a unique strategy to perform buoyancy control among sharks. Benjamin Marsaly
195: Little is known about the range the Rio Grande Sucker (Pantosteus plebeius) in the upper San Francisco River Basin. In this part of the range, Rio Grande Sucker co-occurs with Desert Sucker (Pantosteus clarkii) with evidence of introgressive hybridization at some localities. We are interested in documenting the full extent of the range of Rio Grande Sucker and identifying zones of overlap. We will evaluate morphological and meristic characters that distinguish the two species in allopatry and where they hybridize. To address this, we conducted extensive exploratory sampling throughout the San Francisco headwaters and collected specimens and fin clips for genetic analysis. We then performed geometric morphometric analysis on Desert Sucker and Rio Grande Sucker specimens using tpsDigital for landmarking and the geomorph R package for General Procrustes Analysis, Principle Component Analysis, and Canonical Variate Analysis. We found that species differ significantly in shape but have similar allometric growth trajectories. We will continue this investigation using nextRAD sequencing to document hybridization status and clarify morphological uncertainties associated with introgressive hybridization. Understanding whether morphological characteristics distinguish these species, and how they change with hybridization status, will assist managers in field identification and management of Rio Grande Sucker. Katie Massue-Monat
196: Humans increasingly encounter rattlesnakes in urban settings as human-wildlife conflicts scale with expanding land development. Snakebites at these interfaces pose threats to human and domestic animal safety, and treating these incidents with antivenom is highly expensive. Rattlesnake populations are equally at risk in the form of human-induced mortality and indirect anthropogenic stressors. Snakes are foundational components of ecosystems that control prey populations and disease spread, so it is essential to understand the dynamics between snakes and humans at urban-natural interfaces to minimize conflict and preserve balanced ecosystem function. This study quantifies western rattlesnake (Crotalus oreganus) responses to urbanization and human disturbance across three axes: defensive behavior, body condition, and hydration. Rattlesnakes will be sampled across a continuous gradient of urban and natural habitats in central California using a combination of urban snake relocation services and targeted hiking surveys. Defensive behavior is measured by recording captured individuals with GoPro action cameras and determining overall rattling proportion times and number of strikes during a standardized behavioral trial. Health and hydration are determined using body condition indices and blood plasma osmolality measurements. Fieldwork is underway and will span the spring, summer, and fall of 2026. I hypothesize that habituation to humanrelated stimuli results in reduced defensive behavior of rattlesnakes in urban areas, and that body condition and hydration are likely supplemented by additional prey and water resources in urban habitats. Results will compare urban and natural rattlesnake trends and inform management strategies to promote coexistence with these ecologically critical reptiles. Sara J McClelland
197: Hammerhead sharks (Family Sphrynidae) are some of the most threatened sharks globally, and in 2014, they were added to CITES Appendix II in order to regulate their international trade. The bonnethead shark, Sphyrna tiburo, is found in the western North Atlantic from North Carolina to Belize and is currently classified as Endangered on the IUCN Red List. However, there is still limited information on habitat use and its ecological roles within its range. Previous studies reported that S. tiburo primarily consume Callinectes sp. crabs, often supplemented by other marine invertebrates, thus suggesting a specialized but potentially flexible feeding strategy. This study integrates DNA metabarcoding and stable isotope biogeochemistry, providing a dietary assessment and understanding of the bonnethead trophic ecology. Fin clips, muscle biopsies, and cloacal swabs were collected from bonnetheads from North Carolina, Florida, and Mississippi. Fecal DNA from cloacal swabs was amplified and sequenced using Next Generation Sequencing for prey detection and identification via bioinformatic comparisons with known species sequences. Fin clips and muscle biopsies were assessed for diet origin, composition, and trophic position by using δ13C and δ15N values. Results will provide insight into the bonnethead’s trophic position as well as its ecological role within various locations around the United States. Ultimately, this project will clarify how diet and resources can influence the distribution and persistence of Sphyrna tiburo populations. Caralyn McCollum
198: Land-use change threatens herpetofauna via habitat loss and direct mortality, and the Threatened or At-Risk status of over 90% of lizards in New Zealand reinforces our need to mitigate this threat. Mitigation translocation is used globally to moderate the adverse effects of land-use change on individuals; however, this practice is still relatively new in New Zealand. Endemic lizards are legally protected in New Zealand, and projects that will impact lizards require a permit granted by the Department of Conservation. We reviewed permit documents from the Department’s central database to assess trends in permit allocation, identify and quantify mitigation methods being used, and where possible, evaluate translocation outcomes. Permits issued for lizard mitigation translocations nearly tripled from 2013 to 2023, however these varied considerably by geographic region with over 70% of permits occurring in only 25% of New Zealand’s regions. Proposed release site preparation often included pest mammal control, native planting, and rock or log enhancements; however, enhancement design varied considerably across projects and reports of enhancement outcomes were often unclear. Novel practices come with inherent challenges and in New Zealand, a lack of standardization in translocation design and reporting has left knowledge gaps and an inability to compare mitigation translocations which must be rectified to develop best practice for New Zealand lizards. Standardization will facilitate nationwide comparisons of translocation outcomes and assessment of the efficacy of methods, which is crucial given the short timelines of many land-use change projects, highly uncertain outcomes, and the threat status of New Zealand lizards. Anna Millender
199: The reliable estimation of population vital rates is crucial for the effective management and conservation of elasmobranch populations. Traditionally, estimation of birth length, maturity metrics, and individual growth have been carried out separately. While this is convenient and often generates reasonable results, it is unable to address uncertainty in parameter estimates in a cohesive manner. Using Bayesian hierarchical models, the vitalBayes R package creates a more integrated workflow with which uncertainty is propagated downstream from birth to mortality. This package implements a four-stage workflow for estimating birth length, length- and age-atmaturity, individual growth curves, and natural mortality with survivorship simulation. The growth models used have been reparametrized by deriving the growth coefficient k from observable maturity milestones, thereby grounding growth models in directly observable biological priors rather than mathematical abstract. This allows for the propagation of uncertainty from upstream birth and maturity posterior distributions into downstream individual growth estimation. Four common methods for estimating age-specific mortality are included, and when appropriate have been redefined to be growth model agnostic rather than relying solely on the von Bertalanffy model. Additionally, mortality can be optionally scaled using a target average lifetime mortality rate. When estimating mortality, joint posterior sampling of the best fitting growth model is used, thereby preserving parameter correlation and continuing to propagate uncertainty from birth to mortality. Estimating vital rates in this fashion is particularly suitable for low or skewed sample sizes, uncertain age estimates, or skewed sex ratios for which traditional independent estimation may be problematic. Brian Moe
200: The wedgefishes (Rhinidae) are one of the most critically endangered groups of elasmobranchs.  This includes bowmouth guitarfish (Rhina anclyostoma), which are managed in aquaria globally.  A recent population viability analysis (PVA) determined that establishing ex-situ breeding populations and transferring R. anclyostoma from aquaria could support the in-situ population.  However, transporting this large species can be challenging, thus the PVA identified artificial insemination (AI) as a solution to enable global genetic exchange.  To establish a successful AI program, it is critical to first generate baseline reproductive data, including characterizing reproductive seasonality and developing protocols for semen collection, handling, and cryopreservation.  This study presents initial validations for plasma testosterone analysis in male R. anclyostoma after double ether extraction.  Serial dilutions of pooled extracted plasma yielded a curve parallel to serially diluted synthetic testosterone standard.  Recovery of known amounts of synthetic testosterone added to a pool of extracted serum was 105%.  Analysis of testosterone concentrations collected from one male over two years suggests seasonal variation under managed care.  Analysis of multiple males is required to confirm seasonality and determine when spermatogenesis occurs.  This study also presents preliminary analysis of semen samples from four males.  Ultrasonography was used to identify fluid within the alkaline gland and in the ductus deferens, and semen samples were collected to assess sperm motility before and after cryopreservation.  Semen quality varied between males, likely influenced by seasonal variation, husbandry, collection, and cryopreservation methods.  Future work will focus on comprehensive characterization of semen characteristics and optimization of cryopreservation techniques. Joshua K. Moyer
201: Subgenus Kenoza contains two species well differentiated by morphology and nuclear DNA: Esox americanus (subspecies E. a. americanus and E. a. vermiculatus) and E. niger. Early molecular studies suggested that E. niger carries mitochondrial DNA from E. a. americanus along the Atlantic slope while retaining distinct nuclear ancestry. Here, we expand geographic sampling and use genomic and mitochondrial data to investigate relationships between E. niger and E. americanus across their distributions. Our results reveal four distinct genomic lineages within E. americanus that likely warrant taxonomic revision, and demonstrate pervasive, geographically structured mitochondrial introgression from E. americanus into E. niger, extending beyond Atlantic Coastal Plain populations. Zoë Müller
202: Amphibian oviposition site selection is expected to reflect hierarchical ecological filtering processes, with broad-scale patch size acting as a coarse filter and finer-scale patch-quality variables, such as predation risk and leaf litter identity, shaping recruitment. However, whether these ecological filters extend beyond oviposition decisions to influence recruitment across life stages is not well established. Invasive plants such as Chinese tallow (Triadica sebifera) may complicate this process by introducing novel inputs that alter habitat quality and larval performance. We evaluated how wetland size, predator presence, and leaf litter identity influenced tadpole recruitment in a factorial mesocosm experiment including Chinese tallow, native litter types, and litter-free controls. Tadpole recruitment was quantified using standardized dipnet surveys conducted multiple times across the oviposition period. Predator presence reduced tadpole occurrence, whereas smaller mesocosms and loblolly pine litter increased occurrence. Densities were significantly higher in smaller mesocosms and declined from mid-season to end-season. Main effects of predator presence and leaf litter identity did not significantly affect density where tadpoles were present, although density varied among treatment combinations. No tadpoles were detected in large predator-present mesocosms containing Chinese tallow. These results suggest that patch size and patch-quality variables influenced recruitment at different stages, with predation risk affecting tadpole occurrence and patch size shaping density after recruitment. Chinese tallow may further constrain recruitment under high-risk conditions. Our results indicate that amphibian recruitment reflects hierarchical filtering across life stages and highlight the importance of integrating wetland size, predation risk, and detrital inputs in evaluating outcomes in wetlandbreeding amphibians. Marion Mundy
203: Amphibian population sizes are sensitive to a variety of factors, including invasive species. Melia azedarach, the chinaberry tree, is a common, invasive, ornamental plant with insecticidal properties. Insects are the primary prey of adult anurans. Considering the insecticidal properties, the presence of invasive chinaberry may have a negative effect on foraging success of anurans due to a lack of prey availability. Adult gulf coast toads (Incilius nebulifer) were placed in enclosures permeable to insects with different chinaberry treatments, which may repel or kill insects. Changes in toad mass over time were measured as a proxy for insect availability. The control toads’ mass was greater than toads exposed to Chinaberry material, but the effect was countered by survival. These results are similar to previous work with other anuran species and reiterate the complex roles that invasive species can play in the ecological communities of amphibians within their native ranges. Ryan Munnelly
204: Body condition indices (BCIs) are widely used in ecological studies across taxa as non-destructive proxies for internal energy reserves such as fat and proteins, yet biological processes, such as reproduction, may inflate mass-based indices. Amphibians partially exhibit a suite of traits that can lead to this inflation, such as strong seasonal reproduction, large variation in clutch size and egg load between populations, large increases in mass during gravidity, and opportunistic appearances of females at breeding sites. With túngara frogs (Engystomops (=Physalaemus) pustulosus), we quantified how oviposition effected female body mass and condition and compared male and female body condition after accounting for reproductive investment. Females lost approximately 27% of their body mass following oviposition in both a field population and a laboratory colony. The proportional mass loss scaled predictably with pre-oviposition mass, but not with body length. Using this shared relationship, we estimated post oviposition mass of females in a long-term dataset from Gamboa, Panama, where all females were sampled when gravid but not after oviposition. Male condition was consistent across population, despite differences in snoutto-vent length and environmental conditions, suggesting energetic constraints due to reproduction. These results demonstrate that BCIs derived from gravid females can systematically overestimate somatic conditions, and that the reproductive state of an organism must be accounted for when interpreting sex differences or monitoring population health. Michael Musal
205: Species propagation or translocations for reintroduction or augmentation (PTRA) can increase species survival, population size, and fitness. However, without proper implementation and monitoring, PTRA can also cause outbreeding or inbreeding depression and loss of genetic variation. The Duskytail Darter (Etheostoma percnurum) is a federally endangered fish, threatened by habitat degradation that has contributed to the reduction of its range to just 9 river miles of Copper Creek (Clinch River, VA). Since 2017, Copper Creek has been used as a source site for nest collections to propagate juveniles in captivity that are translocated 62 river miles upstream of the source site to establish a new population of E. percnurum in the mainstem Clinch River and to augment the Copper Creek population. Using a 20-locus microsatellite dataset from 2017-2019 and one generated from samples taken in 2025-2026, we will perform a temporal comparison of E. percnurum from Copper Creek to evaluate the effects of PTRA efforts on genetic diversity of the natural population. Similar analyses will compare the natural population to captive-reared individuals used for introductions to assess the quality and spectrum of genetic diversity between the two groups. For both comparisons, microsatellite genotypes will be used to identify temporal changes in the mean number of alleles, observed and expected heterozygosity, inbreeding coefficients, and effective population sizes. Conclusions will be used to create an adaptive management framework for improvement to propagation and recovery efforts, ensuring the best opportunity for species recovery. Erin Muths
206: New World snakes in the Tribe Dipsadini have evolved dietary specializations for feeding on snails, with morphology and feeding behaviors similar to those observed in Old World snail-eating snakes (Family Pareidae). The Pareidae are a diverse group of gastropod specialists native to Southeast Asia with twice as many teeth on the right mandible compared to the left as an adaptation for efficiently extracting right-coiled snails from their shells. The tribe Dipsadini is also diverse, containing 142 species in the genera Dipsas, Geophis, Plesiodipsas, Sibon, and Tropidodipsas. The single study investigating dental asymmetry in the Dipsadini found support for slight mandibular asymmetry in three species of the genus Dipsas, suggesting that the asymmetry observed in the Pareidae may also have evolved in the Dipsadini. Our project includes species from all five genera of Dipsadini, as well as the closely related outgroup genus Ninia, to robustly test whether asymmetrical mandibular dentition is observed broadly across the significantly younger New World group of snail-eating snakes. To evaluate this potential trend, we generated micro-CT scan data from museum specimens and compared left and right mandibular tooth counts to determine if asymmetry was present. Preliminary results provide evidence of weak asymmetry broadly across the group. This project leverages a “natural experiment” and provides insights into the convergent evolution of gastropod specialization and adaptations for consuming asymmetric prey in two independent lineages of snail-eating snakes. Edward A. Myers
207: Visual depictions of Squalus acanthias musculoskeletal anatomy have remained largely unchanged over the past century, with the exception of the adductor mandibulae complex (AMC). Although S. acanthias is a model species for sharks in comparative anatomy instruction, the AMC’s structure, subdivisions, and insertions are inconsistently documented in scientific texts and visualizations. Our research identifies previously undescribed muscle–tendon architecture within thequadratomandibularis divisions of S. acanthias, indicating more structural and functional variation than previously recorded. In contrast, dissections of Mustelus canis—often mistaken for S. acanthias despite distinct taxonomic and feeding differences—show a less subdivided AMC that more closely resembles comparative anatomy texts. Mechanically, the AMC divisions in S. acanthias produce a broad range of moment arms prioritizing both force amplification and velocity amplification. These characteristics may have evolved with the generalist feeding style of S. acanthias, as obligate suction feeders typically exhibit jaw mechanics associated with rapid jaw closure, while those of bite feeders suggest more reliance on constant force transfer to the prey. Overall, these results highlight some of the variation in AMC structure among sharks. It also suggests that a deeper dive into the realm of jaw muscle architecture and diversity may shed light on the evolutionary and functional significance of their complex designs, for even an old dogfish can still teach us new tricks. Laurel Nave-Powers
208: The Bay Anchovy (Engraulidae: Anchoa mitchilli) and Broad-striped Anchovy (Engraulidae: A. hepsetus) are two abundant species found along the northern Gulf Coast. Anchovies tend to reach their greatest densities in shallow, estuarine habitats such as the Lake Pontchartrain Basin in southeastern Louisiana. Our monitoring team has been investigating spatial and temporal changes in anchovy populations in Lake Maurepas, at the western end of the Lake Pontchartrain Basin, over the last two years using standard trawling methods. For this project, we aim to incorporate environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling into our monitoring to determine if there is a correlation between eDNA read number and anchovy biomass and abundance in Lake Maurepas. Environmental DNA data is being collected simultaneously with anchovy trawling. If eDNA read numbers strongly correlate with biomass and abundance, then eDNA can be used as a fast, non-invasive way to estimate population size. This study will also examine whether this correlation varies seasonally and whether these relationships hold across different anchovy densities throughout the lake. Generally, this study will provide valuable insights into the utility of eDNA data to monitor fish abundance and biomass. Alisa L.
