209: Although the blunt-nosed leopard lizard (Gambelia sila) has been federally endangered since 1967, no standardized range-wide surveys have been conducted in the past few decades, leading to questions about the population status and relative abundance of many historic populations. We set out to survey 24 known historic sites using a combination of traditional (e.g., repeat-visit) and emerging (e.g., time-to-detection) visual encounter survey methods. Our goals were to: 1) record current G. sila status at these historically occupied sites, 2) determine what site characteristics (e.g., ground biomass, shrub presence, human modification, soil clay content) were predictors of occupancy versus extirpation of G. sila, and 3) compare repeat-visits and time-to-detection methods to inform future survey efforts for this species. G. sila were detected at 12 out of 24 historic sites (naive occupancy of 50%). In our traditional models, clay content and percent shrub cover were the two biggest predictors of occupancy. We found that G. sila have high detectability when present on a landscape and detected them within the first 60 minutes of survey in 89% of surveys. Our results suggest that single-visit wandering transects may serve as a cost-effective way to track population trends in years when funding and man-power is limited. Lotanna Micah Nneji
210: Seasonal aggregations of leopard sharks (Triakis semifasciata) along La Jolla Shores Beach (San Diego Count, California, USA) provided a unique opportunity to quantify chafing behavior in a large elasmobranch aggregation. Chafing (rolling laterally to rub the body against the substrate or another organism) is widely documented in fishes but typically reported from solitary individuals or small groups. Here, we used aerial drone footage of aggregations exceeding 100 sharks to quantify the frequency, kinematics, and spatial distribution of chafing/rolling events, visible as bright flashes of the sharks’ white ventral surfaces. Three video sequences were analyzed using the multi-animal tracking program TRex, enabling the tracking of individuals within these groups. Across clips, we documented 223 chafing events. Tracking data allowed us to determine whether individuals rolled multiple times and to quantify roll direction, magnitude, speed, and position within aggregation kernel utilization distributions (KUDs). Roll direction (left vs. right) was evenly distributed, but rotation magnitudes varied. Individuals performing repeated rolls within short intervals tended to repeat direction and magnitude, consistent with attempts to dislodge localized irritants. Roll events were randomly dispersed and slightly more frequent in lowerdensity regions of the aggregation. Concurrent ectoparasite surveys of 24 captured sharks revealed that all individuals harbored copepod ectoparasites (e.g., Pandarus spp., Achtheinus spp.), and CO1 sequencing is underway to confirm identifications. The universal presence and diverse distribution of ectoparasites on sharks’ bodies support chafing as an ectoparasite-removal strategy. This study demonstrates the utility of drone-based tracking for quantifying rare behaviors within large shark aggregations. Ashleigh Novak
211: The Whitetail Shiner (Cyprinella galactura) is a leucisid fish known to host at least two species of Dactylogyrus gill flukes, Dactylogyrus beckeri and D. nuntius. In Alabama, its reproductive season occurs from May to August, coinciding with rising water temperatures. During the spawning period, the host is assumed to divert energy expenditure for gonadal development, with the immune system being compromised. This immune suppression offers opportunities for Dactylogyrus gill flukes attached to the gill filaments, weakening the host. Our study utilized previously collected samples of Whitetail Shiners from April to August in 2013 and 2014, collected from the Flint River in Madison County, Alabama. SL and mass of each preserved specimen were recorded. Gonadal dissection was performed to determine the GSI (Gonadosomatic index) and the sex of the fish. Gill arches were excised and then examined to determine parasite count. This count was used to calculate mean abundance, prevalence, intensity and frequency of infection. Data show parallel trends between GSI and parasite infection both years. Parasite loads increased gradually as GSI rose from April to peak abundance from May to July. By the end of the breeding season in August both parasite abundance and GSI had declined. Parasite counts were higher in April 2014 than in April 2013, likely due to higher water temperatures. Data show that larger hosts tended to have higher parasite loads, particularly males. As commonly observed in other fish species, some hosts had no parasites, while others had high parasite loads. Gabriel Ortiz
212: Coastal habitats support essential ecological functions for many species, including feeding, movement, and reproduction, yet these environments shift through dynamic geomorphological processes driven largely by wave action. Diamondback terrapins depend on these coastal systems for nesting, making them sensitive to shoreline stabilization that disrupts natural sediment erosion and movement. We investigated how terrapin nesting habitat composition varies between natural coastlines and man-made, hardened shorelines to understand how coastal processes influence nest-site selection and predation risk. We predicted that stabilized shorelines would experience long-term increases in vegetation and corresponding shifts in nesting habitat use, whereas natural coastlines would maintain similar habitat proportions over time despite spatial reorganization. We evaluated terrapin nesting ecology across three Chesapeake Bay sites: Janes Island, a natural, highly dynamic shoreline; Poplar Island, a restored and stabilized site with long-term increases in vegetation; and Patuxent River natural sites with extensive microhabitat data. Terrapins typically prefer open or edge habitats with reduced vegetation, yet the loss of open sandy areas on protected shorelines has led to increased nesting in vegetated habitats that also experience higher predation. Using multinomial logistic regression, we found no temporal change in habitat use at natural sites, while on Poplar Island nesting in vegetation increased and nesting in edge habitat decreased. Generalized linear models revealed a significant rise in predation probability over 23 years on Poplar Island, with shaded, vegetated habitats exhibiting the highest risk. These results highlight how shoreline stabilization can reduce habitat suitability and threaten longterm terrapin persistence. Esma Pajt
213: Squamate hemipenes are highly morphologically diverse, and yet we still know little about why they are so variable compared to other anatomical structures. We know even less about the evolution of the homologous hemiclitores and their potential reproductive functionality in squamates. Recent work in snakes has described a high amount of morphological variation in hemipenes between and within species. Lizards are closely related to snakes and are also known to have elaborate genitalia, yet have not been studied in such depth, especially the anatomy of females. Here, we quantify the 3D shape variation of the hemipenes and hemiclitores of the Argentine Giant Tegu (Salvator merianae), a large species of teiid lizard known to have morphologically complex genitalia. Our sample includes at least 40 adult tegus from an invasive population in the Everglades National Park in FL. We prepared hemipenes in their inflated, functional states using traditional methods and created digital, 3D models of those using laser scanning. We analyzed 3D shape variation, patterns of asymmetry, and allometry in these structures using 3D geometric morphometrics and statistical analyses and ordinations in R. We compare the morphology of the hemipenes and hemiclitores of tegus to those of snakes and discuss the evolutionary implications for squamates more broadly. Anjana Parandhaman Anjana Parandhaman; Regina Spranger; Anthony Clemento; Chad Mitcham; Christine Fox; John Carlos Garza; Eric
214: Research has shown that morphological similarities among shark species are common, making them hard to distinguish and confounding conservation efforts. Misidentification is a major obstacle to conservation, especially in light of new data showing that sharks are shifting ranges in responses to global warming. Identification of elasmobranch species is difficult due to the strong similarities that exist between closely-related species, and research has shown that cryptic species, which are physically identical to more common species but can only be identified using genetics, occur often. Here, we used genetic techniques to identify shark species from dried jaws in collaboration with other investigators as part of the Minorities in Shark Science’s Integrated Coordinated Open Network Inclusive Conservation (ICONIC) Oceans project. For this, we extracted and sequenced DNA from the jaws of 32 different individual sharks to amplify the ND2 and D-loop regions of the mitochondrial genome, and compared these to reference sequences downloaded from Genbank. We found that many species belonged to the requiem shark genus Carcharhinus, which are relatively common but have many similar morphological traits that make them difficult to identify, even when a whole specimen is available for study. In many cases, such as in illegally-imported cargos of shark meat or fins, only part of an animal is present, making misidentification more likely. This work highlights the importance of genetic research in species identification and how it can be implemented to better improve conservation efforts worldwide. Kane Petty
215: The Node Height test is a simple way to use phylogenetic independent contrasts (Felsenstein 1985) to estimate change in the rate of trait evolution. Increasing, decreasing, or constant patterns of trait evolution can be consistent with Brownian Motion, Late Burst, and Early Burst models. Previous research used this approach with limited taxonomic sampling (McCann and Hagey 2024). We were curious how different taxonomic sampling may affect the Node Height test results. Using a simulation approach, we generated phylogenetic trees, with and without extinction (Birth-Death Model and Pure-Birth). We then varied how traits evolved on those phylogenies using Brownian Motion, Early Burst, and Late Burst modeling, followed by recreating different levels of missing taxa (0%, 30%, 50%, 70%, and 90%) with randomly dropped tips. We fit our simulated data to the Node Height test to see how consistent our results were. Ellie Phelps Ellie Phelps; Adam Smith; Hannah Thompson; Sarah Christensen; Kaylee Winegarner; Caralyn McCollum; Avery Chapple; Renee Garza; Maddox Moran; Bilal Mustafa; Emily Devine; Natalie Hall; Danielle Gonzales; Daniel
216: Hemidactylus turcicus is an invasive gekkonid species in North America, which is originally from the Mediterranean region, that has the most expansive range of any non-native, building-dwelling gecko in the United States. The factors that have facilitated this species spread in its invasive range are poorly known. Here, we aim to understand the influence of survey- and site-specific factors in H. turcicus colonization of an urban campus in central Texas. Once per month for an entire year, we surveyed 44 buildings on campus during which we counted the number of geckos and recorded environmental variables that impact gecko activity, such as air temperature and wind speed. We also recorded variables that could impact the occupancy of geckos, including number of lights and building age. Using gecko counts, we built an abundance index generated with N-mixture models to determine which factors impact gecko population size. We used presence-absence data to build single-season occupancy models to estimate occupancy and detection probability. Thus far, 1167 geckos have been observed, with an average of 5 geckos per building, with the most in March and least in January. Preliminary model results indicate that most geckos have been found on the west and south side of buildings, and temperature had the most impact on the detection of a gecko. We expect to identify the factors that influence colonization in H. turcicus, which will show why they occupy certain spaces and not others, information that can leveraged to better understand invasive species dynamics in urban environments. Maria Pierce Maria Pierce; Emily Peele; Gregg Poulakis; Andrew Wooley; Lukas Heath; Dylan Yakich; Tonya Wiley; Kara
217: Coral reefs sustain a disproportionate share of global marine biodiversity, yet they are increasingly threatened by disturbances that reduce coral cover and erode ecosystem resilience. As reefs degrade, the loss of visual, chemical, and acoustic signals disrupts essential ecological processes. Ambient acoustic cues are especially important for settlement of marine fishes in a suitable habitat. When natural soundscapes are degraded, corals and juvenile fishes show low settlement rates, and can trigger trophic cascades that ultimately undermine reef condition, coastal protection, and food security. The loud feeding sounds made by parrotfish as they graze on the hard reef substrate stand out as one defining features of the reef soundscape, and reflects their role as dominant herbivores and bioeroders. However, it remains unresolved whether these sounds may influence the behavior of other fish residents on the reef. To address this gap, I am integrating natural history observations with manipulative acoustic playback experiments to examine how parrotfish feeding sounds influence the behavior, abundance, and diversity patterns of coral reef fishes. Preliminary observations show increased aggregation among herbivorous species in high algae, low coral habitats, where parrotfish form groups more frequently and in more diverse species assemblages. This behavioral observation is consistent with the hypothesis that fish use sound cues in group formation, and provides the prediction that reef fish will respond to parrotfish feeding sound playbacks. Experimental presentations of parrotfish feeding sounds in the reef community will provide a direct test of how these acoustic cues may influence fish behaviors and community-level patterns. Jeffrey D Plumlee
218: Sharks are a common host for teleost symbionts given their migratory behavior, feeding opportunities they create, and likeliness to deter other predators. In Southeast Florida, teleost symbionts can generally be classified into families Echeneidae, Rachycentridae, and Carangidae (further classified as Decapterus versus nonDecapterus spp.). To better understand these interactions, this study investigates and compares interactions between lemon sharks (Negaprion brevirostris), nurse sharks (Ginglymostoma cirratum), and teleosts using long-term observational video data (n=2,360 clips) generated by Coral City Camera, a publicly accessible livestream of a reefscape near PortMiami. On average, lemon shark symbiont aggregations were more diverse and abundant than nurse shark symbiont aggregations. Seasonal differences were statistically significant for all measured variables except lemon shark symbiont family diversity. Existing literature suggests these differences may be the result of life history differences between host species, namely movement and migration patterns and feeding strategies. Biological associations are particularly vulnerable to the effects of abiotic change, generating uncertainty regarding how these relationships will fare in increasingly unstable and human-altered habitats. Mason Polencheck
219: Accurate population density estimates are critical for evaluating conservation efforts for at-risk species such as the Mojave Desert tortoise (Gopherus agassizii). Mark-recapture methods are widely used in wildlife monitoring; however, they can yield biased estimates when detection rates are low, model assumptions are violated, or juveniles are excluded. From 2015 to 2025, we conducted mark-recapture surveys across ten 1-km² plots in the Ivanpah Valley, generating spatial encounter data for uniquely identified individuals. We developed an enhanced spatially explicit capture-recapture (SECR) model that incorporates juveniles and accounts for individual variation in detection and movement within a Bayesian framework. Specifically, detection and movement processes were modeled to vary among individuals and sites, allowing for differences in detectability and space use. Additionally, a spatial integration approach was used to address edge effects and uncertainty in individual locations, which enabled robust estimation of population abundance. As a result, the model demonstrates improved computational efficiency and convergence relative to previous implementations, while producing density estimates with reduced uncertainty. Notably, including juveniles produced variable effects on density estimates, with some sites showing substantial increases. Collectively, these results highlight the importance of incorporating all life stages to improve biological realism and avoid underestimation. This framework advances SECR methodology and supports more reliable longterm monitoring of Mojave Desert tortoise populations. Bree Putman
220: Coral reefs function within mosaics of interconnected habitats, where mobile consumers create critical trophic linkages across ecosystem boundaries. White grunt (Haemulon plumierii), an important species for local fisheries in Florida and the Caribbean, exemplifies this connectivity by sheltering on patch reefs during daytime and foraging nocturnally in adjacent seagrass beds. We used DNA metabarcoding to characterize diet composition of white grunt across nine patch reefs varying in seagrass continuity and connectivity in the Upper Florida Keys. Stomach contents from 90 white grunt (10 per reef) were analyzed using COI gene metabarcoding (Leray primers) targeting a 313 bp fragment. After quality filtering and host DNA removal, we retained 331 Exact Sequence Variants (ESVs) from 9.3 million reads. Diet analysis revealed remarkable prey diversity spanning 15 phyla, 25 classes, 43 orders, and 70 families. Malacostraca (crustaceans, 26.8% Relative Read Abundance) and Polychaeta (bristle worms, 23.3%) dominated prey composition, followed by Trematoda (10.8%), Actinopteri (7.8%), and Ophiuroidea (7.8%). Despite significant variation in fish size among reefs (Kruskal-Wallis H=26.09, p=0.001), diet richness and Shannon diversity did not differ significantly among reef patches (H=7.66, p=0.47 and H=10.11, p=0.26), suggesting consistent prey availability across the seascape. Future analyses will integrate seascape variables (seagrass fragmentation, edge habitat, reef connectivity) to evaluate how habitat configuration influences cross-habitat energy flow. These findings provide baseline data on reef-seagrass trophic linkages, informing multi-habitat management strategies for interconnected coastal seascapes. Diego Quirola
221: While historically viewed as solitary, recent research suggests that individuals within many reptile species exhibit repeatable behavioral differences (personalities) and seasonal non-random social aggregations. Such findings challenge dichotomous classifications of species as solitary or social and highlight the need to consider how individual variation structures sociality. While Crotalus oreganus exhibits consistent intraspecific differences in behavior, their effect on social behavior has yet to be examined, limiting our understanding of the structure and importance of sociality for wild populations. Here, I implement Project RattleCam (PRC), a non-invasive livestreaming collaboration that provides the unique opportunity to study wild rattlesnakes across multiple years. Building on this innovative approach, my research will examine how intraspecific variation influences the activity, social structure, and phenology of C. oreganus. Using archived PRC footage, I will identify individuals based on their unique, innate markings and quantify their duration of presence and interactions. To explore whether C. oreganus exhibits non-random aggregations, I will conduct social network analyses. I anticipate that individual snakes will exhibit unique, repeatable social behavior. Additionally, sex, pregnancy, and male dominance are expected to influence activity, gregariousness, and site fidelity. By examining the association between individual variation and social structure, this study will provide novel insight into the drivers of aggregation in ectotherms historically considered non-social. Paula Dominguez Rein-Loring Paula Dominguez Rein Loring; J. Marcus Drymon; Mark Fisher; Fernando Martinez-Andrade; William Driggers;
222: Complex evolutionary processes can result in the expression of adaptive and non-adaptive traits. As such, it is necessary to address the roles that environment and ancestry play in trait evolution when testing adaptive hypotheses. Recently, we found an undescribed morphological trait on the eyelids of Iguanian lizards; namely, palpebral combs or "eyelashes". Palpebral combs are a modification of the outermost palpebral scales on the eyelids, creating a protective fringe at the interface of the eyelid and the eye. Palpebral comb presence and morphology appear to be highly correlated with environment; The trait is most apparent among desert species and reduced within arboreal species, while other ecologies appear to correlate with specific palpebral comb morphs — leading us to an adaptive hypothesis. However, we found that the presence of this trait is widespread within Iguania but relatively absent in all other squamates, suggesting that trait expression is the result of either parallel adaptation or the retention of an ancestral trait. However, no research has formally addressed this topic and its evolutionary significance remains unknown. To test these hypotheses, we will integrate μCT-based 3D geometric morphometrics, ecological data, and phylogenetic comparative methods (PCM) to uncover the influences of evolutionary history (phylogeny) and ecological variables (habitat, diet, locomotion) in the expression and variation of palpebral comb morphology. Relative association of palpebral comb morphology with phylogenetic and ecological variables may disseminate whether this trait is convergent or ancestral within Iguania. Patrick Rex
223: As human industrialization advanced, plastic became an essential resource sustaining modern society. However, over time it began disintegrating into microplastics and sequestering in aquatic ecosystems. Amphibians, particularly anurans, act as bioindicator species as they react rapidly to changes, indicating the health of the overall ecosystem. The American toad (Anaxyrus americanus) is a common species found in freshwater ponds throughout the eastern United States, offering insights into how native amphibians respond to this pervasive stressor. While many studies investigate the effects of microplastics on frogs, few do so in ecologically relevant experimental conditions. In this study we use mesocosms to simulate naturally occurring ecological conditions during larval development either with or without polypropylene microplastics. To test the effects of microplastics, 45 tadpoles were placed into each of ten mesocosms; five serving as controls and five treated with a defined concentration of microplastics. The plastics are interspersed with the algal resources on which the tadpoles forage, allowing us to assess the effects of microplastics when ingested during natural foraging behaviors. By assessing gut and mouth morphology throughout larval development and through metamorphosis, we anticipate seeing that microplastics alter morphological endpoints at multiple life stages. Similarly with behavior, assessing locomotion and foraging tests judgement and decision between individuals in both control and treatment groups. With these results, we aim to provide management guidelines to promote safer ecosystems for future amphibian generations. Radmon Rice
224: As the Earth continues to experience unprecedented ecological shifts, many studies have been able to conclude that climate change can alter phenotypic traits across species. One impacted trait is fecundity which, though studied in a number of plethodontid species, has not been examined long-term across decades for climate change’s potential influence. Our objective is to analyze the fecundity of Plethodon jordani, a species of salamander endemic to high-elevation forests across Tennessee and North Carolina, from 1920-2020. Using museum and live specimens from ten decades in June, July and August, we compared the fecundity and size of P. jordani across season and decade to analyze for differences. We found fecundity varied across decades and months in P. jordani specimens with fecundity decreasing across decades and shifting later in the summer. As climate change continues to accelerate studies examining long-term changes in traits like fecundity, it is imperative to examine potential population-level changes in species. Amber Ringle Amber Ringle; Katherine Polatcheck; Emily Yeager; Colin Foord; Christian Pankow; Julia Saltzman; Catherine
225: Sharks are important hosts for fish in the family Echeneidae, including both sharksuckers (Echeneis naucrates) and remoras (Remora remora). Different attachment sites on a host have advantages and disadvantages, including effects on transportation and hydrodynamic drag, feeding opportunities, and protection from predators. This project aims to determine if there is significant variation in preferred attachment sites for Echeneidae across nurse sharks (Ginglymostoma cirratum), lemon sharks (Negaprion brevirostris), and bull (Carcharhinus leucas) and blacktip sharks (C. limbatus), aggregated as “other carcharhinids”. To assess attachment location variation of Echeneidae among sharks in Biscayne Bay, Florida, this study used 2,360 live feed footage clips collected between 2022 and 2025 from the Coral City Camera Project by Coral Morphologic. Video coding documented the date/time of the video, shark species, and the number and location of Echeneidae present. Results showed lemon sharks had a significantly greater average number of Echeneidae compared to nurse sharks and other carcharhinids. Seasonal variation in symbiont abundance between wet and dry seasons was also observed. There were statistically significant patterns in dominant attachment location across the compared groups. 226: When captured in recreational, commercial, and scientific fisheries, sharks experience physiological stress induced through vigorous movements like burst swimming, which are often exhibited when resisting capture. Concentrations of lactate, a byproduct of exhaustive exercise, have been documented to rise in shark blood based on time on the line, intensity of fight, and water temperature, reflecting physiological stress levels. When multiple blood samples are taken from the same individual at various time intervals post-capture, we can measure changes in lactate over time to gain a better understanding of how sharks respond to and recover from capture-induced physiological stress. Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) is another indicator of stress in teleost fishes and other vertebrates, but change in blood ACTH concentration has only been measured in two shark species. In this study, we attempt to quantify recovery from capture in nurse sharks (Ginglymostoma cirratum), a relatively stress-tolerant species, by measuring the change in both lactate and ACTH from blood samples collected over longer time periods than previous studies have explored, up to several hours apart. Additionally, we use accelerometers to gain insight into how activity during recovery affects resulting changes in lactate and ACTH values. Erica Ro
227: Sufficient reproductive output is essential for amphibian population viability. Therefore, identifying the environmental factors that influence reproductive output is crucial for addressing amphibian declines. The Chiricahua Leopard Frog (Lithobates chiricahuensis; hereafter CLF) is a federally threatened species native to the American Southwest that has experienced population declines throughout its range. Localized bullfrog eradication, the creation of permanent ponds, and translocation efforts have facilitated CLF reestablishment in some parts of southeast Arizona, but reproductive output varies markedly between breeding sites and across rain years. We are investigating how physical habitat structure, water quality, and other characteristics of CLF breeding sites best explain inter-site variation in CLF reproductive output. This study is part of the University of Arizona’s FROG Project which is helping to recover and monitor CLF and their habitat in southeast Arizona. Here we present our sampling design and preliminary data from CLF breeding sites during 2026. Through this work, we aim to increase our understanding of CLF reproductive ecology and inform ongoing efforts to create and restore anuran breeding habitat in the American Southwest. Alison Robertson Alison Robertson; Elizabeth Murphy; John Roman; Sarah Dietrick; Katherine Yang; Andrew Selwood; Ross Boucek; Michael Parsons; Theresa Cody; Dean Grubbs; Ashley Dawdy; Adam Brame; Tonya Wiley; Gregg
228: Illegal take is one of the major threats to sea turtles worldwide. In Bocas del Toro, Panama, sea turtles were exploited for generations to supply local, national, and international markets. However, following the protection of these species and increased conservation efforts in Bocas del Toro, the region became one of the most important sea turtle rookeries in the Caribbean Basin. Nevertheless, illegal take of sea turtles in the region has not been assessed in the past twenty years. This study aims to elucidate the illegal take of sea turtles on seven nesting beaches in Bocas del Toro using data collected between 2003-2025. We applied the IPOACHED framework to predict which species classified as in-demand, passive, obtainable, all-purpose, conflict-prone, hide-able, extractable, and disposable are more susceptible to being taken and therefore more vulnerable. Preliminary results show that at least 1,190 nests and 194 sea turtles have been illegally taken in Bocas del Toro between 2003-2025. These estimates do not include illegal market data. When applying the framework, we found that the hawksbill, green, and leatherback turtles were perceived as in-demand, passive, obtainable, all-purpose, hide-able, extractable, and disposable, aligning with most of the key vulnerability factors. However, the IPOACHED categories vary by species and location. Our findings highlight the importance of integrating empirical data with theoretical frameworks to identify current and emerging threats to sea turtle populations. This approach provides a replicable model for understanding how the illegal take operates and underscores conservation gaps that must be addressed for effective conservation management. Alex Romer Alexander Romer; Melissa Miller; Sergio Balaguera-Reina; Michael Kirkland; Edward Metzger III; LeRoy
229: Shark depredation has led to growing frustration among recreational anglers, prompting negative responses, including the targeting and harvesting of sharks regardless of protected status. Although qualitative evidence suggests depredation is increasing in the southeastern United States, with Florida emerging as a hotspot, quantitative data identifying the primary shark species involved remain limited. This study aimed to characterize shark abundance and seasonality in the highly recreationally fished waters of Palm Beach County, Florida using a combination of snorkel surveys, baited remote underwater video (BRUV) surveys, and fishing surveys. Snorkel results in the upper water column identified 5 species, with bull sharks (Carcharhinus leucas) as the most abundant species followed by sandbar sharks (Carcharhinus plumbeus). A maximum number (MaxN) of 15 bull sharks were sighted in a single snorkel dive. Additionally, snorkel results indicate a strong seasonality of C. leucas with peak abundances during the winter months in January and March, while C. plumbeus showed strong seasonality with peak abundances in May. BRUV surveys identified 7 species and fishing surveys identified 6 species. Both BRUV and fishing surveys were conducted on the seafloor, and both indicated nurse sharks (Ginglymostoma cirratum) as the most abundant species followed by C. leucas and lemon sharks (Negaprion brevirostris). These findings highlight the value of integrating complementary survey methods to develop a comprehensive understanding of shark community assemblages. This work provides foundational abundance and seasonality data for improving our understanding of shark depredation dynamics and informing strategies to mitigate this human-wildlife conflict. Jessica Schulte
230: Invasive Red lionfish (Pterois volitans) are responsible for dramatic declines in native fish abundance and biodiversity. Their success is attributed to their lack of predators in their invasive range in the tropical and subtropical Western Atlantic Ocean. Despite the apparent lack of large predators of lionfish, parasites are often overlooked as predators that could limit the success of invasive species. Low parasitic loads can make for a more biologically fit individual, allowing for higher invasion success. For this reason, it is hypothesized that lionfish carry a lower parasitic load in their invasive range. This project aims to assess the parasite abundance in lionfish collected from along the entire reef slope (0-300 m) in Curaçao in 2019 and 2022. We conducted dissections examining the skin, body cavity, buccal cavity, fins, gonad, liver, spleen, eye, heart, intestine, fillet, and gills under a dissection microscope to carefully check for parasites. We will perform descriptive analyses to summarize parasite presence and quantity by species and body site where they were found. It is most likely that there is a low abundance of parasites within these lionfish, suggesting that the lack of parasites could play a major role in the success of invasive populations. Understanding the role that predation plays in invasive species can help us develop strategies to control their spread and prevent further ecological damage. Benjamin Schuster
231: Aquatic pump gill ventilation is the primary mode of gas exchange for most teleost fishes, yet the extent of kinematic variation in this process remains under-researched. Pump ventilation relies on both the buccal force pump and opercular suction pump. Still, species differ in their dependence on each mechanism, with pelagic taxa generally exhibiting force-pump dominance and benthic taxa tending toward suction-pump dominance. Such distinctions are not universal, and interspecific variation in ventilatory strategy may have important implications for coping with environmental stressors such as warming and hypoxia. This study examines whether teleost fishes exhibit far greater flexibility in their ventilatory kinematics than previously documented. High-resolution videos of respiration were recorded from 52 individuals across multiple species at the National Aquariums and analyzed using DeepLabCut for markerless tracking of the jaw for scalable kinematic analysis. We then used jaw motion to quantify the duration of inhalation and exhalation across individuals. Preliminary results show that resting fishes displayed distinct breathing patterns compared to actively swimming individuals, with species commonly reducing ventilation frequency by lengthening the jaw-opening phase. By expanding this dataset across species and individuals, this project will quantify buccal expansion and compression durations as proxies for pump dominance, identify evolutionary and ecological patterns in ventilatory mechanics, and evaluate whether kinematic flexibility serves as a functional buffer against anthropogenic reductions in oxygen availability. H. Bradley Shaffer
232: Invasive species establishment is a global threat to biodiversity. Florida has more invasive herpetofaunal species than anywhere else in the world, including the better-known Green Iguanas (Iguana iguana) and Burmese Pythons (Python bivittatus). One lesser-known invasive, Argentine Giant Tegus (AGTs; Salvator merianae), established in South Florida during the early 2000s but populations have been documented further north into Central Florida. AGTs are successful invaders because of their broad diet, resilience to low temperatures, and their role as reservoirs for native and invasive parasites. As large, omnivorous lizards in Florida without a native counterpart, AGTs have detrimental effects through depredation of vulnerable, state-listed native species like Gopher Tortoises (Gopherus polyphemus). In collaboration with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, we are monitoring and removing individuals from a potentially emerging population of AGTs in Orange and Seminole Counties, Florida, to understand their current and potential impact on native species. To date, we have removed 9 lizards across the greater Orlando area, represented by a mix of males and females, and all but 1 lizard classified as large adults. Necropsies documented active follicles present in females, but breeding has not yet been confirmed. Gut contents consisted of native and exotic flora and fauna and supplemental anthropogenic food resources. Our removal efforts provide the unique opportunity to further our understanding of the biology and ecology of AGTs within their invasive range, monitor population biology during the establishment phase of invasion, and potentially eradicate AGTs from the greater Orlando area.
233: Increasing urbanization often reduces habitat quality, particularly within aquatic systems with changing hydrology because of altered land use. Semi-aquatic snakes are obligate carnivores, relying on prey populations including amphibians, fishes, and invertebrates, which often are among the first taxa affected by deteriorating habitat conditions. Aquatic and semi-aquatic prey items might also facilitate movement of emerging pathogens such as the invasive lung parasite, Raillietiella orientalis (Ro), which often uses anurans as secondary intermediate hosts and can later infect definitive hosts including snakes. The University of Central Florida (UCF) in Orlando, Florida, has experienced substantial growth during recent decades, yet there have been few studies to monitor the ongoing effects of urbanization on local species. We are conducting a long-term study on UCF’s main campus to monitor semi-aquatic snakes, their prey, and Ro occurrence between wetlands with different flood regimes. By assessing available and consumed prey, we can determine (a) which snake species are more likely to occupy habitats with greater urbanization and Ro and (b) whether snakes might shift prey selection in response to fluctuating resource and habitat availability. Whereas we found no significant difference in prey availability between wetland types, consumed prey did significantly differ by wetland hydrology and snake species. All snakes that tested positive for Ro were found within permanent wetlands. We believe our results will be useful for campus land managers in assessing the health of wetland food webs through long-term monitoring of the prey base and shifting pressures of invasive parasites amidst environmental stochasticity. Analisa Shields-Estrada Analisa Shields-Estrada; Wesley Neely; Sarah Fritts; David Rodriguez
234: Present-day species richness on land-bridge islands was likely influenced by late Quaternary sealevel fluctuations through episodic changes in island size, isolation, and habitat. Despite this, previous studies either failed to account for the dynamic nature of island variables or focused on oceanic islands. Here, we investigate the effects of late Quaternary sea-level changes on the contemporary species richness of squamates and amphibians across the land-bridge islands in South Korea. We compiled richness data across 160 islands by conducting extensive searches of peer-reviewed articles, biodiversity databases, and survey records. We then calculated contemporary and historical spatial predictors of insular species richness, including island size, distance from the mainland, degree of isolation, and changes in these values over the late Quaternary. We fitted generalized linear mixed models using these predictors to test whether changes in island configuration during the late Quaternary influenced contemporary species richness. Our results show that late Quaternary sea-level changes had little effect on present-day insular species richness. Instead, species richness was predicted primarily by contemporary island size for squamates and distance from the mainland for amphibians. This suggests that herpetofaunal diversity in this area equilibrated rapidly following isolation. Our results provide a framework for further investigating the biogeography and evolution of insular herpetofauna in this region. Our current studies using genomic data are providing insight into demographic responses, patterns of genomic divergence, and local adaptation at the community level due to changes in habitats, land area, and isolation associated with sea-level fluctuations. Ayley Shortridge
235: Dendrobatid poison frogs utilize alkaloids that are sequestered through their diet of small arthropods for defense against predators and microbial infection. Dendrobatid alkaloids are known to disrupt normal nervous and muscular system function; however, these frogs are largely considered immune to the effects of their own alkaloids. Locomotor performance can be used as a measure to understand the potential physiological effects of alkaloid ingestion in dendrobatids. A field-based experiment was conducted in northeastern Costa Rica with the dendrobatid frog, Oophaga pumilio, to investigate the effect of alkaloid ingestion on locomotor performance. Our study included three experimental groups: wild-caught frogs, control frogs, and frogs fed tricyclic alkaloids. To quantitatively examine locomotor performance, a racetrack was used to measure distance, time, and speed of individual frogs in each group. Our study found that tricyclic alkaloids significantly decreased the distance and time traveled by O. pumilio, while it significantly increased frog speed. The observed differences in locomotor performance following alkaloid ingestion, suggests a potential physiological cost to alkaloid defense in poison frogs. Dustin Siegel
236: Hemidactylus turcicus has been an invasive species in Texas since it was first reported in 1954, particularly in urban areas, yet we still know very little about their microhabitat preferences and how these may have contributed to their spread. We set out to monitor gecko populations occupying buildings on Tarleton State University’s campus in Stephenville, Texas. We conducted nocturnal surveys and recorded environmental variables about once per week at five structures on campus known to harbor geckos. With the aid of flashlights, we spotted geckos on structures, and then measured perch height, distance to the nearest light source, and distance to the nearest gecko via laser-based digital tape measures. We also categorized geckos as either “small” or “large” based on a visual estimation of their body size. We found that northwest and southwest-facing walls harbored the most geckos, suggesting that geckos may have been occupying these walls because they would be exposed to highest amount of sunlight during the afternoon. Large and small geckos were similarly distributed relative to light sources; however, most geckos were found far from light sources (> 5 m). Larger geckos, nevertheless, perched higher on walls and closer to other geckos than smaller ones. Our results indicate that lights on buildings are not contributing much to microhabitat usage in geckos on Tarleton’s campus. Rather, it seems that wall direction and intraspecific factors likely contributed much more to their microhabitat preferences, where fear and competition from larger geckos may drive smaller geckos to occupy suboptimal perches. Sierra Smith Sierra Smith; Sid Gopalan; Blair Perry; Yannick Francioli; Kaas Ballard; Sam Kerwin; Anthony Saviola; Rich
237: We examined how socioeconomic variation in urban neighborhoods, associated with habitat disturbance and vegetation management, correlates with behavioral traits in urban fauna. We assessed boldness behavior in the native green anole (Anolis carolinensis) and the invasive Cuban brown anole (Anolis sagrei) across habitats spanning a socioeconomic gradient measured in mean household income. Using behavioral indices for boldness and risk-taking — Flight Initiation Distance (FID), Alert Distance (AD), and Distance from Refuge (DR) — we hypothesized that A. sagrei would on average be bolder than A. carolinensis, as boldness is commonly associated with invasive species in the literature. Observations across two sampling seasons (Fall 2025, Spring 2026) and 10 neighborhoods (two at each income level ranging from <$50K to >$150K per year) suggest that socioeconomic status is associated with differences in anole boldness. A. carolinensis showed a negative correlation between boldness and household income, indicative of risk-taking reduction with increasing human affluence. In contrast, A. sagrei increased boldness with increasing affluence. A boldness index derived from residuals of a regression of FID and DR reveals that invasive A. sagrei are consistently less bold than their native counterparts, refuting our hypothesis. The risk aversion of A. sagrei makes them uniquely able to persist in the absence of natural refugia, where bold and aggressive behaviors increase exposure to predation risk. Unraveling the role of natural refugia in supporting native species may inform urban planning and promote equitable investment in greening urban spaces, improving human wellbeing and native biodiversity alike. Meaghan Sorce
238: Manta and devil rays (family Mobulidae, order Myliobatiformes) are among the most distinctive and threatened elasmobranchs. These fully pelagic, ram filter-feeders possess specialized cephalic lobes that funnel water into the mouth. However, their protected status, large body size, and oceanic distribution make their ecology and taxonomy difficult to study. In other chondrichthyans, dermal denticles (tooth-like skin structures) have proven valuable for understanding anatomy, species differentiation, and ecological adaptations using museum specimens. Here, we investigate dermal denticle diversity in two mobulid species: Mobula birostris (giant manta ray) and Mobula hypostoma (lesser devil ray). Using micro-computed tomography on skin samples from museum specimens, we quantified denticle morphology, size, surface area, and density across body regions. Our results reveal pronounced inter- and intra-specific variation. Mobula birostris is entirely covered by large, stellate denticles that vary across the body. Highly stellated denticles occur on the pelvic fins and tail, while less complex forms are found on the head; smaller denticles are present on cephalic lobes and gill regions. This regional diversity challenges the assumption of a single diagnostic denticle morphotype per species. Notably, morphologies previously attributed to other manta species were observed in different body regions of the same individuals. In contrast, Mobula hypostoma exhibits a single morphotype of small, spiny denticles, unevenly distributed, with some areas lacking denticles entirely. These findings suggest that denticle morphology reflects diverse functional and evolutionary pressures and should be used cautiously in taxonomy. Emmy Spadaro
239: The geckolets, genus Sphaerodactylus, are remarkably diverse and found throughout the Caribbean region. Of the 109 species currently described, 34 occur on the island of Hispaniola. Nearly all of these geckolets are endemic to Hispaniola, some with greatly reduced ranges. However, genetic and morphological data indicate that there are many species not yet recognized; 11 new species and 23 elevated subspecies double the number of species on the island. With this new taxonomic resolution, a more complete picture of geckolet functional and phylogenetic diversity on Hispaniola can be drawn. I use a timetree with the new taxonomy to define phylogenetic diversity and I identify morphological characters for functional diversity. I also present maps with the change in diversity metrics and change in protected area coverage between the current and future species diversity in light of predicted extinctions. Abby Spegel
240: The Texas tortoise (Gopherus berlandieri) is characterized by low reproductive rates, long generation times, and limited dispersal, making populations particularly susceptible to habitat loss and climate change. Texas tortoises inhabit Tamaulipan thornscrub in south Texas and northeastern Mexico. Nueces Delta Preserve, located at the easternmost extent of the Texas tortoise range along the Texas Gulf Coast, consists of mixed-habitat patches dominated by lomas (raised clay dunes) that support thornscrub vegetation. A decline in loma coverage at this site has been driven by invasive grasses and reduced freshwater inflow, limiting habitat availability and population connectivity. Despite intensive tracking at other sites, tortoises at the range edge may exhibit distinct movement patterns and habitat use. Texas tortoise movement across fragmented loma remains poorly understood, particularly seasonal and sex-based variation. This study employs long-term GPS tracking of Texas tortoises at Nueces Delta Preserve to characterize seasonal and inter-patch movement and evaluate behavioral response to active management techniques, such as prescribed burns, mechanical brush removal, and herbicide application. We hypothesize that tortoise movement between habitats will vary seasonally and by sex, with males exhibiting greater inter-patch movement and both sexes concentrated within thornscrub during thermally stressful periods. Findings will provide critical baseline data on seasonal and sex-based movement patterns to information conservation and land management decisions.
241: Bonnetheads (Sphyrna tiburo) are common warm-water sharks found in estuarine and nearshore waters along the southeastern US coast. In U.S. waters, their stock status is classified as unknown, highlighting the need for additional information before management strategies can be adjusted and applied. One critical component of fisheries management is the ageing of individuals to create growth curves for populations – typically a time and labor-intensive process. FT-NIRS (Fourier Transform Near-Infrared Spectroscopy), a method traditionally used to assess chemical composition, has shown recent success in estimating age of teleosts accurately and efficiently. We applied this method to approximately 1,500 vertebrae from bonnetheads from the Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico using FT-NIRS to generate chemical composition spectra. Multivariate statistics and machine learning techniques will be used to analyze the spectra, enabling creation, calibration, and training of a model capable of determining age using spectra alone. This approach has the potential to streamline the elasmobranch ageing process, allowing for efficient and accurate population assessments to support better management of coastal shark populations. Edward Stanley
242: The Gila monster (Heloderma suspectum) is a unique, long-lived venomous lizard endemic to desert regions of North America. They are elusive and difficult to study, as they spend most of their time underground in rocky crevices and burrows. As such, knowing the conditions that affect our ability to detect H. suspectum may be invaluable to future conservation and management efforts. We conducted 287 standardized 1-kilometer transect detection surveys across two sites in southern Nevada. Both visual sightings and indirect signs such as tracks and body drags were recorded as a positive detection. Habitat and environmental variables were recorded at five points along each transect. We detected H. suspectum on 22 of the 287 transects (7.67%). Of those 22 detections there was a single visual sighting, with the other 21 occurrences being a sign or track detection. We used a model selection process to determine which environmental covariates had the greatest impact on detection. The highest performing model consisted of substrate structure, prey presence, ground temperature, time of day, and vapor pressure deficit. Substrate structure was the most influential variable, with our model predicting a higher probability of detection in sandier substrates (p < 0.001). Our results show how difficult it is to detect this species using standardized search methods even at sites where they are known to occur and gives insight into the conditions that most influence detectability. Alyssa Stringer
243: The vertebrate inner ear is used for both hearing and balance. It is further specialized in elasmobranchs (sharks and rays) for detection of low-frequency sounds. Changes in the size and shape of the inner ear have been associated with both phylogenetic relatedness and ecological traits in numerous tetrapod groups, but only a few studies have assessed these relationships in fishes. In addition, estimation of evolutionary relationships in the chondrichthyan lineage has been plagued by conflicting results. For example, phylogenies estimated with mitochondrial or nuclear genes have recovered sharks as monophyletic, while those using morphological data and Ultra Conserved Elements have suggested that the Hexachiformes (Six-gill sharks) might be sister to the rest of the elasmobranchs. In order to further understand these relationships, this study uses a dataset of endocasts of the skeletal labyrinth to test if inner ear characteristics can help provide new traits for phylogenetic analysis within elasmobranchs. Bryce Sweely
244: Quantifying trophic interactions can provide insight into the dynamics of high trophic-level marine predators, as these species exert top-down effects that regulate community structure and maintain ecosystem stability. Bulk stable isotope analysis (SIA) has been used as a reliable method for estimating trophic position (TP); however, uncertainty in inorganic nitrogen sources affecting primary producers can bias nitrogen-15 values, skewing these estimates. Additionally, the collection of muscle tissue required for SIA can be invasive and difficult to preserve at remote field study sites. Non-lethal, minimally invasive alternatives, such as dried blood spot analysis, show promise in reducing animal stress and simplifying field sample preservation while providing the data necessary for food web studies. For this project, we collected muscle tissue and whole blood samples to compare TP estimates among silky sharks (Carcharhinus falciformis), sandbar sharks (Carcharhinus plumbeus), and scalloped hammerhead sharks (Sphyrna lewini) captured near Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary. Using a weighted multi-amino acid approach, we calculated TP estimates among these species and revealed a relatively narrow TP range: silky sharks (4.29 ± 0.14), sandbar sharks (4.21 ± 0.14), and scalloped hammerhead sharks (4.62 ± 0.26). Although there was a consistent offset between TP estimates derived from muscle tissue versus whole blood, dried blood spot analysis proved to be an effective alternative for capturing interspecific food web relationships. This method significantly reduces the financial and logistical challenges associated with sample preservation and laboratory preparation, offering a viable option for sampling collection involving elasmobranch species globally. Brett Sweezey Brett Sweezey; Jay Rooker; Michael Dance; Eric Hoffmayer; William Driggers III; J. Drymon; Marissa Nutall; Brondum Krebs; Creed Branham; Landes Randall; Susan Lowerre-Barbieri; Shane Cantrell; Brett Falterman; R. J.
245: The Southern Coastal Plain of the United States is a species-rich ecoregion that has experienced extensive urbanization and invasion over the past century, significantly altering native herpetofaunal communities. Central Florida’s landscape, in particular, has been rapidly fragmented since the 1960s, in association with travel, housing, transportation, and agriculture. To assess how herpetofaunal diversity has changed amid this land conversion, we utilized long-term data of observations at the University of Central Florida (Orlando, Florida) to establish a robust species inventory. We compiled recorded observations from researchers, museum specimens, and participatory science databases from 1963 to the present. Our meta-analysis indicates likely extirpation of listed species including Eastern Indigo Snakes (Drymarchon couperi) and Gopher Frogs (Lithobates capito), as well as a recent potential loss of Pygmy Rattlesnakes (Sistrurus miliarius). 14 invasive species have been introduced, among which the Brown Anole (Anolis sagrei) has become the most abundant lizard species. Varying survey efforts over decades introduced biases and gaps in our data, with recent increases in herpetological research on campus leading to documentation of locally rare habitat specialists within urban refugia including Glossy Swampsnakes (Liodytes rigida), Pine Snakes (Pituophis melanoleucus), and Southeastern Dwarf Salamanders (Eurycea quadridigitata). We emphasize the importance of long-term, consistent monitoring to better understand potential consequences of urbanization. Despite changes in species composition, diversity in this heavily altered landscape persists, showing the importance of preserving remaining habitats. Emalee Swisshelm
246: Leuciscidae is a diverse family of freshwater fishes found throughout North America and Eurasia making up a large portion of the North American freshwater fish assemblages. While their external morphology is conserved compared to other fish families, variation in osteological components have been noted. A divergent morphological trait within Leuciscidae is the pharyngeal jaw, used heavily in processing prey items as this family lacks teeth in their oral jaws. Due to the close connection with dietary habits, the pharyngeal jaw is hypothesized to show morphological variation, possibly even within closely related species. Pogonichthyinae is found exclusively in North America. Cyprinella, the second largest genus in Pogonichthyinae, is consistently found to be monophyletic (with the exception of C. callistia). With continued studies refining the phylogenetic understanding of Leuciscidae, revisiting morphological analysis of key features may shed new light on how these unique characteristics evolved and diversified. Through the visual analysis of cleared and stained specimens, this study aims to describe morphological characteristics of the pharyngeal jaw in Cyprinella. We focus on a small subset of four closely related species (C. luternsis, C. caerula, C. callitaenia, C. callisema, and C. nivea) along with Notropis maculatus as an outgroup taxa and will examine the morphological variation to highlight key difference and similarities among them. Genevieve Sylvester
247: Traditional shark tracking methods, including satellite and acoustic tags, provide valuable data on large-scale movements but lack the fine-scale resolution needed to link swimming kinematics with behavior. Some satellite tags incorporate accelerometers to infer activity levels; however, they do not provide direct visual confirmation, making it difficult to distinguish behaviors such as foraging, schooling, or predator avoidance. To address this limitation, this study used animal-borne data logger cameras to quantify swimming kinematics and behavior in free-swimming sharks. The tag package was mounted on the dorsal fin and recorded tri-axial acceleration, compass heading, gyroscopic orientation, pitch, and lean, alongside synchronized video, to provide a “shark’s-eye view” of the environment. The tag package was deployed on blacktip (Carcharhinus limbatus), lemon (Negaprion brevirostris) and nurse sharks (Ginglymostoma cirratum). The kinematic data revealed tailbeat frequencies of 0.97 Hz for C. limbatus, 0.77 Hz for N. brevirostris, and 0.58 Hz for G. cirratum. Tailbeat frequency differed significantly among the three species. Aerial drone-based observations of free-swimming individuals in the wild were used to independently quantify tailbeat frequencies in non-instrumented sharks. The tailbeat frequencies were similar between free swimming sharks and sharks instrumented with the tag package, suggesting that the tag package does not alter natural swimming behavior. Tailbeat frequency was significantly greater when the shark was pitched upward, compared to when it was horizontal or pitched downward. The ability to use video to ground truth kinematic data with environmental stimuli provides insight into the relationships between locomotion and ecological function. Isabella Szarko
248: In vertebrates, eye size is often closely related to visual ecology, with larger eyes generally associated with greater visual activity or sensitivity, though the relationship between eye morphology and ecological traits remains understudied. Elapid snakes (e.g., sea snakes, cobras, and coral snakes) occupy a wide range of habitats, including terrestrial, marine, arboreal, and fossorial environments, and exhibit diverse diel activity patterns across species. Here, we investigate whether variation in elapid eye size correlates with habitat use and diel activity by measuring eye diameter in 78 species from natural history collections. Ecological data (habitat use and diel activity pattern) were compiled from published natural history sources and SquamBase. We used phylogenetic comparative methods and an existing elapid phylogeny to account for shared evolutionary history when assessing associations between ecology and eye investment (ratio of eye size to body size). We find that eye investment is reduced in fossorial, semifossorial, and marine species, while terrestrial and arboreal species have increased eye investment. Similarly, eye investment is increased in diurnal species and decreased in nocturnal species. Our findings suggest that levels of eye investment are dependent on the role vision plays in species-specific ecology; for example, terrestrial and arboreal species need greater visual acuity for navigating complex environments and active foraging. This research provides novel insight into how ecological pressures have shaped eye evolution in a diverse radiation of snakes. Brendan S. Talwar
249: How do individuals choose their mate? Mate choice could be based on many things, including qualities of the mate (color, size, ornamentation, genes, etc.) and/or quality of the territory, spawning location, etc. Previous lab research has shown female cichlids preferer larger males. There are two possibilities: 1. biggest is best, i.e., a female always choses the biggest male, or 2. a female choses a male that matches her size but is slightly bigger, i.e., assortative mating, in which big females mate with big males and small females mate with small males. To test which of the two is happening in the field, for 3 weeks in January 2026, I visited ten rivers of northeast Costa Rica to examine breeding pairs of six species of cichlid fishes. Because I could not catch the fish without disturbing their parental care, I positioned a model of known size next to each fish to estimate its size. I got data on 108 pairs of cichlids across six species. For each species, I analyzed the data using a least-squares regression of male length on female length. There was a strong positive relationship between male size and female size (n=108). Four of the species analyzed individually shared the same significant relationship, strongly indicating that there was positive size–assortative mating. The results of this study will add to our understanding of mate choice, evolution and sexual selection in neotropical, substrate spawning cichlids. Taylor Thomisee
250: The purpose of our study is to understand how neighborhood socioeconomic status affects the relative densities of native versus invasive lizard species in urban environments. We hypothesized that lower socioeconomic neighborhoods, which typically experience greater anthropogenic disturbance and less managed vegetation, would favor invasive species over native congeners. We conducted this analysis across ten neighborhoods of varying socioeconomic status in the New Orleans metropolitan area, quantifying the abundance of the native green anole (Anolis carolinensis) and the invasive Cuban brown anole (Anolis sagrei) along standardized transects at each site. Accounting for interspecific behavioral differences, including the greater disturbance tolerance of A. sagrei, we hypothesized that A. sagrei would exhibit higher abundance in lower socioeconomic (highdisturbance) urban zones, while A. carolinensis would be more prevalent in higher affluence areas with greater habitat complexity. Analysis of preliminary data supports this hypothesis, with significantly greater abundance of A. sagrei in lower socioeconomic neighborhoods nearly excluding A. carolinensis. Additionally, A. sagrei also showed high abundance in higher affluence neighborhoods, suggesting broad displacement of A. carolinensis across the urban socioeconomic gradient. Our findings support the hypothesis that high-disturbance zones, particularly urbanized environments, facilitate the establishment and spread of invasive populations. We attribute the disproportionately higher invasive densities in lower affluence zones primarily to reduced managed vegetation, which decreases shelter availability and increases predation risk for the more behaviorally cautious A. carolinensis. Anna Thonis Anna Thonis; Blackwell Emily; Olivia Weklar; Maram Al-Busaidi; Isabella Gaba; Delaney Kenshock; Ryder Kern; Leona Li; Michelle Lin; Mia Loran; Calista Lynch; Lena Olson; Shagun Sinha; Avery Wong; Kaijun Xie; Kristin
251: Shark fishing techniques, whether recreational, commercial, or scientific, are essential in researching a wide variety of shark species. Longlining and drumlining are two common methods of surveying sharks. However, it is important to assess mortality rates between the two methods and across species. Data were examined from multiple sources from drumlined and longlinged blacktips throughout Southern Florida. Preliminary analysis indicates that longlined blacktips have a higher mortality rate than drumlined blacktips. Other factors, including lactate, sex, and maturity, were also noted and analyzed, suggesting that stress metrics are higher in long-lined blacktips than in drum-lined blacktips. Further research should be done to determine which fishing gear and protocols the elasmobranch research community could implement to reduce mortality rates, whether at-vessel or upon release. Kevin Torgersen
252: Habitat availability is a key determinant of estuarine fish abundance, yet species-specific responses to habitat loss and environmental disturbance in urbanized systems remain unclear. We tested the hypotheses that (1) fish abundance is positively associated with natural habitats (e.g., seagrass, mangroves, oyster reef), (2) artificial structures partially compensate for natural habitat loss for structure-associated species, and (3) disturbance events (e.g., freshwater discharge, cold snaps, harmful algal blooms) drive shifts in habitat use and abundance. We analyzed long-term fisheries-independent monitoring data (1997–2019) from the St. Lucie River and southern Indian River Lagoon, Florida, focusing on Sheepshead (Archosargus probatocephalus) and Spotted seatrout (Cynoscion nebulosus). Field-collected habitat data (shoreline, bottom type, and bottom vegetation) were integrated with available habitat maps (seagrass, mangrove, oyster) to quantify habitat availability through time. We applied generalized additive models, Ivlev’s electivity index, principal component analysis, and kernel density estimation to evaluate relationships among catch-per-unit-effort, habitat use, and environmental variability. Results supported all three hypotheses with species-specific differences. Sheepshead were strongly associated with structured habitats and exhibited increased use of artificial shorelines where natural habitats declined, whereas spotted seatrout abundance was closely linked to seagrass availability and declined following periods of reduced water clarity which has led to seagrass habitat loss. Disturbance events corresponded with shifts in abundance and hotspot locations for both species. These findings demonstrate that habitat-specific dependencies mediate fish responses to environmental change and provide guidance for restoration and management in urbanized estuarine systems. Benjamin Torres
253: For ectothermic species whose behavior dictates much of their life history traits, thermal decisions also influence their ability to combat disease. Individuals’ environmental histories affect their vulnerability to infection and can provide insight into within species variation in infection. To assess the average relationship between environmental temperatures and host temperatures, and its resulting influence on Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) load, we will use Notophthalmus viridescens (Eastern newt) to conduct isolated temperatures experiments in conjunction with studying movement in the field to better understand the behavioral aspect of the host-pathogen-disease relationship. We aim to answer: 1) How does newt temperature influence in-host pathogen growth? and 2) How does newt behavior affect the relationship between environmental temperature and amphibian temperature? We will hold newts in two types of enclosures: ones designed to experience narrow temperature ranges (warm and cool) and others that are designed to allow behavioral choice in temperature. Studying this temperaturesensitive relationship may provide clarity on how certain amphibians species are better able to combat infection by this fungal pathogen. This information can also be used to inform what kinds of environmental manipulation may better serve amphibians infected with Bd. Dominic Troiani Dominic Troiani; Eli Greenbaum; Chifundera Kusamba; J. Maximilian Dehling
254: Microplastics are one of the most common pollutants that are ubiquitous throughout the world. They enter the environment either directly through the manufacture of microplastics (primary microplastics) or as a result of larger plastics breaking down as a result of weathering, UV radiation, and physical abrasion (secondary microplastics). At acute exposures, environmental microplastics are known to have negative impacts on many invertebrates, fish, and even mice. This research aimed to understand the effects of chronic exposure to environmentally realistic levels of polyethylene microplastics on the development and ossification in African Clawed Frog (Xenopus laevis) tadpoles. Tadpoles were raised in a control group or a treatment group of 50 ug/L of polyethylene microplastics ranging from 740 nm - 4990 nm in diameter until they reached Nieuwkoop and Faber developmental stage 59. Developmental timing, development of scoliosis, and skeletal development were assessed. Results indicated no effect on developmental timing, but there was an effect of microplastics on the development of scoliosis. Testing is ongoing to determine differences in ossification between the microplastics and control groups. While Xenopus laevis are known to be resilient to various environmental conditions and degraded habitat quality, effects of microplastics were found. More work should be done analyzing these effects across amphibian species, especially those that may be more susceptible to damage via microplastic pollution. Jacob Twersky
255: Some species exhibit different morphotypes throughout their range which may have varying selective benefits based on differing environmental characteristics. The timber rattlesnake (Crotalus horridus) has a black and yellow morphotype throughout their range. Recent research has shown that black morphotypes are more abundant within cooler climates at either northern latitudes or higher elevations (Allsteadt et al. 2006). Despite this shift in morphotype abundance, the yellow morphotype still persists in cooler environments which may suggest a selective benefit for individuals exhibiting this phenotype. The objective of this project will be to determine if different morphotypes of timber rattlesnakes have different rates of predation and if this differs based on the color of the substrate the snake is sitting on and the habitat type it resides in. To test this, we will measure predation on black and yellow morphotype foam models on differing backgrounds (black, yellow, and natural backgrounds) in three different environments: Right-of-way, Deciduous Forest, and Burnt Deciduous Forest. Instances of predation will be recorded on camera in each habitat. Results from this study may shed light on why yellow morphotypes are still abundant within cooler environments. Anastasia Umstott
256: The introduction of non-native species can have harmful effects on native ecosystems. Examination of established non-native species and their dispersal paths can help create strategies to reduce the harmful effects of these species on the native ecosystem. Aspidoscelis neomexicanus is a hybrid parthenogenetic whiptail native to the Rio Grande river basin, and introduced populations of this species exist in northern Utah and northeastern Arizona with putative introductions in southern Utah and northwestern New Mexico. Preliminary analysis of mitochondrial and microsatellite loci indicate that the majority of non-native populations are sourced from the same native region, but because of the recency of dispersion little variation is present within loci we targeted, limiting our ability to identify specific dispersal patterns. To gain better resolution of the dispersal paths and source populations of these introduced populations, we generated whole-genome PacBio DNA sequence data from individuals at nine different sites (five non-native and four native). Here we describe our bioinformatics pipeline and early results from our genomic analysis. Eric VanDerSluys
257: As microplastics pollute waters more and more, they are affecting wildlife in freshwater environments. These pollutants are present in every stage of these freshwater organisms' development and can affect their behavior, development, and anatomy. This study was done to observe how ultra-low, environmentally realistic levels of microplastics may influence tadpole physiological function and morphology. Northern Leopard Frog tadpoles were exposed to 1ug/L of 34-50um polyethylene microplastics during development, then assessed for physiological and anatomical changes. Tadpoles exposed to microplastics had higher oxygen consumption rates than controls. The tadpoles were then staged (average stage Gosner stage 27), weighed, and photographed to observe jaw sheath morphology using Image J. No statistically significant effects of microplastics were found on tadpole jaw sheath anatomy. In the future, we hope to assess other morphological characteristics. Research on microplastics can help us better understand their effects on tadpoles, as well as every other species in ecosystems polluted by microplastics.
258: In many cases, the identification of fish eggs is not always possible via just visual inspection. To help properly identify the species in a stretch of the Flint River (Saginaw River watershed) that passes through the campus of the University of Michigan-Flint, DNA barcoding is used in this project to identify eggs without a known associated adult. DNA barcoding relies on a small fragment of the mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COI). The COI barcodes of the unknown species were compared to the database of known COI sequences from the Barcode of Life Data (BOLD) Systems. The goal of this project is to create an egg identification reference library of local Michigan fishes (Mid-Michigan) with both photographic and barcode references to assist in egg identification via external appearance and gross morphology, when possible. Anna Velten
259: Increasing human impact on aquatic systems often leads to deteriorating fish health and more frequent disease outbreaks. This study investigates whether identifying early physiological symptoms can help assess and control the spread of these diseases regionally. This study establishes a baseline health assessment for various freshwater and marine fish species common to the southeastern United States through a visual evaluation scale. The primary objective is to create a qualitative monitoring list and tool by translating external physical observations into a quantitative health index for regional fish populations. By utilizing a standardized 1-10 scale, analysis of individual fish condition and body morphology will facilitate the identification of aquatic environmental issues and the spread of disease. Preliminary development of this scoring system indicates that the 1-10 scale provides a consistent and reproducible framework for distinguishing varying levels of health. A score of ten represents optimal health, while lower scores correlate with physiological stress, physical trauma, or disease presence. Implementing this systematic scoring system across aquatic environments establishes a benchmark for identifying disease prevalence in these areas. This visual assessment framework offers a practical, rapid-response methodology for biologists and resource managers to monitor the well-being of a region's fish population without harm. Hardin Waddle
260: Coastal estuaries serve as shark habitats and can be hotspots for contaminant accumulation. This study investigates how habitat urbanization and feeding ecology shape exposure to total mercury (tHg) and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) across three shark species. Two studies were conducted: (1) a comparison of broadnose sevengill sharks (Notorynchus cepedianus) from urbanized (San Francisco Bay, CA) and less-urbanized (Willapa Bay, WA) estuaries, and (2) an evaluation of finetooth (Carcharhinus isodon) and sandbar (Carcharhinus plumbeus) sharks from South Carolina with differing diets. Contaminant concentrations were analyzed in shark blood, muscle, prey, water and sediment, and stable isotopes (δ¹³C, δ¹⁵N) were used to assess trophic position. Subadult sevengill sharks exhibited significantly higher muscle tHg concentrations in Willapa Bay versus San Francisco Bay, while blood tHg did not differ significantly, indicating greater long-term accumulation than recent exposure differences. PFAS concentrations exhibited no significant differences across habitats, life stages, or sexes, suggesting baseline exposure across locations. Sandbar sharks displayed significantly higher tHg than finetooth sharks, increasing with size in both species. Teleost prey had significantly higher tHg concentrations than invertebrates (p < 0.05), suggesting biomagnification through trophic transitions.
