Isotopic signatures revealed finetooths as pelagic specialists (narrow δ¹⁵N range), while sandbars revealed broader shifts toward benthic foraging (broader δ¹⁵N range, enriched δ¹³C). While finetooth neonates exhibited the lowest summed PFAS concentrations, juveniles reached levels commensurate to adults. Overall, mercury accumulation may reflect trophic position and habitat use, whereas PFAS exposure may be driven by early-life accumulation and species-specific physiological plateaus. Whitney G Walkowski (She/Her)
261: Stream-breeding salamanders in the Eurycea and Desmognathus genera play a vital role in nutrient cycling, the food web, and overall ecosystem functioning in streams and riparian forests. However, the population dynamics and habitat use of stream-breeding salamanders are poorly understood, especially in low elevation regions like Virginia’s Coastal Plain. It is crucial to understand how stream-breeding salamander ecology varies across regions, life stages, and species to manage populations. To improve our understanding of local stream-breeding salamander ecology, we used cover-board transects to survey adult southern two-lined salamanders (Eurycea cirrigera), three-lined salamanders (E. guttolineata), and northern dusky salamanders (Desmognathus fuscus) in riparian forests surrounding nine headwater streams in Williamsburg, Virginia. We then created statistical models to predict salamander abundance based on combinations of microhabitat, landscape, and climatic variables. We found that differences in soil moisture and temperature between the board and surrounding soil, day of year, proximity to stream, proportion of evergreen forest in the watershed, and cumulative precipitation over 5 days were important predictors of the abundance of stream-breeding salamanders. Additionally, we found that each species utilized a different amount of terrestrial habitat around the stream, with a 14.2-m buffer for E. cirrigera, 7.3-m buffer for E. guttolineata, and 1-m buffer for D. fuscus.These results highlight the need for the protection and restoration of riparian and upland forest buffer zones improve salamander habitat quality. In the future, our models will be combined with previous research on larval populations to understand overall trends in stream-breeding salamander populations. Olivia Weklar
262: In 2009, Lowry et al. published a study detailing a new method and tool for assessing shark bite marks on both biological and man-made objects using the relationship between interdental distance (IDD) and bite circumference with the total lengths (TLs) of fourteen species of shark. When combined with knowledge of geography, habitat, and species-specific feeding behavior, it was possible to use their tool to obtain an accurate estimate of shark size and potential species. However, the species included in this study and the sizes of sharks sampled were limited to those available in three shark jaw collections in Florida. Sample sizes for four species (Carcharhinus falciformis, Negaprion brevirostris, Sphyrna lewini, S. mokarran) were not sufficient to include the IDD-based total length estimates in the tool. Since 2009, users of this tool have also requested that the number of species be expanded to include other species that leave bite marks on various objects and prey. Therefore, this study seeks to update the 2009 study in two ways. The first is increasing the sample sizes for all fourteen of the original species, which will not only make the TL estimates more statistically robust, but will also allow both IDD and bite circumference to be used to estimate TL for all of those species. The second update is to add data for three new species: C. longimanus, Notorynchus cepedianus, and S. zygaena.
263: Dendrobatid poison frogs sequester defensive alkaloids from dietary arthropods. Alkaloids are known to vary significantly within and among species, and understanding the factors involved in this variation remains an active area of research. Although differences in arthropod availability appear to drive most of the alkaloid variation, there is emerging evidence that alkaloid modification and differences in sequestration efficiency may also play a role. Most sequestered alkaloids retain the same chemical structure as those found in arthropods, but some species of dendrobatids can chemically modify dietary alkaloids, such as the N-methylation of decahydroquinoline (DHQ) and hydroxylation of pumiliotoxins. Our project had two goals: (1) to determine if dietary piperidine (PIP) can also be N-methylated, because it is a secondary amine and structurally similar to DHQ.; and (2) to investigate differences in sequestration efficiencies between PIP and DHQ alkaloids among different species. In one experiment, we fed PIP to three species of poison frogs (Dendrobates auratus, Epipedobates anthonyi, and Ranitomeya variabilis) to determine if they could N-methylate, and in a second experiment, we fed D. auratus and E. anthonyi DHQ to compare differences in N-methylation and sequestration efficiencies to frogs fed PIP. No evidence of PIP Nmethylation was found, but there were differences in sequestration efficiency between frogs fed DHQ and PIP. Surprisingly, we found that D. auratus and E. anthonyi can hydroxylate DHQ, which represents an entirely new alkaloid modification in poison frogs. We provide a comparison of alkaloid modification and an evaluation of sequestration efficiency among dendrobatid poison frogs. Caroline J Wiernicki Caroline Wiernicki; James Turnbull; Jérôme Pinti; Camille Pagniello; Barbara Block; Matthew Oliver; Aaron
264: Predator-prey interactions involving large sharks and coastal dolphins have been documented through the observation of shark bite wounds on surviving dolphins and recovered carcasses. Characterizing shark bite occurrence across dolphin life stages and over time is critical for understanding predation risk and its ecological consequences. Yet determining when bites occur is rarely possible without consistent, long-term field observations. To address knowledge gaps in the demographics and timing of shark–dolphin interactions, we used data collected by the Sarasota Dolphin Research Program, which has monitored the long-term resident bottlenose dolphin (Tursiops truncatus) community in Sarasota Bay, Florida for over five decades. Digital photos from field projects and necropsy records of pre-mortem wounds were used to identify fresh shark bites. For each shark bite, we recorded the year and month it occurred and classified the dolphin’s life stage. A generalized additive model was used to assess trends in shark bite occurrence over time. Results suggest that calves were bitten more frequently than other life stages, reflecting their greater vulnerability to predatory sharks. Fresh bites occurred primarily during May through October, corresponding with seasonal presence of bull sharks (Carcharhinus leucas) and tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier) – the primary predators of Sarasota Bay dolphins. Preliminary annual trends suggest an increase in shark bites that has stabilized in recent years. Our findings underscore the value of long-term, individual-based data for understanding how demographic vulnerability and temporal variability interact to shape basic patterns of predator– prey ecology in marine ecosystems. Keiffer Williams
265: Sharks occupy multiple ecological niches and exhibit a wide range of lifestyle strategies. In this study, we examined the morphological diversity of skulls (neurocrania) of sharks using two-dimensional (2D) geometric morphometrics on almost all the known genera of extant sharks and several extinct taxa. Our analysis includes ~ 33% of all extant shark species (N = 178) and indicates that the rostral length and cranial width are the most variable parts of the shark neurocranium, where there appears to be only one general neurocranial morphology in sharks that is characterized by a relatively slender skull with a short rostrum. Whereas this morphological condition is regarded as plesiomorphic, our study reveals that the general neurocranial morphology could be evolutionarily modified in two different ways: elongating the rostrum or broadening the cranial width. Our study also indicates that, like the overall body form morphology, neurocranial morphology in sharks is tightly connected to their lifestyle. The skulls of most examined fossil sharks are represented by the generalized neurocranial morphology, but Lamniformes exhibit the greatest neurocranial diversity among all the shark orders examined. By integrating taxonomic order, ecomorphotypes, and body types with neurocranial morphology, our study represents the most comprehensive survey of the morphological diversity of neurocrania in sharks to date, providing new ecological and evolutionary insights. Sidney Woodruff (she/they)
266: Studies have shown that elasmobranchs accumulate significant quantities of the toxic metal mercury (Hg), which can pose health risks for both human consumers and the animals themselves. The collection of muscle samples for use in evaluating Hg burden can be accomplished non-lethally but is still invasive and could result in animal stress. The goal of this study was to determine if fin clips can be utilized as a less invasive surrogate for measuring internal Hg burden compared to muscle biopsies in bonnethead Sphyrna tiburo and scalloped hammerhead sharks Sphyrna lewini. Paired muscle biopsies and fin clips were collected from individual bonnethead and scalloped hammerhead sharks sampled from northeast Florida and southeast Georgia estuaries using bottom longline and drumline fishing techniques. Hg concentrations were measured using a Direct Mercury Analyzer (DMA-80). The association between fin and muscle concentrations will be presented, along with a comparison of results from similar studies on other shark species. Tina Wu
267: We focused on Ariake Bay, Japan, recently identified as the first nursery ground for the scalloped hammerhead Sphyrna lewini in the northwestern Pacific, to clarify how this bay functions as an important nursery habitat. In this bay, juveniles with stretched total length (STL) ≤ 80 cm predominated. Adults appeared only from May to June, from the central bay to the mouth, and disappeared in July when salinity decreased during the rainy season. Neonates with open umbilical scars (mean STL 52.3 cm) occurred only in and around June, grew to a mean of 68.3 cm by September, and were largely absent during winter as water temperature declined; few individuals remained until summer of the following year. Neonates showed relatively high empty stomach rates, and although the hepatosomatic index slightly decreased during the first two months after birth, no decline in condition factor was observed. In the inner bay, age-0 individuals occurred in lower salinity waters (minimum 26) than older juveniles. Almost all adults caught by longline near the bay mouth were males aged 10–38 years; catch-curve analysis estimated an annual survival rate of 0.85. Male growth followed a Gompertz model and was faster than in other regions. Stomach contents included fish, squid, guitarfish, and conspecific neonates, suggesting that adult males may act as predators of juveniles. We conclude that, following parturition, the rainy season may exclude potential predators from the bay, and together with Ariake Bay’s unique physical environment and abundant prey availability, create an optimal nursery habitat for this species. Alexander Yan
268: Sharks are crucial apex predators that maintain ecological balance, aquatic biodiversity, and resilient ecosystems. The long lifespans, low reproductive rates, and high trophic positions make sharks particularly susceptible to mercury bioaccumulation. Initially released into the atmosphere by industrial pollution, mercury is then deposited into aquatic reservoirs. Through methylation, inorganic mercury is converted into a highly toxic organic form. We are exploring species and age-related differences in bioaccumulation among the apex predator, broadnose sevengill sharks (Notorynchus cepedianus), and the mesopredators, leopard sharks (Triakis semifasciata) and brown smooth hound sharks (Mustelus henlei). We hypothesize that, as apex predators, broadnose sevengills will have the highest tHg levels, and that older sharks will have higher tHg levels than younger sharks. We quantify mercury concentrations using direct thermal-composition amalgamation atomic absorption spectrophotometry, following EPA Method 7473. This process combusts the sample, and the released mercury binds to the amalgamator because of its high affinity for gold. Total mercury concentrations were highest in the broadnose sevengill sharks. There was a significant positive correlation between total length and tHg observed in both broadnose sevengill and leopard sharks (p < 0.0001), indicating a size-related increase in mercury accumulation. These findings may indicate that mercury accumulation increases with age and size, as well as the primary diet of the shark species, informing risk assessments for predators of estuarine environments. Jessica Zhong Jessica Zhong; Delson Hays; Fernando Melendez-Vazquez; Julian Gallego-Garcia; Jonathan Armbruster; Pamela
269: Transitions to planktivory are often coupled with benthic-to-pelagic transitions and are abundant throughout the evolutionary history of fishes. In percomorph fishes, there have been multiple independent transitions across a large variety of timescales. Despite this, the molecular basis of these transitions is understudied. We analyzed chromosome-level genomes of 14 percomorph fishes spanning 7 independent planktivore transitions to garner a holistic view of the genomic basis of planktivory. Using comparative genomic techniques, we analyze both coding and conserved nonexonic element (CNEE) regions associated with transitions to planktivory. Using OrthoFinder and TOGA2 with the Comparative Annotations Toolkit, we were able to identify 7717 orthologous coding regions. Contrasting a recent study by Santaquiteria et al., on surgeonfishes and their allies, our positive selection analyses found no evidence of positive selection in protein-coding genes. However, using PhyloAcc, we were able to identify 188 CNEEs with accelerated evolutionary rates in planktivore lineages, with 49 CNEEs in 2 or more transitions, 7 in 3 or more, and 1 of which was shared among six out of seven independent transitions. This pattern aligns with a growing body of work, particularly in birds and mammals, showing that convergent phenotypic transitions are more often accompanied by accelerated evolution in conserved regulatory elements than by recurrent positive selection in protein-coding genes. This study allows us to better understand the genomic landscape of these dietary transitions. Future directions aim to study not just orthologous genes, but also multi-copy genes, to gain insights into possible instances of neofunctionalization associated with planktivores.
270: The Neotropical freshwater fish fauna is one of the most diverse in the world. However, the species and functional diversity of some regions, such as the Brazilian Northeast, remain poorly understood. To reduce this knowledge gap, we conducted a survey of the distribution and occurrence of fish species in the Brazilian Northeast and linked these data to a matrix of ecological traits. This approach allowed us to obtain ecological information for nearly all species in the region. Two spatial delimitation scenarios were used to determine species occurrence and perform the analyses. The first scenario considered the division into ecoregions, while the second followed the Brazilian classification of hydrographic regions. Subsequently, we calculated alpha (richness, functional diversity, divergence, dispersion, and evenness) and beta functional diversity metrics. Alpha diversity analyses showed that communities in the Northeast, regardless of species richness, exhibit a set of functional traits concentrated within a small portion of the available functional niche space, maintaining a similar niche structure. Furthermore, despite differences in richness, the species present tend to be functionally distinct from one another, suggesting that functions are relatively evenly distributed within the functional space. Beta diversity analyses indicated that most of the variation is explained by the turnover component, whether considering species composition or their functional attributes. Therefore, we emphasize that understanding functional diversity is also a key element for the conservation of species that make up the freshwater fish communities of northeastern Brazil. Dean Adams
271: Organismal biologists commonly use landmark-based geometric morphometrics to characterize and compare biological shapes. Advances in three-dimensional imaging hold potential to catapult morphometric studies, but quantifying shape from 3D surfaces in an efficient manner remains challenging. Several surface-based GM procedures have been proposed, which align surface scans and use their differences as the basis of shape analysis. Comparisons of landmark-based and surface-based methods have revealed mixed results, but these studies utilized empirical datasets where the true patterns of shape differences are unknown. In this study we performed a simulation experiment where the true shape differences between objects were known, and evaluated the performance of two landmark-based and four surface-based methodologies under these conditions. Several procedures, including landmarks plus semilandmarks, as well as the surface-based method DAA (and to a lesser extent auto3d), most consistently recovered the known patterns of shape variation. Results from other procedures (GPSA and pseudoLM) were more variable. Notably, patterns in more complex shapes were better characterized than patterns in simpler shapes, implying that automated surface-based methods were challenged when presented with shapes whose principal axes were similar, or where structures contained few localized shape differences for these methods to properly orient the surfaces. Overall, our findings highlight that while biologically informed landmarking remains imperative as a foundation for morphometric analyses, some surface-based procedures do offer a powerful and efficient means of characterizing shape, and hold promise for morphometric studies. Jon Adamski
272: Leopard geckos (Eublepharis macularius) are one of the most popular and common lizards kept by reptile enthusiasts. Here, we study the dentition of a pet trade leopard gecko, who displays an abnormal tooth count. We compare it with two specimens from their native distributional range (Gujrat India, Balochistan Pakistan). We found remarkable differences. We also examined x-rays from two additional captive specimens, which showed normal dentition. The captive specimen exhibits hyperdontia (increased tooth count), this pathology has only been reported four times prior in lizards (Uta stansburiana [1], Petrosaurus mearnsi [2], Homonota marthae [1]). Compared to the native geckos, the number of tooth loci corresponds to the expected number for its size; premaxillary 13, maxillary 32,37, and dentary 31,37, however, when we look at the teeth, we find many instances of multiple teeth in the same loci (3–5). Another anomaly we found in this specimen is reduced resorption pits in most teeth, and shifting of teeth into a more palatal position. In the premaxilla, we saw no teeth, but some irregularshaped structures occupying the dental positions. This phenomenon is rare in lizards, and there is no clear cause for the occurrence of this pathology. It may be related to dysfunction in dental epithelial stem cells, signaling pathways, or odontoclasts. James Anderson
273: Compensatory responses in life history traits have been recognized in depleted populations among a variety of fishes and may serve as mechanisms of population regulation for sharks. Reduced population densities can decrease intraspecific competition and increase prey availability, resulting in faster growth and earlier maturation. These density-dependent changes in life history traits are often attributed to high fishing pressure and may be relevant to population dynamics. The Blacknose Shark, Carcharhinus acronotus, is a small coastal species vulnerable to bycatch in the Gulf of America (GoA), where its stock status is uncertain but declines in abundance have been reported. Given these pressures, this species provides a useful model for evaluating potential compensatory responses in exploited shark populations. To examine temporal shifts in Blacknose Shark growth, vertebral samples collected from the GoA between 1992 and 2025 (n = 259) were analyzed. Resulting von Bertalanffy growth parameters revealed distinct shifts over time. Growth coefficients increased from 0.26 yr⁻¹ in the 1990s to 0.51 yr⁻¹ in recent years, while asymptotic size declined from 105.8 to 95.1 cm fork length. These patterns indicate faster growth to smaller sizes, consistent with density-dependent responses following exploitation. These findings highlight the need for continued monitoring to better characterize GoA Blacknose Shark population dynamics and to support effective management and regulatory measures. Thomas L. Anderson
274: Global plastic production has increased exponentially since the onset of large-scale industrialization in the 1960s, resulting in pervasive contamination of marine ecosystems. To date, more than 1,300 marine species have been documented ingesting plastic debris, with microplastic particles (<5 mm) identified in fish gastrointestinal tracts as early as 1949. Despite growing recognition of this issue, long-term trends in microplastic ingestion spanning pre- and post-industrial periods remain understudied. In particular, comparisons between shallow-water benthic fishes and mesopelagic fishes are limited, in part due to an incomplete understanding of plastic transport pathways in marine environments. Here, we investigate microplastic ingestion in shallow-water benthic fishes and mesopelagic marine fishes across eight decades (1940s–2010s) using archived museum specimens. Southern California fish species with three different feeding behaviors were selected: planktivore, invertivore, and piscivore. Gastrointestinal tracts were dissected under contamination-controlled conditions, chemically digested in KOH, and vacuum filtered onto glass microfiber filters. Using Raman spectroscopy, hyperspectral maps were collected from each filter to quantitatively and qualitatively analyze potential plastics. Polyamide and polystyrene were found to be the most prevalent microplastics. Additionally, fish species collected in enclosed water systems and nearby industrial areas were more likely to be found with microplastics. This study provides a temporal assessment of microplastics in marine fishes, informing future monitoring and policy strategies aimed at mitigating marine plastic pollution. Dahiana Arcila
275: Zeiformes (dories, oreos, and tinselfishes) are a morphologically disparate marine clade whose family-level relationships have remained contentious. Previous studies relied on both molecular and morphological characters to test the monophyly of the six currently recognized families, but left several deep nodes poorly resolved. For this study, we generated a new phylogenomic dataset of 1,126 nuclear markers for 25 zeiform species (covering all six families) and seven paracanthopterygian outgroups, and we inferred relationships under both coalescent (ASTRAL) and Maximum Likelihood (RAxML-NG) frameworks. The two analyses yielded congruent topologies: Cyttidae, Zeidae, Oreosomatidae, Parazenidae, and Grammicolepididae (sensu stricto: Grammicolepis plus Xenolepidichthys) were each resolved as monophyletic. For the first-time, our dataset includes molecular data from the rare deep-sea genus Macrurocyttus. Macrurocyttus acanthopodus originally described by Fowler in the monotypic family Macrurocyttidae and subsequently subsumed into Grammicolepididae (subfamily Macrurocyttinae) base exclusively on morphology, was resolved as sister to Zenion in both ASTRAL and RAxMLNG trees, removing it from Grammicolepididae. Short internal branches at the base of the crown clade are consistent with a rapid radiation, and the deep divergence of Macrurocyttus from both Grammicolepididae and the remainder of Zeniontidae supports its historical recognition as a distinctive lineage. Our markers provide a genomic backbone for future comparative work on zeiform morphological evolution, biogeography, and deep-sea diversification. Jon Armbruster
276: Human relationships with snakes are complex, with interactions ranging from persecution to stewardship. Fear-based attitudes can lead to hostile interactions, endangering people and snakes, moving researchers to work to identify factors that lead to conflict or coexistence. We conducted a systematic literature review to synthesize the factors that form both the positive and negative attitudes that influence our behavior towards snakes. Our first objective was to understand the state of knowledge about the factors influencing people’s attitudes and behaviors toward snakes. Our second objective was to document the geographic, demographic, and taxonomic representation among the human-snake attitude and behavior literature. We modified the PRISMA framework for systematic literature reviews. We included papers if they 1) collected original empirical data, and 2) measured one of the following: affective, cognitive, or conative attitudes about snakes, knowledge about snakes, or human behaviors toward snakes (for example, killing or relocating). This review will help us understand the factors that impact cognitive and attitudinal dimensions, which may ultimately influence people’s behaviors. Because human-wildlife interactions research is often context dependent, we hope to uncover biases in snake taxonomic groups, demographics, and geographies studied in human-snake research. This literature review will identify a larger breadth of attitude-behavior pathways and other factors influencing human-snake interactions. Our holistic review can guide interventions to not just mitigate snake-conflict, but also promote support for conservation and coexistence. Owen Bachhuber
277: Hybrid unisexual whiptail lizards exhibit lower endurance and mitochondrial respiration compared to their parental sexual species. We hypothesize that this may be due to mitonuclear incompatibility either derived from hybrid-derived or clonally-derived genetic variation. In eukaryotes, the nuclear and mitochondrial genomes must work in unison to facilitate energy production through oxidative phosphorylation. As a result, coevolution between these two genomes is vital for organism fitness, and ancestral (hybrid-derived) or de novo (clonallyderived) variation in their interacting genes can result in functional consequences. Here we examine patterns in the context of the hypothesis that hybrid-derived incompatibilities are responsible for lower endurance and mitochondrial respiration. Specifically, we assess the expression patterns of N-mt genes (nuclear encoded genes that localize to the mitochondrion), with special attention focused on genes that interact directly with mitochondrial gene products. Under this hypothesis, we predict that the expression of paternal N-mt alleles, which aren’t coadapted to the maternally-inherited mitochondrial genome, should exhibit expression levels equal-to or greaterthan those of the maternal N-mt alleles. Our preliminary results showed a parental bias in mitochondrial-interacting nuclear genes, notably within protein-protein interactions, and within the mitochondrial inner membrane. Our analysis of protein models shows spatial proximity of paternal-biased N-mt genes with mitochondrial genes, which could negatively affect mitochondrial respiration. Leah Bakewell Leah Bakewell; Carrie Alfonso; Karla Aleujevic; Samantha Fontaine; Jaden Keller; Yanileth Lopez-Tacoaman;
278: Digitized fish specimens represent a rapidly growing resource for biodiversity research, yet much of the information they contain remains difficult to access and analyze at scale. This poster explores how artificial intelligence and machine learning can be used to extract, standardize, and expand biological information from specimen images and associated data. We present several complementary approaches. First, orientation-aware object detection models are used to identify and localize multiple components within museum images, including specimens, eyes, labels, scalebars, barcodes, and calibration targets, despite variation in orientation, scale, and layout. Second, automated morphological pipelines generate biologically meaningful representations, such as finsuppressed silhouettes and midlines, enabling consistent extraction of traits related to body shape, curvature, and feature position across species. These methods support scalable morphometric analyses that are not feasible through manual workflows. We also highlight FishAIR, an AI-ready image infrastructure that integrates automated metadata extraction, image quality assessment, and provenance tracking to support reproducible workflows. Within this framework, derived artifacts such as segmentations, bounding boxes, and trait measurements are systematically linked to source images. The AIR vocabulary further standardizes descriptors for image quality, biological content, and computational outputs, enabling interoperability and consistent reuse across datasets and analytical pipelines. Together, these efforts demonstrate a shift from image repositories toward integrated, computation-ready data systems. By combining AI/ML methods with structured, provenance-aware data, this work enables more efficient data curation, improves data quality, and supports new forms of large-scale analysis in ichthyology, including phenomics, trait-environment studies, and evolutionary comparisons.
279: I used DNA barcoding of fecal pellets to determine the diet of Eleutherodactylus rogersi (Bahamian Flat-headed Frog), The Bahamas only endemic frog. In 2023, I sampled on four islands: Cat, Eleuthera, Long, and San Salvador. In 2024, fecal pellets (at least 10 / island; 82 total) were mailed to the NAU Bat Ecology & Genetics Lab “Species from Feces” for DNA barcoding. They amplify a short section of cytochrome oxidase subunit I (COI) using the ANML primer and compare sequencies against reference libraries derived from the Barcode of Life Database (BOLD), limited to arthropods only. Fifty dietary taxa (OTUs) were detected from the 82 fecal pellets. Of these, 5 were identifiable only to phylum (Arthropoda), 4 to class (2 Arachnida, 2 Insecta), and 19 to order (6 Araneae, 4 Sarcoptiformes, 1 Symphypleona, 3 Lepidoptera, 1 Amphipoda, and 4 Isopoda), and 22 OTU’s were identifiable to genus or species. E. rogersi is neither a strict specialist nor a full generalist. It consumes small, terrestrial prey items with spiders (Araneae), isopods (Isopoda) and ants (Hymenoptera: Formicidae) being the most common, composing 56% of all prey items detected. Only 2 taxa, Arachnida and Isopoda, were common to all 4 islands, with ants consumed on 3 of 4 islands. Surprisingly, only one beetle (Chrysomelidae), and no centipedes or millipedes were detected. Other prey items were lepidopterans (2), hemipterans (2), and dipterans (1). While identification of prey to species is limited to published sequences, DNA barcoding can detect rapidly digested softbodied prey and is non-lethal. Neil Balchan
280: Tropical forests across Malaysia, Indonesia, and Borneo create complex habitats that support high species richness, yet many regions remain poorly understood. Mountains, rivers, and elevational gradients can isolate animal populations, promoting evolutionary divergence. Amphibians are particularly useful for studying evolution because they are sensitive to environmental conditions and often have limited dispersal abilities. Even small geographic barriers can separate populations and eventually lead to the formation of new species. One amphibian group that reflects these patterns is the frog genus Leptobrachella (family Megophryidae). These frogs are small and typically live on the forest floor, concealed in leaf litter near clear streams in undisturbed tropical forests. Many species are similar in size, coloration, and body structure, making them difficult to distinguish using physical traits alone. Because of this similarity, traditional identification methods may underestimate true species diversity, making Leptobrachella an important system for studying cryptic biodiversity. This research investigates the evolutionary relationships of Leptobrachella species from the Kalimantan Timur of Indonesia through comparison of mitochondrial 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequences. Using Bayesian and maximum-likelihood analyses, we compare DNA sequences to construct phylogenetic trees and determine the placement of specimens collected from the Meratus Mountains within the genus, thereby expanding known species distributions across the Bornean landscape. Shannon Barry Shannon Barry; Matthew Ajemian; Charles Bangley; Laura Garcia Barcia; Jayne Gardiner; J. Marcus Drymon; Bryan Frazier; James Gelsleichter; R. Dean Grubbs; Neil Hammerschlag; Michael Heithaus; John Morris; Bradley
281: A team of researchers and educators at the California Academy of Sciences collaboratively developed an educational game with supporting resources that teach the principles of epidemiological modeling. The game is designed to simulate emerging knowledge of the chytridiomycosis pandemic in amphibians and the use of modeling to test hypotheses about disease dynamics in different contexts. First, students are introduced to the topics of amphibian diversity, the life cycle of the pathogen Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis, and ongoing amphibian chytridiomycosis research through three short videos. Next, students model the spread of chytridiomycosis in a population of frogs using a simple Susceptible-Infected-Recovered epidemiological model. Once students are comfortable with the basic S-I-R model, they move on to more complex models that simulate disease dynamics in different areas of the world with different communities of amphibians. The modeling evolves into more of a game, where students try to save their amphibian population by strategically choosing conservation actions and their populations are also subject to random events that can change things up. Google Sheets templates for recording data allow students to see the effects of their choices for their population in real time and to easily compare with their classmates. Through completing the activity, students learn about biodiversity, climate change, disease ecology, mathematical modeling, conservation strategies, and the scientific process while having fun fighting to save their frogs! This activity uses inexpensive materials and can be adapted to high school and undergraduate classrooms for one or multiple class periods with optional extension activities. Emma Bell
282: Reintroduction of species can help prevent extinction and maintain biodiversity. Many factors can play a role in the success or failure of reintroductions. Here, I present data on population dynamics of wood frogs (Rana sylvatica) in both an introduced population, and the source population the introduced population was drawn from. Like other early-spring breeding amphibians, warmer winter temperatures were associated with earlier breeding. In several years during this study, rapidly warming temperatures triggered the initiation of early breeding, but rapid freezing paused breeding. Prolonged freezes increased egg mortality, in some years killing all the eggs laid during the initial breeding bout. Over the course of the study, the introduced population remained smaller than the source, and also had a higher coefficient of variation in population size. Although earlier breeding can present benefits to some amphibian populations, rapid fluctuations in temperature and subsequent egg mortality present a cost. Populations in the initial phase of introduction are likely more vulnerable to extinction from these temperature fluctuations. Michael F. Benard
283: The Eastern Newt (Notophthalmus viridescens) is a common species that occupies ponds across eastern North America. Newts can act as a keystone predator on amphibian guilds in some scenarios. However, recent evidence suggests that keystone predation function may result from sexually dimorphic effects. For example, Eastern Newts are sexually dimorphic in 1) morphology head size with females having wider gapes and 2) the areas of ponds they occupy with females foraging primarily in benthic areas of ponds. Surprisingly, records of natural variation of sex ratios within ponds is lacking with limited published data reporting the sex ratios are most often male dominated, with additional evidence showing the ratio can shift over seasons. Multi-year sampling from ponds in Missouri and multi-month sampling from ponds in North Carolina help identify patterns in the sex ratios of newts within ponds over seasons. This sampling allows us to test for evidence of habitat/behavior partitioning between sexes as well as potential bias in capture method. Preliminary analysis suggests that sex ratios are on average strongly male dominated and trends show highest male dominance in the first quarter of the year. This study provides data on natural variation and can serve as a basis for future experimental work. Rebecca Frances Bentley
284: Glucocorticoid hormones (GC), such as corticosterone and cortisol (CORT), are commonly used indicators of physiological stress in vertebrate animals. However, their interpretation relies on developing baselines for typical GC concentration and how they vary by season, sex, and age-class. We examined CORT metabolite concentrations in wild and captive-reared Blunt-nosed Leopard Lizards (Gambelia sila), an endangered species endemic to central California. Despite having endangered status for over 50y and substantial research on decline of native habitat, no information is available on CORT physiology in G. sila. This knowledge gap limits our ability to assess relative stress levels among extant populations or in response to environmental stressors such as habitat degradation or captivity. We first quantified seasonal variation in CORT concentrations from fecal samples collected directly from wild lizards and opportunistically from the environment. Pooled across all samples, CORT concentration displayed a parabolic pattern, first increasing and then decreasing across the active season. Results from known lizard samples suggest that this pattern is driven by increased CORT concentrations in gravid females during the first half of the active season. One-year old animals also displayed higher CORT than older animals in both sexes. We next compared CORT concentrations between the wild-collected samples and samples collected from a closely-related captive-breeding colony at Fresno Chaffee Zoo. CORT from captive animals was indistinguishable from wild animals. Our results provide an important CORT baseline for future G. sila studies and will inform ongoing efforts to repatriate and restore this endangered lizard. Moisés A. Bernal
285: As weather events and temperatures become more extreme, amphibians are at higher risk of population decline. Plethodon cinereus (Eastern Red-backed Salamander) is commonly known for its color polymorphism, but the proximate and ultimate factors behind that polymorphism are unknown. Previous work has found life strategy differences between the striped (red-back) and unstriped (lead-back) color morphs. These differences include increased stress and predation of the unstriped morph (Davis, 2010). Corticosterone (CORT) is a stress hormone found in amphibians that can be quantified using dermal skin swabs and enzyme-linked immunoassay (Santymire, 2018). This study aims to determine whether stress levels (CORT) are affected by increased ambient temperatures or color morph. Salamanders were sampled using natural cover objects in Richmond, VA, Ithaca, NY, & Susquehanna, PA. Upon collection, salamanders were swabbed with a sterile cotton swab to establish baseline cortisol levels. After being transported to the lab, salamanders were held for one hour at the average collection temperature before beginning the experiment. Individuals were randomly assigned to control or experimental groups. Control individuals were held at collection temperature while experimental individuals were held at +6° for one hour each. Salamanders were swabbed again before being returned to the collection site. This work is being conducted during the 2026 field season, and data analysis will occur upon completion of the season, before presentation. Chloe Bestgen
286: This study investigates regionalization (i.e., modularity) of the anterior vertebral column in basal ostariophysan fishes. The superorder of Ostariophysi is comprised of two subgroups/series, Otophysi and Anotophysi. Otophysi (e.g., carps, minnows, catfishes) is diagnosed by the presence of a Weberian apparatus, which consists of a modified series of anterior vertebral elements arranged in a linear sequence connecting the swim bladder to the inner ear, and functions in high frequency sound transmission. The series Anotophysi (order Gonorynchiformes) although not possessing a functioning Weberian apparatus, exhibits several modifications of the anterior vertebral region (e.g., expanded neural arches and supraneurals, modified pleural ribs) that some researchers hypothesized are precursors to Weberian apparatus elements. Recent studies have determined that the Weberian apparatus in otophysans is a functional module (i.e., a semi-autonomous set of highly correlated traits within larger units). Modularity of the anterior vertebral region in gonorynchiform fishes has until now, not been investigated. The goal of this project is, therefore, to investigate modularity of the anterior vertebral region in two key gonorynchiform taxa (i.e., Chanos and Gonorynchus) using 3-D geometric morphometric analyses based on microCT scans. The results from this study will provide a better understanding of regionalization of the anterior vertebral column in Ostariophysi, and hopefully provide insights into the evolution of the Weberian apparatus. Jordyn Bharratsingh
287: The thorny catfishes (Doradidae) are readily diagnosed by a midlateral series of bony scutes bearing thorns, a flexible parapophysis associated with a specialized protractor muscle and firmly connected to the swim bladder wall forming the elastic spring apparatus involved in sound production, and a broad cephalic shield extending posteriorly and connected to the dorsal fin. Currently, 96 valid extant species are recognized, in addition to one extinct species, Doras dionae. Several well-preserved fossils from different localities and ages have also been tentatively assigned to extant doradid genera. This study describes a second extinct doradid species, assesses its phylogenetic position, and identifies its diagnostic features. Comparative analyses were conducted between fossil material and dry skeletons of extant species, and both two- and three-dimensional imaging techniques were used to document the new taxon. A total evidence phylogenetic analysis was performed, including 180 morphological characters coded for the new extinct species, Doras dionae, and 90 extant doradids, combined with data from three molecular markers. Results indicate that the new extinct species is closely related to the two extant species of Centrodoras, forming a clade sister to Lithodoras + Megalodoras. The new extinct species is assigned to Centrodoras and distinguished by a relatively large anterior nuchal plate, a narrow interorbital distance, and shallowly concave lateral margins of the middle nuchal plate. The species is based on six fossils from the upper member of the Urumaco Formation, in Venezuela, dated to approximately nine million years ago. Joseph Bizzarro
288: Reconstructing time-calibrated phylogenies for species-rich clades remains a major challenge due to incomplete taxonomic sampling and the computational demands of large genomic datasets. Ovalentaria is a diverse clade of percomorph fishes with broad variation in reproductive strategies, making it a strong system for studying trait evolution. Despite this diversity, a comprehensive time-calibrated phylogeny for this clade has been lacking. Here, we infer a fossil-calibrated phylogeny of Ovalentaria using a multilocus dataset of exon-capture sequences spanning 576 taxa across all major lineages. Divergence times were estimated in BEAST 2 under a Bayesian relaxed-clock model, incorporating 23 fossil calibrations as hard minimum constraints and soft maximum bounds derived using the Hedman (2010) approach. A Birth-Death tree prior was used to model diversification, and posterior distributions of trees were summarized to generate a maximum clade credibility chronogram. To improve taxonomic representation beyond the backbone dataset, additional taxa were incorporated by grafting phylogenies from 21 previously published studies and from newly inferred trees based on publicly available sequence data. Secondary dating on subtrees was conducted using the PhyloChronoRank pipeline and trees were grafted onto the fossil-calibrated backbone following methods outlined by Betancur-R., increasing taxonomic coverage while preserving the temporal framework inferred from the Bayesian evolutionary analysis. The resulting phylogeny with over 3,500 taxa represents a substantially expanded, time-calibrated hypothesis of relationships across Ovalentaria and provides a foundation for large-scale comparative analyses. This framework enables future tests of reproductive trait evolution and other macroevolutionary hypotheses within one of the most diverse radiations of teleost fishes. Ella Boback
289: Invasive reptile species may play a role in the environmental dissemination of foodborne pathogens. The Argentine black and white tegu (Salvator merianae), an invasive species established in Florida, frequently inhabits agricultural environments, increasing the potential for fecal contamination of fresh produce. This study investigates the prevalence and antibiotic susceptibility of Salmonella spp. isolated from tegus in Florida. Fecal and cloacal samples were collected from 98 wild tegus captured through established USDA management programs. Samples were processed using standard microbiological culture methods for the isolation and identification of Salmonella. Confirmed isolates will undergo antimicrobial susceptibility testing for the following antibiotics including ampicillin, azithromycin, cefoxitin, ceftriaxone, chloramphenicol, ciprofloxacin, gentamicin, meropenem, nalidixic acid, tetracycline, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, in accordance with established clinical guidelines. This study characterizes the prevalence and antibiotic resistance of Salmonella in an invasive species to assess its role as a potential environmental reservoir. Because tegus inhabit agricultural areas, the findings may have important implications for food safety and public health. Jack Boyette Jack Boyette; Tamilie Carvalho; David Rodriguez; Wesley Neely; Daniel Medina; Renato Martins; Robert Ossiboff; Zaira Gomez; William Vuyk; Shannon Buttimer; Karen Paniagua Torres; Ananda Brito de Assis; Carlos Navas;
290: Natural History Collections are invaluable sources of biological information for research, education, conservation, and public outreach but often lack the resources, programming expertise, and infrastructure needed to create custom digital tools for data accessibility. Large scale data aggregators facilitate data access but partially address common institutional needs. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has rapidly changed the way developers create, maintain, optimize, and test code, lowering the technical barrier to software creation. AI-assisted coding can accelerate the development of tools for digitization, data management and visualization, and public accessibility in Natural History Collections. In this project, I demonstrate the use of AI-assisted coding in the development of two custom web applications designed to address common institutional needs. I built two web applications using GPT 5.3 Codex based on data exported from the Cornell University Museum of Vertebrates database. The first tool is a specimen search portal enabling multi field filtering, data export, and mapping of localities. The second contains an interactive map to visualize the sampling of localities for four collections and a cumulative graph of specimens and lots sampled through time. Both applications performed the intended functions accurately, demonstrating that AIassisted coding can be used to generate operational, lightweight applications for Natural History Collections. The development of web applications through AI-assisted coding reduces technical barriers, enabling the creation of tailored tools with minimal infrastructure. Careful prompt design, refinement, and attention to data security are essential for robust results and safe adoption of this technology. Michael Britton
291: Lampreys are an ancient lineage of jawless fishes, spanning over 300 million years of evolution. Within Petromyzontidae, a unique process of speciation referred to as the ‘paired-species concept’ proposed that non-parasitic lamprey species are directly derived from parasitic ancestors. Nearly all extant brook lampreys evolved within the past 60 million years, which suggests over two-thirds of all lampreys are derived from relatively recent ecological speciation. However, the species limits within most paired species are under-explored, leaving doubt regarding the status of disjunct populations of brook lampreys. We evaluate the potential for cryptic species within Ichthyomyzon gagei, a nonparasitic species with a disjunct northern and southern population that may constitute two species. We examine morphological and genetic variation among the two populations of I. gagei to identify functional differences due to the population split and potential speciation between them. Detecting speciation within brook lampreys has implications for understanding the processes that drive diversification within lampreys and may indicate alternatives to the paired-species concept. Brett O. Butler
292: Maintenance of genetic diversity and successful reproduction of captive stock is integral to the sustainability of zoological collections. However, many captive breeding programs suffer from low reproductive success, which increases inbreeding susceptibility and hinders conservation efforts. The Eastern Massasauga Rattlesnake (Sistrurus catenatus) is an imperiled viper that poses several challenges to captive reproduction. Specific aspects of female S. catenatus reproductive biology, such as long-term sperm storage (LTSS) and the ability to produce multiple paternity litters, reduce confidence in inferred ancestry and could alter current understanding of relatedness and genetic health of captive individuals. Studies are needed to determine how multiple paternity and LTSS impact reproductive success. Current genomic approaches can provide fine-scale measures of genetic diversity and relatedness, thus offering increased accuracy to programs aimed at making informed breeding recommendations. We will estimate genetic health and first-order relationships using high-throughput Restrictionsite associated DNA sequencing (RADseq) of captive populations across the Eastern Massasauga Saving Animals From Extinction (SAFE) program in the United States. Results of this study will equip zoo husbandry managers with molecular pedigrees and metrics of inbreeding to make high-confidence pairing recommendations Angelo Cantu
293: Behavioral lateralization is widespread among vertebrates, including fish, amphibians, and reptiles, yet evidence in snakes remains scarce and inconsistent. We investigated ambush-posture laterality in the Chinese green tree pit viper (Trimeresurus stejnegeri), a nocturnal sit-and-wait predator, using 283 independent observations from northern Taiwan. Data were compiled from long-term nocturnal field surveys (2014–2025) and verified citizenscience records (2013–2025). Ambush direction was determined from photographs using a standardized, anatomically based method, with ambiguous cases excluded. We tested for population-level bias across three sites and evaluated potential effects of age class and perching height. Here, 36 of 55 individuals (65.5%) at Yangmingshan exhibited a significant rightward bias, whereas no population-level laterality was detected at the other sites. Neither age class nor perching height influenced ambush direction. These results provide evidence for site-specific population-level lateralization in a snake and suggest that lateralization is context-dependent rather than fixed. This study highlights the value of integrating long-term field surveys with citizen-science data to address questions in behavioral ecology and reptile evolution. Hung-Chia Chang (Vincent)
294: The integration of citizen science platforms into undergraduate education provides opportunities to engage students in authentic biodiversity documentation. This study evaluates the use of iNaturalist as a tool for documenting Puerto Rican herpetofauna in a zoology laboratory course. Across four semesters (2021–2023), 156 students submitted photographic or audio observations as part of a structured assignment requiring a minimum of five anuran and five reptile species per student. Students collectively generated a dataset representing multiple taxonomic families of amphibians and reptiles, demonstrating broad taxonomic coverage. Shannon diversity indices (H′ ≈ 2.0) indicate consistent diversity in the assemblage documented by students. Observations were dominated by common native anurans, including Eleutherodactylus coqui, E. antillensis, E. cochranae, and Leptodactylus albilabris, along with introduced species such as Rhinella marina and Osteopilus septentrionalis. Among reptiles, frequently recorded species included Anolis cristatellus, Iguana iguana, Pholidoscelis exsul, and Hemidactylus mabouia. Differences in the relative representation of taxonomic families suggest variation in detection and observation patterns, likely influenced by species visibility and student behavior. Overall, iNaturalist effectively engaged students in documenting local biodiversity while producing a dataset with meaningful taxonomic breadth. These findings support the incorporation of citizen science platforms into laboratory curricula to promote active learning, field observation skills, and contributions to biodiversity databases. Luiza Chelotti
295: The Common Fangtooth, Anoplogaster cornuta, is a deep-sea generalist feeder notable for its impressive dentition. Their oral jaws have long, recurved, fang-like teeth whose function has confounded scientists for over a century. There few teeth on the lower jaw, with teeth usually paired on the left and right sides in a 3+3, 4+4, or 5+5 arrangement. The anterior-most tooth is the longest while the posterior teeth are substantially shorter and feature rounded, knob-like caps at their tips. The relationship between tooth shape and tooth function is not straightforward, as the placement of teeth along the jaw can also influence tooth function. We analyzed tooth morphology in A. cornuta to test for functional homodonty or functional heterodonty. Micro-ct scan data was obtained from 25 individuals of A. cornuta, ranging in size from 80-125 mm SL. Specimens included the 3+3, 4+4, and 5+5 arrangement of teeth, plus specimens with unequal tooth numbers of 3+4 and 4+5. This is the first time that unequal tooth numbers on the dentary has been reported. There was no significant effect of fish size and tooth number. The software package Dental Dynamics was used to assess functional homodonty and heterodonty in A. cornuta. The results of this study reveals the functional significance of the unique tooth arrangement in the Common Fangtooth. Antrelle D. Clark
296: Advancing science in invasive species can sometimes seem at odds with immediate management objectives. By the time an invasive species gains attention, it simultaneously requires management to prevent spread and research to optimize management decisions and tools. Efficient management cannot occur without knowledge of the species, and in some cases, information about ecology, reproduction, and impacts are lacking and may differ from information available from its native range. Limited budgets and personnel provide challenges to optimizing management, but collaborative efforts can help overcome these challenges. We present a case for collaboration across disciplines in the Argentine Black and White Tegu, Salvator merianae. This tegu is a large omnivorous lizard with notable cold tolerance that is expanding its invasive range in the United States. Trapping efforts are ongoing but face challenges in population reduction potential. There are needs to understand its reproductive ecology, develop effective lures, and quantify impacts to improve management efficacy. We partnered with ongoing removal efforts from state and federal agencies to obtain tegus to advance science in multiple avenues. From 98 tegus removed from Florida by managers in 2025, we are pursuing efforts with multiple collaborators from universities and zoological institutions to quantify reproductive hormone cycling from blood samples, investigate changes in chemical compounds associated with reproductive seasonality and their potential as pheromonal and visual attractants, describe seasonal changes in reproductive anatomy, screen for pathogens, and contribute data to ongoing diet analyses on this species. We present preliminary data on these efforts to advance invasion science. Rebecca Clemons
297: A non-native Petroscirtes blenny was documented off Kona in Hawaiʻi. Using morphology and a COI barcode, the species was determined as Petroscirtes breviceps, which has an established range of over 5,000km west of the Hawaiian Islands. While the path of introduction is unknown, the most likely explanation is from marine debris. Petroscirtes blennies are capable of long-distance dispersal by associating with drifting debris. Although this is the first confirmed record of Petroscirtes in Hawaiʻi, two additional iNaturalist records were posted the same year. Monitoring and further research will be necessary to determine if a population is becoming established, what impacts this blenny might have on native species, and if marine debris introductions will become more common as the ocean continues to accumulate debris. Lexi Cochran
298: Space-for-time substitution is the assumption that ecological relationships found along space or time are equivalent, allowing temporal patterns to be extrapolated into space and vice versa. This assumption has been widely debated in the ecological literature, with support contingent on scale and ecological context. Space-for-time substitution has been used in many areas of ecology, such as the study of ecological succession, but few studies have investigated its usefulness in population ecology modeling. Here, we used space-for-time substitution to extrapolate demographic rates across the distribution of the tropical lizard Tropidurus torquatus, based on 25 years of capturemark-recapture data. We used a Pradel model to estimate the effects of climate variables, thermal physiology, and breeding phenology on survivorship and seniority rates in a monitored population. Seniority rates were then used to derive per capita recruitment. We then used the same model to extrapolate demographic rates from the monitored population across the entire range of T. torquatus, using equivalent spatial predictors related to climate, thermal physiology, and breeding phenology. We then derived population growth rates across the species’ range from survivorship and per capita recruitment rates. Lastly, we tested whether estimated population growth rates were better predictors of local occurrence than climatic variables. Population growth was not a better predictor of occurrence than climate, suggesting that space-for-time substitution did not yield reliable estimates of demographic rates in T. torquatus. We discuss processes that may violate this assumption and propose avenues to improve the spatial extrapolation of demographic rates. Tim Colston Edgardo Rosado-Ramos; Jacob Adam; Eneilis Oliveras; Fabian Feliciano-Rivera; Gualberto Rodriguez; Alberto
299: Microbes found living on or inside vertebrate hosts are widely known to impact a suite of traits related to host fitness, including development, immune response, nutrient acquisition, and reproduction. Reptiles are one of the most threatened vertebrate groups and among the least studied regarding their associated microbiota. The Puerto Rican Boa (Chilabothrus. inornatus) is an Endangered Species and an icon of endemic Puerto Rican herpetofauna. We characterized the skin, oral and gut microbiome (bacterial and fungal) of the Puerto Rican Boa via culture techniques and a combination of next-generation and traditional sanger sequencing. Samples were collected from cave populations in Arecibo, Isabela, Cabo Rojo, Aguadilla and Hatillo on the main island of Puerto Rico. By cataloging the microbiome diversity of this enigmatic species, we can begin to understand the role of the microbiome in host pathogen defense (e.g. against invasive fungal pathogens, such as Ophidiomyces ophidiicola) as well as the begin to document how the microbiome shifts under changing climatic in a dynamic tropical island ecosystem. Andrea L. Colton Andrea Colton; Thomas Akre; Quinn Bozek; Kira Cates; Elizabeth Culp; Matt Elliott; Andrew Grosse; Jeffery Hall; Emma Kendrick; John Kleopfer; Ivana Mali; Jonathan Mays; Kevin Oxenrider; Chris Polinski; Lisabeth Willey;
300: The Sharpnose shiner Notropis oxyrhynchus is endemic to the Brazos River drainage of Texas. At the time of original description (1951), this species occurred throughout almost the entire length of the Brazos River mainstem, as well the Double Mountain Fork of the Brazos River, a major tributary in the upper part of the system. Since 1951, Sharpnose shiner have undergone a major range contraction and are now restricted to the uppermost part of the Brazos River drainage, above Possum Kingdom Lake, and the species was placed on the US endangered species list in 2014. Despite its endangered status, the Sharpnose shiner has received little attention from ichthyologists, and there is currently no information available on the anatomy of this species beyond that reported in the original description (limited to counts of fin rays and pharyngeal teeth). To advance understanding of the biology of N. oxyrhynchus, and the anatomy of leuciscid minnows more generally, we present an anatomical atlas for the Sharpnose shiner. Our atlas, which covers both male and female anatomy, stems from a combination of traditional and contrast enhanced CT-scanning, scanning electron microscopy, serial sectioning, and gross dissection of formalin-fixed museum specimens (most collected in the 1980s and 90s). Using our atlas, we document (for the first time) organs of the abdominal cavity (in both sexes) and aspects of the musculoskeletal system. We also document (for the first time), the existence of externally visible secondary sexual dimorphism in the Sharpnose shiner, represented by nuptial tubercles on the head and pectoral fin of males. Though basic, our atlas may contribute to the conservation of the species (e.g., by allowing managers to identify the sex of an individual more easily in the field based on external characters). Ryan Cook
301: Head up displays were observed in Aneides aeneus during aggressive interactions in lab and field. Male A aeneus in SE Kentucky have large, bifurcated mental glands located under the chin that are important in courtship behavior. The color of the mental gland ranges from white to yellow to orange which is unique among north american plethodontid salamanders. Two individuals with orange mental glands were observed in the lab raising their heads at an angle of about 45 degrees in the presence of intruding males. Five other males with lighter mental glands also exhibited the head up display. This display alone may serve as a threat to intruding males. The head up posture plus the orange color of the mental gland could represent a territorial display as well. This behavior may also occur in females. In the field, a head up display was observed three separate times by a single female brooding eggs in a rock crevice. The female was between the eggs and the crevice opening. This behavior was displayed once each month during July, August and September in response to a flashlight and a stick probe introduced into the crevice. In each instance, the female raised her head up and down several times which may be a further development of the head up response observed in males. Also, the female bit the probe in each instance. These display behaviors observed in A. aeneus may be intraspecific displays that help in maintaining territories and /or preventing oophagy. Tobey Curtis Tobey Curtis; Daniel Daye; Ian Miller; Delisse Ortiz; Alyssa Mathers; John Carlson; Daniel Crear; Brad McHale;
302: Non-native species can directly and indirectly compete with native species for access to resources, negatively affecting individual health and fitness and resulting in reduced population sizes of native taxa. The Moorish Gecko, Tarentola mauritanica (Phyllodactylidae), is a large species native to the Mediterranean Region of Europe and northern Africa. As with many other gecko species, T. mauritanica has been introduced outside its native range. Recently, non-native populations of T. mauritanica have been established in Texas, USA. To better understand the ecological impact of T. mauritanica, we examined the species’ diet from populations in south-central Texas. Voucher specimens were collected annually during the month of September for three years (2023–2025). During preservation, stomachs of individuals were removed and stored in 10% buffered formalin and later transferred to 70% ethanol. Later, we examined stomach contents using a dissecting microscope, identified prey items to order, and estimated the volume of each prey item. In total, we collected 245 specimens of various age, size, and sex across the three years. Of these, 214 (87%) contained diet items in their stomach. Our data show that the diet of T. mauritanica primarily consists of invertebrates, matching previously published reports, with flies (Diptera), termites (Isoptera), and moths (Lepidoptera) being found most frequently. By volume, crickets (Orthoptera), moths (Lepidoptera), and cockroaches (Blattodea) were most significant. This research represents the first detailed account of the diet of T. mauritanica in the USA and may be a step toward understanding consequences of this species’ introduction. Isabella V. Davis
303: Across taxa and worldwide, emerging infectious diseases are threatening wild populations. Amphibian species have experienced rapid population declines in recent years and are the most threatened vertebrate class worldwide. Likewise, infectious diseases impact 29% of amphibian species worldwide. Three major pathogens contribute to declines across amphibian populations: Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (fungus), Ranavirus (virus) and Amphibian Perkinsea (protist). Recent analysis of long-term aquatic monitoring datasets across the southern two-thirds of the Everglades have revealed dramatic decreases in amphibian abundances, but amphibian disease assessments are lacking in this region. To assess whether disease may contribute to population declines in the Everglades, 8 species of amphibians were sampled from all six major sub-basins in the Water Conservation area. Custom Taqman qPCR on DNA extracted from toe or tail clips was run to detect and quantify infection with Bd, Rv, and Pr. We found no Pr in any of the amphibians sampled for this study. We found a lower prevalence of Bd than Rv in the Everglades. We found higher prevalence of Rv in the invasive species, Osteopilus septentrionalis. This project will address a critical knowledge gap by quantifying infections with three major amphibian pathogens across Everglades species and populations, thereby advancing our understanding of disease ecology in amphibians from an iconic World Heritage site. Rebecca Davis
304: Ultrasonography is widely used in reproductive research. In many species, changes in follicular size, shape, echogenicity, etc. are easily tracked indicating the stages of female reproductive development. However, ultrasound is an under-used method in reproductive research in males, and even more so in non-mammalian species. Until now, the study of annual reproductive cycles of male snakes have included the use of lethal procedures. Here, we applied the same concepts of female tracking via ultrasound to male reproductive anatomy. The length, width, and height of the testes of male Louisiana pinesnakes (Pithuophis ruthveni) were measured to calculate total volume. While multiple formulas have been published for calculating the volume of elliptical-spheroid organs (i.e., testes), the final equation was chosen due to the results matching closest to the verified displacement measured from a small subset of excised testes. The testes of 20 male pinesnakes were images via ultrasound monthly throughout the active period (March through October). Measurable changes in size and echogenicity were seen across the active period, suggesting ultrasound as an alternative to lethal procedures for observing seasonal gonadal development and the tracking of annual reproductive cycles in male snakes. Madeline Davis
305: Only two published scientific studies have focused on barracuda stress physiology. One found that great barracuda exposed to stressors associated with fishing took much longer to find refuge and displayed signs of decreased mobility and disorientation, while another found the species generally showed low levels of lactate, a byproduct of exhaustive exercise, after angling. This project aimed to better understand stress in barracuda by evaluating bycaught individuals captured in fisheries-independent longline and drumline shark surveys for stress. It also validated the use of a point-of-care device for barracuda lactate levels using laboratory assays. Data shows sea surface temperatures positively correlated with higher lactate values in bycaught individuals. Future studies should focus on the recovery of barracuda from angling to expand understanding of capture stress and recovery rates in great barracuda within Southeast Florida. David A. Davis
306: Urbanization of the Chicago metropolitan area has drastically altered the landscape of northeastern Illinois over the past two centuries. Once dominated by forest and marshy wetlands, the region is now characterized by dense urban centers highly fragmented by several major roadways. The resulting loss of natural habitat has impacted regional abundances of some turtle species, such as the state-endangered Blanding’s Turtle (Emydoidea blandingii). Despite modern environmental protections, fragmentation and degradation of the remaining habitat provide little opportunity for populations to expand or recolonize their former range naturally. We sampled 18 publicly owned forest preserves, conservation areas, and mitigation sites for aquatic turtles to determine species richness, diversity, and evenness of the present assemblages. Species richness ranged from 1 to 5, with most assemblages comprising common species considered resilient to anthropogenic disturbance, such as the Painted Turtle (Chrysemys picta) and Common Snapping Turtle (Chelydra serpentina). Diversity indices ranged from 0 to 1.31, while evenness indices varied from 0.38 to 1. We intend to continually reassess turtle assemblages at all sites on a five-year rotation to gain a long-term temporal understanding of demographic trends. Wesley Aaron Dillard
307: The earliest vertebrates possessed dermal skeletons consisting of bony plates capped with various dental tissues. Most extant bony fish lineages have reduced or lost this dental element of their armor with only the derived bony element remaining, present either thin overlapping scales or dense dermal scutes. However, nine disparate lineages of teleost fish have re-evolved odontodes, tooth-like structures consisting of dentine and a pulp cavity, as part of their dermal armor. Amongst this group, only armored catfish (Loricarioidae) have evolved both bony and dental elements despite having evolved from a scaleless ancestor, mimicking the armor of stem vertebrates despite it being a derived trait. Here we investigate the utility of the bristlenose armored catfish, Ancistrus spp. as a potential model for the evolution and development of dermal armor in bony fishes. We use a variety of techniques including immunohistochemistry, Computed Tomography (CT), small molecule inhibition, and diaphonization to examine questions about morphological development, developmental origin, and developmental pathways. We show the unique development of odontocomplexes in armored catfish throughout early development with influence from putative developmental pathways. Together, these data highlight ways in which studying armored catfish development contributes to our understanding of the evolution of the dermal skeleton in teleosts. Samantha Dillon
308: Heightened national security concerns continue to drive administrative goals to secure the U.S.-MX international border by any means necessary. The construction of a contiguous, impermeable barrier along the southwestern border has raised ecological concerns among conservationists and wildlife managers. The Texas tortoise (Gopherus berlandieri) is a small tortoise found throughout the Tamaulipan biotic province and is listed as threatened in Texas. The installation of a large, linear barrier across the southern tip of Texas potentially threatens to the persistence of G. berlandieri by disrupting suitable habitat connectivity, leading to cascading impacts to population stability over time. Our objectives were to characterize suitable habitats using ensemble habitat suitability modeling and estimate their potential functional connectivity by using model outputs to establish a framework for circuit-theoretical connectivity analysis. We used this multi-scale modeling approach to investigate long-term ecological impacts posed by the U.S.-MX international border barrier system on populations of G. berlandieri along the southernmost borderland of Texas. Samantha Dillon
309: The 4 July 2025 flood in the upper Guadalupe River in central Texas took over 100 lives and impacted many thousands more. The unique combination of a concentrated, high-energy storm and the location of heaviest precipitation in the uppermost watershed meant that the volume and velocity of flood waters in the main river channel across Kerr County attained destructive power unprecedented in this system. Using a combination of original survey data and iNaturalist records, biodiversity was assessed before and after the flood, with a focus on fish, amphibians, and reptiles. The river channel was inaccessible for surveying for approximately two months after the flood. As surveys became possible, biodiversity detections indicated that only a portion of species recorded before the flood are still being detected. Local distributions of some species were affected. Even accounting for bias toward large and culturally important species being overreported in iNaturalist, depletion of most species appears to persist. Lan Do Lan Do; Ella Neuenschwander; Brittney Parks; Ariana Brown; Devon Haley; Brooklyn Upp; Bryan Juarez; Maggie
310: The family Triglidae comprises a morphologically distinctive, circumglobally distributed group of benthic marine fishes, commonly known as searobins or gurnards. Members of this family are characterized by head and body armament (i.e. spines and boney plates), large wing-like pectoral fins, and sound production involving the swim bladder. Their most notable attribute is the presence of free pectoral rays that bear chemosensory structures and are associated with modified skeletal elements and musculature, allowing triglids to “walk” along the bottom and detect infaunal prey. Currently, the family contains 177 recognized species across 14 genera and four subfamilies. Previous phylogenetic reconstructions generated for the family have yielded conflicting relationships at multiple hierarchical levels, including among subfamilies, genera, and species, likely due to variable taxon sampling and differences in phylogenetic signal among morphological and molecular datasets. To further examine these relationships, we generated a phylogenomic dataset using target enrichment of ultra-conserved DNA elements (UCEs) for 69 triglid species and eight outgroup taxa. Results from maximum likelihood (IQ-TREE) and species tree (ASTRAL-III) analyses recover congruent topologies, providing a framework for testing biogeographic hypotheses and understanding processes driving diversification in this family at a global scale. Natalie H. Donato
311: Eurycea sosorum individuals in the City of Austin (COA) salamander assurance colony have experienced a reduction in toe, foot, and sometimes limb length. Because pH and calcium concentrations in captivity differed from conditions in the wild, we experimentally tested whether they caused appendage reduction. We tested two replicates of three combinations of “low” (~7.1) and “high” (~8.1) pH with “low” (~35 mg/L) and “high” (~100 mg/L) Ca2+ concentration. Two controls were fed with groundwater to replicate pH and Ca2+ conditions in the wild. We stocked each tank with 12 adult captive-reared E. sosorum. The salamanders were visually assessed quarterly and photographed at the start and every six months for 1.5 years. Measurements of total length, body length, and toe length of each foot were made at the start and the end of the experiment. Over 1.5 years, appendage reduction did not occur. Our results indicate that the tested water chemistry changes of low calcium, the combination of high pH and low calcium, or a static system mimicking the conditions in the wild do not result in appendage reduction in E. sosorum. Paige Donkers
312: Ringneck snakes (Diadophis punctatus) are often thought of as generalist predators that feed on a variety of invertebrates and vertebrates. However, quantitative assessments of their diet remain limited. To address this gap, we used stable isotope analysis to estimate the contribution of four co-occurring plethodontid taxa to the diet of D. punctatus. Using sampled tissues from D. punctatus, four Plethodon species (Plethodon montanus, Plethodon cylindraceus, Plethodon yonahlossee, Plethodon cinereus) and a suite of invertebrates (earthworms, slugs, ants), we analyzed isotopic overlap to infer trophic relationships within forest floor ecosystems of northwestern North Carolina. Previous work has shown that tail tips can provide coarse information on salamander diets without the need to sacrifice individuals.
