We calculated isotopic niche space and diets of each species using tail tips from all field-collected salamander tail tissue. Our results suggest that salamanders make up a substantial portion of D. punctatus diet. Among the species examined, Plethodon yonahlossee contributed the least to the assimilated diet, indicating potential prey selectivity. This pattern may reflect ecological or behavioral differences, including the larger body size of P. yonahlossee or its broader diet, which may reduce temporal or spatial overlap with actively foraging snakes. This reinforces the significant role that salamanders can play in structuring forest floor food webs and suggests a more specialized diet in Diadophis punctatus in certain environments. Kylie Dowd
313: Contemporary freshwater fish distributions and biodiversity in eastern and central North America reflect episodic Pleistocene climate cycles, during which alternating glacial and interglacial phases repeatedly restructured interior hydrology. Northern fish populations were shaped by cyclical dispersal: advancing glaciers displaced populations into southern refugia, followed by recolonization during glacial retreat. As a result, northern population genetics were influenced by refugial isolation, transient dispersal corridors, topographic barriers, and intrinsic biological constraints. The bigmouth shiner (Ericymba dorsalis) occupies a largely northern distribution within previously glaciated regions of the upper Mississippi River and Great Lakes basins. It is widespread in tributaries of the Red, Missouri, Mississippi, and Illinois rivers, with fragmented, disjunct populations in western Michigan, Ohio, western New York and Pennsylvania, and northern West Virginia. These eastern populations are of conservation concern, being listed as threatened in several states and likely extirpated from West Virginia. Mitochondrial phylogeography reveals a basal east–west divergence (~1.4 Ma), indicating long-term isolation between major population groups. A more recent western divergence (~0.5–0.7 Ma) among Missouri, Mississippi, and Illinois river clades corresponds to mid-Pleistocene drainage reorganization and isolation in multiple western refugia. In the east, divergence between an Allegheny River lineage and a Great Lakes lineage (~1.1 Ma) suggests prolonged isolation in an upper Ohio–Teays refugium, possibly alongside a separate Atlantic refugium. These patterns indicate that deep lineage structure predates the Wisconsin glaciation and was reinforced by repeated glacial vicariance and postglacial recolonization. Tim Earley
314: This study investigates the phylogenetic relationships among species of the North American subfamily Pogonichthyinae (family Leuciscidae) using the complete mitochondrial genome. We accomplish this through the analysis of whole mitochondrial genomes of 85 species. By comparing our phylogenetic trees to those produced using other genetic material, we contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of these relationships. We demonstrate the monophyly of Pogonichthyinae as a subfamily among closely related outgroup species. Our results confirm the hypothesis of several other authors: for example, the monophyly of the group containing Tiaroga, Oregonichthys, and Rhinichthys. However, we also increase support at some previously ambiguous nodes and note some interesting differences in relationships to other published studies. Emily Echevarria
315: Seahorses (Hippocampus spp.) produce clicking sounds through a stridulatory mechanism by snapping their heads in a rapid, stereotyped motion. These clicks are commonly produced during feeding, mating, social encounters, and stressful situations. We characterized the acoustic behavior of click production of Hippocampus erectus during feeding events, and quantified the acoustic characteristics that include peak frequency, amplitude, duration, and click rate before and after feeding. Two tanks of H. erectus at the Waikiki Aquarium were remotely monitored using a hydrophone and Raspberry Pi system, with recordings captured daily during 0900 and 1400 feeding sessions. Ambient sounds were collected for five minutes pre and post feeding of frozen mysid shrimp and analyzed using Raven Pro. Click sounds were recorded during both periods, but there was a behavioral shift in acoustic output following the introduction of prey with an increase in click rate post-feeding. Additionally, the postfeeding clicks exhibited lower mean peak frequencies and amplitudes than those recorded before the feeding event. These results could indicate that feeding clicks may be distinct from social or stress-related vocalizations, potentially reflecting the mechanical feeding mechanism or a shift in behavioral state. Maddie English Maddie English; Bonnie Hamilton; Alexandra McInturf; Deven Guerrero; Auguste Tveit; Olivia Boisen; Reilly
316: The Texas A&M University Biodiversity Research and Teaching Collections (BRTC) is an important university-based collection of vertebrate biodiversity in the southern United States, with strong holdings in fishes, amphibians, and reptiles. Founded in 1936 as the Texas Cooperative Wildlife Collection, the BRTC has developed into an internationally recognized research facility supporting specimen-based scientific research. Specimens housed in this collection include fluid-preserved specimens, skeletal preparations (cleared-and-stained, dry skeletons, and digital datasets resulting from CT scans), and tissue samples suitable for genetic and genomic work, enabling comprehensive research in systematics, taxonomy, biogeography, morphology, and genomics. The ichthyological collection houses 1,018,283 specimens in 66,816 lots, representing over 4,475 species. This includes freshwater and marine species from over 70 countries, and all major ocean basins, with particular strengths in Texas and the Gulf of Mexico. The collection ranks among the 25 largest ichthyological collections in the United States by number of specimens and lots. The herpetological collection, one of the 15 largest university-based collections in the country, includes more than 112,207 specimens representing 2,480 species across 106 families. Although especially strong in the southern United States and Mexico, it also includes important Neotropical, Afrotropical, Australasian, and Palaearctic material. The BRTC supports a broad range of scientific studies through active loan programs, onsite access, and integration with digital platforms like iDigBio, FishNet2, VertNet, and MorphoSource, while maintaining extensive collaborations with researchers worldwide. Current activities include a collection-wide reorganization of ichthyological material and the implementation of a standardized labeling system in the herpetology collection, further improving accessibility, organization, and research capacity.
317: Understanding animal ecosystem dynamics at the individual and population levels is essential for uncovering life-history patterns and important areas for management and conservation. Marine fish species often face minimal geographic barriers to movement, but intrinsic barriers like philopatry and site fidelity can dictate gene flow. Atlantic nurse sharks (Ginglymostoma cirratum) present a unique opportunity to investigate patterns of population structure and connectivity in benthic large-bodied sharks that have the capacity for wide dispersal but are also extremely philopatric. Previous research on their population genetics using microsatellite genetic markers revealed little population differentiation throughout the western Atlantic Ocean, but new genomic methods using data such as single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) may uncover previously unrecognized genetic structure. Using tissue samples from 95 nurse sharks across North and Central Bahamas and an atoll in Brazil, we performed double digest restriction site-associated DNA sequencing (ddRAD-seq), extracting a final 5,629 SNPs. After performing a suite of qualitative and quantitative genomic methods, we uncovered weak but significant population structure among sampled regions, however, most observed genetic diversity occurred within samples. We attribute their population structure to the strong reproductive philopatry of nurse sharks. Our findings suggest they also experienced a recent population expansion, leading to an excess of rare loci that could be creating weak signatures of population differentiation and explaining the higher diversity within samples. In light of nurse sharks being wide- ranging and performing seasonal migrations, reproducing migrants may also contribute to the observed low genetic structure by maintaining gene flow between populations. Gustavo Ruano Fajardo
318: Several amphibians have developed a close relationship with bromeliad plants, which provide moisture, prey, and shelter. However, climate change and habitat loss could alter the interactions between amphibians and phytotelm bromeliads. There is a lack in the understanding of how environmental change affects the skin microbiome of amphibians that use bromeliads. The question of whether bromeliads serve as a refuge or as an ecological trap for these species is unresolved. We are evaluating the hypothesis that climate stress may induce dysbiosis in the skin microbiome of the bromeliad-associated salamander Bolitoglossa helmrichi, increasing their susceptibility to infection by the chytrid fungus. We are using a pyramidal epidemiological framework to investigate associations with microbiome dysbiosis in this microecosystem. We designed a field experiment in Guatemala, where natural bromeliads may or may not be used by salamanders under cloud forest conditions. In addition, to control for microbiome environmental input, we are using artificial bromeliads in forest conditions. We compared local climatic conditions, the presence of chytrid fungus, the amphibian host microbiome, and the bromeliad microbiome. Additionally, we utilized bromeliad environmental characteristics, including structure, pH, temperature, and dissolved oxygen. Preliminary results suggest a difference in microbiome composition between salamanders and the bromeliad microbiome. Ongoing analyses aim to determine whether these patterns are consistent. Furthering this research can help develop a framework for associating the role of amphibian-bromeliad interactions in a changing world. Sydney Falcon
319: Salamanders are widely regarded as a generalist species that shows no preference of prey item. However, very few studies have been conducted on the diet of salamanders in order to confirm the assumptions of them being generalists. Feeding habits in particular of Ambystoma salamanders are largely unknown due to the lack of gut content studies available on the genus, with most information on the genus pertaining to the larval stage, not metamorphosed adults. Gut content analysis will be performed on specimens of A. opacum, A. talpoideum, A. texanum, and A. maculatum in order to determine the diet of these widespread Ambystoma species. These four species also have a history of co-occurring with each other and can be found in similar habitats. Specimens that originate only in Louisiana from the Southeastern Louisiana University Vertebrate Museum will be used in this study. The diets of each species will then be compared to determine if these species of salamander partake in niche partitioning while occurring with other species in the Ambystoma genus. The found diet will also provide information on the life history of the salamanders and since this study is the first proper diet analysis of these species, will provide an actual representation of the realized niche. Nicholas A. Farmer Nicholas Farmer; John Carlson; Michael Schram; Brian Moe; Adam Brame; Andrew Wooley; R. Dean Grubbs;
320: Runoff from mining wastes can contaminate nearby wetlands with heavy metals, even decades after mining operations have ceased. For many species, acute exposure of metal-naïve individuals to heavy metals leads to a variety of negative effects, including effects on behavior. Few studies have tested whether negative effects are present in individuals that have experienced long-term (multi-generational) exposure to heavy metals. We collected tadpoles of Boreal Chorus Frogs (Pseudacris maculata) from contaminated ponds in the Tri-State Mining District (TSMD) and tadpoles from uncontaminated reference sites. The TSMD is a US superfund site that continues to have elevated levels of heavy metals in terrestrial and aquatic habitats despite remediation efforts. Data collection is in progress at the time of the submission of this abstract. We first are verifying that heavy metal levels are elevated at our specific collection sites and also are determining whether other water-quality variables differ among our sites. Behavioral trials are ongoing in the laboratory, where we are using a two-factor design to compare responses of tadpoles from the two habitats (contaminated versus control) to cues from predators versus nonpredators. This correlational study should contribute to our understanding of how chronic exposures to heavy-metal contamination impacts amphibian populations. Elizabeth Favor
321: Mutations that help organisms overcome one selective challenge can also compromise other aspects of performance. In garter snakes (Thamnophis sirtalis), resistance to tetrodotoxin (TTX) from toxic Pacific newts (Taricha) evolves through amino acid substitutions in the skeletal muscle sodium channel (Nav1.4), the molecular target of TTX. Our previous work shows that the same substitutions that reduce toxin binding also impair channel function. These biophysical tradeoffs scale upwards, leading to slower and weaker muscles in the most resistant snakes. Here, we extend that work by testing whether the physiological costs of TTX-resistance depend on temperature. We isolated skeletal muscle from snakes with different Nav1.4 genotypes and measured mechanical performance across ecologically relevant temperatures. Muscles from snakes carrying the highly resistant channel variant (1.4LVNV) performed worse at lower temperatures, showing greater declines in excitability and contractile performance than muscles from less resistant or TTX-sensitive snakes. These results suggest that the costs of extreme resistance are magnified in cold conditions. This temperature-sensitive tradeoff may help explain a longstanding geographic pattern in the snake-newt arms race. Although toxic newts range far north along the Pacific coast, snakes with the most resistant sodium channel genotypes are restricted to a relatively small region of central and northern California. Our findings suggest that cold environments may constrain the spread of extreme TTX resistance by amplifying its physiological costs. Kelsey Fenner
322: Amphibians host a plethora of parasites, including lungworms of the genus Rhabdias. In vertebrates, helminths elicit a T-helper type 2 (Th2) immune response with upregulation of proteins such as IL-4Ra, IL-13Ra1, IL-25, IL-6, IL-10, while inhibiting the release of Th1 stimuli, such as IFN-γ. Parasite presence impacts host’s fitness by disrupting central endocrine axes and mediating important trade-offs. Currently, amphibians face critical threat from emerging pathogens worldwide, and much attention has focused on Th1 responses and natural plasma antibodies, while Th2 responses have been overlooked in this context. Herein, we experimentally infected cane toads (Rhinella marina) with lungworms (Rhabdias pseudosphaerocephala) and tracked the local (lung) and systemic (spleen) gene expression of Th2 proteins, in addition to systemic IFN-γ at 1, 3, 14, and 30 days post-infection (DPI). In the spleens, lungworms caused an upregulation of IL-4Ra at 3 DPI, and marginal upregulation of IL-25. In the lungs, IL-6 was the only upregulated cytokine, and IL-4Ra decreased at 14 DPI. IL-13Ra1 and IL-10 were not altered in either tissue, and IFN-γ mRNA was not detected. These results indicate that the most pronounced immune responses occurred systemically rather than at the site of infection. Despite evidence of Th2 activation in the spleen, lungworms remained in the lungs through 30 DPI, suggesting a mismatch between systemic signaling and local immune activity. This pattern suggests immunomodulation or tolerance mechanisms that may limit host responses in lung tissue and facilitate parasite persistence. Further studies are needed to clarify the mechanisms underlying this tissue-specific immune regulation. Walter Flynn
323: The University of Puerto Rico Mayagüez Fish Collection (UPR) was a significant biorepository of marine fish biodiversity in the Caribbean, encompassing historical data from 13,000 specimens, comprising >650 species, >375 genera, and 165 families. This collection originated in the 1930s and was formalized by Donald Erdman in the 1950s. It grew significantly with the arrival of Jack Randall in 1961, and steadily under Dannie Hensley to the final Curator, Matt Craig. Without formal oversight, an active curator and institutional funding and support, the collection deteriorated after 2013. It was also subject to loss of climate control following Hurricane Maria. In 2022, the National Science Foundation awarded funds to rescue and facilitate the transfer of the collection to another institution. UPR is now integrated into the Marine Vertebrate Collection at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography (SIO). SIO is a leading marine fish collection in the United States, housing over two million specimens and has previously integrated collections including the University of California Los Angeles Ichthyology Collection and the Pitman Epipelagic Collection, providing accessibility to this valuable material. Herein, we present the final statistics on what was recovered from UPR and is now available for research. The over 2,300 lots increased nearshore and deep-benthic Caribbean holdings substantially, adding over 230 previously unrepresented species as well as over 20 paratype lots previously inaccessible. All records were digitized and georeferenced following significant metadata forensics and are available on public data repositories Additionally, this effort trained ten undergraduates in fish systematics and collection management. Yannick Z. Francioli Yannick Francioli; Justin Bernstein; Richard Adams; Hannah Guss; Drew Schield; Siddarth Gopalan; Dylan Maag;
324: The taxonomic history of the Western hognose snake (Heterodon nasicus) has at times included three subspecies (nasicus, kennerlyi, and gloydi) and at other times included three full species. To clarify the systematics of H. nasicus, we collected ddRADseq and whole mitochondrial genome data from Texas populations, where all three subspecies were known to occur, as well as resequencing data from a formalin-fixed gloydi specimen. Analyzed using a newly-sequenced reference genome, we found that delimitation approaches do not support three separate species, and that gloydi is genetically indistinguishable from nasicus. Despite gloydi being rare (and perhaps extinct) in Texas, these results imply that efforts are not needed to conserve this subspecies. Christian Furness
325: Bermuda’s anchialine ponds have been described geophysically and biologically, but not bioacoustically. Bioacoustics allows us to passively monitor wildlife through their vocalisations, and can be linked to measurements of biodiversity. This study is the first application of passive acoustic monitoring in Bermudian anchialine ponds, with the aim of gathering new perspectives on species diversity in these protected habitats. We deployed underwater audio recorders in two ponds from 18 May – 16 June 2025, gathering a total of 797 hours of audio data. We marked biotic sounds in the recordings and labelled them with the lowest taxonomic level possible. Preliminary results indicate that there are diel cycles of acoustic activity, although the diversity of sounds differs between ponds. Fishes are audible on the recordings but cannot be confidently identified, and Lesser Antillean whistling frogs (Eleutherodactylus johnstonei) are heard beneath the water despite vocalising terrestrially. This is the beginning of a broader study of Bermuda’s anchialine ponds. Future study will broaden the spatial and temporal scope to include additional ponds and lunar cycles. Jackie Galvez Jacquelyn Galvez; Joanna Chen; Sophia Paz Fogel; Malia Magbual; Antonia Schwartz; Samantha Torres; Connie
326: Fragmentation and isolation of populations within a species may lead to genetic and morphometric differences between populations. This divergence can be the result of several factors, including genetic drift, phenotypic plasticity, and rapid evolution. Recently, such differentiation among populations has been found across geographic scales much smaller than previously thought, possibly driven by differences in flow regime, predation, human impact, or surrounding habitat differences. Rhinichthys atratulus, the Eastern Blacknose Dace, is a wide ranging minnow found throughout the Eastern United States. Previous evidence suggests population-level genetic divergence among R. atratulus populations within the region. Here we examined morphometric variation of R. atratulus populations among six sites within a 1km section of Allyn Brook in Durham, CT. Approximately thirty fish per population were collected and scanned and sixteen homologous landmarks were digitized for each specimen. The raw coordinates were then Procrustes transformed. We used PCAs and MANOVAs to test null hypotheses of homogeneity of shapes and allometries among populations, and found significant differences in body shape among three site groupings. These results suggest strong microgeographic variation within a small section of Allyn Brook lacking physical barriers to gene-flow among populations. Michael J. Ghedotti
327: Ponyfishes in the Family Leiognathidae uniquely possess a complex bioluminescent system with an esophageal light organ containing bioluminescent bacteria, a reflective gas bladder, and transparent windows through adjacent tissues that allow light emission distant from the light organ to produce camouflaging counterillumination and, in some species, intraspecific communication. Despite having bacterial light production, a type of light production that cannot be changed rapidly, researchers observed many species of ponyfishes rapidly blinking. The equulitine ponyfishes form a well diagnosed clade in which males have lateral transparent windows on the body, and males of one species, Equulites elongatus, were observed in the wild to blink rapidly. This group allowed us to explore bioluminescent organ anatomy in a sexually dimorphic group and describe the morphology associated with blinking. We used gross anatomical, histological, and radiological methods to investigate the light organ-system of ponyfishes in the Tribe Equulitini. We provide the first detailed description of the internal structure of the bioluminescent light organ in Leiognathidae, identify the esophageal homologs of the light organ’s tissues, and describe the novel mechanism for blinking involving longitudinal muscle of the muscularis propria that moves mucosal connective tissue shutters. Although males have larger light organs and transparent lateral windows on their flanks, both males and females have a similar morphology and have structures consistent with the ability to blink. Katie Gheysen
328: South Texas estuaries provide essential habitats and putative nurseries for bonnetheads (Sphyrna tiburo), spinner sharks (Carcharhinus brevipinna), and cownose rays (Rhinoptera bonasus). These systems support multiple life stages, yet the degree to which these species partition habitat in space and time remains unclear. We analyzed acoustic telemetry data from 14 bonnetheads, 8 spinner sharks, and 15 cownose rays between 2024 and 2026 to quantify spatial, temporal, and social segregation. Comparisons of habitat utilization distributions (UDs) revealed species-specific core use areas (50% UD). Bonnetheads occupied the largest proportion of unique core habitat (21%), compared to cownose rays (11%) and spinner sharks (4%). Core-area overlap occurred primarily between bonnetheads and cownose rays (46%), with only 5% shared by all three species. Broader home ranges (95% UD) showed greater spatial overlap, with 36% shared among species. To examine co-occurrence patterns, weighted social networks were constructed to assess community structure (modularity, measuring how individuals form groups), identify individuals connecting groups (betweenness centrality), and evaluate whether species preferentially associate with conspecifics (species assortativity). Modularity revealed a non-random community structure with both species-specific and mixed-species groups, while betweenness centrality highlighted individuals acting as connectors across groups, suggesting shared movement pathways or temporal overlap in space use. Species assortativity showed a tendency toward conspecific associations, with comparisons of within- and between-species edge strengths (reflecting the intensity of shared space use) indicating stronger within-species connections. Together, these analyses demonstrate that elasmobranchs partition habitat and time while maintaining overlap, with implications for essential fish habitat designations and coexistence. Ricardo Galaz Gibert
329: Due to their secretive behavior, snakes are notoriously difficult to detect during field surveys. Thus, studies of snake behavior, habitat use, and demography often suffer from a low sample size, limiting conservationbased inference and applications. Traditional survey methods rely on above-ground activity; however, temperate snakes enter brumation during the winter months, restricting field surveys to a narrow active season window. Borescopes are well-suited for detecting fossorial or saxicolous wildlife, but no prior research has evaluated the rate of false-negatives (i.e., failing to detect snakes when they are present). In winter 2025–2026, we initiated borescope surveys at the Marine Corps Recruit Depot, South Carolina, USA to collect preliminary data and develop a protocol for addressing the following objectives: 1) quantifying false-negative detection errors by scoping hibernacula in use by telemetry-equipped eastern diamondback rattlesnakes (Crotalus adamanteus; EDBs), 2) determining if borescope surveys disrupt winter dormancy, and 3) characterizing features associated with hibernaculum selection. Preliminary surveys (n=13) resulted in five false-negatives, no evidence of hibernaculum abandonment, and four instances of intraspecific communal brumation. On average, EDBs selected south-southeast facing hibernacula with a depth of at least 54 cm, including tip-ups (n=4), stump holes (n=2), bank roots (n=4), logs (n=2), or anthropogenic structures (n=1). Our findings will pose implications for the utility of a contemporary survey technique and improve understanding of EDB overwintering behavior and microhabitat requirements. Matthew G. Girard
330: Amphibians and reptiles are sensitive indicators of environmental change, yet many recently protected landscapes lack baseline data needed to inform conservation and management. The Eagleville Barrens Conservation Area in Orange, Massachusetts is a recently protected property lacking standardized data on amphibian and reptile communities. This study aims to establish a baseline herpetofaunal inventory to inform longterm monitoring and management. Surveys were conducted during the spring and early summer of 2026 across a range of habitats including vernal pools, wetlands, upland forest, and transitional areas. Multiple survey methods were used to maximize detection probability, including visual encounter surveys, vernal pool dip-netting, coverboard arrays, and aquatic turtle trapping. Individuals were temporarily captured for identification and basic morphometric data collection before being released at the point of capture. Preliminary results document species presence across habitat types and provide insight into habitat associations within this mixed-use landscape. This inventory establishes a repeatable framework for future monitoring efforts on Mount Grace properties and contributes to regional data on herpetofaunal distribution. Additionally, this project supports conservation planning by identifying species of concern and highlighting the importance of protecting small, heterogeneous habitats for amphibian and reptile communities in Massachusetts. Luis Gonzalez
331: All North American pitvipers express maternal attendance, whereby post-parturient females stay with their offspring until the natal shed. The nature of maternal attendance has been long debated; the benefit to progeny is often considered passive protection (i.e., discouraging predation attempts via proximity to young), despite some evidence of active maternal defense from ex situ research and limited field observations. In August–September of 2022 and 2024, we placed timelapse cameras at eastern diamondback rattlesnake (Crotalus adamanteus; EDB) birth sites (n=29) to evaluate behaviors of post-parturient females and neonates. Preliminary results provide observations of attending females engaging in vigilant behaviors and agonistic defense of offspring. We thus report field-based evidence of active maternal care in a live-bearing pitviper, with implications for the evolution of parental care and sociality in squamate reptiles. Kim Gray
332: Traits favored in the pet trade, including rapid growth, high fecundity, and generalist diets, also characterize successful invaders, helping explain their overrepresentation among invasive species. These traits also threaten native species by promoting displacement and altering behavior. The convict cichlid (Amatitlania spp.) exemplifies this pattern as a popular aquarium species and emerging high-risk invader. In 2018, we recorded a new population of convict cichlids in the crater lake Apoyo, Nicaragua. Lake Apoyo harbors one of the few welldocumented cases of sympatric speciation, the Midas cichlids radiation (Amphilophuss spp.), making it of particular conservation and evolutionary interest. To characterize this new population, we used Rad-seq to sample 84 individuals across the native range of Amatitlania siquia. Fst statistics and population structure PCA indicate that the Apoyo population is highly divergent from the other populations we sampled. Moreover, PCA suggests this Apoyo population is composed of two genetic clusters. Admixture analyses support this pattern, identifying two ancestral components, with some individuals showing single and others mixed ancestry. Consistent with these patterns, Tajima’s D was strongly positive in Lake Apoyo, indicating an excess of intermediate-frequency alleles expected under recent admixture between differentiated source populations, outweighing the negative values typically associated with rapid population growth in invasive species. Interestingly, phylogenetic analyses recover both genetic clusters of Apoyo as sister taxa of the Lake Xiloá population. However, admixture analyses suggest that Xiloá’s population consists of admixed individuals from three ancestral sources, two shared with Apoyo. We hypothesize that these are likely from the pet trade. Aaron Griffing
333: Chemosensation is commonly used among animals to convey information including location, identification, reproductive status, and social dominance. Some vertebrates (particularly squamates) possess specialized structures for the production (femoral glands) and detection of chemical signals. The production of femoral gland secretions from male lizards is regulated by androgens and, consequently, varies between the mating (when secretion activity peaks) and non-mating periods. Additionally, the biochemical properties and/or concentrations of the volatile lipids within the secretions also vary between the mating and non-mating seasons and therefore might function as a sex-attractant pheromone, and/or indirectly guide female mate choice by conveying information regarding the social dominance and fighting ability of males. The reflectance spectrum of femoral secretions has been shown to vary visually between sympatric lizard species enabling species recognition. Because many lizard species, such as the Argentine Black and White Tegu (Salvatore merianae), possess the ability to see ultraviolet wavelengths, we wished to determine if the reflectance of femoral pore secretions vary seasonally, between the sexes, and across the ultraviolet and visible spectrum in wild caught S. merianae. The reflectance of femoral secretions from males during the mating season varied from all other groups (non-mating season males, mating season females, and non-mating season females). Additionally, there existed a direct and negative relationship between male secretion reflectance and Julian day in the northern hemisphere. Our results indicate that the reflectance of S. merianae femoral pore secretions may be of primary importance during the mating season. Rachel Gutner
334: Emerging infectious diseases, especially fungal diseases, can pose significant threats to wildlife and are of growing conservation concern. Snake fungal disease, also called ophidiomycosis, is an emerging fungal disease caused by the keratinophilic fungus Ophidiomyces ophidiicola. Here, I explore how ophidiomycosis impacts the threatened eastern indigo snakes (Drymarchon couperi) by analyzing how seasonality in ectotherm immune capacity may drive dynamics of Ophidiomyces ophidiicola. I propose that the seasonal variations observed in the prevalence and severity of ophidiomycosis in eastern indigo snakes are driven by the mismatch between: 1. Fluctuations in host immune capacity caused by differences in environmental temperature and 2. Fluctuations in optimal temperature conditions for the survival of Ophidiomyces ophidiicola. To explore this idea, I describe the empirical dynamics of ophidiomycosis in this system and propose a preliminary mechanistic model of my hypothesis.
335: The taxonomic status of Nerodia clarkii has been in question for decades, but recent work has informed our understanding of the relationships among its subspecies and its relationship with Nerodia fasciata. Those findings fuel a new perspective on lingual luring by N. c. compressicauda. I will present an update and thoughts on the use of lingual luring by adult saltmarsh snakes and a discussion of avenues of future behavioral and morphological research in light of this new view of the relationships among the N. clarkii subspecies. I will also provide insights on methodologies relevant to the pursuit of proposed behavioral and morphological research. Railee Harbo
336: Hatchling freshwater turtles face significant challenges during early life stages, including predation, desiccation, and habitat loss. Despite their ecological importance, little is known about their movements and habitat preferences due to their cryptic behavior and small size. In this study, we utilized fluorescent powder tracking, a non-invasive method, to investigate the spatial ecology of hatchling turtles in southern Belize. Forty-seven hatchlings from five species (Kinosternon acutum, K. leucostomum, Trachemys venusta, Claudius angustatus, and Chelydra rossignonii) were tracked across old-growth rainforest and pine savanna habitats. Hatchlings exhibited movement distances ranging from 3 to 1987 cm, with most activity concentrated in high-elevation rainforest, particularly in ephemeral aquatic habitats such as puddles and ditches. Species-specific preferences were observed, aligning with adult habitat use. Notably, the longest movement was recorded for a C. rossignonii individual, which travelled over 19 m in two days. Significant differences in habitat use were found between ephemeral, permanent, and upland microhabitats, highlighting the importance of temporary aquatic environments during the rainy season. The study confirmed the effectiveness of fluorescent powder tracking as a low-cost, low-impact tool for monitoring hatchling turtles. Despite potential concerns about increased visibility to predators, only one potential predation event occurred during tracking. These findings emphasize the critical role of ephemeral habitats in supporting hatchling survival and provide valuable insights for conservation planning. By addressing a key knowledge gap, this research supports efforts to protect threatened freshwater turtle species in Belize's rapidly changing ecosystems.
337: Coastal shark species comprise one of the most threatened marine vertebrate groups. Prevailing ecological paradigms generalize that small-bodied sharks use shallow-water resources across ontogeny, and that inshore presence of large-bodied species is largely constrained to nursery-associated juveniles that shift to deeper offshore environments as they mature. Shark trophic position and niche size are proposed to increase with age, but limited resolution of life history ecology in many taxa may obscure the true complexity and diversity of ontogenetic resource-use strategies. Using a hierarchical probabilistic model of muscle δ13C and δ15N values, we reconstructed continuous, sex-specific isotopic niche trajectories across full- or late-ontogeny of nine coastal shark species around Biscayne Bay, Florida. Posterior probabilities of change states (positive, negative, or stable) along trophic-position, habitat-movement, and niche-breadth axes revealed high divergence in ontogenetic strategies across species. Modeled sex-specific deviations from species-level trends were minor. This diversity in ontogenetic niche dynamics largely supports generalized habitat-use and niche-breadth patterns for coastal sharks but challenges the expected trophic upgrading trajectory, revealing trophic function is more complex across ontogeny than previously recognized. These findings underscore the importance of ontogeny-sensitive investigations to ecosystem-based management, providing a probabilistic framework for exploring ontogenetic shifts across systems and taxa. Katie Hoffman
338: Peter’s Rock Agama (Agama picticauda) invaded South Florida during the 1970s and is now quickly expanding its invasion range to include much of Central Florida. However, little is known about this species in the northernmost portion of its invasion range or what specific factors may drive establishment in these new locations. To properly determine the impact of this species on the landscape, it’s crucial to understand how habitat selection and seasonality may facilitate their establishment and spread. Here, we sought to utilize observations from the citizen science platform iNaturalist to determine the rate of spread for this species in Central Florida and to assess the influence of habitat type and seasonality on the abundance of A. picticauda observed. In January 2026, we exported all available research-grade observations of A. picticauda from iNaturaist from 2015 to 2025, totaling 1126 observations across 15 counties in Central Florida. A. picticauda presence and abundance significantly increased by year across the 15 counties (p < 0.001). Using the Global Human Footprint Index, we observed that A. picticauda exhibited higher abundance in highly urbanized habitats (p < 0.001). Seasonality was also associated with the abundance of observations, with spring and summer months having significantly more observations than winter and fall (p< 0.001). This study furthers our understanding of A. picticauda’s general ecology in Central Florida, shows the use of citizen science data, and serves as a guide that land managers can use to identify optimal areas and times of year to sample or remove them. Darcae Holmes
339: Gobiesox yuma was described in 1917 based on a single specimen collected 12 miles off the coast of Sanibel, western FL. The holotype (and only known specimen) of G. yuma, was taken aboard the auxiliary ketch yacht “Yuma” via anchor and reported to exhibit black and white markings on the body and median fins. Following Briggs (1955), Gobiesox yuma is currently considered a junior synonym of the wide-ranging G. strumosus Cope 1870, occurring in shallow coastal waters of the Western Central Atlantic from New Jersey (USA) to the Yucatán Peninsula (Mexico). Underwater photographs of G. strumosus made available by recreational divers, show individuals with markedly different color patterns, including: (1) an olive-brown body with darker brown mottling and dark brown fins without a white margin, and (2) a solid black body with fine white markings and black fins with a translucent white margin. Individuals exhibiting the different color patterns also exhibit consistent differences in body and fin shape, counts of papillae contributing to region C of the ventral adhesive disc, and in mitochondrial DNA (p-distance >5%). Based on this evidence, we conclude that G. strumosus, as currently defined, is a complex of two species: the olive-brown G. strumosus and the black and white G. yuma. Taryn Hood
340: Teleost fishes are an ideal model to study the relationships between groups of traits (i.e., integration, modularity) due to their expansive trophic ecology, ontogenetic complexity, and the evolution of pharyngeal jaws. This two-jaw system may allow for functional decoupling between prey acquisition via the oral jaws and prey processing via the pharyngeal jaws. However, the functions of each jaw vary widely across fishes, and ontogenetic influences on the oral and pharyngeal jaws are understudied. Pricklebacks (Stichaeidae) are a useful model for studying fish feeding, as certain species have convergently evolved omnivory and herbivory, and shift in diet over ontogeny. Pricklebacks also possess diverse oral jaw morphotypes, with physiological and morphological differences across species. Here, we use high resolution micro-CT imaging to explore the relationship between oral and pharyngeal jaw shape over ontogeny in five species of pricklebacks with diverse diets. We describe and compare the shape of the upper and lower oral and pharyngeal jaws using 3D geometric morphometrics. We found that diet structures patterns of modularity, while species and ontogeny influence integration. Individual jaws have idiosyncratic multivariate groupings and some species undergo ontogenetic convergence and divergence, but species differences generally outweigh influences of allometry on shape. Lastly, pharyngeal jaw size covaries with diet and may increase processing capabilities. In pricklebacks, widespread modularity of the oral and pharyngeal jaws may contribute to the flexibility in morphology and diet observed in the pricklebacks, and increased modularity may be a factor in the evolvability of new diets in teleost fishes. Ren Horn
341: As many as 75% of humans will reside in cities by 2050. Urbanization often benefits introduced species, where biotic filtering, introduction effort, and species-specific traits interact to regulate co-occurrence patterns. Community assembly among non-native species is shaped by interactions such as competition and colonization history, especially priority effects. Introduced geckos are ideal vertebrate models for testing such theories because they are readily available at exceptionally high densities on buildings, which function as spatially replicated systems. The Gecko Grid is an emerging research network designed to investigate the ecology and evolution of introduced geckos across campuses in the United States and beyond by establishing standardized, student-friendly protocols for field surveys and statistical analyses. By integrating course-based undergraduate research experiences with coordinated gecko sampling, The Gecko Grid will enable students across institutions to contribute comparable data to a centralized database while analyzing data on their campuses' geckos. Preliminary results from initial protocols developed by Tarleton State University’s “Team Gecko” based on studies of Hemidactylus turcicus indicate structured microhabitat use, with larger individuals occupying higher perches, and no effect of artificial lighting on presence. Occupancy models reveal variable detection probabilities across buildings and survey conditions, while flight initiation distance trials show greater escape distances at lower perches. Protocols are readily extendable to multispecies assemblages, and early empirical data suggest interactions consistent with competitive exclusion and character displacement. The Gecko Grid aims to advance urban ecology while fostering student research on campus through a common repository of gecko data generated by standardized, scalable procedures. Anna McCallum Humphrey
342: A central question in invasion biology and evolutionary ecology is whether populations exposed to novel environments evolve in predictable ways. Although morphological divergence following introduction has been documented in many taxa, it remains unclear whether introduced populations repeatedly evolve similar phenotypes across species. We addressed this question using citizen-science photographs from 22 lizard species (11 anoles and 11 geckos) represented by native and introduced populations. From standardized images, we quantified head dimensions, forelimb and hindlimb segments, total limb lengths, and tail length (original tails only), expressing all traits relative to snout–vent length (SVL). We compared native and introduced populations using mixed-effects models, meta-analyses, and species-level effect sizes. We further used Miami, Florida, as a natural experiment to test whether independently introduced species coexisting within the same city exhibit convergent morphological evolution. Morphological divergence between native and introduced populations was widespread. However, most traits showed little evidence of predictable evolutionary change. Species differed markedly in both the direction and magnitude of divergence, suggesting that responses to introduction are largely contingent on species-specific biology and ecological context. The only consistent signal across taxa was a tendency for introduced populations to exhibit relatively longer distal limb segments, potentially reflecting weak but repeatable adaptation to novel structural environments. The Miami analysis yielded a similar result: despite experiencing a shared urban environment, introduced species showed limited morphological convergence. Our results suggest that morphological evolution following introduction is common but only weakly predictable, with only subtle and potentially repeatable changes emerging in locomotor morphology. Ian Solon Ito
343: The Puerto Rican Boa (Chilabothrus inornatus) is an endemic species to Puerto Rico, where it often inhabits subterranean environments such as caves which serve as both refugia and hunting grounds. The PR Boa has been federally listed as endangered since 1973 due to habitat destruction and invasive species. Environmental DNA is an effective tool in monitoring biodiversity, and detecting endangered, cryptic, or invasive species. The implementation of an eDNA assay protocol will complement traditional survey methods to better understand the PR Boa island-wide distribution. Further, invasive species, the Reticulated Python (Malayopython reticulatus) and the Common Boa (Boa constrictor) have proliferated in Puerto Rico creating established populations which can lead to false positives. In this study, we collected soil samples from five caves with known populations of PR Boa and developed species-specific primers for the development of an eDNA assay for the PR Boa. Soil samples were collected in a targeted approach ranging from five different microhabitats. Species-specific primers for the PR Boa were created in the NADH dehydrogenase 4 mitochondrial complex; in addition, a primer targeting the cytochromeb mitochondrial complex (cyt-b) was tested after successfully amplifying members in the same genus, Chilabothrus (Reynolds et al. 2013) will also be tested for efficacy. All samples will be subject to Sanger sequencing and qPCR to quantify target species abundance per sample. Surface eDNA was also collected via swabs for PR Boa and invasives to compare efficacy of soil and swab samples.
344: Gatineau Park is a conservation park located in the Ottawa-Gatineau Region of Canada. Gatineau Park comprises over 50 lakes home to a wide diversity of aquatic species, including up to six freshwater fish species at risk. Introduced species have negatively impacted native species diversity. Prior to the establishment of Gatineau Park, park lakes were stocked during the 1930’s with sportfish for recreational fishing. Species diversity surveys conducted between 1970 and 2007 have documented that declines in small-bodied freshwater fish species richness over time, particularly minnow species (Leuciscidae), correlate with introductions of predatory piscivorous fishes; however, data of native species at risk and invasive predatory fishes from previous studies are almost 20 years old. Therefore, our main research goal was to thoroughly describe distribution patterns and assess distributions of Gatineau Park fish species. Using a combination of traditional fishing survey methods and eDNA metabarcoding, we sampled 40 of the known 50 lakes within Gatineau Park. For eDNA metabarcoding, water samples were collected and pumped through filter papers that were later extracted and sequenced. We selected two genes for metabarcoding: 12S and COI. Almost half of the lakes within the park are currently data deficient with no previous sampling records. We documented species within 14 data deficient lakes, providing baseline records as a point of comparison for future surveys. We found evidence of predatory fishes that have spread to new lakes since the previous survey, but have also identified lakes that do not currently contain introduced predatory fishes. Ben Jellen
345: The Ornate Box Turtle (Terrapene ornata) is a terrestrial turtle species found in prairies throughout the central United States. Their populations are declining primarily due to habitat loss, road mortality, and the pet trade. They are protected throughout much of their range and are listed as threatened by the Illinois Department of Natural Resources. I studied movement patterns and habitat use in a population of ornate box turtles in a 16-ha remnant sand prairie within a fragmented suburban landscape in southwestern Illinois. Turtles were fitted with radio transmitters attached to the carapace and tracked twice weekly from May to November. Average home ranges (MCP) were 0.75 ± 0.15 ha with substantial overlap among individuals. Ornate box turtles exhibited a heavily female-biased sex ratio of 17:1, likely due to environmental sex determination combined with arid nesting conditions. Results from this study are being used to inform management practices to ensure long-term protection. Whitney Jones
346: Dietary data is essential in understanding predator-prey interactions and how changes in prey availability impact different species. However, for larval fish their trophic ecology remains poorly resolved due to limitations in identifying prey. Although larvae have traditionally been considered opportunistic plankton feeders, growing evidence suggests they exhibit selective feeding behaviors. In this study, we used next-generation DNA metabarcoding to analyze the stomach contents of wild-caught larval fish across multiple families in Hawaii. This approach provided greater taxonomic resolution than conventional visual methods and allowed for more precise characterization of larval diets in the wild. Our results revealed clear differences in diet composition among larval fish groups, with some taxa dominated by a single prey type and others exhibiting more diverse diets. Diet composition also varied between assays, reflecting differences in taxonomic coverage and emphasizing the value of complementary molecular markers. These findings demonstrate that larval fish occupy distinct trophic niches and vary in their degree of feeding selectivity, highlighting their more structured and specialized role in marine planktonic food webs than previously recognized. Ingrid M. Kaatz
347: Catfish disturbance sounds were described from 13 families. Temporal patterns of swimbladder and stridulation sounds showed significant positive correlations between pulse number and duration: swimbladder n = 2,784 sounds, 28 spp., 6 families, r = 0.876, r2 =0.767); stridulation n = 4,226 sounds, 26 spp., 8 families, r = 0.390, r2 = 0.152.Temporal differences were found among eight families. Aspredinids produced the longest mean duration and pulse numbers calls for stridulation sounds per family as well as the longest mean pulse number calls for swimbladder sounds per family. Species differed in duration and pulse number in three families (# species): 9 stridulation, 19 swimbladder doradid; five auchenipterid; and seven mochokid. Both traits differed for both mechanisms in doradids and auchenipterids; and stridulation in mochokids. Sounds of doradid and auchenipterid males and females differed in temporal traits for stridulation (5/6 species) and swimbladder sounds (2/6 species). Trachelyopterus galeatus female sounds were longer in duration and greater in pulse number for both mechanisms. Catfish sounds can provide taxonomic characters in phylogenetic studies and their diversity will lend support to acoustic monitoring of natural ecosystems. Kristin Kabat
348: Islands that are severely impacted by storms or hurricanes are frequently re-colonized by species that were present prior to extirpation. Many species that colonize these islands are faced with new ecological conditions that either vary between islands, or that differ substantially from the mainland. Such environmental heterogeneity can act as a driver of trait values through both natural selection and/ or phenotypic plasticity. In 2014 and 2022, Anolis sagrei were collected from two populations on small spoil islands in the Tomoka River, Florida. These islands differed with respect to temperature, moisture, and canopy cover, and are subjected to repeated disturbances. We selected males and females from each island population from both time points. We measured external morphological traits and dissected individuals to measure the morphology of various organs. We then compared these measurements within and between the islands and time points to quantify spatial and temporal variation in morphology. We hypothesized that the environmental drivers of phenotypes are consistent across time, leading to consistent trait value within islands regardless of year. By testing for repeatable environment-phenotype association, our results will demonstrate how strong and persistent ecological conditions might shape morphology and provide insight into the processes that shape phenotypic variation in populations. Eva Kerr
349: Parthenogenetic whiptail lizards of the genus Aspidoscelis are a compelling system for studying hybrid polyploidy, as many species originate from crosses between two or more sexual species and reproduce clonally as all-female lineages. Aspidoscelis exsanguis is one such triploid parthenogen derived from hybridization among three ancestral sexual species (A. burti, A. arizonae, and A. scalaris), yet a high-quality reference genome for this species is lacking. Here we present a de novo whole-genome assembly of A. exsanguis generated from PacBio HiFi long-read sequencing. The total assembly size of the assembly is 5.1 Gbp — approximately three times the estimated haploid genome size of 1.78 Gbp — and gene completeness analysis with compleasm shows 96% of sauropsida orthologs present in exactly three copies, consistent with triploidy. The resulting reference genome will be a valuable resource for the broader research community studying parthenogenesis and hybrid speciation in Aspidoscelis. Jaden Kinney
350: Organisms with limited dispersal capabilities commonly fragment over space and time into a complex of forms exhibiting patterns of morphological distinctiveness and lineage independence. This poses a taxonomic and biogeographic challenge that is best solved by geographic sampling. Of particular interest are the contact zones where divergent lineages interact. One example of a difficult complex is the Plethodon wehrlei complex of woodland salamanders, which has recently been split into five separate species, but transition zones between species have never been characterized. Here, we present expanded geographic sampling across the southern range of the complex with the goal of characterizing geographic ranges, patterns of population structure, and points of secondary contact. We incorporate and additional ddRAD sequencing library for a total of 18 localities. We build on previous analyses of population admixture and isolation by distance using the programs STRUCTURE and conStruct. Results will inform further investigation of species delimitation and zones of secondary contact. Andrea Kroetz Andrea Kroetz; Alyssa Mathers; Zachary Siders; Andrew Wooley; Lukas Heath; Dylan Yakich; Rachel Scharer;
351: Pacific Chorus Frogs (Pseudacris regilla) are widely abundant across western North America including on three of the Channel Islands of southern California. Despite being one of the most regionally common amphibians, their origin on the Channel Islands is unknown. Island populations provide a unique opportunity to estimate the effects of isolation and dispersal on patterns of genetic and phenotypic variation due to their simplicity, replication, and well-documented histories. Our project investigates the evolutionary history of P. regilla on the Channel Islands by identifying patterns of genetic and phenotypic variation to understand how geological, ecological, and anthropogenic changes throughout history have influenced population divergence among islands and the mainland. Our first objective is to reconstruct colonization history of each island by using genomic data to estimate the geographic patterns and timing of divergence and to characterize demographic histories in relation to environmental changes. Our second objective is to investigate the effects of geographic isolation on phenotypic variation by characterizing variation in male advertisement calls and comparing acoustic properties among island and mainland populations. Results from our study will reveal how the effects of historical scenarios such as vicariance by sea-level rise and human occupation that alter population connectivity and size influences genetic diversity and phenotypic traits among populations. Insights gained from studying a widespread and locally abundant amphibian species will help inform predictions for how more sensitive and cryptic amphibian species may respond to future environmental changes. Kole M. Kubicek
352: Clearing and Double Staining (C&S) is a widely used technique enabling researchers to examine cartilage and bone in situ and is particularly useful for studying the skeleton of small vertebrates (e.g., fishes and amphibians). Traditional C&S protocols use an acidic solution to stain cartilage, which can result in the decalcification of bones in tiny specimens (e.g., larvae and early juveniles), compromising the quality and accuracy of bone staining. This is problematic as many developmental studies utilize the uptake of Alizarin Red S by bone as the main indicator that an ossification is present. To address this issue, an acid-free C&S protocol using MgCl₂ instead of glacial acetic acid was developed. However, the protocol for this technique was originally designed using a single species, Danio rerio (Zebrafish) and tested on a single developmental stage. Additionally, the study did not evaluate how duration spent in the staining solution could impact overall staining quality. Given that the ideal concentration of glacial acetic acid and duration in the cartilage staining solution have been shown to vary depending on the species and size of specimens, the same could also apply to the acid-free method. To optimize the acid-free C&S protocol for the earliest life stages of vertebrates, we test the effects of both staining time and concentration of MgCl₂ in the cartilage staining solution on the quality of cartilage and bone staining in multiple species. Results indicate both factors affect the uptake of Alcian blue in non-target tissues but do not affect bone staining. Bernie Kuhajda Bernie Kuhajda; Dave Neely; Alexey Chernyak; Akbarjon Ro'zimov
353: The Laurel Dace, Chrosomus saylori (Leuciscidae), is a federally endangered species restricted to a few headwater streams along Walden Ridge on the Cumberland Plateau in eastern Tennessee. The Tennessee Aquarium has been leading Laurel Dace research for 13 years, including status surveys, microhabitat assessment, life history studies, and developing propagation protocols. Unfortunately, Laurel Dace continue to decline from extreme siltation and degraded water quality from poor agricultural practices, competition and predation from invasive centrarchids, and drying streams during drought. In 2022, the Tennessee Aquarium partnered with the Natural Resources Conservation Service on a Regional Conservation Partnership Program (Ridges to Rivers) to address water quality concerns by assisting farmers with implementing best-management practices. This project invests $21.8 million into the region over five years. However, in 2024 an exceptional drought led to the emergency rescue of 300 Laurel Dace from two streams. These individuals overwintered at several facilities, and most were released into the wild in March 2025. Meanwhile, the Tennessee Aquarium formed a technical work group and embarked upon actions to manage this critically endangered species, including establishing ark populations, assessing genetic and disease risk, and strengthening local outreach. Strong community engagement led to the inaugural Laurel Dace Day festival and 5K in nearby Spring City, which adopted the Laurel Dace as their official town fish. This program has demonstrated the potential to engage communities and drive meaningful on-the-ground conservation efforts to save this species from extinction. More good news, summer 2025 surveys rediscovered Laurel Dace in a third creek. Arianna Kuhn
354: The Guana Tolomato Matanzas Estuary (GTM) provides essential habitat to several ecologically and economically important species, including serving as nursery habitat to a variety of shark species, most notably the scalloped hammerhead (Sphyrna lewini). Spanning the Northeastern Florida coast, it is home to over 50 endangered or threatened species and hosts several habitat restoration projects due to the GTM Estuary’s ecological significance. Due to its proximity to developed areas along the coast, it can be threatened by human influences, such as pollution. While the negative effects of human interaction with the environment are of growing public interest, the effect of pollution in the GTM Estuary has not been well studied. Therefore, the overall purpose of this project was to examine pollutant exposure in species residing within the GTM Estuary, specifically that of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). PFAS have been shown no clear pattern of accumulation or biomagnification in marine taxa and pose significant health risks to marine organisms and the humans that consume them. This presentation will discuss PFAS data in a variety of shark species and their prey, including sandbar sharks (Carcharhinus plumbeus), bull sharks (Carcharhinus leucas), and scalloped hammerheads. These results will be compared to Maximum Contaminant Levels in drinking water as identified by the EPA to identify overall risk within the system. Zachary Laughlin
355: In many ecosystems, species abundances, as well as community diversity and evenness fluctuate predictably across seasons. In the Southern Appalachians seasonality is associated with variation in temperature, precipitation, evapotranspiration, species abundances and community structure. Salamander life cycles are tightly coupled with seasonal variation in abiotic and biotic variables. While seasonal variation is often studied in macrobial communities, it is important for shaping microbial communities as well. We are investigating the impact of seasonality on the skin microbiota of Plethodon shermanii, Plethodon teyahalee and P. shermanii X P. teyahalee hybrids. We traveled to the Nantahala National Forest (Coweeta) where we sampled 277 salamanders in total across seasons for microbial, genetic, and ecological information. We used 16S sequencing to gather information about the salamander skin microbial community and analyzed our findings in R. In our findings we look at the influence of seasonality on Plethodontid salamander skin microbiomes. Our study hopes to provide greater understanding of the ecological, evolutionary, and microbial properties of Plethodontid salamanders. Sarah Laurino
356: Burbot (Lota lota) are the sole freshwater representative of the Order Gadiformes, which includes marine cod species, and have a circumpolar distribution north of 40o. Despite the ubiquity of burbot, little is known about the habitat selection and activity patterns of juveniles and how these behaviors shift across distinct seasons. Quantifying these behaviors is essential for understanding the energetic trade-offs and habitat requirements that underpin early-life survival, particularly as northern systems experience rapid winter warming. We investigated juvenile burbot habitat use and activity using radio frequency identification (RFID) telemetry within a controlled artificial stream system containing both pool and moderate-flow riffle sections. We simulated seasons by manipulating water temperature and photoperiod to reflect winter and summer conditions. Within each seasonal treatment, we compared responses to varied structural habitats (wood versus rock complexes). Under simulated winter conditions, juveniles favored riffle habitats over pools with occupancy jumping from 49.1% in summer to 62% in winter. Habitat structure further shaped occupancy patterns: wood treatments elicited significantly greater site fidelity and prolonged residency compared to rock substrates. Activity varied with both habitat type and season, but overall increased more than 3.5-fold from summer to winter. Notably, this heightened winter activity contrasts with the reduced activity observed in many other freshwater species during cold periods. Understanding the seasonal habitat selection and activity patterns of juvenile burbot is increasingly important as climate-driven shifts in temperature regimes across northern systems may have cascading consequences for juvenile survival and long-term population stability in this cold-adapted species. Alexia Leone
357: Wood turtles (Glyptemys insculpta) are an endangered riparian species that are primarily affected by habitat degradation. Our local population’s habitat, especially their nesting habitat is overtaken by anthropogenic structures and invasive species like knotweed (Reynoutria spp.). Artificial nesting mounds are one conservation method commonly used for other turtle populations. This thesis project aims to study how restored nesting habitat affects nest viability. We will have six test areas with three habitat types in each: artificial nesting mound, raked area, and natural area. An iButton will be installed in each habitat type to measure temperature. We will then survey for and track females and protect their nests. We will compare the nest success of nests laid in each habitat type. This work will be conducted during the May 2026 nesting season, so results have not been collected yet, but they will be prepared in time for the conference. We hope to use the findings of our study to improve future conservation of the wood turtles in the Susquehanna River Basin. Andrea Leontiou
358: The African notopterid subfamily Xenomystinae comprises two genera partly differentiated by dorsal-fin presence/absence, and three valid species: Papyrocranus, with two finned species, and Xenomystus, with one finless species. We test the monospecific Xenomystus hypothesis using molecular, morphological, and osteological data, which differentiated seven distinct species across Xenomystus’s geographic range, including five new species. The previously synonymized Xenomystus nili should be resurrected and its geographic range expanded to the Lake Chad basin. The currently valid Xenomystus nigri is redescribed and restricted to the Niger Basin and coastal rivers between the Dahomey Gap and Cross River, including the Ouémé, Ogun, and Kwa-Ibo rivers. Three of the five new species are endemic to the Congo Basin, a fourth is widespread in the Congo and Ogooué basins, and the fifth is endemic to coastal river systems of Sierre Leone (Upper Guinean ichthyofaunal province). Exploratory phylogeographic analyses using COI sequences reject mitochondrial monophyly of Xenomystus, instead supporting three distinct subclades made paraphyletic by Papyrocranus: Xenomystus nigri was recovered as a West African (Nilo-Sudan province) reciprocally monophyletic sister lineage to a central African clade (Congo + Lower Guinean provinces) of three undescribed species. At least 14% COI sequence divergence and hyo-branchial skeletal characters differentiate theses major lineages. A third lineage sister to all other Papyrocranus + Xenomystus comprised an undescribed Congo Basin endemic Xenomystus sister to an undescribed Papyrocranus from the Rokel River (Upper Guinean province). These findings highlight the importance of integrative taxonomy for resolving African ichthyofaunal diversity and informing conservation efforts. Oliver Ljustina
359: The dunes sagebrush lizard (Sceloporus arenicolus; DSL) is an endangered species endemic to the Mescalero-Monahans Shinnery Oak Dunes system of southeast New Mexico and west Texas. Many researchers use 18.9-L (5-gal) buckets for pitfall traps to survey lizard populations, including the DSL. Texas A&M Natural Resources Institute (NRI) and SWCA Environmental Consultants (SWCA) evaluated whether smaller 13.2-L (3.5gal) buckets could reduce the installation effort and increase efficiency, without reducing its efficacy as a pitfall trap for DSL. NRI installed a total of 90 pitfall traps within six 39.5-acre sites in the Texas portion of the DSL range. SWCA installed a total of 108 pitfall traps in a 365-acre site in the southeast New Mexico portion of the DSL range. Both NRI and SWCA kept the pitfall traps open for a total of 5 days or until a DSL was captured. SWCA recorded the snout-vent length (SVL) for each lizard captured. Results from NRI and SWCA’s trapping efforts indicate that smaller buckets were effective at capturing DSL and other larger lizard species. Two DSL, 46 side-blotched lizards (Uta stansburiana), and 17 marbled whiptails (Aspidoscelis marmorata) were captured by NRI. Eighteen sideblotched lizards (SVL: 4.1-5.5 cm) and 54 marbled whiptails (SVL: 5.9-9.8 cm) were captured by SWCA. NRI and SWCA found that smaller buckets reduced manual labor and installation time without reducing the efficacy of capturing DSL. These findings suggest that 13.2-L buckets are an efficient and effective alternative to traditional 18.9-L pitfall traps for DSL surveys. Isamar Lopez-Argueta
360: First described in 1864 based on one specimen from an imprecise locality in northeastern South America, the predatory characin Scissor macrocephalus has remained an ichthyological mystery and the only member of its genus for over 160 years. 21st century expeditions by the Royal Ontario Museum and University of Michigan Museum of Zoology to Guyana’s Mazaruni and Upper Kuribrong rivers yielded fresh specimens, tissues, and photos of both the original S. macrocephalus, and four putative undescribed congeners. While morphologically distinct, males of all forms share similar laterally projected bony hooks on fin rays, contrasting with the Acestrorhamphidae pattern in which hooks are projected posteriorly. Scissor macrocephalus males have bony hooks projecting anteriorly from unpaired-fin unbranched rays and laterally from branched rays. Two new putative sister species, respectively from the Kuribrong and Mazaruni rivers, share the same pattern but with greater hook development. The remaining two new species, also putatively allopatric sister species from the Kuribrong and Mazaruni rivers, have both laterally and posteriorly projected bony hooks on the anal fin. The putative Scissor clade also can be diagnosed by having darkened fins, with species being differentiated from one another by predorsal scale organization, maxillary teeth counts, presence or absence of caudal-fin blotches, and distinctive bony hook morphology. The clade is endemic to rivers draining the northeastern corner of the western Guiana Shield highlands, and is hypothesized to be an early branching lineage in the Stygichthyinae, a subfamily whose extant diversity is greatest in southeastern Brazil. Annaleise Lukens
361: Proceratophrys is a widely distributed South American frog genus that occurs across multiple ecoregions, including Amazonia, Atlantic Forest, Caatinga, Cerrado, and Chiquitano Forest, occupying both forested and open environments. The genus currently comprises 42 recognized species and exhibits remarkable morphological variation, including the presence or absence of palpebral appendages among closely related taxa. During a revision of Cerrado populations of Proceratophrys based on museum specimens, recently collected material, and mitochondrial DNA data, we discovered an undescribed species from the western Cerrado of Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil. Here, we describe this new species using an integrative approach based on adult morphology, advertisement call, and mtDNA evidence. The new species is known from the municipalities of Campo Grande and Alcinópolis. Adult males measure 28.88–39.45 mm snout–vent length (31.36 ± 4.16), whereas females measure 36.47–45.99 mm (42.43 ± 2.79). Molecular analyses indicate that the new species is more closely related to P. dibernardoi, P. huntingtoni, P. moratoi, and P. salvatori. Within these related species, genetic distances range from 1.3% (P. salvatori) to 6.7% (P. strussmannae). The advertisement call has a duration of 0.150–0.183 s (0.166 ± 0.01), with 13–15 pulses per call (14 ± 0.70), pulse rate of 81.83–87.77 pulses/s (mean = 86.11 ± 1.99), and dominant frequency of 9375–10312 Hz (9960 Hz). These results emphasize that integrative approaches, combined with exploration of previously unsampled regions, continue to reveal new lineages in Proceratophrys, even in areas where the genus was historically under documented. Justin Mann
362: Niche partitioning occurs when two ecologically similar sympatric species vary in resource use to reduce competition. Species that use behavioral strategies to partition niche space may vary in peak daily activity times, temperament, and/or diet preferences. Woodland salamanders of the genus Plethodon are an ideal study system for examining niche partitioning due to their territorial behavior, reliance on moist microhabitats, and frequent overlap with other species. Additionally, Plethodon salamanders display a striped/unstriped color polymorphism, and consideration of these morphs in behavioral niche partitioning studies is crucial as color morph niche divergence has been previously observed. In this study, we examine behavioral niche partitioning between two sympatric color polymorphic Plethodon species, the Eastern Red-backed Salamander (P. cinereus) and the Northern Zigzag Salamander (P. dorsalis), by testing which species and color morph will occupy higher-quality habitat in laboratory-based behavioral trials. Based on past work, we predict that P. cinereus will outcompete P. dorsalis and striped morphs will outcompete unstriped morphs. This research provides new insights into the ecology and morph differences in the little-studied P. dorsalis and explores species and morph co-occurrence from a behavioral perspective. Maria Manz
363: Hemidactylus turcicus is a non-native gekkonid species that has invaded much of the southern United States. Their invasion success is linked to thriving in urbanized environments, but how they have behaviorally adjusted to living with humans is unknown, which many animals perceive as predators. Here, we set out to examine the fear response in H. turcicus occupying buildings of our campus in Central Texas. We determined behavioral responses of geckos to humans by measuring flight initiation distances (FID). Given that visual colors can affect animal behavior, we also tested the effect of varying T-shirt color on FID. To measure FID, we conducted nocturnal surveys of buildings on campus with dim lights to not disturb geckos. When geckos were spotted, we measured our start distance, and then one of us walked towards the individual at a consistent pace and stopped as soon as the gecko fled, at which point we measured the distance between us and the gecko. We categorized the size of the gecko as “small” or “large” based on a visual estimation, whether the gecko was perched above or below our eye-level, and if there was a nearby refuge. From 5 surveys with black T-shirts and 67 FID measures, preliminary results suggest that geckos that are smaller and those perched below eye-level exhibit the largest FIDs. These baseline data using a neutral T-shirt color suggest that both ontogenetic and habitat-specific factors may influence a gecko’s decision about when it is the best moment to flee from an approaching predator. Michael W. McCoy Garrett Maggio; April Blakeslee; Sarah Goodnight; Iris Segura-Garcia; Jeb Byers; Jason Williams; Krista McCoy;
364: The order Tetraodontiformes, commonly known as pufferfishes and their relatives, includes 447 species across ten families. Several families in Tetraodontiformes, such as Balistidae, Monacanthidae, and Tetraodontidae, have sexually dimorphic characteristics exhibited by some, but not all species. We found that dimorphisms exhibited by tetraodontiform fishes include size, body and fin shape, and coloration. Studies show that some of the same dimorphisms exhibited within a family do not always occur in closely related species. For example, in the family Monacanthidae, male Rudarius minutus specimens have long quill-like spines, a characteristic that is also seen in Amanses scopas, despite the two species not being closely related. Through literature review and specimen assessments, we present a summary of the types of sexual dimorphisms exhibited by Tetraodontiformes, along with a phylogenetic analysis of the order and occurrences of sexual dimorphism within each family. Caleb McMahan
365: Anthropogenic land development and biological invasions drive rapid evolutionary change. We investigated whether urbanization and invasive competitors correlate with morphological shifts in Anolis lizards, hypothesizing that urban environments select for larger body sizes (snout–vent length, SVL) and that invasive populations exhibit greater morphological variation between habitats. We compared the green anole (Anolis carolinensis), native to the southeastern United States, with the invasive Cuban brown anole (Anolis sagrei).
