We conducted a weighted random-effects meta-analysis using data from 73 populations across 23 published studies spanning five decades, analyzing effects of species, sex, habitat type (urban vs. forest), and invasion status on SVL. We examined temporal trends over three decades (>30 generations) to assess morphological shifts associated with environmental change and interspecific interactions. Results revealed that body size varied significantly by species and sex, with males consistently larger than females and A. carolinensis larger than A. sagrei. A. sagrei were significantly larger in their invasive range than in their native range (Cuba and the Bahamas); within the invasive range, forest populations exceeded urban populations in size. Temporal analyses showed native A. sagrei (Cuba and the Bahamas) increased by approximately 5–7 mm per decade, with sex-based variation and faster growth in urban populations, while invasive A. sagrei exhibited no significant change. Conversely, A. carolinensis decreased by 10 mm per decade in urban habitats. Our findings suggest urbanization and competition with invasive species generate overlapping yet distinct selective pressures on Anolis morphology, with implications for understanding contemporary evolution in human-modified landscapes. Christopher Meehan
366: Diamondback Terrapins (Malaclemys terrapin) are native to the Atlantic and Gulf Coasts of the United States, and are imperiled across their range due to habitat loss and road mortality. Mark-recapture studies are critical for long-lived organisms because long-term data is needed to detect trends in population demographics. Despite their benefit, the majority of long-term mark-recapture studies of terrapins have been conducted on the Atlantic Coast. Since 2012 terrapins within the Barataria estuary have been part of a mark-recapture program. Terrapins are captured with unbaited fyke nets and given scute notches for identification when recaptured. Fourteen Cormack-Jolly-Seber models were generated and provided annual survival and capture probabilities between the sexes, which were then used in a Jolly-Seber model to estimate annual population sizes. 445 terrapins have been captured, 254 females, 190 males, and 1 juvenile, and there have been 49 recaptures. Abundance estimates were lowest in 2013 for females (416.6 ± 84.6) and males (278.3 ± 56.4), and highest in 2014 for females (918.3 ± 157.9) and males (618.9 ± 104.6). Female survival probability ranged from 75-87%, and male survival probability ranged from 79-91%. Despite yearly differences, annual abundance and survival probability has remained relatively consistent throughout the study. Survivability and abundance are both high, but neither metric is at the historical maximum of our study. Our population's consistently high abundance and survival estimates may be a reflection of limited interactions with humans. Emily N. Meese Emily Meese; Echelle Duffield; Ryan Logan; Miranda Haggerty; Kimo Morris; Lance Adams; Ryan Freedman;
367: Sunshine viruses (Sunviridae) are a recently discovered novel major clade of pathogenic viruses known, until now, from only one viral type isolated from captive collections of Australian pythons in Australia. We discovered a second, genetically divergent, genotype in captive sidewinders at Zoo Atlanta and traced the origin of the pathogen to the wild source-population in Yuma, Arizona, USA. Ongoing efforts are surveying taxonomical and geographical range for the virus. It is not yet know if this virus presents any conservation threat to snake species. Joseph R. Mendelson III
368: While high-throughput sequencing costs have plummeted, the 30× gold standard depth remains a financial and computational bottleneck for large-scale phylogenomic studies, limiting taxonomic sampling breadth. Low-coverage Whole Genome Sequencing (lcWGS) has emerged as a compelling alternative, reducing costs while retaining key advantages over targeted approaches, such as relaxed tissue requirements, reduced laboratory workload, and access to a broader marker diversity. Yet whether lcWGS faithfully captures the evolutionary signal needed for reliable phylogenomic inference in large radiations remains an open question. Zhang et al. (2019) suggested that depths as low as 5× and 20× suffice for UCE and BUSCO locus recovery respectively in insects, but it remains unclear whether these thresholds translate to other radiations, especially in vertebrates. The hyperdiverse Cypriniformes (4000+ species) provide an ideal case study, combining extensive prior genomic resources with typical genome sizes (~1.5 Gb) comparable to the insects of largest genome sizes previously studied. We exploited publicly available NCBI data, generating a sequencing depth gradient (10×, 15×, 20×, 30×) through in silico downsampling, and evaluated its impact on sequence assembly through length and % sequence identity and phylogenomic inference through locus recovery rate, alignment length, parsimony-informative sites, mean bootstrap support, and Robinson-Foulds distances between topologies. Results suggest that 10× coverage is sufficient to recover stable topologies congruent with higher coverage, inducing only marginal increases in nodal support at higher depths. This indicates that the core phylogenetic signal is captured at low coverage, making 10× an effective threshold for resolving complex radiations without redundant sequencing costs.
369: The alligator snapping turtle (AST, Macrochelys temminckii) occurs across the southeastern United States, but fundamental aspects of its ecology, such as its trophic ecology, are still lacking across much of its extensive range. Stable isotope ratios of carbon (δ13C) and nitrogen (δ15N) are elemental tracers that can be used to track energetic pathways and infer trophic position of consumers within food webs. We collected tissues of AST, local basal resources, and consumer (fishes, turtles) in three streams in East Texas (Alazan Wildlife Management Area, Shawnee, and Attoyac) to investigate aspects of trophic ecology and energy pathways maintaining populations of AST in these streams. We used stable isotope ratios of δ13C and δ15N in tissues collected from May to August 2023 from where the focal species was known. A total of 31 individuals of M. temminckii (average straight line carapace length = 36.0 cm; range =13.0 to 58.4 cm) were included. Macrochelys temminckii collected from Alazan had a narrower isotopic niche compared to individuals collected from Shawnee and Attoyac systems. Stable isotope ratios of carbon suggest that M. temminckii are supported by autochthonous (e.g., seston) rather than allochthonous (e.g., terrestrial plants) basal resources. Based on vertical position occupied by centrarchids, catfishes, and turtles, and their nitrogen ratios enrichment, these consumers appear to be important prey supporting M. temminckii. Sampling across broader spatial and temporal extents will provide context as to the variability in their isotopic niche. The isotopic niche variation across sites suggests that M. temminckii is a generalist consumer in their habitats. Clinton J Moran
370: Hemidactylus turcicus is an invasive species in the United States, which was first recorded in Florida in 1910. Other gecko species have been introduced, although none exhibit the rapid range expansion seen in H. turcicus, which may be linked to phenotypic, historic, and environmental factors. However, it is not clear why H. turcicus has been such a successful colonizer, especially when facing competition from other building-dwelling geckos. Priority effects likely shape the assembly of invasive gecko communities, where the earliest colonizing species can continue to occupy the niche spaces of future invaders even when late-arriving species are better adapted for the niche. Rapid sympatry of ecologically similar geckos can lead to character displacement and shifts in abundance. Here, we will study priority effects and competitive displacement among three non-native gekkonid species (H. turcicus, Tarentola mauritanica, and Cyrtopodion scabrum) that co-occur in San Antonio, Texas. Two of these species arrived recently, while the third, H. turcicus, has been established in Texas since the 1950s. We will use count data and environmental covariates to estimate relative abundance of geckos in areas of sympatry, while also measuring functional trait data (morphometrics and microhabitats) to determine if character displacement is evident among these competitors. Our data will elucidate competition outcomes of ecological interactions among these gecko invaders. We anticipate that priority effects better explain community assembly in nonnative geckos as the most established species (H. turcicus) will display hallmarks of competitive displacement in areas of sympatry but remain numerically and geographically dominant. Maddox Moran
371: In California, the foothill yellow-legged frog (Rana boylii) is a widely distributed endemic species that has experienced significant declines for a variety of reasons (Kupferburg 2012; Adams et al. 2017). R. boylii habitat is primarily found in rivers and streams, but within these, it exhibits a wide range of differences in temperature, vegetation, stream hydrology, and elevation (Lind 2004). Acoustic communication is important for successful reproduction in frogs, yet how specific habitat parameters, such as elevation, influence this trait remains poorly understood. Liao and Liu (2008) conducted a literature review examining the relationship between anuran acoustic organs (vocal sacs and tympana) and altitude across a wide range of frog taxa, finding that they decline and degenerate with increasing altitude. To determine whether a similar relationship exists in R. boylii, we examined museum specimens from the California Academy of Sciences and the Museum of Vertebrate Zoology, collected from two distinct elevational zones: low-elevation (0–300 m) and high-elevation (700–1,000 m). Tympanum and body length measurements were taken from 66 male specimens. We hypothesized that due to very different ecological pressures associated with elevational differences, tympanum size correlates with elevation. We found that frogs in the high-elevation zone have a mean tympanum diameter smaller than that of those collected from the lowelevation zone. Results from the Mann-Whitney U test and the T-Test indicate a highly significant difference between these two groups. These findings suggest that the elevation may be a driving force behind variation in tympanic morphology in R. boylii. John Morris
372: Competition among anuran larvae can slow development and result in smaller body size at metamorphosis. Potential effects include decreased survivorship or smaller adult body size, either of which can decrease recruitment rates through direct or indirect mechanisms. Within the continental U.S., Cuban Treefrogs (Osteopilus septentrionalis) are established in Florida and Louisiana and have invasive potential beyond the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plains, possibly affecting native anurans at multiple life-history stages. To examine the potential effects of larval O. septentrionalis, we quantified growth and activity levels of their tadpoles and those of two anurans native to eastern Texas: Green Treefrogs (Dryophytes cinereus) and Gulf Coast Toads (Incilius nebulifer). Tadpoles of the three species were raised in single or multi-species treatments. Both total and net growth of D. cinereus were lowest in the presence of O. septentrionalis, whereas only net growth of I. nebulifer was lower in treatments when O. septentrionalis larvae were present. Both activity level and net growth of O. septentrionalis were greatest when reared in isolation, potentially indicating density-dependent intraspecific competition. Together with the dietary generalist nature of the adults, the impacts of larval O. septentrionalis on native anurans that breed syntopically present challenges for persistence of the native species. To minimize the risk of potential declines in native anuran populations at local and regional scales, management of Cuban Treefrogs should focus primarily on preventing establishment of new populations. Lindsay Mullins
373: The flatfish family Soleidae is one of the most speciose families of the Pleuronectiformes with approximately 29 genera and 139 species recognized within the family. The soleid genus Soleichthys contains approximately 15 described species with another 6-7 species recognized but not formally described. Members of Soleichthys inhabit relatively shallow tropical waters from east Africa and the Red Sea, to southern Japan, both coasts of northern Australia and many insular locations throughout the Indo-west Pacific Ocean. These small-sized, often colorful, species are infrequently captured, and with few exceptions are not well represented in fish collections. Juveniles have a different color pattern than adults which often complicates identifications. Unfortunately, most of the specimens do not have associated tissue samples, which would help identifications and help to match color morphs within a species. Although these species overlap in meristic and morphological characters, they can be sorted into high and low meristic groups and together with color features can be diagnosed. Several new species are presented herein based on morphological characters and pigmentation features. Eric C. Munscher
374: Treefrog species of Bokermannohyla are often difficult to identify phenotypically, which is further challenged by known hybridization in this clade. In southeastern Brazil, many individuals in overlapping areas were traditionally assigned to B. circumdata or B. luctuosa, very similar in calls and morphology. A recent phylogeny restricted the distribution of these species, leaving a large proportion of specimens without taxonomic assignments. We aimed to phylogenetically delimit lineages within this complex and investigate possible hybridization across their geographic range. We generated genomic data for 99 individuals spanning ca. 1200 km and inferred phylogenetic relationships by combining our sequence data with additional GenBank sequences of 49 species included in the most recent Bokermannohyla phylogeny. We then evaluated genetic structure and admixture (i.e., possible hybridization) using ca. 8700 SNPs. We recovered nine species that matched those defined by the most recent phylogeny, including B. circumdata and B. luctuosa. Genetic clustering largely corresponded to distinct species. Notable exceptions included B. sp. 4 and B. izecksohni, which shared the same genetic cluster despite forming separate clades, and B. vulcaniae, which exhibited two genetic clusters that match two locations. We identified 12 admixed individuals in different areas, involving the combinations B. luctuosa and B. vulcaniae, B. sp. 5 and B. circumdata, B. diamantina and B. vulcaniae, and the two B. vulcaniae clusters. These results reveal a complex evolutionary history that could reflect incomplete population differentiation, taxonomic over-splitting, and the influence of hybridization and/or retention of ancestral polymorphisms among lineages. Chloe Nash
375: Selective constraints are limitations imposed on organisms by their environment that shape which traits are favored by natural selection and limit evolutionary changes. Head-first burrowing is an example of constraint, where the shared selective pressures of burrowing constrain variation in body plans, such as in the sand lances (Ammodytidae) and the sand burrowers (Creediidae). Not only do sand lances burrow head-first in the benthos, they also school and feed in pelagic environments providing an interesting comparison to the exclusively benthic sand burrowers. This research investigates how head-first burrowing in sand lances and sand burrowers is imposing different selective constraints along the body through the lens of modularity and integration and in the context of life history spent in benthic and pelagic habitats. Using CT scanning and geometric morphometrics we determined how many modules are present, presence and patterns of integration, and if shape variation is different for the modules associated with burrowing compared to modules not associated with burrowing. We expect to recover two modules with the head forming a module separate from the rest of the body, and signals of integration among the modules. We also expect smaller variation in shape of the head module, shown by a lower disparity of the head compared to the rest of the body reflecting the strong selective pressure of head-first burrowing that results in a constraint on morphology. This research sheds light on the morphology associated with head-first burrowing, as well as how constraint is shaping adaptations within these families. Eli Nettlebeck
376: Sequential hermaphroditism, or sex change during an individual’s lifetime, increases the reproductive success of a species. It may be utilized to compensate for an inability to locate mates, or other factors like, small populations, reduced size, short lifespans, and microhabitat occupation. This is particularly true for small coral reef fishes. Those previously mentioned traits, coupled with strict microhabitat requirements, can limit options for reproduction. The association between microhabitat specialization and hermaphroditism, however, is still poorly understood, and it remains to be seen whether the strict lifestyle requirements a species may face could encourage hermaphroditism. The Gobiosomatini tribe is a group of fishes with various microhabitat associations to other organisms, such as sponges, corals, and urchins. Some species also live generalist lifestyles, tending to be larger, and without microhabitat associations. Sex change can be described in these fish by the presence of pAGS (precursive accessory gonadal structures), tissue mounds on the gonad that catalyze sexual transition, or the simultaneous presence spermatozoa and oocytes present in the same gonad. Functional hermaphroditism has been confirmed in one microhabitat specialist, though it’s unknown if other related taxa are also hermaphroditic. Histology will be used to examine the gonad structure of species within the Gobiosomatini tribe, and test for a relationship between hermaphroditism and microhabitat associations. The gonad structure of habitat specialists and generalists will be also compared. Whatever findings regarding hermaphroditism may help bolster existing phylogenetic connections between taxa and create a better understanding of the reproductive and ecological dynamics of hermaphroditic reef fishes. Matilda Newell
377: Flotant marshes in the Barataria and Terrebonne basins provide numerous ecosystem services including nutrient abatement, as well as habitat and resources for aquatic organisms. However, many flotant marshes in south Louisiana are becoming degraded, reducing the provision of habitat for aquatic biota. Although flotant marshes provide critical habitat for numerous fishes and invertebrates, including commercially harvested species, there has been little research on flotant marsh stability on aquatic faunal communities. Therefore, the purpose of this study is to examine aquatic faunal communities at healthy and unhealthy flotant marshes in the Barataria and Terrebonne basins. Healthy and unhealthy flotant marshes were sampled monthly in Lac des Allemands, Lake Boeuf and Lake de Cade. Faunal sample efforts employed multiple passive sampling methods including minnow traps, crab traps and experimental gill nets. Catch per unit effort, abundance, species richness, and size of individuals were recorded. Fish and macroinvertebrate abundance and diversity and water quality were compared among basins and between healthy and unhealthy flotant marshes. Preliminary results indicate that healthy and unhealthy flotant do not significantly differ in species richness but significantly differ in Shannon-Weiner diversity (Welch’s F1,34.6 = 6.59, P = 0.040). Results demonstrate the importance of preserving stable healthy flotant marsh to maintain aquatic species diversity and community composition. Examination of the ecological function of healthy and unhealthy flotant marshes can help inform conservation and preservation efforts for south Louisiana’s aquatic ecosystems. Andrew Nosal
378: The deep sea is an understudied biome comprising nearly 95% of all livable space on Earth. Traditionally, studying life in the deep sea requires the use of remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) using visual surveys through the ROV camera. However, the capacity to analyze filtered water for the DNA signatures of marine life increases the scope to census this remote habitat. As such, ROVs have been recently retrofitted to collect water samples at depth for environmental DNA (eDNA), a method using high-throughput sequencing to detect DNA in water samples. In April of 2023, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Association Ocean Exploration Program (NOAA-OE) conducted the 2023 Shakedown + EXPRESS West Coast Exploration (EX2301) in the northeastern Pacific Ocean with a specific mission to test the use of eDNA to explore the deep sea biome. During the expedition, water samples were collected to research whether eDNA can be used to characterize different biological communities and to determine spatial assemblage patterns of different taxa using different DNA markers. Using eDNA as a standalone method, assemblage patterns were detected, distinguishing mesopelagic and bathypelagic zones using the cytochrome c oxidase 1 (COI) and 12S mitochondrial DNA (12S) markers. Within the mesopelagic, dominant substrate types were distinguishable. Across bathypelagic sites, we found a high degree of dispersion, suggesting that greater numbers of replicate sampling would be necessary to characterize them. The results presented in this study provide a framework for assessing the ability of eDNA to capture the diversity of the deep sea biome. Megan O'Brien
379: Understanding how freshwater species diversify across river systems remains a central question in evolutionary biology. Geographically structured lineages of the African catfish genus Amphilius (Family: Amphiliidae) tend to resemble each other morphologically, complicating species delimitation and obscuring evolutionary relationships. This study investigates phylogenetic relationships and species boundaries within Amphilius from Gabon using an integrative approach. A COI gene tree reveals multiple well-supported lineages, many of them limited to specific river basins such as the Komo or Ogooué-Ngounié systems, a pattern consistent with diversification driven by geographic isolation. Several individuals provisionally identified as A. cf. longirostris and Amphilius sp. form independent clades, suggesting the presence of undescribed species. In contrast, morphospace analyses based on linear morphometrics show substantial overlap among genetically defined lineages, and meristic data reveal no clear differentiation, although qualitative traits such as coloration may offer additional diagnostic value and merit further evaluation. These patterns indicate that morphological similarity does not reflect shared ancestry and is more consistent with morphological conservatism, in which lineages retain an ancestral rheophilic morphology despite accumulating substantial genetic divergence across drainage basins. This integrative framework highlights the limitations of morphology-based taxonomy in Amphilius and reveals unrecognized lineages, at least some of which may merit recognition at the species level. Future analyses will use landmark-based geometric morphometrics to quantify body shape variation and microCT scanning to generate high-resolution 3D skeletal reconstructions for detailed functional and evolutionary analyses across Amphiliidae.
380: Amphibians are threatened by numerous anthropogenic changes to the environment, including habitat modification and the widespread introduction of livestock, such as cattle, to the landscape. Aquatic larval amphibians are especially vulnerable to changes in water quality, due to their small size and thin membranes for respiration. Cattle add nutrients to watersheds through their waste and stir up sediment through their trampling. High enough nutrient concentrations may be toxic to larvae and lead to eutrophic conditions, depleting oxygen levels. In this experiment, 192 larval tiger salamanders (Ambystoma tigrinum) were divided between 24 cattle tank mesocosms, which were divided into 6 treatment groups in a 3 x 2 factorial design. The larvae are exposed to either 0 g, 250 g, or 1250 g of fresh cattle waste, and the presence or absence of trampling. These treatments are repeated bi-weekly. Every month, chlorophyll, dissolved oxygen, ammonia, phosphate, nitrate, and nitrite concentrations are assessed, along with the larvae’s mass and SVL. In June, daily monitoring will start to retrieve metamorphosed salamanders. The experiment will conclude once all salamanders have metamorphosed. We expect to see negative effects on salamander development and survival rates in tanks exposed to increased turbidity from trampling and higher levels of waste, though trampling may allow sediment to bind to and remove toxins from the water column, mitigating the negative effects. Emily Olson
381: Nuptial tubercles are keratinized structures that develop on the heads and bodies of male minnows (Cyprinidae) during breeding season. While their functional role is not fully understood, tubercles are often associated with conspecific interactions, spawning behaviors, and mate recognition. Environmental conditions often drive phenotypic variation, and we hypothesize that nuptial tubercle dispersal and allometry may differ across habitat types. In this study, we examine whether tubercle dispersal patterns and body morphometrics vary across habitat-associated forms, including taxa occupying both lotic and lentic systems. Rather than treating species as strictly benthic or pelagic, we consider a continuum of habitat use reflected in morphology, such as fusiform body shapes associated with greater use of the water column and dorsoventrally depressed body shapes associated with benthic, substrate-oriented habitats. We measured standard length, body depth, and head width, and recorded the number and spatial distribution of tubercles across the head and body. Preliminary analyses show no statistically significant differences in tubercle distribution across habitat categories or body forms. Instead, variation in tubercle distribution is driven by species identity, indicating that species-specific factors structure these patterns rather than broad environmental or habitat classifications. These results demonstrate that tubercle distribution cannot be predicted from generalized habitat associations and instead reflects species-level differences, emphasizing the need for taxonomically explicit approaches when evaluating the evolution and function of secondary sexual characteristics in freshwater fishes. Lynette Ong
382: Hemogregarines of the genus Hepatozoon (Apicomplexa, Hepatozoidae) are common hemoparasites found in all major vertebrate lineages globally. Despite their high diversity in reptiles and potential ecological significance, hemoparasites that infect squamates in Southern Africa are historically understudied, and key aspects of their biology, taxonomy, evolutionary relationships, and geographic distribution remain poorly understood. Using a combination of molecular and morphological techniques, we assess hemogregarine diversity in squamates from São Tomé and Príncipe (STP), Angola, and Namibia. Blood smear analysis from 954 specimens yielded a 2.2% positive infection rate for Hepatozoon parasites: 1 (0.7 %; n = 127) from STP, 11 (3%; n = 322) from Namibia, and 9 (2%; n = 505) from Angola. Snakes had the highest prevalence (36%; n= 9/25) with positive individuals in Viperidae (n=2), Pseudaspididae (n=1), Pythonidae (n=4), and Elapidae (n=2). Positive infections were identified in 12 lizard individuals (1.2%; n = 929) from the families Scincidae (n=11) and Gekkonidae (n=1). Ongoing work will link parasite morphologies to their genetic data to evaluate their phylogenetic relationships. This multispecies survey reveals high hidden hemoparasite biodiversity in Southern Africa and significant potential for new species records in Hepatozoon. Gregory B. Pauly
383: Although a mostly aquatic lineage, some Desmognathine salamanders in the Southern Appalachians have been observed foraging in more terrestrial environments than in aquatic ones. This study examines foraging via isotopic niches of blackbelly salamanders (Desmognathus mavrokoilius) in areas of both with and without shovelnose salamanders (Desmognathus marmoratus). We hypothesized that in co-occurring habitats, blackbelly salamanders would forage more terrestrially to avoid high competition. Currently, 6 streams (3 sympatric and 3 allopatric) have been sampled from to collect tail tissue samples, as well as a variety of aquatic and terrestrial invertebrate prey items. Preliminary stable isotope results indicate a trend that aligns with the proposed hypothesis. In sympatric streams, blackbelly salamanders have isotope signatures that match those of terrestrial invertebrates. In allopatric streams, this isotopic signature appears more mixed with aquatic invertebrates. Additional stream sites are to be sampled along an elevation gradient to examine any trends that could be affected by that factor. Protein lipid analysis of tissue samples, along with stomach pumping data, will also be used to further elucidate any overlap in foraging and potential for competition. Emileo Peralta
384: The genus Macrhybopsis contains 12 species of benthic, barbeled minnows that are distributed throughout central and eastern North America (including Canada, Mexico and the US). Members of Macrhybopsis demonstrate fewer secondary sexual characteristics than some other North American minnows, with most species having monomorphic unculiferous tubercles, roughly ovoid aggregations of keratinized epidermal cells, each with a keratinized projection (unculus) at the surface. Among species of Macrhybopsis unculiferous tubercles are present in both males and females as well as juveniles of at least 18 mm SL in four distinct conditions. In addition to unculiferous tubercles, male Macrhybopsis also possess typical conical (“nuptial”) tubercles on the dorsal surface of the pectoral fin in association with the anterior rays. To compare the tuberculation in Macrhybopsis with that of other North American minnows, we used scanning electron microscopy (SEM), histology, micro-computed tomography and a recently published methodology that allows the coding of tubercle presence by cephalic region. We then test the hypothesis of whether ecological traits in minnows (e.g., habitat) may be related to different aspects of tuberculation by analyzing their relationships using phylogenetic comparative methods.
385: Human activities over the past few centuries have caused extensive fragmentation of wildlife populations, primarily through urban growth, agricultural development, and aquatic habitat modification. While studies have quantified the effects of these anthropogenic activities on population diversity, few have compared natural historical fragmentation to recent anthropogenic barriers. The common mudpuppy (Necturus maculosus) is a fully aquatic salamander sensitive to population fragmentation, and widespread declines have been documented across the Midwest. During the last glacial period, connections between the Mississippi and Souris-Red-Rainy water basins allowed mudpuppies to colonize northern regions. As the glaciers retreated, these basins became isolated, resulting in long-term natural population separation. However, dam construction has resulted in drastic population fragmentation across these basins. Thus, we aimed to assess the relative effects of long-term natural barriers and short-term anthropogenic barriers on genetic differentiation in the common mudpuppy. Mudpuppies were sampled across Minnesota, representing two major water-basin populations separated for approximately 11,000 years, as well as populations separated for up to 150 years by series of dams. Tail tissues were collected, and ddRADseq was used to characterize genomic variation. Genetic diversity metrics were estimated using Stacks, and PCA was used to assess population structure. Preliminary analyses indicate stronger genetic differentiation among populations separated by dams than among populations isolated by basins, despite the latter being separated for two orders of magnitude longer. These results suggest that anthropogenic barriers may rapidly reduce genetic connectivity in fully aquatic species, with potential implications for population persistence and river management in the upper Midwest. Sinlan Poo
386: Roads are among the most pervasive anthropogenic alterations to natural spaces over the last century. For some wildlife, roads are significant dispersal barriers, restricting movement and causing mortality during crossing attempts, both of which can impact population demographics and lead to declines. Thus, understanding the spatiotemporal predictors of road mortality events is critical for implementing effective mitigation measures for species of conservation concern. We used landcover data and observations of snake and turtle road mortality around Carlyle Lake, Illinois, collected from 2000–2002 to determine if landscape features predict spatial patterns of road mortality. We recorded a total of 266 road mortality events across five snake and two turtle species, including 41 mortalities of the now federally threatened Eastern Massasauga. Using landscape variables in a logistic regression model to compare observed versus random locations, we found that predictive ability varied among the species examined. Our road surveys identified areas with high mortality historically, but our results for some species can also be used to identify areas where road mortality is predicted to be highest under current landcover conditions. Mitigation measures and monitoring could be focused on these locations to benefit species of concern. Wes Pratt
387: Wolffishes and the Wolf Eel (Anarhichadidae) are cold-water, durophagous fishes that live in the Northern oceans. They are morphologically distinct from other perciformes, characterized by robust, molariform dentition organized into toothplates that are used in crushing invertebrate prey items. Because of their ecological significance and unique morphologies, we performed a comparative analysis of craniofacial morphology and mechanics among all five anarhichadid species. We characterized interspecific variation in craniofacial morphologies across the family by performing 3D geometric morphometrics on high resolution microCT scans of each species. Next, we use biomechanics to better understand the crushing processes used by these species during prey capture. It is likely that their durophagous diet has influenced various cranial elements to favor their unique feeding ecology. To shed light on these relationships, we evaluated the mechanical advantage of the lower jaw. We next measured the cross-sectional area of the molariform tooth plates of the upper jaw to evaluate how plate geometry relates to durophagy performance across species. Lastly, we aim to compare ontogenetic shifts between the Atlantic Wolffish (Anarichas lupus) and the Pacific Wolf Eel (and Anarrhichthys ocellatus) to determine if their divergent morphologies are due to variation in ontogenetic trajectories. Together, these analyses allow us to test how the durophagous feeding system has driven evolutionary shape change through feeding and ontogeny. Bennett Price
388: Little is known about the secretive and fully aquatic salamander: the Three-toed Amphiuma (Amphiuma tridactylum). Although these salamanders are abundant in Louisiana, they are understudied, and their ecology remains poorly understood. We propose to radio-track five male and five female A. tridactylum each week via radiotelemetry to document their locations, movements, and behaviors. This data may provide insight into homerange size, whether this species exhibits sex-specific movement patterns, and whether home ranges differ during and outside the breeding season. We also plan to record individuals' habitat selection to gain further understanding of habitat preferences in this understudied species. Griffin Pugh
389: Sternopygus is a genus of weakly electric Neotropical knifefish with a wide distribution across South and Central America, extending from Panama to Argentina. This genus is currently composed of 12 valid species with five being endemic to the trans-Andean region of South America and lower Central America, and seven being found in all major cis-Andean South American basins. Among these, S. macrurus has its type locality broadly defined as “Brazil,” and the type specimen is taxidermized, which limits detailed morphological comparisons. Recent studies suggest that S. macrurus likely represents a complex of several undescribed species distributed across multiple cis-Andean South American basins. Two populations frequently attributed to S. macrurus are those inhabiting the Paraguay and upper Paraná rivers in central South America. Based on an integrative analysis of external morphology, osteology, genetic haplotypes, and molecular species delimitation techniques, these two populations are described as two new species. Phylogenetic analyses of the mitochondrial COI gene and haplotype network reconstruction recovered nine haplotypes across the La Plata basin—five in the upper Paraná and four in the lower Paraná and Paraguay basins—suggesting strong hydrographic structuring of genetic diversity across the region. ABGD, ASAP, and GMYC supported the delimitation of all Sternopygus species and the phylogeny recovered the two new species as sister to each other. The recognition of these taxa increases the number of valid species of Sternopygus to 14 and further supports the hypothesis that the widely distributed S. macrurus, as previously recognized, represents a complex of several distinct species. Austin Rejcek
390: Understanding how island biodiversity originates and persists is central to evolutionary biology and conservation. Islands of the Puerto Rico Bank, shaped by repeated cycles of isolation and connectivity, provide a natural laboratory to evaluate how dispersal, divergence, and introgression interact during diversification. Here we use low-coverage whole-genome data from modern and historical specimens of Caribbean Spondylurus skinks, sampling 14 of 17 currently recognized species, to reconstruct the evolutionary history and assess current genetic diversity of this insular radiation. Phylogenomic analyses of mitochondrial and nuclear SNPs reveal pervasive discordance among gene trees, extensive introgression, and reject a simple stepping-stone model of diversification across the Caribbean. Instead, Spondylurus diversification reflects repeated long-distance dispersal, gene flow following divergence, and persistence on small islands and cays. Genomic patterns of diversity, runs of homozygosity, effective population sizes, and genetic loads show strong contrasts among species with different recent demographic histories, including severe inbreeding, elevated realized genetic load, and sharp population declines associated with invasive predators. Historical specimens exhibit higher heterozygosity and lower genetic load than contemporary samples, indicating rapid genomic erosion over the last century. Together, our results highlight introgression as a persistent force shaping Caribbean skink evolution and reveal urgent conservation risks driven by recent demographic collapse and loss of genomic resilience. Josh Rivera
391: Ambystoma talpoideum are facultative paedomorphs, exhibiting a life-history polyphenism where individuals either remain as aquatic larvae through sexual development and into adulthood, or undergo metamorphosis to become terrestrial adults. These divergent ontogenetic pathways are adaptively significant, and highly dependent on the environmental conditions. This study aims to investigate the independent influence that varied temperature and food availability have on the frequency timing, and size at which A. talpoideum transition between life history stages. I will quantify developmental outcomes, specifically including incidence and timing of metamorphosis, and associated morphological traits, such as growth rate, under a factorial design of food and temperature regimes. While previous studies largely used large pond and mesocosms, where complex interspecies interactions are inevitable, this study utilizes individual housing in a controlled laboratory approach. By growing the salamanders in individual containers, the physiological effect of environmental temperature and food availability can be studied independently. By decoupling the effects of temperature and nutrition from the effects of interspecific crowding or competition, the proximate environmental cues that drive these life history transitions in A. talpoideum can be clarified, progressing knowledge of their life history. Abigail Robison
392: Chemical cues are central to mate choice in many vertebrates, yet the role of female signals and their hormonal regulation remains poorly understood. Estrogen is a key regulator of sexual receptivity across vertebrates, but its influence on female signaling in reptiles is not well known. In eastern fence lizards (Sceloporus undulatus), males rely on femoral pore secretions for chemical communication, while females lack such glands and may instead produce chemical cues via lipids on the surface of their skin. We tested whether estrogen influences female signaling and sexual receptivity by surgically manipulating estrogen levels to create low-estrogen (ovariectomized) and high-estrogen (sham surgery) females. Male odor preferences were measured in a three-zone choice arena to assess whether males respond to potential chemical cues from females and whether female estrogen levels affect such responses. Additionally, live male-female interactions were staged to quantify female receptivity and male courtship intensity. Together, these approaches evaluate how estrogen shapes both potential chemical signals and behavioral contributions to mate choice. This work provides new insight into the hormonal regulation of female signaling and its role in lizard courtship. Amanda Rocio
393: Biofluorescence, the absorption of short-wavelength light and its re-emission at longer wavelengths, has been documented across diverse taxa. While recent work has begun to characterize the chemical and physiological mechanisms underlying fluorescence in frogs, little is known about how this trait changes throughout development. Understanding the ontogeny of fluorescence is essential for interpreting its potential ecological and functional roles, including signaling, camouflage, or sexual cues. This study examines temporal changes in biofluorescence in a cohort of ten juvenile Ceratophrys cranwelli. A longitudinal design was employed using two complementary methods. First, spectrometer measurements were collected to quantify the brightness of fluorescence. Second, changes in fluorescent patch size and spatial distribution relative to body growth were assessed using geometric morphometric analyses of standardized fluorescence images. Data collection for both approaches was conducted weekly. By integrating spectral and spatial analyses, this work provides insight into how fluorescence patterns emerge and shift through time, contributing to a broader understanding of how they influence both intra- and interspecific communication.
394: The Guaviare region (Colombia), due to its strategic position between Amazonian and Orinoco ecosystems, exhibits vast biogeographic complexity. Historically, the study of its ichthyofauna has been insufficient, constrained by limited access to the territory and public order dynamics that hindered fieldwork in past decades. This study characterized fish biodiversity through sampling in ecosystems associated with the Guaviare, Inírida, and Vaupés rivers, along with their main tributaries in the Guaviare political region. Community-based sampling was conducted with local fishers across the four municipalities (San José, El Retorno, Calamar, and Miraflores), using various fishing techniques and exploring multiple aquatic habitats (morichales, lagoons, streams, and main river channels). A visual catalog was developed and designed, including diagnostic descriptions of 377 species, along with ecological aspects, trophic and reproductive habits, conservation status, and photographic records that facilitate field identification. Additionally, new records for the department of Guaviare were reported, significantly expanding current knowledge of regional fish diversity. The catalog is the result of more than three years of collaborative work with local communities, presenting a detailed inventory that provides a solid baseline for future ecological studies, while also serving as a tool for the conservation of aquatic ecosystems and for environmental education through the social appropriation of knowledge. Alejandro Romero
395: Chinook salmon (Oncorhynchus tshawytscha) and steelhead trout (O. mykiss) runs that spawn in rivers on the West Coast of the US experience multiple stressors throughout their life cycle. Changing ocean food webs, increased prevalence of harmful algal blooms (HABs), contaminant exposures, and many other stressors combine to cause population declines. Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency complex (TDC) may be a symptom of these multiple stressors, or an additional cause of population-level impairments. It is still unknown how TDC may arise. This project combines field sampling, controlled laboratory experiments, and modeling to assess potential causes and effects of thiamine deficiency at critical stages of salmonine life cycles, and interactions of TDC with other known stressors. Here we present our research plans for experiments to explain the role of HABs in thiamine dynamics, and investigate whether common stressors (e.g., temperature, copper exposure, disease challenge) contribute to an increased thiaminase production within prey. We also present preliminary data on ocean prey base nutritional profiles (lipids, thiamine, and thiaminase) from the initial year of Pacific coast-wide monitoring of salmonine egg thiamine. There is strong evidence that anchovy-dominated prey bases are linked to TDC in salmon. Furthermore, TDC as indicated by egg thiamine appears widespread. This is the largest effort to-date that will integrate patterns from California to Alaska. This multi-year effort brings together an interdisciplinary team to investigate how multiple stressors and salmonine life history and physiology interact to perpetuate poor recruitment of these culturally and economically important fishes. Freya Rowland Freya Rowland; Elizabeth Schyling; L. Kealoha Freidenburg; Mark Urban; Jonathan Richardson; A.Z. Andis
396: Ectothermic organisms such as rattlesnakes have activity levels that directly correlate to environmental temperature, however, human interference often limits our ability to accurately quantify and analyze activity levels in wild animals. In recent years, the use of live-streaming camera technology allows researchers to observe wild animals remotely and in real time, allowing for a constant stream of activity data without human influence on behavioral patterns. The aim of this study is to investigate, quantify, and predict the relationship between weather data and the activity patterns of the Western Rattlesnake (Crotalus oreganus) using an archive of video data taken from a live-streaming camera. California Polytechnic State University San Luis Obispo established Project RattleCam in the Fall of 2021, a livestreaming camera shared through YouTube that broadcasts live footage from a rookery of C. oreganus. By comparing daily weather patterns to documented rattlesnake thermoregulatory behavior, we will quantify the impact of environmental temperature on snake activity and create a predictive model to estimate activity levels as temperatures change. The collection of the data that will be used to create the initial algorithm is still in progress and will be completed in Spring of 2026. When collection is complete using data for 2021, the model will generate a prediction for snake behavior in later years based on weather data inputs, and its effectivness will be judged by comparing it to the observed data collected from 2023. Molly Russell
397: Satellite telemetry has transformed the study of shark movement ecology by enabling researchers to track animals across vast, otherwise inaccessible marine environments. For decades, the Argos satellite system has been used to track marine megafauna. Recently, Argos operations expanded into an integrated Argos-Kineis constellation that includes a fleet of nanosatellites designed to increase transmission frequency and improve localization performance. While these advances promise finer-scale tracking of wide-ranging species, changes in satellite architecture and localization algorithms may influence derived movement metrics, raising questions about whether ecological inferences remain comparable across telemetry platforms and between new and historical telemetry datasets. We evaluated how differences in satellite-receiving systems and analytical workflows influence ecological inference from animal tracking data. Using satellite-tagged sharks from South Florida as a case study, we compared key properties of telemetry datasets generated by legacy Argos processing and the newer Argos-Kineis constellation. Specifically, we examined differences in transmission dynamics, including the timing and frequency of location estimates, and how these differences propagate into commonly used movement metrics. We then assessed how alternative processing approaches affect derived estimates of animal space use. Across individuals, we compared transmission intervals, patterns of data density, inferred behavioral state, and spatial estimates of habitat use derived from kernel-based utilization distributions. By examining how evolving telemetry systems shape the structure of tracking datasets and downstream analytical outputs, this study evaluates whether methodological differences among satellite platforms influence ecological interpretations of shark movement, fine-scale behavior, and space use. Jade Samples
398: Wildfires are increasing in frequency and intensity worldwide, altering habitat structure and potentially reshaping predator-prey interactions. Because many antipredator defenses rely on visual signals, firedriven changes in background and vegetation structure may influence the effectiveness of defensive coloration. Here, we experimentally tested how fire affects predation risk across different antipredator strategies in snakes in the Pantanal and Humid Chaco, two fire-prone Neotropical ecosystems. We deployed 900 clay snake replicas representing five color-pattern morphs associated with camouflage, mimicry, and aposematism across burned and unburned habitats. Overall predation rates did not differ between fire treatments. However, the effectiveness of defensive strategies varied with habitat context. Cryptic morphs experienced higher predation in burned areas, consistent with reduced background matching in simplified post-fire environments. In contrast, aposematic and mimetic patterns maintained lower attack rates under these conditions, suggesting that conspicuous warning signals remain effective despite increased detectability. Imperfect mimicry showed limited protection in burned habitats, indicating that signal accuracy may be critical when visual exposure is high. These results demonstrate that fire can alter the selective landscape of antipredator traits by modifying the visual environment in which predators detect prey. Our findings highlight that disturbance-driven changes in habitat structure can differentially affect the performance of defensive strategies, with potential consequences for the persistence and evolution of phenotypic diversity in fire-prone ecosystems. Aintzane Santaquiteria Aintzane Santaquiteria Gil; Mark Sabaj Pérez; Alessio Capobianco; Matthew Burnett; Olga Otero; Alison Murray; Diogo Mayrinck; Nathan Lujan; Milton Tan; Melissa Rincón Sandoval; Lily Hughes; Jonathan Armbruster; Giorgio
399: Southeast Asia is a geologically complex region, characterized by the convergence of major tectonic plates, the uplift of mountain ranges, and frequent sea level changes. The presence of geographic barriers can limit population connectivity and dispersal, leading to reduced gene flow and, ultimately, allopatric speciation. These dynamics have led this region to become a global biodiversity hotspot with potential for cryptic species. Ahaetulla prasina is one of the widely distributed arboreal snakes in Southeast Asia. This species has long been treated as a single species, but its taxonomy and phylogeny has not been fully resolved. Historically this species in Southeast Asia has been described under several subspecies which later end up in synonym (e.g., Dryophiops prasinus chinensis, Dryophiops prasinus indicus, & Dryophiops prasinus var. prasinus). Previous work with their mitochondrial phylogeny shows that this species might consist of several lineages, reflecting cryptic diversity. Although it provides preliminary understanding of A. prasina some uncertainties remain regarding the taxonomic status of Southeast Asian populations. To address these gaps, more extensive sampling across the species known distribution needs to be conducted to establish more precise species boundaries. Recognizing that mitochondrial DNA alone is insufficient for resolving complex tokogenetic relationships, my research will utilize genome-wide Single Nucleotide Polymorphism (SNP) data. By combining mitochondrial phylogeny and population genetic structure using SNP, I aim to elucidate the boundaries between species and populations and subsequently resolving taxonomy of this species. Sarah Sargent
400: The Slimy Salamander (Plethodon glutinosus) complex is a group of terrestrial plethodontids distributed from New York to Texas, consisting of 15 parapatric species described using allozymes. These species are morphologically conserved, making phenotypic differentiation difficult. This complex is suggested to exhibit narrow hybrid zone between geographically adjacent species both within the species complex and outside of the traditionally assigned species complex, such as the P. jordani, P. shermani, and P. metcalfi. Many of these lineages are range restricted and face threats of habitat loss from anthropogenic development and climate change. Several regionally confined studies have called into question several of these taxa using mitochondrial and nuclear evidence, however were limited in the geographic and taxonomic coverage. In this study, we re-assess the phylogeographic diversity of the P. glutinosus complex with near complete taxonomic sampling - 13 species - in addition to 10 outgroup species which may or may not hybridize with the in-group. We identify 4-6 lineages which exhibit extensive geneflow at almost all contact zones. We also find little phylogeographic structure across historically suggested geographic barriers such as the Mississippi River, however fine the Appalachian Mountains as potentially impactful on geneflow and population connectivity. Kristie Semanchik
401: Human-wildlife conflict is one of the most urgent challenges facing conservation efforts in Nepal today. It poses a significant threat to both wildlife populations and local communities, making it one of the greatest obstacles to conservation succes. The vulnerable mugger crocodile (Crocodylus palustris), an apex predator in the wetlands and rivers of lowland Nepal, is predominantly found in Chitwan National Park(CNP). Recent conservation successes have increased crocodile populations in protected areas and adjacent buffer zones. However, this has led to frequent human-crocodile conflicts, particularly in community and aquaculture ponds, posing risks to both local communities and crocodiles. Despite extensive research on human-wildlife conflicts in Chitwan, human-crocodile conflicts remain understudied, and many incidents, including human fatalities, are underreported. This study addresses this research gapby examining conflict patterns in the buffer zone of CNP. We used interview-based occupancy analysis to assess the spatial distribution of crocodiles and conflict occurrences, while semi-structured interviews provided insights into the types and intensity of conflict. Secondary data from the Department of National Park and Wildlife Conservation supplemented the findings. Our results show that crocodile populations have spread throughout the buffer zone, with conflict prevalent in multiple areas. Conflicts include attacks on humans, livestock, economic losses in fish farming, and resource competition, most of which remain undocumented.The park's records focus primarily on human casualties, overlooking other conflict types. The rising conflict threatens local communities and jeopardizes hard-earned mugger crocodile conservation success. This is leading to emerging coexistence issues for people and this vulnerable species. Aidan Shaw
402: The evocatively named Cottus confusus of the Columbia drainage has long represented one of the most enigmatic of Western sculpins, difficult to recognize in the field and defying attempts by numerous ichthyologists to separate it cleanly in morphological keys. Using a genome-wide data set of 5236 post-filtering SNPs, we demonstrate that the taxon’s elusive definition stems from its polyspecific nature. Phylogenetic (IQTREE) and populational analyses (ADMIXTURE, STRUCTURE), reveal unequivocally that the classic concept of Cottus confusus spans at least six and possibly as many as ten distinct evolutionary lineages that merit recognition at the species level. While several hybrid zones exist, most localities appear pure in clustering analyses run under a range of possible K values, and there is no evidence of rangewide introgression. The holotype locality in the Salmon River falls within the range of a highly divergent and well-supported clade that appears limited to a portion of the Snake River system of central Idaho, implying that distinct evolutionary lineages elsewhere in the range of the species complex will likely require formal taxonomic description, such as (but not limited to) lineages restricted to the Willamette, Deschutes, and Wallowa systems. Phylogeographic analysis reveals several cases of Upper Columbia lineages in the east closely related to lineages inhabiting the slopes of the Cascades in the west, possibly implying more than one historical episode of downstream migration. Mara Sidloski
403: The purpose of this poster is to provide an open forum for discussions with the leadership of the American Society of Ichthyologists and Herpetologists (ASIH). What can we do better to (1) grow and support our diverse membership, especially students; (2) foster greater membership involvement and organizational fiscal stability; (3) improve JMIH and Ichthyology & Herpetology; (4) prioritize resources to meet future obligations and goals; and (5) reinforce what we already do well? We can also deliberate the future of ichthyology and herpetology or anything else members wish to discuss with the President, President-Elect, and other members of ASIH leadership. We are here to listen to compliments, critiques, and ideas to improve our Society. We will also share drink tickets (if we have any left) with members who stop by to chat! Colin A. Simpfendorfer
404: Parental investment varies widely across ray-finned fish. One method is coating eggs with a distasteful or lethally toxic compound that deters or outright kills egg predators. However, not all ichthyotoxins are created equally, and their chemical composition and synthesis pathways also vary. The toxic attribute of gar (Lepisosteidae) eggs has been known for nearly two centuries, with consumption by humans resulting in foodborne illness. Previous studies have also found that gar egg derivatives were inconsistently cardiotoxic to both vertebrates and invertebrates, but the chemical identity and structure remained unknown. We report here initiation of an investigation of the presence of this toxin in Spotted Gar (Lepisosteus oculatus) eggs. Bioassay guided fractionation studies using Red Swamp Crayfish (Procambarus clarkii) confirm the presence of a lethal toxin. Results also support the conclusion that the ichthyotoxin is a small molecule that may complex to proteins, with both the independent and complexed structures proving to be toxic. Future work seeks to structurally characterize this compound using spectroscopic and mass spectrometric techniques. Samantha Skerlec
405: The gopher tortoise (Gopherus polyphemus) occurs in nearly all terrestrial habitats in the southeastern U.S. and is one of the most frequently translocated reptiles in North America. There is a need to determine which habitats are most suitable to support translocated tortoises and to provide restoration and management targets across different habitats. To address these needs, we used existing line transect distance sampling data to predict tortoise densities in different land cover types using a Bayesian implementation of a hierarchical distance sampling model. Data were collected from 2014 through 2020 as part of Florida’s gopher tortoise monitoring program for state conservation lands, and our models included two covariates describing habitat condition, soil depth to water table, and canopy cover. The predicted gopher tortoise densities varied by land cover type but generally increased with decreasing canopy cover. Among land cover types and under average soil depth to water table and canopy conditions in each land cover type, coastal strand, sandhill, coastal grassland, and coniferous plantation had the highest predicted tortoise densities (>1 tortoise/ha). Under the same conditions, the lowest predicted densities occurred in upland pine, upland coniferous, xeric hammock and mesic flatwoods (<0.40 tortoise/ha). This study demonstrates how extensive monitoring data and metrics of land cover condition can be used to inform future translocation protocols and habitat management and restoration. W. Leo Smith Caitlin Schoeck; Erik Grafel; Jack Newmark; Logan Penny; Ella Rogers; Laura Stewart; Sophia Volovoy; Alex
406: The University of Kansas Biodiversity Institute (KUBI) is actively incorporating a large, orphaned fish collection. These fishes were collected by the Missouri Department of Conservation from 1980 to 2000. This material, collected during statewide stream surveys, is adding substantially to the KUBI collection, which recently surpassed 46,000 cataloged lots representing more than 555,000 specimens. We estimate that the Missouri collection will ultimately contribute more than 78,000 additional specimens and further strengthen KUBI as a leading repository for Great Plains freshwater fishes. Work to date has processed 222 sites, yielding 2,190 identified and cataloged lots comprising 16,462 specimens, with 339 pre-sorted family-level jars and 25 additional unsorted fivegallon buckets awaiting processing. Prior to the incorporation of these specimens, our Missouri holdings included approximately 550 sites, 3,700 lots, and 52,000 specimens, so this will more than double our holdings from the state. This project has been supported by the University of Kansas and has provided extensive training of one graduate student and six undergraduates. The undergraduates are gaining valuable training in fish identification, curation, digitization, and hands-on museum collections work. We look forward to the complete digitization and publication of these records into online biodiversity repositories where they will be useful for research, management, and conservation. Orphaned collections are costly to absorb, but the results of this effort highlight their value. Blaire Smith
407: Unisexual salamanders in the Ambystoma laterale-jeffersonianum complex coexist with blue-spotted salamanders (Ambystoma laterale), yet distinguishing these lineages in the field remains difficult without genetic analysis. To address this challenge, we developed a standardized photographic workflow to generate highresolution, repeatable images for non-invasive phenotypic analysis. During the 2025 spring migration at Presque Isle in Marquette, Michigan, we collected dorsal and ventral images of over 200 individuals using a controlled camera setup with consistent lighting, positioning, and scale calibration. This image dataset supports three complementary research objectives. First, we quantified color variations using image-derived gray values to test whether spot-body contrast differs between diploid (LL) and (LLJ) individuals. Second, we evaluated whether external morphology captured in images can be used to accurately determine sex as well. Third, we extracted body length measurements from calibrated images to assess size differences between LL and LLJ individuals. Average contrast differed significantly between ploidy groups, driven primarily by variation in body coloration. We were able to clearly determine sex and successfully evaluated morphological variation in the complex. Together, these approaches demonstrated the versatility of standardized imaging as a non-invasive tool for studying amphibian phenotypes. By enabling simultaneous analysis of coloration, morphology, and size, this workflow reduces reliance on genetic and invasive methods while creating a permanent digital dataset for future research. Carol Spencer
408: In February 2026, AmphibiaWeb added the 9,000th amphibian species to its database, a remarkable milestone for biodiversity science and a testament to decades of careful fieldwork, taxonomy, and collaboration across the globe. From rainforest leaf litter to mountain streams, amphibians continue to reveal an extraordinary diversity of forms, life histories, and adaptations, reminding us how much of the natural world remains to be discovered. This achievement celebrates not only the richness of amphibian life, but also the scientists, local communities, and conservationists whose efforts make these discoveries possible -- roughly three new species are described each week since AmphibiaWeb started! At the same time, it underscores both the urgency and the opportunity of our moment: even as amphibians face unprecedented threats– the 9,000th species added to our database, Tylototriton wufengensis (Li et al 2026), is already proposed to be listed as Vulnerable -- our growing knowledge strengthens the foundation for protecting amphibians and the ecosystems they help sustain. Here at AmphibiaWeb, we declare this to be the year of the 9,000th amphibian species. Leah Spoolstra
409: Salivary glands have not been studied thoroughly in plethodontid salamanders; the enzyme contents of glands of the buccal cavity are poorly understood. Previous enzymatic studies in other families of amphibians have identified proteases and amylases in the oral cavity, which are thought to be secreted from the intermaxillary gland and lingual gland. We used immunohistochemistry to identify the presence of amylase, protease, and lipase in buccal glands of three species of Eurycea, and hematoxylin and eosin staining to describe gland morphology. Amylase and protease were present in the intermaxillary gland and in the surface epithelium of the tongue. Unlike the lingual gland of other amphibians, salivary enzymes were not detected in the lingual gland of Eurycea. Preliminary results indicate the possible presence of lipase in the oral cavity. Our study confirms the intermaxillary gland as a major salivary organ. Future work investigates a hypothesized evolutionary link between the plethodontid mental gland and salivary glands. Katie Steffen
410: Houston Toads (Anaxyrus houstonensis) have been federally listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act since 1970 due to a multitude of factors contributing to the loss and alteration of this species’ native habitat. Currently, there is a multipronged collaborative effort involving federal, state, and local agencies working on a Houston Toad management and recovery program. The prongs of this program include protecting and restoring habitat, propagating and supplementing individuals into the wild, establishing a monitoring program, and educating the public through outreach programs. As a part of this recovery program, the Natural Resources Institute was tasked with monitoring and surveying for wild chorusing Houston Toad populations in Robertson and Leon Counties, TX. To detect chorusing Houston Toads, we established 60 roadside auditory survey points in each county based on historical records and results from habitat models. To supplement the driving surveys, we also deployed 20 automatic recording devices (ARDs) each year on private lands throughout these counties. In total, we conducted 200.4 hours of roadside auditory surveys and the ARDs collected approximately 17,864.3 hours of recordings across the three-year study. The surveys were unsuccessful in detecting wild chorusing Houston Toads, but we did detect the presence of 12 anuran species calling during the study. Here, we present the results of our three-year frog call study in Leon and Roberston Counties. Ben Stegenga Benjamin Stegenga; Kira Cates; Thomas Akre; Chris Polinski; Ivana Mali; A Nowakowski; Matthew Kamm;
411: Understanding the combined effects of land use and climate stressors on reproduction and hatchling survivorship of long-lived turtle species is key to developing effective management strategies. In freshwater turtles, high adult survivorship often masks the long-term reproductive consequences of these stressors. Here, we studied how microclimate variability – fine scale temperature and moisture conditions – affects reproductive success of Spotted Turtles (Clemmys guttata) at both the northern and southern extents of their range. We deployed soil temperature and moisture sensors across available nesting habitat at known Spotted Turtle sites in Georgia and Massachusetts. In conjunction, we attached radio transmitters and thread bobbins to female turtles to locate nests. We placed additional sensors in and adjacent to nests to measure seasonal variation in nest temperature. All sensor data were used to assess microclimate conditions at nest sites relative to the available surrounding habitat. In Georgia, we tracked 9 turtles and located 14 nests, while in Massachusetts, we tracked 11 turtles and located 7 nests. Turtles in both populations consistently selected warmer nest sites when compared to random locations, and nests also had higher soil moisture than random sites in Massachusetts. Fifteen turtles hatched in Georgia, and 25 turtles hatched in Massachusetts. Upon hatching, we monitored growth and righting responses in a lab for approximately 6 months. Warmer nest temperatures were associated with higher growth rates in Massachusetts turtles, but righting time increased with nest temperature in Georgia. These results will help guide habitat management decisions where Spotted Turtles are a conservation priority. Adam Steinfeld
412: We previously identified invasive mammalian predators as the primary cause of lizard extinction globally, especially on islands. But what are the non-lethal impacts of invasive mammals to native lizards? How are some species able to coexist with invasive threats while others cannot? In St. Croix, US Virgin Islands, invasive mongooses have been implicated in the extinction or extirpation of multiple reptile species. However, the St. Croix Anole (Anolis acutus) remains numerous despite this threat. These lizards are widespread on the main island in sites of variable mongoose density as well as on four mammal-free offshore cays. We collected habitat, behavior, and morphological data on anoles at sites across St. Croix to examine the influence of mammalian predator density on anole biology. At each site, we recorded habitat and ecological data as well as lizard perch height, temperature, and flight initiation distance. We also captured as many individuals as possible and measured limbs, toes, body length, and counted the number of toepad lamellae. We found that mammalian predator density has significant associations with behavior and morphology. Our results highlight how invasive species can impact native wildlife and the provides valuable insight into the mechanisms of how naïve prey and introduced predators can coexist. Johanna Stewart
413: Although traversing sand is difficult for most animals, many snakes can do so easily using sidewinding locomotion. Sidewinding snakes alternately plant some body segments while lifting and propelling others forward, causing the snake to travel in an overall direction oblique to the long axis of its body. Sidewinding has evolved multiple times throughout snake phylogeny, and it differs markedly from a more widespread form of locomotion—terrestrial lateral undulation. While biomechanical differences between sidewinding and lateral undulation have been well established, it is unclear whether these modes represent discrete forms or exist as two extremes along a continuum. One subfamily, Natricinae, provides ample opportunity to investigate the potential existence of such a continuum, as its species vary in their frequency and ability to sidewind. Hence, we investigated the biomechanics of sidewinding and lateral undulation in one natricine species, the Diamondback Watersnake (Nerodia rhombifer). From dorsal-view videos of snakes moving across sand and pebbles, we tracked and extracted the coordinates of the snout and four reflective body markers. Using these data, we tested which metrics are most useful for rigorously quantifying differences in the kinematics of sidewinding versus lateral undulation. Developing a quantitative methodology to distinguish these two modes of locomotion can facilitate future studies examining which aspects of biomechanics, morphology, and control are key to effective sidewinding performance.
414: Type localities are a fundamental concept in taxonomy. The type locality corresponds to the original locality from which the name-bearing type specimens were collected. The concept of types and priority also helps to enhance stability of identifications of samples. Sampling topotypic samples, therefore, can be important for ensuring data are representative of name-bearing types, especially genomic data which may be difficult to obtain from the original type specimens. In addition, type localities are fundamental for linking biological characteristics to taxonomic names via species distributions. We assessed the type localities of all valid species of North American Leuciscidae from Eschmeyer's Catalog of Fishes. Type localities with coordinates were recorded directly. We also compiled previously georeferenced coordinates from FishNet2. Finally, we used GeoLocate to georeference type localities without available georeferenced coordinates. Exact or hypothetical coordinates are assigned to nearly all type localities for species of North American Leuciscidae, although estimated precision for hypothetical coordinates varies considerably. We also investigate and resolve the type locality of Cyprinella camura. These type localities will guide sampling for comprehensive taxonomic sampling of genomic data for the North American Leuciscidae. Samuel Taylor Samuel Taylor; Timothy Earley; Joseph Coolon; Adelina Rodriguez; Phillip Harris; Jeremy Wright; Antonio
415: Understanding how ectotherms interact with their thermal environment has been a major herpetological research area for decades. Body temperature data, commonly measured via a probe inserted into the cloaca, is critical for this research. As part of a larger effort to rewild endangered Blunt-nosed Leopard Lizards (Gambelia sila), we measured thermoregulation using conventional thermal gradient trials with thermistor probes inserted into the cloaca. Animals were assessed in batches of 6-12 and typically released within 48h of measurement. However, in 2023, we delayed releasing a batch of 11 animals (6M:5F) and four males died 3-8d post assay. Animals were asymptomatic prior to the day of death. Gross necropsy showed no damage near the cloaca or obvious cause of death. Specimens were submitted to Northwest Zoo Path for histopathology which revealed that deaths resulted from an ascending bacterial infection from the cloaca into the urinary tract which led to sepsis. Observed bacteria were common cloacal flora and the cloacal probe most likely moved fecal material from the colon into the urinary tract leading to infection. We recommend that future studies either avoid cloacal body temperature measurement or perform a pilot study where a few individuals of all sexes and age classes are held for at least 10d post measurement for observation to confirm assays will not cause infection. For smaller species, we recommend collecting external rather than internal body temperature data and we present results comparing methods in G. sila. Rory S. Telemeco
416: The Canadian Museum of Nature houses over one million specimens of fishes, amphibians, and reptiles, representing a wide diversity of taxa and preparation techniques. To increase the accessibility and research value of these collections, specimen imaging plays a central role in ongoing digitization efforts. Because no single imaging method captures all biologically-relevant features, assessing complementary approaches is essential. We explore ultraviolet (UV) photography as a supplementary imaging technique for revealing surface features not apparent under standard visible-light conditions, providing a “hidden” perspective on preserved collections. Specimens were imaged under ultraviolet illumination using a full-spectrum converted camera fitted with UV/Infrared-cut hot mirror filters, documenting UV-induced visible fluorescence. Specimens from multiple herpetological and ichthyological taxa, collection ages, and preservation types were examined. UV photography revealed surface features in some taxa that were not visible under conventional illumination, demonstrating the potential of UV-based imaging to enrich digital specimen records and highlight otherwise overlooked morphological detail. For example, lumpfish tubercles exhibited strong green UV-induced fluorescence. Specimens with surface features that strongly interacted with ultraviolet light represent candidates for future UV-reflectance analyses to evaluate potential UV-sensitive fish, amphibian, and reptile species. Distinguishing biologically-meaningful fluorescence from preservation-related artifacts remains a key challenge. Overall, UV photography is a promising but context-dependent addition to collection specimen imaging workflows, with important limitations that must be considered.
