417: Natural oscillations in climate have repeatedly forced landscapes across North America to undergo restructuring, which has created opportunities for divergence, specialization, and secondary contact in many populations. Western aquatic garter snakes (Thamnophis) occupy lentic, lotic, and coastal systems that have been shaped by unique geological and hydrological histories, but the extent to which climatic restructuring has influenced their divergence, distribution, and functional morphology remains unresolved. In this study, I am integrating ecological niche models and quantitative morphometrics to test whether current population distributions and phenotypic diversity within this complex are consistent with geographic isolation acting on conserved niches, or adaptive differentiation into distinct climatic regimes. Niche models constructed under contemporary conditions are being projected onto paleoclimate reconstructions of the mid-Holocene (~6ka) and Last Glacial Maximum (~22ka) to infer regions of climatic refugia based on continuous areas of suitable habitat, range shifts, and niche overlap between species. Morphological variation in cranial shape and body proportions within and among species is being quantified from museum specimens and compared to identified climatic niche positions. By integrating morphometrics and ecological niche models, this study will help determine if the effects of late Quaternary landscape dynamics are expressed in both species distribution and functional divergence. The results from this work will help shed light on the ecological and evolutionary patterns shaping western aquatic Thamnophis, and provide a foundation for future integrative evolutionary analyses in identified regions of stability or instability.
418: Ecological niche models (ENMs) are widely used to evaluate changes in species distributions over time. In Texas, land cover changes, hydrologic alterations, and climate change have contributed to the designation of many freshwater fishes as Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN), highlighting the importance of assessing distributional changes. We created ENMs to quantify species range shifts between historical (1980–2000) and contemporary (2012–2024) time periods for six cyprinid species listed as SGCN in the Neches and Sabine River basins of East Texas. Occurrence records for both time periods were obtained from online databases, with additional contemporary data collected through surveys conducted in 2023–2024. Environmental predictors described aspects of hydromorphology, land cover, and climate. All six species exhibited shifts in their range and changes in habitat suitability between historical and contemporary time periods. The Mississippi silvery minnow Hybognathus nuchalis exhibited range contractions and declined in overall habitat suitability. Fluvial specialists such as Sabine Shiner Notropis sabinae and Shoal Chub Macrhybopsis hyostoma showed range contractions and were associated with increased habitat suitability, likely reflecting their restriction to core habitats where environmental conditions remain favorable. Pallid Shiner Hybopsis amnis, expanded its range despite decreased suitability, suggesting its dispersal into less suitable environments in response to environmental changes. Similarly, Blackspot Shiner Notropis atrocaudalis and Suckermouth Minnow Phenacobius mirabilis exhibited expansion and increased suitability, indicating improved environmental conditions over time. These contrasting patterns of species distributions and habitat suitability may capture multiple ecological processes that can inform conservation of SGCN in Texas rivers. Nicole Valenzuela
419: Home range size has long been the standard for explaining the spatial ecology of many organisms. Common choices for estimating home range size include Minimum Convex Polygons (MCPs), which have limitations that have been recognized by many. It has been only recently that alternative estimation methods have been proposed, and even more recently that these methods have been compared for animals that are more sedentary, like some herpetofauna species. Ten veiled chameleons (Chamaeleo calyptratus) were radio-tracked over 100 days in southwest Florida. We compared two methods of home range estimation for these lizards: MCPs and Autocorrelated Kernel Density Estimates (AKDEs). We found that home range size is highly individualized among lizards, but both MCP and AKDE appear to overestimate space use for certain individuals to some extent, depending on the specific model used. More home-range estimation method comparisons should be done on herpetofauna species, and the information presented in this study may prove useful to those who are planning to do so. Anna Velten
420: The Trachylepis variegata species complex has long been subject to taxonomic difficulties, and recently the systematics of the Angolan specimens was revised. However, the clade as it exists outside of Angola has not been thoroughly addressed, and specimens long considered as Trachylepis punctulata may represent a separate species which has been tentatively labeled Trachylepis triebneri. In this study, significant sampling gaps have been filled, and a well-sampled mtDNA phylogeny has revealed population structure that supports T. triebneri as an evolutionary unit, as well as two previously unrecognized clades. Whole-genome sequences have been obtained for each mitochondrial clade, and the data will be leveraged to further assess the species status of these groups and to confirm the relationships recovered in the mtDNA tree. These findings will be coupled with morphology to assess the status of T. triebneri and the two new clades as full species. The timing of divergence between T. triebneri and T. punctulata will be determined, and the role of the Kunene River as a barrier driving speciation will be evaluated. Trachylepis triebneri and T. variegata share a large range boundary, and ecological niche modeling via MaxEnt will be used to test the hypothesis that these taxa are kept separate by an environmental barrier, likely coinciding with a west-east rainfall gradient in Namibia. The majority of the world’s Trachylepis museum samples will be revised, and morphological accounts and ranges will be updated for all members of the complex. Peter C. Wainwright
421: The whitespotted eagle ray, Aetobatus narinari, is a protected species commonly found in nearshore waters of Florida, including within the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary (FKNMS). This ecologically important and biodiverse region is well studied, yet the movement ecology, habitat use, and behavior of A. narinari within the Florida Keys remain poorly understood. Previous aerial surveys revealed that habitats near Tavernier Key may represent local hotspots of A. narinari. To better understand the significance of this area, this study assessed fine-scale movement, habitat use, and behavior of A. narinari using drones. Drones were deployed to continuously track the movement and behaviors of individual rays for up to 2.5 h. By maintaining the ray within the center of the frame and orienting the drone in the direction of movement, geospatial maps of fine-scale movement were generated. Observations revealed a range of intra- and inter-specific interactions, including group formations (1–8 individuals), following behaviors that may be related to courtship, and associations with teleosts, sharks, and other ray species. Foraging occurred primarily within sparse seagrass habitats. Leaping behavior was also documented and may function in communication, parasite removal, or avoiding threats. Anthropogenic interactions included movements within boat channels with active vessel avoidance and proximity to fishing gear. This study highlights the ecological importance of this region for A. narinari. Continued drone surveys in this high-abundance area will generate multi-year datasets on the ecological role and behavior of A. narinari, supporting effective management of the species within the FKNMS. Christian Walker
422: In many animals, social experience shapes how individuals evaluate and choose mates, yet the mechanisms underlying these shifts in mate choice behavior remain poorly understood. The túngara frog (Physalaemus pustulosus) provides an excellent model system for investigating this due to its well-characterized acoustic communication system: males produce advertisement calls ranging from simple "whine-only" calls to complex "whine+chuck" calls, with females strongly preferring the latter in mate choice trials. This study investigated how prior exposure to social stimuli of varying attractiveness influences subsequent mate choice behavior in female túngara frogs. Gravid females were assigned to three treatment groups: asocial control (green noise), whine-only calls, or whine+chuck calls. Frogs were exposed to these simulated nightly choruses for one week. Behavioral trials then assessed mate choice preference by measuring female phonotaxis toward whineonly or whine+chuck speakers. Data analysis revealed that exposure to any social stimulus (whine-only or whine+chuck) significantly increased the likelihood of females choosing a speaker compared to asocial controls, indicating that social experience enhances behavioral responsiveness. Further, exposure to the highly attractive, whine+chuck social stimuli led to increased choosiness. These females preferentially chose the whine+chuck speaker and exhibited longer choice latencies compared to females exposed to the less attractive, whine-only stimuli. This suggests enhanced discrimination and evaluation of mate quality. Brains were collected for single-nucleus RNA sequencing to examine how social experience influences the physiological basis of these behavioral shifts. Preliminary findings from these analyses will be presented, providing insights into the mechanisms underlying experience-dependent changes in mate choice behavior. Danielle Walkup Danielle Walkup; Bret Collier; Kevin Skow; Wade Ryberg; Toby Hibbitts; Kathryn Steffen; Lee Fitzgerald; Roel Lopez
423: Extreme temperature and precipitation events (e.g., heat waves, drought) are affecting vital rates, abundance, and distribution of many species, resulting in population declines, local extinctions, and losses of ecosystem function. Amphibians may mitigate the effects of such events through dispersal, phenotypic plasticity, or genetic adaptation. I reviewed the literature to assess what is known for amphibians about variation in species’ traits as they relate to climate-induced thermal tolerance and resistance to water loss. I explored taxonomic differences in these traits and, where possible, distinguished between the roles of phenotypic plasticity and evolutionary adaptation. I examined over 160 studies on acclimation, tolerance, sensitivity, and adaptation of physiological traits in response to climate-induced variation in thermal conditions and water loss. The majority of studies focused on responses to increased temperatures rather than to potential water loss. Moreover, more research has been done with anurans than with salamanders. As past reviews have documented, phenotypic plasticity is well-established in amphibians whereas evidence of genetic adaptations remains uncommon. Information on tropical species has increased significantly in recent years, especially those along elevational gradients. This increase in knowledge about tropical species is particularly significant given that loss of terrestrial water storage is resulting in ecosystem water deficits, widespread tropical drying and, thus, longer dry seasons in regions like southern Amazonia. Many species possess physiological mechanisms for coping with hydrothermal variation; uncovering these mechanisms could provide insight into how species may respond to future climate change. Cathy Walsh
424: Efficient data discovery remains a central challenge in using large, specimen-based biodiversity resources. This poster presents recent improvements to the search and query capabilities of FishNet2, with an emphasis on enabling more effective exploration and retrieval of fish biodiversity data. The updated system introduces flexible spatial query tools that allow users to search using points, polygons, and hydrologically relevant features such as river systems and coastal regions. These capabilities support ecologically meaningful queries and can be saved and reused for reproducible workflows. Taxonomic searches are now synonym-aware, improving the completeness of results and reducing data loss due to naming inconsistencies. Guided query interfaces, autocomplete functions, and dynamic filtering further simplify navigation across large and heterogeneous datasets. User and data provider dashboards extend functionality beyond search. Users can access saved queries, track usage, and review dataset summaries, while providers can monitor dataset status and usage patterns. The platform also introduces data flagging, enabling users to report potential issues such as taxonomic errors or geospatial inconsistencies. These flags initiate direct communication between users and data providers with tracked workflows, supporting targeted corrections and continuous improvement of data quality. A live demonstration will showcase query construction, spatial search, dashboard functionality, and data flagging in real time. These enhancements position FishNet2 as a more interactive and user-centered platform for accessing and working with large-scale fish biodiversity data. Alice Wang
425: Arboreal habitats are uniquely structurally demanding on their inhabitants because of their inherent complex three-dimensionality. As such, scansorial animals often exhibit morphological and functional adaptations that enable them to reversibly attach to surfaces. Geckos are widely known for their subdigital pads that generate temporary adhesion. Most geckos also possess claws, which can mechanically interlock with rough substrates, puncture soft substrates, and generate friction to enable reversible attachment, but their form and function have been less intensively explored. A recent study investigated variation in claw morphology of a padless genus of gecko, revealing intriguing inter- and intraspecific patterns. Specifically, it identified significant variation between the claws of the manus and pes, as well as between digit I and the other digits. However, that study was limited to four congeneric species. This raises the question of whether such trends are exhibited by geckos more generally. Here we provide preliminary results of a morphologically comprehensive study assessing the intra- and interspecific variation in claw morphology more broadly across the Gekkota. Specifically, we took multivariate measures of claw morphology of all clawed digits of the left appendages of 16 species representing the six limbed gekkotan families. In addition, we sampled five species representing two limbed, lepidosaur outgroups. Preliminary findings reveal significant interspecific differences in claw size and shape, while intraspecific and intraindividual variation is more subtle. We report not only on the identification of general morphological patterns in gecko claws but also provide baseline data pertinent to future work on the ecomorphology of geckos. Gregory J. Watkins-Colwell
426: Zoos and natural history museums are both collections-based institutions with important missions in biodiversity research and education. Animals in zoos are a repository and living record of the world’s biodiversity, whereas natural history museums are a permanent historical record of snapshots of biodiversity in time. Surprisingly, despite significant overlap in institutional missions, formal partnerships between these institution types are infrequent. Life history information, pedigrees, and medical records maintained at zoos should be seen as complementary to historical records of morphology, genetics, and distribution kept at museums. Through examining both institution types, we synthesize the benefits and challenges of cross-institutional exchanges and propose actions to increase the dialog between zoos and museums. With a growing recognition of the importance of collections to the advancement of scientific research and discovery, a transformational impact could be made with long-term investments in connecting the institutions that are caretakers of living and preserved animals. Sydney Wayne
427: A re-activated ASIH IACC (Institutional Animal Care Committee) will revise the 2014 Guide for Use of Fishes in Research in collaboration with representatives from the American Fisheries Society. The updated document will guide investigators as they develop IACUC protocols for research on diverse fish species. It has been agreed at a national level (National Academy of Sciences) that the standards and practices in the documents provided by each of the taxon-specific vertebrate societies will be cited in and will take precedence over The Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (National Academies Press) with respect to taxon-specific care and use issues. As ichthyologists we can have important impacts on standards for animal use and care practices that will benefit the entire fish community. The Committee has agreed on the need for significant revision of the Fish Guide as well as the addition of new topics to address fish diversity, working with everything from larvae to large pelagics and other wild species, and animal welfare in the context of lab work, aquaculture, and field work including monitoring and collection of museum material. We will seek input from the ichthyology community on these topics at JMIH and will encourage attendees to identify problems/challenges faced during the IACUC protocol approval process and articulate how the current (2014) guidelines may have run counter to the generation of high-quality data. Community input will be incorporated into the revised Guide, as appropriate. Jeffrey Weinell
428: Leukocyte profiles can be useful in assessing physiological states of vertebrates. Specifically, heterophil:lymphocytes (H:L) ratios are increasingly utilized to measure physiological stress due to its cost effectiveness and relative ease of sampling. However, accurate assessment of stress metrics using leukocyte profiles heavily depends on well established baselines achieved by wide spatial and temporal sampling. Established H:L baselines for vertebrates are lacking in general but are especially sparse for squamates. In our study, we collected blood samples from two species of watersnakes found in urban canals in southern Florida: Nerodia taxispilota (Brown Watersnake), and Nerodia floridana (Florida Green Watersnake). Using established staining techniques, we describe leukocyte profiles for these two species including relative proportion of heterophils, leukocytes, eosinophils, basophils, and monocytes. We further quantify H:L ratios for each individual sampled to assess variation in association with factors such species, sex, and apparent infection by Ophidiomyces ophiodiicola, a pathogen responsible for snake fungal disease (SFD.). These data contribute to our understanding of how leukocyte profiles vary regionally for these species and in association with factors such as habitat modification following urbanization. Julia Wester
429: In low-relief landscapes, small fluctuations in water level can alter hydrologic connectivity among wetlands, influencing dispersal pathways for aquatic organisms. We developed a high-resolution framework to model temporal surface-water connectivity among eleven wetlands on a university campus in southwest Florida by integrating LiDAR-derived elevation data with continuous groundwater monitoring. Hourly groundwater levels were used to estimate water surface elevations and compared against least-cost flow paths derived from elevation and surface type. Connectivity was defined as the presence of a continuous surface-water pathway and assessed at 1inch vertical increments across a narrow elevation range (17–19 ft) to capture short-term hydrologic linkages. We compared modeled connectivity metrics, including frequency of connection, with species occurrence and abundance data from >30 minnow trapping surveys targeting aquatic and semi-aquatic taxa. Analyses focused on species reliant on aquatic dispersal. This approach provides a framework for studying dispersal pathways and potential invasion processes in highly dynamic wetland system. Mark Wildhaber
430: In 2020, the Museum of Comparative Zoology Ichthyology Collection received a massive collection of mostly three-spined sticklebacks (Gasterosteus aculeatus) that were soon to be orphaned from the closing FosterBaker Lab at Clark University in Worcester, MA. There were almost 40 years of ball jars at the Foster-Baker lab loaded with specimens and buffered formalin, also with rich accompanying data and copious field notes. The roughly 500,000 specimens over 3,500 lots were collected mostly from the same 90 lakes in South Central Alaska that were sampled regularly over the course of roughly thirty years. While the collection is atypical in museums for its extreme focus on one taxon from a limited range, the now well-databased and curated collection of wild-caught model organisms will hopefully offer interesting opportunities in evolutionary biology research. Additionally, efforts to digitally extend the collection can make this a broadly used resource with reach far beyond the lab(s) that collected the specimens. Samuel Wilson
431: Body and caudal fin (BCF) swimming is a common locomotor strategy in fishes that is traditionally divided into four modes: anguilliform, subcarangiform, carangiform, and thunniform. These modes have historically been classified based on locomotor mechanics inferred from body shape. However, emerging mechanical and kinematic evidence challenges this framework, suggesting that individual species may display characteristics from multiple modes depending on ecological context, and that clear kinematic distinctions between modes are not always evident. This study investigates differences between adjacent BCF swimming modes – carangiform (Seriola dumerili, Coryphaena hippurus) and thunniform (Thunnus atlanticus) species (n = 6 per species) – using a comparative biomechanical approach. Vertebral shape was assessed using skeletal morphometrics and mechanical properties were obtained from compression tests. Preliminary analyses of stiffness (E) revealed differential patterns between the carangiform and thunniform swimmers, whereas second moment of area (I) exhibited species-specific patterns; flexural stiffness (EI) is currently being calculated to further evaluate these differences. Integrating mechanical and morphological metrics will help evaluate structural patterns (i.e., vertebral column regionalization) that may contribute to functional variation in locomotion and refine biomechanical interpretations of BCF mode classifications. Jessica Wimmer
432: Many amphibian populations have been declining due to disease, habitat destruction, and anthropogenic stressors. This is in part due to the permeability of amphibian skin as this trait makes them vulnerable to pollutants entering their body, such as salt. Two stressors that co-occur in roadside freshwater habitats are road deicing salt and artificial light at night (ALAN). Exposure to road deicing salt can decrease survival, alter behavior, and decrease growth, and exposure to ALAN has been found to decrease tadpole immune function and increase susceptibility to other stressors. Despite ALAN and road deicing salt being common roadside pollutants, no studies have examined the impacts of ALAN on salamander larvae, and no studies have been conducted on how the cooccurrence of these stressors impact amphibians. This study seeks to answer how ALAN and road deicing salt impact small-mouth salamanders and leopard frogs, and if there are interacting effects between the stressors. To answer these questions, I conducted a mesocosm-based experiment. I set up 4 cattle tanks at 6 different distances from a commercially available solar powered streetlamp for a total of 24 tanks, and half of the tanks at each distance received a sublethal road deicing salt treatment. We will have collected data for survival, snout-vent length, and mass to determine how ALAN and salt impact amphibian fitness. Andrew Wooley
433: Natural history museum collections are crucial archives of past and present biodiversity, and thus serve as an essential resource for scientific research and education. Within collections, holotypes hold an especially important role as unique individuals used to define and describe new species. Because of their special status, loaning of holotypes is extremely limited to ensure the safety and longevity of these specimens. While necessary, this can severely limit the use of holotypes in research capacities. One way of circumventing this is to utilize nondestructive digitization methods. Using a Bruker SkyScan 1273 High Capacity 3D X-ray Microscope, we are creating highresolution µCT scans of the NHMLA Ichthyology holotype collection. This digitization effort documents the skeletal anatomy of our holotypes and creates a publicly accessible resource of high-resolution anatomical data. These data can serve as a resource for taxonomic research and for the creation of educational curricula and models, showcasing the importance of museum collections to not only researchers but also to the wider public. Jennifer Wyffels Jennifer Wyffels; Ashley Dawdy; R. Dean Grubbs; Tonya Wiley; Gregg Poulakis; Lukas Heath; Andrew Wooley; Dylan Yakich; Stephen Anderson; Jill Arnold; Shane Boylan; Chris Buckner; Lynne Byrd; Carolyn Cray; Whitney
434: While the presence and composition of megafauna-associated fish assemblages is well-documented across numerous transient marine species, exploration and understanding of the ecological relationships underlying these symbiotic communities remains limited. To better understand cryptic ecological dynamics in elasmobranchassociated teleost communities, we assessed the composition, stability, spatial use, and niche partitioning of fishes associated with five individually identifiable lemon sharks (N. brevirostris) in Florida, USA. A total of 315 passive video observations collected between September 2022 and January 2025 were analyzed. Stability of assemblages were assessed using Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and NMDS ordination. Niche usage and partitioning was characterized from standardized Levins’ B, Schoener’s D, and Pianka’s O. We found that lemon shark-associated fish assemblages were dominated by fishes in families Carangidae and Echeneidae with less frequent occurrences of fishes in the Haemulidae, Kyphosidae, Lutanjidae, and Pomacentridae families. Spatial distribution relative to the host varied by family but consistently deviated from randomly distributed occurrence across all sharks and symbiont families. Niche assessments revealed specialist tendencies in Haemulidae and Decapterus spp. and moderate generalist tendencies in Carangidae and Echeneidae. Niche overlap was variable and driven by individual shark host, but assemblage composition remained relatively stable across observations. These findings underscore the complex role of marine megafauna in shaping ecological communities and suggest these communities function as independent, mobile mini-ecosystems. Deepening scientific understanding of these transient communities highlights the importance of comprehensive conservation practices that manage both stationary ecosystems and the mobile communities that move through and connect them. Eren Yigit
435: Yawning is a behavior people commonly associate with tiredness. However, in most animals, “yawning” (e.g., extended gaping of the mouth) is poorly understood and could have a number of functions. Prairie rattlesnake (Crotalus viridis) yawns have captivated hundreds of viewers on Project RattleCam’s YouTube livestream of a rattlesnake den in Colorado. Viewer-driven curiosity and attention around rattlesnakes opening their jaws and exposing their fangs sparked our research question aiming to quantify and understand the predictors of yawning behavior in this species. Previous research shows that fasting snakes yawn to help aid in jaw readjustment after consuming prey, yet these behaviors have not been studied in wild contexts and may be associated with other physiological or behavioral traits. Using footage of >600 rattlesnake yawns obtained from the summer of 2024, we tested the following hypotheses: (1) yawning initiates upcoming ecdysis, serving as a mechanism to crack the skin to start the process of shedding, (2) yawning assists with odor detection by facilitating the capture of chemical cues and transportation to the vomeronasal organ, (3) yawning signifies a transition between two behavioral states, and (4) yawning helps reset the vomeronasal organ to enhance its function. We analyzed Project Rattlecam footage for spikes in yawning frequencies to observe seasonal differences, identified the body position commonly associated with yawning, and differentiated yawning between neonates and adults. More data is currently being collected to understand rattlesnake yawning behavior by using non-invasive techniques that reduce disturbance to note the natural behavior of this cryptic species.
436: The invasive hemlock woolly adelgid (HWA) has decimated Eastern and Carolina hemlock populations in the Southern Appalachian Mountains. Imidacloprid, a neonicotinoid insecticide, is widely used to suppress HWA and conserve hemlock forests, but its persistence in organic matter and mobility in soils raise concerns about non-target impacts on stream-dwelling amphibians. Previous research in our lab documented reduced terrestrial adult abundance of stream-breeding salamanders in imidacloprid treated systems, despite no significant changes in larval abundance. We hypothesize that imidacloprid may have sublethal effects on salamanders exposed in streams as larvae, that lead to greater long-term impacts under chronic exposure. We assessed this through controlled pulse exposure experiments on common Appalachian stream species: larval blackbellied salamanders (Desmognathus amphileucus/folkertsi) and two-lined salamanders (Eurycea wilderae/cirrigera). Larvae were exposed to environmentally relevant concentrations of imidacloprid across repeated 5-7-day dosing intervals to simulate run-off dynamics while measuring growth rate, feeding latency, and cover use. Preliminary results show shifts in growth trajectories over time and increased feeding latency in higher dose groups of the Desmognathus species, indicating reduced foraging efficiency and possible changes in developmental timing. While mortality was not impacted, these sublethal results begin to provide a mechanistic explanation for observed field patterns. By examining the risks imidacloprid poses to salamander development and behavior in headwater systems, our findings provide valuable insight for forest managers seeking to balance invasive species control, hemlock conservation, and long-term amphibian population resilience. Hadley Copeland
437: The combined acoustic and visual characterization of fish social interactions in natural aquatic environments is challenging due to limitations in direct observation, signal attribution, and background noise. As a result, many fishes remain classified as non-soniferous due to a lack of evidence rather than evidence of absence. Here, we document the first known instance of sound production within the order Aulopiformes during courtship behavior in the lizardfish (Synodus intermedius). Using a paired small-aperture acoustic array and 360° video system, we recorded two independent courtship interactions on 4 June 2023 and 10 March 2026 along the house reef of the Curaçao Sea Aquarium (Bapor Kibra, Curaçao). Over approximately three hours of observation, individuals produced discrete acoustic trains. These signals had a peak frequency of ~125 Hz, were organized into pulse trains, and were temporally associated with pectoral fin movement and cranial elevation, suggesting a behavioral and mechanical linkage. Dissection revealed a previously undescribed morphological feature that may underlie sound production in this species, providing a novel hypothesized acoustic mechanism. Together, field observations, synchronized recordings, and morphological analysis suggest that acoustic communication may play a broader ecological role in this cryptic mesopredator than previously recognized. These findings expand the known distribution of soniferous fishes and highlight the potential for passive acoustic monitoring to detect and track species within Aulopiformes. Future work will assess the distribution of this mechanism across the order and its applicability for long-term monitoring. Matt Duggan
438: The behavioral displacement hypothesis posits that behavioral interactions drive niche divergence, making these interactions potential determinants of invasive species success and distributions. House Geckos (Hemidactylus spp.) are widely distributed human-commensal invasive lizards. Over the past century, Mediterranean House Geckos (H. turcicus) have established populations in the southern USA, followed by Tropical House Geckos (H. mabouia) in southern Florida, and Sri Lankan House Geckos (H. parvimaculatus) in southern Louisiana and Texas. These species are ecologically similar, leading to speculation of competitive displacement of H. turcicus, which no longer occurs in southern Florida and is increasingly rare in southern Louisiana. Yet, no study has documented competition among these species. We ascertained the competitive-dominance hierarchy among these three species through staged encounters in lab arenas. Individual H. turcicus were randomly paired with geckos of both competitor species (n = 3/species) and a conspecific control, pairs were introduced to arenas where behavioral interactions were video recorded. Predefined behaviors were quantified and categorized to assign dominance ranks and compared via GLM to determine the dominance order among species. Hemidactylus turcicus was submissive to H. mabouia in 81% of encounters yet evenly matched against H. parvimaculatus. Competitor sex was not a significant predictor of competitive outcomes. Mass may be an advantage for the larger H. mabouia, which used an escalating aggressive strategy. Whereas, the smaller H. parvimaculatus used an avoidance strategy similar to H. turcicus. Our findings will broaden our understanding of the role of behavior as a mechanism of competitive displacement among co-occurring invasive species. Sarah Gibson
439: The flexible stem hypothesis elevates phenotypic plasticity as a key mechanism in adaptive radiation. For example, the jaws of cichlids are known to have morphological plasticity, allowing acclimation to different diets. In studies of morphological plasticity, significant behavioral plasticity may take place well before substantial morphological changes occur. Specialized morphology is assumed to improve performance, but few studies investigate the effect of experience on performance. The Mesoamerican cichlid Amatitlania nigrofasciata was used in the current study to investigate whether this cichlid species can learn and improve benthic feeding performance with behavioral modifications alone. The novel prey used in this experiment was a crushed pellet and gelatin mixture allowed to set on microscope slides. Thirteen individuals were separately housed and each given ten trials with this food at regular intervals over four weeks. Trials were filmed and analyzed for components of performance, including the number of bites, the mass of food removed, and the time spent eating. Our prediction was that there would be an increase in feeding performance, and our initial results confirm this. By analyzing behavioral aspects of the fish during feeding trials, we expect to identify how the fish improve their performance with experience through taking more food per bite, taking more bites, or modifying feeding kinematics, such as by altering their orientation to the substrate. This study serves as a stepping stone into investigating how morphological and behavioral plasticity (learning) work together to improve performance on novel prey. Stephen M. Kajiura
440: Anuran amphibians rely heavily on auditory signals to obtain mates. Shifts in signaling can greatly impact female choice, with some frogs altering call frequency, timing, or duration. The social environment, such as male density or position within a group, also influences signaling behavior. Previous work on our study species, the bird-voiced treefrog (Hyla avivoca), has shown that males modify calling tactics in large groups and that females prefer nonoverlapping, long-pulsed calls. Our study builds on this work by examining how grouping behavior during calling influences auditory signal parameters. During the late spring and early summer, we monitored the position of calling males within choruses and the density of male groupings. We then correlated social positioning with changes in call parameters (frequency, duration, and pulse number). We found that call positions located near the center of the chorus or in densely packed areas were associated with distinct calls. Males in these positions produced longer, lower-frequency calls, traits favored by females when selecting a mate. These findings demonstrate that chorus position predicts the production of female-preferred call traits, highlighting parallels between anuran choruses and lek-based mating systems in other taxa. Irene Kitson
441: Various North American minnow species engage in nest association, and current hypotheses indicate it is mutualistic with reduced egg predation risk through a dilution effect. While the nests confer safety to the eggs, the conspicuous adults are also susceptible to predation while in mixed-species spawning aggregations. The skin of North American minnows contains club cells that release an alarm cue (Schreckstoff) which induces anti-predator fright responses in fish that detect it. The chemical composition is species-specific, and while it has been found that individuals have the strongest response to conspecific Schreckstoff, they can respond to heterospecific Schreckstoff. Through interspecific responses to Schreckstoff, nest association may also serve as an alarm system to reduce the threat of predation on adults. To investigate if nest association serves as a Schreckstoff-mediated predator avoidance mechanism, we exposed mixed-species shoals containing nest associating Southern Redbelly Dace (Chrosomus erythrogaster) to Schreckstoff from Southern Redbelly Dace and non-native Zebrafish (Danio rerio). We predicted that spawning aggregations over Largescale Stoneroller (Campostoma oligolepis) nests would have more intense fright responses to associate Schreckstoff and limited responses to non-native Schreckstoff, and that this difference in intensity would be more pronounced in spawning aggregations compared to non-spawning shoals. Surprisingly, the response to associate Schreckstoff was not more intense than the response to non-native Schreckstoff in any of the conditions. However, there were differences between the responses of spawning aggregations and non-spawning shoals. These results suggest that variations in the fright response may be more dependent on context rather than the species. Jenna Palmisano
442: The Beartooth Butte Formation, with outcrops in Northern Wyoming and Southern Montana, has been thoroughly studied from a paleobotanical perspective. However, this Early Devonian (Lochkovian-Pragian) formation preserves a rich assemblage of fishes. The vertebrates of the Formation have been relatively neglected since the works of William Bryant in the 1930s, but fish plates from the Cottonwood Canyon locality have been incidentally collected by a team of (mainly paleobotany) students and professors from Cal Poly Humboldt (Arcata, California) every few years since the mid-2000’s. Many of these specimens are now deposited at the American Museum of Natural History Fossil Fish Collection, with some scattered fish material co-occurring with fossil plants which were then studied at Cal Poly Humboldt. We assessed the shape and ornamentation of numerous fish plates within these specimens using Bryant’s original descriptions as a guide. Within this collection there are various cephalaspidomorph ostracoderms, along with arthrodire placoderms like ‘Euryapsis’, the pyctodontid ‘Bulbocanthus’, and a relatively 3-dimensionally preserved cranial plate. Newer techniques like CT scanning, combined with the traditional preparation of fossils, provide us with a fresh look at these fishes of Cottonwood Canyon, shining a light onto this 405 million year old community nearly 100 years since its initial description.
443: Electric organs evolved independently multiple times across the fish tree of life. Electric fishes can be broadly characterized both by the strength of their electric discharge as well as the temporal pattern. The Neotropical electric knifefishes (order Gymnotiformes) provide a powerful framework for studying the evolution of electrogenicity, as the order exhibits diversity in both electrical strength and pattern. However, phylogenetic relationships between the gymnotiform families remain contested, which has limited our ability to accurately reconstruct the tempo and mode of electrogenic evolution. Here, we examine the spatiotemporal evolution of electrogenicity in Neotropical knifefishes by assembling the most comprehensive dataset to date, including broad taxonomic sampling (72% of known diversity) with over 1,000 exon markers from the FishLife project. Within this framework, we reconstruct the evolutionary history of three electrogenic-related traits (electric signal pattern, adult electric organ type, and pacemaker nucleus arrangement), correlating these traits with ancestral reconstructions of habitat use and geographic distribution. Michael D Burns
444: The Mimic Shiner (Paranotropis volucellus) is a freshwater fish of the minnow family Leuciscidae widely distributed in North America, but its taxonomic status is uncertain, with suspected cryptic diversity, a common issue among North American minnows. Untangling such complexes is critical for accurate biodiversity assessment and effective conservation. We employed an integrative approach using Restriction-site Associated DNA sequencing (RADseq) and morphology to evaluate the species boundaries and evolutionary history of the P. volucellus complex across its range. We analyzed 946 specimens of Paranotropis, yielding 7,790 unlinked Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs). Phylogenetic analysis recovered the P. volucellus complex as monophyletic, composed of three highly divergent geographic clades: a northern clade (Mimic N), a southern clade (Mimic S), and a geographically disjunct western-eastern clade (Mimic WE). Population structure analyses (ADMIXTURE, fineRADstructure, and PCA) supported a high degree of structure, suggesting the presence of up to 12 distinct genetic clusters within the complex. Species delimitation under the Multispecies Coalescent model (BPP/HHSD) provided evidence for multiple distinct species-level lineages within the currently recognized P. volucellus. Morphological analyses (traditional morphometric and meristic data) partially aligned with the genetic structure, although some clades showed significant phenotypic overlap, highlighting the cryptic nature of this diversity. Our results indicate that P. volucellus represents a complex of several cryptic species, clarifying the evolutionary units within the complex, while providing a robust phylogenomic framework for the genus Paranotropis. This study underscores the necessity of genomic tools to resolve species boundaries when morphological overlap blurs accurate species delineation. Alexis Culley
445: The Eastern Continental Divide (ECD) follows the Appalachian Mountains in North America and acts as a major biogeographic barrier for freshwater fishes by separating drainages flowing towards the Mississippi River and Atlantic Ocean. Asymmetric erosion rates across the ECD have caused the drainage divide to slowly migrate toward the interior of the continent. As the drainage divide migrates, flow from one drainage basin can be abruptly diverted into another in a process called river capture. River capture generates characteristic topographic signatures and can transfer freshwater organisms to opposing sides of drainage divides, thus generating disjunct distributions and opportunities for allopatric speciation. Here, we investigate the origin of geographically disjunct populations within the Saffron Shiner, Hydrophlox rubricroceus, using a suite of phylogenetic and population structure analysis of genomic data. This small-bodied, headwater specialist minnow is widespread on the western side of the ECD with disjunct populations documented in multiple river systems on the eastern side of the ECD. Preliminary results match expectations under the river capture hypothesis, with our maximum likelihood phylogeny recovering Atlantic-slope drainages east of the ECD as independent lineages that are sister to neighboring rivers west of the ECD. Additionally, TreeMix analysis indicates a history of multiple river captures that facilitated gene flow across the drainage divide within the Linville River (Atlantic draining), a result consistent with topographic evidence. Taken together, our analysis of genomic and geomorphic data support the hypothesis that river capture is responsible for the presence of disjunct populations across a major biogeographic barrier. Grayce Cunningham
446: Dispersal into a new geographic region that lacks predators, competition, or offers an abundance of underutilized resources can reshape the evolutionary trajectory of a lineage. Under these conditions, evolutionary theory predicts an initial burst of lineage and morphological diversification that slows down through time as vacant niches become saturated—a signature pattern of an evolutionary radiation. Here, we test for a continental-scale evolutionary radiation in Mastacembelidae, a speciose family of elongate fishes known as spiny eels. Molecular evidence suggests that spiny eels originated in Southeast Asia and dispersed into the Afrotropics during the Middle Miocene (16-10 Ma), where 70% of the species reside today. We combined a linear dataset, which samples 58% of the known species diversity, and phylogenetic comparative methods to compare the tempo and mode of lineage and morphological diversification of Asian and African spiny eels. We find that lineage diversification rates are high across Mastacembelidae but do not significantly differ between the two geographic regions. In contrast, we detect a shift toward accelerated rates of phenotypic evolution at the base of the African clade, indicating faster rates of morphological change compared to their Asian relatives. However, we find no evidence for initial high morphological and lineage diversification rates followed by a slow down after dispersing into Africa. Nevertheless, African species show greater morphological diversity, which we hypothesize is driven by divergent microhabitat occupation across the Afrotropics. These results highlight the importance of geographic colonization in shaping the evolutionary history of freshwater fish diversity. Nathan Dehaut
447: Ray-finned fishes (Actinopterygii) are the most species-rich vertebrate clade, with more than 35,000 described species divided between 540 families. Efforts to resolve relationships among species and higher-level groups, whether wielding morphological or molecular datasets, have clarified several major nodes but left many others unresolved or contentious. Here, we present a new perspective of ray-finned fish evolution. We inferred a backbone topology from 260 chromosome-level genomes using the novel phylogenomics pipeline ROADIES, which analyzes 64,000 single- and multi-copy loci under the multispecies coalescent while accounting for paralogy. We expanded upon this backbone using a second recently-published pipeline, uDANCE, by integrating four additional marker sets (BUSCO genes, UCEs, and two sets of FishLife exons). The resultant trees (n = 20, to capture topological uncertainty and methodological biases) include more than 10,000 species, a nearly-tenfold increase in taxon sampling over all previous efforts. This dataset is also the first large-scale fish phylogeny to incorporate formalin-fixed museum specimens, an emerging approach that enables for genome-scale sequencing from rare, protected, and even extinct taxa. Historical tissues used for this phylogeny include multiple representatives of otherwise unsequenced families and genera, allowing us to compile the first molecular phylogeny of Actinopterygii with 100% taxon sampling at the family level. We find robust support for a large suite of traditional clades, confidently place multiple higher-level taxa for the first time, provide cursory resolution for some once-contentious nodes, and uncover several overlooked non-monophylies of major families and orders. Alyssa Head
448: Genome size varies by more than three orders of magnitude across Tetraodontiformes, from the smallest vertebrate genome on record (ca. 0.4 Gb in Takifugu) to 1.1 Gb in some boxfishes and spikefishes. The reduced genomes of pufferfishes reflect intron compression and loss of repetitive elements, yet the ecological and evolutionary pressures that favored such contraction, and whether similar forces shape genome size variation across the rest of the order, remain unresolved. Here, we inferred a new time-calibrated tetraodontiform phylogeny for 308 species (ca. 71% taxonomic coverage) from genome-wide data and assembled genome size estimates for 161 tetraodontiform species. Our phylogenomic analyses resolved well-supported interfamilial relationships, with the exception of the monotypic family Triodontidae, whose historically unstable placement remained unresolved in our topologies and warrants further study. Preliminary ancestral state reconstructions identified two major lineagespecific shifts in genome size: a contraction in Tetraodontidae and an expansion in Ostracicoidea. We then coded ecological variables (depth, habitat) and integrated morphological data and paleoclimatic curves to test the relationship between genome contraction and expansion and tetraodontiform diversification dynamics. These results identify Tetraodontidae and Ostracicoidea as the two principal axes of genome size change within the order and establish a phylogenomic framework for testing how such changes relate to ecology and morphological evolution in Tetraodontiformes. Michael Chukwudi Ikegwu Chukwudi Ikegwu; Amari Hutchins; Layla Smith; Natanim Ambaye; Winnie Mambo; Zion Vaughn; Segun
449: The Mud Sunfish, Acantharchus pomotis (Baird, 1855), is a unique member of the centrarchidae family originating from the eastern United States. The species is primarily distributed along the Atlantic slope from southern New York to Florida, simultaneously appearing in a handful of Gulf drainages in Georgia, Florida, and Alabama. Despite its broad distribution, the species’ apparent low density, cryptic life history, and preference for difficult to sample blackwater habitat have left it relatively neglected through decades of systematic and ecological research. This study intends to employ whole-genome sequencing to evaluate populations from both the Gulf and Atlantic slopes in order to identify evolutionarily significant units and provide clarified historical inference. Mitochondrial genomes sequences were also produced for some major Mud Sunfish populations for additional comparison. Mud Sunfish were collected and acquired throughout their entire range, including a recently discovered, disjunct population from Washington Co. Alabama. We seek to investigate the status of the currently synonymized A. pomotis mizelli (Fowler, 1945); in addition, we aim to characterize the Alabama Mud Sunfish to determine whether they represent a native relict population or anthropogenic introduction. Our results hope to provide contribution to the understanding of Mud Sunfish, and highlight evolutionary history among freshwater fish populating blackwater coastal plain habitat in the Eastern United States. Gregg Poulakis
450: The cobra diversity of Myanmar has long been a source of confusion, complicating public health responses to snakebites. By integrating distributional data, natural history information, and clinical evidence, we clarify the composition and distribution of Myanmar’s cobra fauna and evaluate the implications for envenoming and snakebite management. We confirm the presence of five cobra species (Naja fuxi, N. kaouthia, N. mandalayensis, N. siamensis, and N. sumatrana) in Myanmar and identify one additional species (N. sagittifera) that may occur in the country. Encounter data show pronounced seasonality, with the highest numbers recorded in December (n = 30), and most observations occurring near human habitation, suggesting seasonal associations with anthropogenic environments. These patterns differ from wet-season activity peaks documented elsewhere, indicating that reported encounters may be shaped more by human behavior than by snake activity. Review of clinical and toxicological information shows that only one species is represented in locally produced antivenom, raising concern about limited cross-neutralization. Traditional practices remain common in many communities and include harmful methods that delay access to medical care or worsen injuries. Clinical evidence demonstrates that neurotoxicity, respiratory failure, and localized tissue destruction are the principal complications of cobra envenoming, often requiring antivenom therapy, airway support, and surgical intervention in severe cases. The broader-than-recognized diversity of cobras in Myanmar, combined with high encounter probabilities, synanthropic tendencies, and gaps in public awareness, continues to hinder effective management of snakebite. Improved community education, expanded venom and antivenom research, and timely access to appropriate medical care are essential for reducing the burden of cobra envenomation in Myanmar. Kirsty Ballard
451: Many fishes and aquatic salamanders employ suction feeding for prey capture. They accomplish this by rapidly expanding the buccal cavity to generate a pressure differential that drives water and food into the mouth. These suction flows are actuated by the muscles and connective tissues of the cranium and hyobranchial apparatus, thereby using these skeletal elements as a lever system that indirectly captures prey within a fluid bolus. The dynamics of these musculoskeletal and fluid systems can change through an organism’s ontogeny and with body size if the physical components of the feeding apparatus or movements therein scale allometrically. These dynamics may also change if the surrounding fluid behaves differently across the studied size range. We targeted the scaling and ontogenetic changes of suction feeding flows within a paedomorphic species of salamander (Ambystoma mexicanum) to 1) provide baseline values for comparison with previously studied suction-feeding vertebrates and 2) describe in-detail the spatiotemporal patterns of fluid motion across varied feeding events. We used morphological and muscle mass data of the feeding apparatus; high-speed video footage and particle tracking; and the mathematical relationships among flow, pressure, and power to make inferences on salamander suction feeding behavior. We aim to broaden our findings beyond animal movement and behavior, and into the fundamental principles of suction generation mechanics constrained by biology.
452: Niche partitioning is a mechanism that enables the coexistence of species-rich assemblages. In this study, we assess the dietary niche partitioning among five sympatric stream and woodland salamanders (Plethodontidae) along a small first order stream in central Alabama, United States. We utilize δ13C and δ15N stable isotope analysis to estimate the dietary patterns of larval and adult salamanders informed by results from gastric lavage. We aim to quantify trophic position, the relative contributions of aquatic versus terrestrial prey, and ontogenetic shifts. Larval salamanders exhibit significant niche overlap, relying principally on aquatic insects and crustaceans. Adult salamanders exhibit more variable intra- and inter-specific isotopic signatures, and rely heavily on terrestrial prey such as crickets, worms, and snails. All species exhibit ontogenetic diet shifts that broadly fall into three categories: body size positively correlated with δ15N, positively correlated with δ13C and δ15N, or negatively correlated with δ15N. These patterns reflect ontogenetic transitions to larger and/or more terrestrial prey. Semiaquatic adult salamanders integrate the aquatic and terrestrial food webs but are more reliant on terrestrial resources. This research provides important insights into the complexity of resource use among sympatric salamanders and their ecological roles integrating aquatic and terrestrial food webs. Our findings emphasize the importance of the stream-side terrestrial environment as a nutrient source for stream and woodland salamanders and may inform conservation strategies in the face of global climate change and habitat loss. Ben Gonzalez
453: Stable isotope analysis of δ13C and δ15N is a powerful tool that can be used to investigate the dietary niches of reptiles and amphibians. Fluid-preserved museum specimens are vital resources that can provide insight into historic dietary niche space, but it can be challenging to recover unaltered isotopic data, as preservation methods have been well-documented to deplete or enrich δ13C and δ15N in tissues. To extract accurate isotopic data, it is imperative to determine how wet-preservation methods alter the isotopic signature of tissues over time. Shifts in δ13C and δ15N measurements due to preservation methods have been previously investigated in fishes, mammals, birds, and invertebrates, but there are few publications for herpetofauna. Here, we examine δ13C and δ15N signatures in the tissues of six species of reptiles and six species of amphibians preserved in ethanol over a period of nine months. Preliminary data reveal that the shifts in isotopic signatures of herpetofauna tissues are non-linear and rapid, where the steepest shift (enrichment or depletion) occurs immediately after preservation. Additionally, shifts after this point remain minimal through time which is consistent with previous studies of other taxonomic groups. We aim to develop correction factors to reconstruct unaltered isotopic signatures in preserved tissue, and it may be necessary for herpetofauna specimens to be corrected on a species-specific basis. These results will increase the utility of herpetofauna museum specimens and ensure that the isotopic information obtained from them is an accurate reflection of historical dietary and ecological dynamics. Devya Hemraj-Naraine
454: Human expansion into natural habitat is transforming ecosystems and driving rapid biodiversity loss. Anthropogenic changes are major drivers of habitat loss and population declines for environmentally sensitive species like reptiles. However, little is known about reptilian tolerance to human activity or traits that may allow them to persist amid anthropogenic changes. We used 4,861,566 global community science observations of squamates and a continuous measure of landscape modification to derive human tolerance scores for 2,290 species. We integrated life history data from 11,767 species to determine which traits predict tolerance to human modification. We found that many squamates (78%) exhibit moderate tolerance of human modification, with wider ranging, larger bodied, faster reproducing species showing the highest tolerance. Intolerance to modification was linked to extinction risk across squamates, as species classified as “Least Concern” had higher tolerance values than species in all other IUCN classifications, supporting the idea that human activity is a primary driver of reptile declines. This is the most comprehensive study of tolerance to human modification in reptiles, and our findings highlight the importance of considering species’ life history when predicting vulnerability to human development and the need to incorporate these data into conservation planning as human-modified landscapes spread. Cristian Hernandez
455: Due to the detrimental nature of their expansion's pressure on the ecosystems they establish in, invasive species place a heavy burden on regional economies to manage their various impacts. However, these exotic species offer remarkable opportunities to assess short-time adaption, symbiosis, and speciation parameters. This study compared specimens of the “Argentine black and white tegu” lizard, Salvator merianae, from invasive populations in southern Florida and captive-bred specimens across the United States, in order to investigate divergences from an ecological evolutionary perspective. We further compared various crosses of hybridizations occurring in captivity within the genus Salvator, for comparison to natural occurrences in South America from the literature. We sampled twelve morphological variables on all captive and invasive specimens, including five established scale counts for determining squamate classification, and two new scale count parameters developed by this work. Blood samples from over 200 living and deceased specimens were used for a variety of genetic analyses, both genomic (microsatellite) and mitochondrial. This study offers the most extensive genetic analysis performed to date on Salvator merianae and Salvator rufescens, both in sample size and the degree of genetic investigation. The goal of this project is to better evaluate species parameters within Teiidae, gauge hybridization potential among invasive reptiles, and ultimately assist efforts in both South American endemic Salvator conservation, & US insavive Savlvator eradication. Amanda Pinion
456: Sceloporus genus lizards represent one of the most diverse radiation of reptiles in North America. Few groups within the genus show unclear species boundaries, particularly those that have recently diverged and stretch across diverse geographical systems. The Sceloporus formosus group is one such example, where many taxa are morphologically conservative despite sometimes showing notable differences in external traits. Earlier studies using mitochondrial DNA and morphology have likely inferred hybridization between members, but genome-wide evidence has been limited, leaving uncertainty about both species limits and evolutionary relationships. Here, we use genome-wide SNP data generated with ddRADseq to examine population structure and phylogenetic patterns across the S. formosus group. Our dataset includes more than 300 individuals sampled across the geographic range, from southern Mexico to Costa Rica, using tissue collections from the Amphibian and Reptile Diversity Research Center at The University of Texas at Arlington. The results show strong genetic structuring overall, with most individuals clustering by geography and currently recognized taxa. However, this pattern is not consistent everywhere. In some regions, particularly where ranges overlap, we find signals consistent with localized hybridization, suggesting that gene flow does occur but appears to be limited. The data also supports the presence of several deeply divergent lineages within the group, likely shaped by geographic isolation and historical processes. Ongoing work is focused on quantifying gene flow and refining evolutionary relationships among species and populations. Overall, these findings highlight the value of genome-wide data for resolving species boundaries and understanding diversification in complex systems. Brian L. Sidlauskas
457: The Malagasy Leaf-nosed Snake Langaha madagascariensis Bonnarterre, 1790 is an arboreal pseudoxyrhophiine snake endemic to Madagascar. This species is unique in possessing an extremely elongate nasal appendage, as well as conspicuous sexual dimorphism in appendage shape and body coloration. Females are generally gray with transverse bands and a broad and bristle-shaped nasal appendage, whereas males are uniform brown with yellow undersides and a finely pointed, lanceolate nasal appendage. We predicted that these differences are a result of ecological divergence in diet and microhabitat between sexes. We examined over 60 specimens of L. madagascariensis to investigate unexplored patterns of sexual dimorphism in ecologically-relevant morphological traits and report new aspects of geographic variation, ontogenetic allometry, and feeding ecology. We found that allometric coefficients differ significantly between sexes in several ecologically-important cranial measurements, including head length, head width, and snout length. We also found that allometric intercepts differ in other morphometric traits, including the nasal appendage length itself. Eight snakes contained stomach contents, with females generally consuming arboreal lizards more frequently than males, though statistical tests were not possible due to small sample size. Overall, we hypothesize that conspicuous sexual dimorphism in this species likely originated or is maintained by ecological differences, perhaps driven by preferences in canopy height or microhabitat. Jake Vos
458: Rattlesnakes are widespread throughout the western United States, where urban expansion could lead to increasing encounters with people. Fear, exacerbated by sensational media portrayals, is linked with the persecution of snakes. In 2024, Project RattleCam launched the first 24-7 livestream of a wild Prairie Rattlesnake (Crotalus viridis) rookery (nursery) to improve public understanding and attitudes toward snakes while engaging them in community science. To extend Project RattleCam’s mission to younger audiences, we led a team of undergraduate students in developing a science curriculum for third through fifth graders, called RattlEd. Our eightday curriculum aligns with Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS), engaging students in activities such as practicing the scientific method, creating models, playing games, and engineering wildlife crossings. In 2025, teachers in California, Colorado, Utah, and Oregon taught RattlEd in their classrooms and surveyed students before and after the unit. Because children’s attitudes are complex, we used a combination of drawing and writing prompts alongside survey questions to assess students’ perceptions. Overall, students reported decreased fear, negativity, and disgust toward rattlesnakes following the unit. Students’ drawings shifted from mostly depicting snakes as predators towards depictions of social, thermoregulatory, and drinking behavior following the unit. All RattlEd teaching materials are available at RattleCam.org. The integration of wildlife livestreams in education can effectively engage students in science while fostering empathy and encouraging safe coexistence with wildlife. Luke Bailey
459: Roadways have severe negative impacts on migratory amphibian populations through direct vehicle caused mortality. Many migratory amphibians move to and from breeding areas in the Spring and juveniles disperse from natal wetlands in the Fall. While the impact of road mortality on adult amphibians in the Spring is well studied and commonly mitigated, recently metamorphosed juvenile amphibians are severely understudied and subject to little to no mitigation despite constituting a major component of amphibian population viability. We address this gap in knowledge by investigating the road mortality rates of juvenile A. maculatum (spotted salamander) using (1) an established method to estimate mortality probability and (2) a novel semi-automated camera trap method to estimate how mortality rate changes within migration season and night. We monitored A. maculatum road mortality in March-May and July-November 2025. To measure mortality rates, we recorded individual survival immediately before and after crossing using a novel drift fence/camera trap design. To estimate the probability of road mortality, we measured the crossing velocity of adult and juvenile salamanders. We present the first estimates of salamander road mortality by age class, hour, and month as well as compare estimates of mortality using a novel and established method. We found that the probability of juvenile road mortality was three times higher than adult road mortality. This suggests that previous studies have underestimated juvenile salamander road mortality. These results will help improve salamander road mitigation by encouraging the inclusion of the juvenile stage in population projections and mitigation efforts. Patty Brennan Patty Brennan; Summer Sit; Rachel Keeffe; Joshua Gunn; Samuel Krauss; Christopher Friesen; Robert Mason; Brandon Hedrick; M. Rockwell Parker
460: Cascade torrent salamanders (Rhyacotriton cascadae) are headwater-obligate species endemic to the western slopes of the Cascade Range in Oregon and Washington. Recent work using a dataset of molecular markers from across the genome has shown that the species consists of six genetically distinct populations, with one showing a large degree of divergence. Building upon this genomic dataset with an additional dataset of ultra-conserved elements, we expand upon this work by providing divergence time estimates for each population, linking the divergence time to past geologic events. While present-day phylogeographic barriers explain genetic structure in some cases, we show that the identity of the divergence group traces back to Miocene era earth movements, and that the divergence reflects incipient speciation. As more recently diverged populations in the species do not share gene flow despite a lack of phylogeographic barriers preventing dispersal, we highlight the causes and potential consequences of secondary contact with diverged groups in the species. As this species is currently being reviewed for listing under the Federal Endangered Species Act (ESA), we highlight the immediate conservation concerns for both R. cascadae as a species, and the diverged group as an evolutionarily unique lineage. Amelia Coykendall
461: Effective species management is informed by reliable estimates of abundance and density, yet traditional methods for estimating abundance such as capture-mark-recapture are not feasible for many situations. Alternative approaches are especially desirable when dealing with an invasive species, where removal is the primary goal. Additional challenges arise when dealing with a cryptic species in a difficult habitat, as is the case for estimating Burmese python (Python bivittatus) abundance in southern Florida. To address these challenges, we developed a Bayesian hierarchical removal model that incorporated spatially explicit removal counts, survey effort, habitat covariates, and telemetry data to estimate local abundance in the Everglades and Francis S Taylor Wildlife Management Area. We found that survey effort influenced detection probability, and that inclusion of telemetry data improved interpretation of the spatial pattern of abundance. Our future work will extend this model across seasons to estimate population trends in support of science-based management of Burmese pythons in southern Florida. Giavanna Harrington
462: Cryptogenic species - species whose native and introduced ranges are unknown - pose a challenge to conservation. The Lesser Antillean coqui (Eleutherodactylus johnstonei) is one such species, with a current distribution throughout the Caribbean islands and mainland South America. Previous work identified two clades: a western Lesser Antillean clade native to Montserrat (subsequently described as E. montserratae) and a widely introduced clade (E. johnstonei sensu stricto) whose native island is unknown. Fossil evidence suggests the Barbuda Island Bank as the potential native range for E. johnstonei. To evaluate this hypothesis, we sampled frogs across Antigua and Barbuda and sequenced the cytochrome b gene to estimate the genetic diversity of each island population and place the islands in a broader phylogeographic context. We found high levels of genetic diversity on Antigua compared to all other island populations, and that haplotypes of E. johnstonei across its introduced range were nested within the Antigua clade, supporting the hypothesis that Antigua is the native range of the species. Additionally, we report the presence of the Cuban tree frog (Osteopilus septentrionalis) on Barbuda - another nonnative species that has been introduced to several Caribbean islands. These results will inform conservation and invasive species management in the Lesser Antilles, as well as support Eleutherodactylus as a promising system for understanding the factors influencing invasion potential and success in widely distributed species. Michelle Le
463: Animal translocation is commonly used to mitigate the impacts of land-use change. However, for many commonly translocated taxa such as herpetofauna, empirical evidence to support its efficacy is lacking, due to limited ecological and biological knowledge, low species detectability, and a lack of standardized processes. A review of government-issued translocation permits in New Zealand revealed high geographic unevenness in how lizards are considered during land-use change and inconsistencies in reporting, suggesting weaknesses in current processes. To understand the drivers of these patterns and how policy and process might be improved, we sought the diverse perspectives of key local and national actors including consultant and government ecologists, government planners, and Department of Conservation faunal management advisors. The focus of these interviews was to gain perspective on 1) the main barriers for considering lizards during land-use change, 2) the expected versus realistic outcomes of lizard mitigation methodologies, and 3) practice-informed recommendations for improvements. Barriers to improved practice identified by the 22 interviewees included a lack of experience in lizard management within local government, time pressures within the permitting and land-use change processes, a lack of available, suitable translocation release sites, and an outdated toolbox for designing herpetofauna mitigations. Suggested improvements included better collaboration between ecologists and governmental bodies, improving local knowledge of lizard ecology and distribution, and developing standardized management and reporting guidelines. Combining perspectives and experiences from ecological and governmental sectors is a crucial, though underutilized, approach for improving current policy and practices of land-use change mitigation to obtain better outcomes. Diana Methner
464: The giant gartersnake (Thamnophis gigas) is a federally threatened species endemic to California’s Central Valley. Following the widespread loss of natural wetlands, the giant gartersnake has become highly reliant on rice agriculture as surrogate habitat. Given their high site-fidelity to these chemically managed landscapes, long lifespan, and apex trophic position, they are ideal candidates for studying pesticide exposure and bioaccumulation. In collaboration with the U.S. Geological Survey, we investigated the detectability of pesticides commonly applied in rice cultivation using non-lethal tail-tip tissues. From May–August 2024, we collected samples across the Sacramento Valley from sites within or adjacent to active rice production. To enhance detection limits for lowconcentration compounds, samples were composited based on snout-vent length, mass, and capture location. Our analysis revealed detectable pesticide concentrations in 84% of composite samples (n = 41 detected; n = 8 not detected). To evaluate the drivers of this internal burden, we integrated California Department of Pesticide Regulation Pesticide Use Reporting data using a GIS-based approach. We modeled the relationship between tissue concentrations and the cumulative pesticide load applied within site-specific buffers over a 60-day retrospective window prior to sampling. Furthermore, we assessed the relationship between snake mass and contaminant load to evaluate evidence of bioaccumulation. Our study highlights a significant conservation concern and validates the use of tail tips as an effective, non-lethal tool for monitoring the real-time environmental exposure of this threatened species. Erin Toffelmier
465: Freshwater biodiversity decline is increasingly driven by the combined pressures of habitat modification and invasive species. We investigated the responses of native Northwestern Pond Turtles (Actinemys marmorata) and invasive Red-eared Sliders (Trachemys scripta elegans) to long-term anthropogenic and interspecific pressures in an urbanized waterway and a nearby natural reserve. By analyzing abundance, demography, body condition, and blood stable isotopes, we examined how human-altered environments mediate interspecific dietary overlap and the efficacy of short-term invasive species removal. After a decade of cooccurrence, native pond turtles declined by nearly 60% as sliders rose concomitantly, shifting species ratios from 1:3 (invasive:native) in a natural reserve to 4:1 in an urban waterway. Stable total populations in the urban waterway indicate near-total species replacement by the slider. Further, high juvenile abundance of sliders suggests urban landscapes function as productive recruitment hubs for the invasive species. Stable isotopes revealed persistent dietary overlap, with natives maintaining a more specialized dietary niche while sliders exhibited more opportunistic foraging. Although urban nutrient subsidies supported higher relative mass in native turtles compared to those in the reserve, these benefits disproportionately favored the slider’s opportunistic life history despite removal efforts a decade prior. Our results demonstrate how urbanization exacerbates invasive impacts by creating conditions that favor generalist invaders over native specialists. Effective conservation requires shifting from isolated removal efforts toward comprehensive strategies that include habitat restoration and policies addressing introduction pathways. Daniel Woods
466: Genetic diversity within populations is essential to a species’ ability to persist and adapt to their environment. The loss of genetic diversity often precedes population extirpation and frequently leads to inbreeding depression. Therefore, conservation decisions can be better informed by incorporating genetic information with ecological models, allowing for the estimation of adaptive potential and climate vulnerability. Mole skinks (Plestiodon egregius) are semi-fossorial lizards with five subspecies. One subspecies (P. e. lividus) is federally listed as Threatened, and two insular subspecies (P. e. egregius and P. e. insularis) are proposed to be listed under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). There are currently no studies quantifying genetic connectivity among all five subspecies.
