Through this project, we aim to assess genetic diversity, model future habitat suitability under different climate scenarios, and identify candidate adaptive loci in mole skink populations. Our initial draft genome is ~1.5Gb spanning 38 contigs, with a contig N50 of 164.3 Mbp, an L50 of 4, and a BUSCO completeness score of 98%. This de novo reference genome will be used to map nextRAD (n=178) and whole genome (n=25) data. Preliminary analyses support the current five subspecies and that there is minimal gene flow among them. We found high population structure among both island subspecies, which are at risk of extinction due to sea level rise in less than a century. One goal of this project is to help inform ESA policy decisions for P. egregius subspecies and facilitate conservation management strategies for the subspecies at risk of extirpation. Juan David González Corredor
467: Predicting patterns of dispersal is an important goal of ecology, evolution, and managing invasive species. Human-mediated dispersal complicates both dispersal patterns and our ability to predict them. Mediterranean House Geckos (Hemidactylus turcicus) are ideal for studying human-mediated dispersal given their reliance on us for long-distance dispersal. Since their introduction to southern Florida ~1910, these geckos have colonized 26 US states despite their limited natural dispersal abilities (<20 m/yr). We reconstructed the historical dispersal patterns of H. turcicus across the US based on colonization records and population genomics. Geckos were collected from 68 sites representing 24 counties in seven US states. A dataset representing 350 geckos and 16,048 single-nucleotide polymorphisms was generated using a RADseq protocol. Analyses of population structure, genomic diversity, phylogeography, migration, and tests for isolation by distance were used to determine source populations within the US and categorize gecko dispersal into one of three hypothetical models. Western populations (AZ, CA, NM) likely originated from those introduced to east Texas. Eastern populations (AL, AR, MD, VA) likely originated from those introduced to Louisiana and Florida. On a continental scale, genetic variation was explained by isolation by distance, supporting a stepping stone model of dispersal. However, dispersal patterns varied by region and there were several instances of long-distance “jump” dispersal. Older populations (e.g., east Texas) even showed patterns of genetic variation consistent with panmixia. More broadly, our study offers a conceptual framework for inferring the often-complex movement histories of invasive species in an increasingly human-dominated world. Chris Distel
468: Species can respond to changing environmental conditions through behavioral adjustments that buffer against costly or lethal stress. Such responses are likely among the most immediate and important mechanisms by which organisms cope with climate change. Behavioral flexibility may be especially important in terrestrial plethodontid salamanders, whose physiology is tightly coupled to ambient thermal and hydric conditions. In the color-polymorphic Eastern Red-backed Salamander (Plethodon cinereus), previous work suggests that morphs (striped and unstriped) may occupy distinct thermal niches. Here, I used laboratory thermal gradient and thermal buffering experiments to examine how three Plethodon species and their color morphs behaviorally respond to increasing temperatures. I found that species differed in the temperatures utilized in thermal gradient trials and during thermal buffering trials, morphs tolerated increasing temperatures differently, and these morph-specific responses varied across species. Felicity Eriksson
469: Diamondback terrapins (Malaclemys terrapin) are a keystone species that occupy brackish water habitat and are listed as vulnerable. Terrapins have Type 1a temperature-sex determination meaning nesting conditions of 31°C or higher will result in more females, while temperatures below 27°C result in predominately male development. Low humidity egg chambers favor females. This suggests temperature and humidity can impact sexual development and may explain the female bias reported in populations. Although significant female bias was observed in Connecticut, preliminary results suggest that the sex ratio can vary among sites sampled. My research applies iButton technology to measure temperature and humidity in soil with various physical features (vegetation, soil substrate, and sun exposure) along the Connecticut coastline to sample the microclimate of terrapin beaches. Soil temperature is affected by physical parameters and can explain the clustering effect observed as well as the female bias seen in Connecticut. “Potential nests” (tagged with iButtons) were placed in a grid along a transect to record daily/seasonal changes and used to confirm there is a behavioral microhabitat preference for fecund females. Preliminary results indicate that soil temperature varies significantly along the coastline. Understanding thermal variation will identify optimal and diverse nesting habitat that support healthy populations, improving the sustainability of terrapins, and may explain why nesting occurs in some spots and not others. Ally Gravgaard
470: Amphibians face the highest extinction risk among vertebrates, yet large-scale patterns of species richness and climate vulnerability remain poorly understood in tropical Africa. We analyzed spatial patterns of amphibian richness, environmental drivers, intrinsic vulnerability, and climate change impacts across Nigeria. We compiled 5,066 occurrence records from GBIF, AmphibiaWeb, and IUCN Red List. After taxonomic validation, we retained 1,110 georeferenced records representing 119 species. Species richness was mapped at 5 km and 10 km resolutions. Environmental drivers were analyzed using boosted regression trees, and intrinsic vulnerability was assessed with trait-based metrics. Species distribution models were developed for 25 species using BIOMOD2 (GLM, Random Forest, GBM, MaxEnt) and combined into performance-weighted ensembles. Future projections were made under CMIP6 scenarios (SSP1–2.6, SSP3–7.0, SSP5–8.5) for mid- and end-century periods. Species richness ranged from 1 to 33 species per grid cell, peaking in southern forests and montane regions. Models explained 78% of the richness variance, with precipitation as the strongest predictor, showing a threshold response above approximately 1,500–1,800 mm. Human Footprint Index showed a positive relationship with richness. Traitbased analysis identified 39 species (32.8%) as highly vulnerable, mainly range-restricted montane taxa. Model performance was high (mean AUC = 0.857; mean TSS = 0.430). Climate projections suggest redistribution and turnover rather than reversal of current richness patterns, with range contractions exceeding expansions. Southern forests and montane regions remain critical refugia, although projected losses are greater outside protected areas. Conservation efforts should focus on these refugia while expanding protections into vulnerable, unprotected landscapes. Katriina L. Ilves Katriina Ilves; André Martel; Tim Haxton; Sarah Steele; Noel Alfonso; Anita LeBaron; Elise Millar; Roger Bull;
471: Many species in the lungless salamander family Plethodontidae use chemical signaling for communication. These cues can evoke a multitude of behavioral responses that are often crucial to an animal’s survival and reproduction (e.g. mate attraction, territoriality). However, the majority of previous studies regarding the function of chemical communication were conducted on a limited number of taxa. The objectives of this study were to (1) determine if the ensatina (Ensatina eschscholtzii) -a species endemic the Pacific coast of the U.S. -can discriminate between conspecific scents and scent from a food source and (2) if their preference for conspecific versus food scents vary between two times of year. To address this objective, we conducted behavioral trials in November 2025 and in February-March 2026. Adult salamanders (15 females and 15 males) were individually presented with different combinations of scents (female vs male and opposite sex vs food). The behavior of each animal was filmed for one hour and we analyzed the relative time spent on each substrate. Preliminary results show that neither male nor female ensatina exhibited a significant preference for conspecific or food scent in the fall but tended to spend more time on the scent from the opposite sex in the spring. These results indicate that ensatina may have more motivation to mate than find food during the months they have been observed courting. Rocky Parker Samuel Krauss; Natalie Haydt; Abby Kepley; Joshua Gunn; Isabella Davis; Kristopher Kubow; Lorin Neuman-Lee;
472: An organism’s elemental composition changes across ontogeny due to stage-specific developmental processes. This is especially true in vertebrates with biphasic life histories, such as amphibians, where shifts in elemental demands can influence an organism’s ionome (the complete elemental makeup required for biological function), and could be altered by factors like temperature. Amphibians can exhibit plasticity in growth and development when exposed to varied thermal regimes, however, the effect of underlying temperature interactions with ontogenic processes to structure the ionome of larval anurans remains poorly understood. We addressed this gap by rearing Lithobates blairi tadpoles across seven controlled thermal regimes (16-28℃) and sampled individuals at four time points to estimate the ionome of larval anurans at multiple temperature-driven developmental stages and body sizes. We quantified whole-body ionomes alongside growth, size, and development metrics to assess how temperature-dependent responses structure elemental composition. Ionome profiles shifted across ontogeny: early larval stages were characterized by growth-related elements (C, N, P), while later stages were represented by elements linked to bone production (Ba, Ca, P, Sr). Temperature further influenced these patterns, with larger body sizes observed at moderate temperatures (20, 22℃), and faster developmental rates at warmer temperatures (26, 28℃). These temperature-driven physiological differences correspond with distinct ionomic profiles, including elevated concentrations of trace metals under warmer conditions (Cu, Cr, Fe, Li). Our results demonstrate that temperature and ontogeny interact to shape the larval anuran ionome, highlighting the need to integrate physiological and ecological frameworks to understand organismal responses to environmental change. Khalil T Russell
473: Rigorous models that produce unbiased estimates and accurately propagate uncertainty are key to making good management decisions but are often challenging for data-limited, rare or hard to detect species. Monitoring methods and data gaps may vary with life stages, environmental conditions, logistical limitations, or management jurisdictions. We demonstrate the use of a multi-method integrated Bayesian community occupancy model to jointly estimate species occupancy among wetlands across multiple landscapes. Our model integrates multiple methods (e.g., acoustic recording units and dipnet surveys) that might be used differently among sites, when temporal and spatial sampling effort vary, and when some species only occur in some landscapes due to range limitations or extinctions. The model leverages taxonomic and ecological groupings of species to generate estimates of rare or enigmatic species. The use of multiple methods and grouping variables led to good model convergence, even for rare and seldom detected species. Relationships between amphibian occupancy and wetland conditions were highly uncertain and species dependent. Our results provided more realistic estimates of amphibian species’ relationships to wetland conditions, including the high uncertainty of how species will respond to wetland restoration at a wetland within a landscape. Our model demonstrates the utility of integrating multiple data sources rather than trying to settle on a single “best” approach, and how to leverage relationships among species to generate estimates of data-limited species. Michael W. Sandel Michael Sandel; Kayla Fast; Andres Aguilar; David Neely; Peter Unmack; Sergei Kirilchik; Jacob Daane;
474: California’s Channel Islands are a young near-shore archipelago of oceanic origin, making them an opportune system for studying dispersal, diversification, and evolution more broadly. Differences in each island’s geomorphology, climate, and human presence have strongly influenced local community assemblages, levels of endemism, and biogeographic distributions. The Common Side-blotched Lizard (Uta stansburiana) is widespread on five of these islands. While analysis of mitochondrial DNA suggests these lizards are recently introduced to several islands, the timing, source, and mechanism of dispersal to each island is unclear. We assemble and analyze a SNP library from 350 individual U. stansburiana along their coastal California distribution and on the islands they inhabit. Specifically, we produce a phylogeny, characterize population genetic diversity and structure, calculate divergence timing between populations, quantify island-mainland migration, and identify change in island population size since establishment. By determining the timing, source, and mechanism of dispersal to each island, our results will allow us to determine which island U. stansburiana populations are long-standing versus recently introduced and will elucidate the role of humans in transporting lizards to and among islands. Further, characterizing consistent patterns of movement, establishment, and population growth of this species will improve our understanding of the processes of dispersal, colonization, and diversification on the Channel Islands and on islands more broadly. Ava Ivy
475: Understanding population connectivity given landscape features, evolutionary history, and humanrelated histories can provide insight into how populations evolve and persist in heterogeneous environments and on a changing planet. This project uses genomic data from the Common Side-blotched Lizard (Uta stansburiana) on California’s Channel Islands to investigate how colonization history, local habitat characteristics, and humanactivity impact patterns of differentiation and connectivity. The Common Side-blotched Lizard occurs on five of the eight Channel Islands through at least three colonization events, and each island varies in geology, vegetational composition, climate, and anthropogenic influences, offering a natural experimental system to study evolutionary processes. We are investigating how colonization history, local habitat characteristics, and human-activity impact patterns of differentiation and connectivity across island populations of this species. We analyze a RADseq library of 575 individuals sampled across the islands to assess population structure and diversity. We additionally use a landscape genomics approach to determine which landscape features best predict connectivity and how these patterns vary within and among islands. Because each island is unique, we predict that islands will differ in which landscape features influence connectivity and the Northern Channel Islands will be more similar to each other than to the southern islands which are associated with distinct colonization histories. Studying a widespread, generalist species in an isolated island system provides a unique opportunity to explore the relationships among connectivity, diversity, and isolation in heterogeneous environments. Additionally, these insights into the effects of landscape on connectivity can be used to better inform ongoing habitat management. Bri Johnson
476: Biofluorescence, which occurs when an organism absorbs and reemits light, has been discovered in hundreds of species in many animal groups including amphibians. While biofluorescence has been reported in eight of the ten salamander families, no studies have performed a comparative assessment of the sources of biofluorescence to reconstruct how this phenotype might have evolved. We used microscopy and histology to assess the distribution, sources, and patterns of biofluorescence in twelve species from Plethodontidae, the largest and most diverse family of salamanders. Biofluorescence was found in the skin of all twelve species but varied widely in its distribution and sources both within and between species. Most species possessed at least one type of biofluorescent chromatophore while many also possessed biofluorescent skin glands. Our histological analysis revealed at least four distinct types of biofluorescent skin glands that may have descended from a common ancestor or evolved convergently. We also discovered male-biased biofluorescence in three species of Plethodon, female-biased biofluorescence in Aneides and two species of Desmognathus, and that biofluorescence is typically present in the skin of juvenile salamanders. Together, our results suggest that biofluorescence is ubiquitous across Plethodontidae and may have been shaped by selective pressures to serve different functions in different lineages including crypsis, mate attraction, competition, territorial scent-marking, and species or sexual identification. Our results also imply that many plethodontids could be valuable models to investigate the visual-signaling roles of biofluorescence. Benjamin R. Karin Benjamin Karin; Jeffrey Frederick; Amir Hamidy; Awal Riyanto; Evy Arida; Djoko Iskandar; Indraneil Das; Adi
477: Feeding on substrate-bound prey characterizes nearly half of reef fish species and is a source of considerable ecological and functional diversity. Recent studies have begun to clarify the mechanisms used by these fishes, but comparisons between major lineages are lacking. We described feeding kinematics in 28 species from 5 prominent families of benthic feeding coral reef fishes: Acanthuridae, Chaetodontidae, Pomacanthidae, Siganidae, and Zanclidae. We used 1000 FPS video to track head and jaw movements during feeding on substrate-bound prey. For each strike, we quantified five prominent motions of the jaws and head. We found distinct kinematic patterns in most families. Pomacanthidae exhibited the highest kinesis, with large ranges of motion in jaw rotation, head elevation, upper jaw protrusion, and lower jaw protrusion, while Chaetodontidae were characterized by very small mouth gapes and diversity in upper and lower jaw protrusion. Pomacanthidae and Chaetodontidae, sister clades, did not overlap in multivariate kinematic space, but the two families formed a continuum of strike kinematics. Acanthuridae and Siganidae overlapped in kinematic space with reduced movement, while Zanclidae fell in between all families. Our results indicate that variable reduction in jaw and skull kinesis is a major axis of diversity in benthic-feeding reef fishes, with herbivory associated with the least skull mobility. An expansive picture of benthic feeding kinematics will allow us to describe and compare the kinematic diversity and underlying mechanisms of extracting attached prey across reef fish, providing insight into its role in fish diversification.
478: Reproductive isolating barriers limit gene flow between species, yet species boundaries often remain permeable, resulting in hybridization. Understanding how genomic architecture and environmental factors shape introgression is critical for explaining hybrid zone formation and stability. Whiptail lizards (Aspidoscelis) are known to hybridize frequently, often resulting in independent parthenogenetic lineages. However, sexual species also have signatures of introgression in their genomes. Here, we characterize a hybrid zone between Aspidoscelis gularis and A. septemvittatus to investigate how genomic architecture and environmental change shape patterns of introgression between closely related species. We address three primary aims: (1) evaluate how genomic architecture and recombination landscape influence heterogeneous introgression across the nuclear genome, (2) test for asymmetric introgression and cytonuclear discordance to assess whether gene flow differs across the nuclear and mitochondrial genome, and (3) integrate demographic inference with microclimate modeling to reconstruct the timing and environmental drivers of secondary contact. Using ddRADseq and whole mitochondrial genome sequencing, we identify a narrow geographic region of hybridization with clinal transitions supporting asymmetric introgression biased towards A. gularis. Patterns of genomic and geographic structure indicate a stable, multi-generational hybrid zone. We further identify genomic regions with excess ancestry, suggesting localized deviations from neutral introgression, which may reflect selection or genomic constraints in the hybrid zone. Analyses integrating demographic inference and microclimate modeling are ongoing and will further clarify the timing and environmental drivers of this secondary contact. Steve Mullin
479: Adaptive changes to the visual system are a primary response to variation in light environments. One important mechanism underlying visual adaptation is the evolution of retinal photoreceptor proteins that govern the earliest stages of vision, including light absorption and signal transduction (phototransduction). While evidence of adaptive alterations in phototransduction are found across vertebrates, turtles remain an understudied lineage. Turtles provide an ideal system to investigate phototransduction evolution due to their deep divergence (~200 million years) into two suborders, Pleurodira and Cryptodira, as well as their occupation of habitats (marine, freshwater, and terrestrial) that differ drastically in their spectral properties. We hypothesized that the long divergence time combined with unique selective pressures imposed by the distinct light environments has resulted in considerable functional differences in phototransduction between and among suborders. To test this hypothesis, we extracted phototransduction genes from one pleurodiran eye transcriptome, eight pleurodiran genomes, 47 cryptodiran genomes, and from 31 other representative reptile genomes. We recovered all expected phototransduction genes in turtles, with no major differences between suborders. Codon-based evolutionary models revealed that these genes are highly conserved across turtles, a pattern that is unusual across reptiles. Although we detected shifts in selective pressure, these patterns were more strongly associated with phylogenetic relationships than with habitat differences, with distinct signals observed in softshell turtles. Overall, our results suggest that light environments may not play as important a role as expected in turtle visual evolution and that, remarkably, turtle vision may be largely conserved over ~200 million years of evolution. Martha Patricia Pérez-Villanueva Martha Pérez-Villanueva; Alfonsina Romo-Curiel; John Mohan; Juan Pérez-Jiménez; Sharon Herzka; Nathan
480: Anura (frogs and toads) represent one of the most diverse vertebrate lineages, yet genomic resources remain limited across much of their evolutionary breadth. This gap constrains comparative studies of trait evolution, especially in lineages that lack high quality reference genomes or are represented primarily by preserved museum material. To address these challenges, we developed and evaluated a targeted sequence capture framework designed to recover phylogenetically and functionally informative loci across deeply divergent frog lineages. We focused on genes related to visual function, development, and phylogenetic inference, using a probe design built from high quality gene references spanning three divergent frog lineages to maximize probe diversity and enhance sequence recovery across long evolutionary distances. Gene capture performance was assessed using metrics including locus recovery, coverage depth and breadth, and exon completeness. To evaluate the utility of this framework in an evolutionary context, we inferred phylogenetic relationships within Afrobatrachia, a diverse African frog radiation whose relationships remain incompletely resolved despite substantial ecological and morphological diversity. Preliminary results suggest that targeted capture can accurately recover both phylogenetic and functional gene data across the frog tree of life. This enabled us to, in combination with existing sequences, reconstruct the most complete phylogeny for Afrobatrachia to date. using both concatenated and coalescent-based approaches. Together, this work establishes targeted capture as a scalable genomic tool for amphibians and generates new insight into the diversification of one of the major radiations of African frogs. Danielle Rivera Danielle Rivera; Nahíra Arocho-Hernandez; Jan Zegarra; Erin Rivenbark; Kevin Chovanec; R. Graham Reynolds; Kevin de Queiroz; S. Blair Hedges; Alberto Puente-Rolón; Luis Gonzalez-Arocho; Nathan Hostetter; Jaime Collazo;
481: Vision is one of the most important sensory systems in many animals, but species inhabiting lightlimited environments are expected to undergo visual regression due to relaxed selective pressures. This has been described in several lineages, including fossorial mammals and cave-dwelling fish. However, these evolutionary pathways remains understudied in amphibians and reptiles. Caecilians and several lineages of squamates have convergently evolved morphological adaptations to their fossorial lifestyles including limbless bodies and regressed eyes, but molecular analyses remain limited. We predict that vision-related genes will show convergent patterns of regression across these independent evolutionary transitions to fossoriality. However, in addition to regression, we hypothesize that a subset of genes, and their proteins, will show evidence of adaptation to the fossorial environment. To test these predictions, we supplement existing amphibian and squamate genomic resources through the sequencing of new genomes three fossorial taxa. Vision-related genes from fossorial and non-fossorial taxa are compared to determine the extent of gene loss and molecular evolutionary models used to estimates selection pressures including relaxed and positive selection. We found that fossorial taxa maintain more vision-related genes than expected, with caecilians maintaining up to 32 visual genes and some squamates up to 30. These results suggest potential adaptive evolution or co-option for non-visual functions. However, evolutionary analyses suggest that these lineages may not have converged on the same visual adaptations to fossoriality, possibly due to distinct life histories. Overall, our results suggest that fossorial adaptation is complex, inadequately summarized by gross visual regression, and requires further study. Kara E. Yopak
482: Introduced species have strong impacts on global biodiversity, often altering community structure and ecosystem function. For ectothermic organisms, temperature strongly influences survival, performance, and reproduction, making thermal physiology a critical factor in determining establishment success following introduction. We tested whether an introduced population of the Italian wall lizard (Podarcis siculus) in San Pedro, California, introduced approximately 30 years ago, has undergone shifts in thermal physiology in response to novel environmental conditions. We quantified four key thermal traits: optimal sprint temperature (Topt), preferred body temperature (Tpref), and critical thermal limits (CTmin and CTmax). We measured the same traits in the source population in Taormina, Italy to assess change following introduction. The introduced population exhibited lower Tpref and CTmin that better matches their new climate, but higher Topt and no difference in CTmax between populations. This pattern indicates that thermal traits have shifted in different directions rather than as a single coordinated response. These results suggest that thermal physiology can change rapidly and in complex ways following introduction, with different components responding independently. Understanding how introduced species respond to abiotic constraints such as temperature is essential for predicting their establishment, spread, and ecological impact under current and future climate conditions. SSAR Siebert Award: Morphology, Physiology and Behavior
483: An animal’s sensory system dictates its ability to navigate its environment. Although pitvipers are known to integrate mechanoreception, chemoreception, infrared, and visual perception while navigating, we have limited understanding of the relative importance of these cues for different orientation or navigation tasks. Many pitvipers make repeated annual movement to and from hibernacula, foraging grounds, and rookeries, even in the absence of chemical cues, suggesting that pitvipers may partially rely on spatial landmarks for piloting. In this study, we investigate the ability of pit vipers to discriminate between two similar visual shapes to solve a navigation task (identifying an accessible refugia). Snakes were trained to first associate the open refugia with a specific shape, and then were tested to determine how readily they could discriminate that specific shape from a similar cue. Some individuals could rapidly learn this task whereas others made repeated mistakes, suggesting that personality may influence learning efficiency. In a subsequent study, we will adapt this initial bioassay to test if pitvipers can use their infrared-detecting pit organs to solve an identical task discriminating between thermal shapes. Brian Kacerski
SSAR Siebert Award: Morphology, Physiology and Behavior
484: Ontogenetic dietary shifts occur in a wide range of vertebrates and are often associated with morphological changes that accommodate these new life history traits. Snakes are hypercarnivores that consume a range of prey items, with wide variation in the degree to which species undergo ontogenetic dietary shifts. Because head shape acts as a predictor of prey preference in many species previous work has suggested morphological changes which occur via allometric scaling potentially correlate with associated dietary shifts. Watersnakes (Genus: Nerodia) exhibit variable dietary shifts through ontogeny, with some species exhibiting discrete changes to functionally different prey groups, others exhibiting more continuous variation in diet and some exhibiting little change in diet through ontogeny. In this study, we use two-dimensional geometric morphometrics to quantify head shape in six species of watersnake across an ontogenetic series. We test the hypothesis that species which undergo discrete dietary shifts would exhibit greater positive allometry in head size and more substantial shape change through ontogeny to accommodate prey with distinct handling characteristics relative to those which exhibited continuous or limited dietary shifts. We further compare results of different analytical approaches using alternate landmarking configurations frequently utilized in studies examining head shape in snakes. We present little evidence to support our hypothesis, instead recovering relationships that suggest species which undergo continuous dietary shifts exhibit the strongest positive allometry in head size and greatest degree of shape change. We further describe significant variation in how different landmarking configurations characterize head shape variation through ontogeny in snakes.
SSAR Siebert Award: Morphology, Physiology and Behavior
485: Microplastics are one of the most prevalent forms of pollution today. The synthetic material is found in abundance in waterways and oceans, and has been found in the tissues of various animal species. Due to the pervasiveness of microplastics in nature, they may be hazardous to amphibian populations, which are declining on a global scale. However, we know little about their effects on amphibian biology. In this study, we aimed to determine if microplastics would have any effects on froglets that had been exposed to microplastics throughout all of their tadpole development. Frogs were placed into a tank bisected into two zones, one illuminated by a lamp, and the other cast in shadow. Frogs were placed in the center of the tank. Microplastic-treated frogs were less likely to move, including being less likely to move between zones when compared to the control group. Due to changes in these locomotory behaviors, we decided to examine the brains of each froglet for any discrepancies between the microplastic-treated group and the control group that could potentially contribute to these effects. Brain analyses are currently ongoing. The long-term effects of microplastics are largely unknown. However, microplastic abundance is steadily increasing. It is therefore imperative to understand how microplastic pollution is affecting amphibian populations so we can better conserve at-risk species. Robert E. 486: Urbanization drastically restructures environments and can often impose thermal and hydric constraints on urban-dwelling organisms. In urban areas, increased temperature (Urban Heat Island Effect) and increased water availability (Urban Oasis Effect) work in tandem to produce novel conditions that might not exist otherwise. Despite increasing human activity, we lack a general understanding of how relative and combinatorial effects of urban conditions affect wildlife. The objective of this study was to analyze how the thermal and hydric characteristics of microhabitats relate to ectotherm physiology. Across 11 Southern California colleges, we logged microclimatic conditions at paired urban and non-urban sites. During spring (rainy) and fall (dry), we measured the hydric physiology of Western Fence Lizards (Sceloporus occidentalis) at each site. We discovered that urban sites had higher ambient humidity and soil moisture. This was associated with lower temperatures, likely due to greater water availability. Regardless of site, plasma osmolality was lower in spring compared to fall. Urban lizards had lower osmolality both in spring and fall, indicating higher hydration than non-urban lizards. Cutaneous evaporative water loss of lizards was similar between sites in spring, but declined in non-urban lizards in fall, likely to prevent desiccation during the dry season. Our results suggest that irrigation on college campuses may mitigate the detrimental effects of urbanization. This work has implications for sustainable urban planning and highlights the importance of microhabitats for urban-dwelling organisms. Stella Raymond
SSAR Siebert Award: Morphology, Physiology and Behavior
487: Understanding how reproductive strategies shift during biological invasion is crucial for identifying the traits and processes that facilitate establishment in novel environments. The Italian wall lizard (Podarcis siculus) is an emerging model organism for studying biological invasions. Understanding reproductive behavior in this species is especially relevant where introduced populations may alter interactions with native congeners and invaded communities. Here, we examine whether responses to reproductive chemical cues differ between native and invasive populations. We conducted a behavioral assay across males, females, and gravid females to quantify patterns of chemosensory investigation, space use, and time allocation in the presence of scent-marked stimuli. Our analyses indicate that behavioral responses to reproductive cues vary with invasion status and that these differences are not uniform across sexes (p < 0.05). We identified an interaction between invasion status and sex, indicating that males, females, and gravid females from invasive populations allocate their interaction time with scent cues differently than their native counterparts. These findings suggest that invasion may be associated with changes in how individuals perceive and respond to social information, suggesting mate assessment as a potentially important mechanism for invasion success and the conservation of native communities exposed to introduced species.
SSAR Siebert Award: Morphology, Physiology and Behavior
488: Organisms often find change stressful. Though humans are the cause of drastic environmental changes, we have little understanding of how stress affects the organisms around us. By inducing specific, controlled hormonal elevations and measuring performance, we can elucidate specific aspects of stress physiology. Glucocorticoids are an intrinsic aspect of the neuro-endocrine stress response and are key hormones that regulate energy use and storage, inherently affecting behavior. This is especially true in ectotherms such as reptiles who rely on behavioral thermoregulation for metabolic processes. Therefore, we can experimentally induce controlled elevations in glucocorticoids such as corticosterone (CORT) to investigate the relationship between this stressrelated hormone and behavior. As CORT responses are often unique to taxa, the ecologically relevant dosage of CORT must be verified for each new species. Here we present the dermal dosage (0.255 µg CORT/ g lizard) we verified to elevate blood CORT to an ecologically relevant level for the Italian Wall Lizard (Podarcis siculus), a widely studied and globally introduced lacertid species. We calculated this dosage from a predictive model based on the dosing curve at four different dosages of dermally applied CORT and the maximum CORT elevation seen after a 5-min chasing stressor. Our findings suggest the ecologically relevant dosage required is significantly lower in Italian Wall Lizards than dosages previously tested and widely used in other closely related lacertid lizards. Though this dosage is unique to the Italian Wall Lizard, it allows future work to explore the impact of ecologically relevant levels of CORT across species. Daniel Sinopoli
SSAR Siebert Award: Morphology, Physiology and Behavior
489: Macrostomy, or enlarged gape, is a key innovation of the snake feeding system that is integral to their feeding behavior and diversification. The skeletal adaptations associated with enlarged gape, such as the unfused mandibular symphysis, are well studied, but the effects of macrostomy on the cranial soft tissues are relatively unknown. For example, the effects of macrostomatan gape on jaw muscle architecture or the biomechanics of the jaw apparatus are nearly unstudied. Here, we used DiceCT and 3D fiber tracking to visualize and quantify the muscle architecture and biomechanics of the jaw and palatal muscles of three Florida banded watersnakes preserved in positions at 0%, 50%, and 100% of their maximum gape. We used Xfiber for Avizo 3D to model and quantify the fiber architecture of the jaw and palatal muscles, including fiber lengths, orientation, and pennation angles. We also measured muscle vectors using segmented attachment sites. At maximum gape, nearly all muscles became less pennate with longer muscles fibers, though the changes were more pronounced in the more superficial muscles. At maximum gape, the positional shift of the mandibles and caudal palate caused the vector orientations of most muscles to shift laterally. These data provide initial insights into the muscular function of snakes at macrostomatan gapes and are a key foundation to further study of the mechanics of the snake feeding system. Ferris Zughaiyir
SSAR Siebert Award: Morphology, Physiology and Behavior
490: Two central ecological questions are how body size varies across geographic gradients and what factors shape that variation. Bergmann’s rule predicts that organisms should be larger in colder climates to aid heat retention, yet amphibians—particularly salamanders—often do not conform. It is likely that evaporative water loss (EWL) is the primary constraint, favoring larger body sizes with lower surface-area-to-volume ratios in warmer, drier climates. Plethodon salamanders are especially sensitive to dehydration because they are fully terrestrial and rely on cutaneous gas exchange. Adapting body size to climate also correlates with life history variation; most growth occurs before maturity, making larger size require delayed maturity or rapid growth. Delayed maturity is constrained by the effects of mortality on lifetime reproductive success. For amphibians, warm, dry environments constrain foraging and increase mortality, favoring rapid maturity, but conversely favor delayed maturity to a larger size to compensate for more dehydrating environments. We used local (16 km2 area) and regional (6,460 km2 area) surveys of Plethodon across Southern Appalachia to estimate the relationship between mean daily vapor pressure deficit—our hydroclimate variable—and minimum size at maturity. We found that minimum size at maturity increased significantly with increasing mean daily vapor pressure deficit and increased slightly with a more southern facing aspect and steeper slope. Our focus on minimum size at maturity demonstrates that body size is a key adaptation among Plethodon and that life histories evolve to accommodate this adaptation. Maddisyn Braun
491: Thermal plasticity is a key mechanism of climate change adaptation, providing an avenue for organismal resilience in the face of intensified climate pressures. Surprisingly, sexual dimorphism in intrapopulation thermal plasticity has received comparatively scant attention. Given both sexes are required for reproductive success, research investigating the role of thermal plasticity in population persistence should consider thermoregulatory strategy in both sexes to most accurately inform conservation predictions. Preliminary results in my research group have revealed significant sex differences in physiological acclimation to ecologically relevant temperatures in Plethodon cinereus. However, it is unclear how these patterns may impact behavior or downstream reproductive opportunity. To expand on this work, I conducted a large-scale investigation examining sex-specific thermal plasticity via two metrics: physiological thermal acclimation and behavioral avoidance strategy. I acclimated male and female salamanders (36 of each) to a warm or cold thermal regime in the laboratory before measuring metabolic and water loss rates using flow-through respirometry. I then used soil microcosms to simulate natural semi-fossorial environments and record movement events along a vertical temperature gradient. I predicted that all females will depress metabolic and water loss rates to maintain costly gamete development, with subsequent effects on behavioral opportunities. Warm-treatment males may not depress metabolic rates, likely to facilitate territoriality and mate searching behaviors. I will report on variation in sex-specific thermal acclimation and behavior in Plethodon cinereus, which represent novel patterns of acclimation in the genus and may prove relevant to species of conservation concern. Jack D. Budd
492: Passive acoustic monitoring may provide a non-invasive method for documenting breeding activity in crocodylians, yet its application to courtship vocalizations has not been systematically evaluated. This study assessed the utility of autonomous recording units (ARUs) for detecting American alligator (Alligator mississippiensis) bellows during the breeding season and tested whether recording frequency influenced detection performance. Three Song Meter SM4 units were deployed at a captive alligator facility in El Campo, Texas, from 20 March to 10 June 2025 and programmed to record daily from 07:00 to 08:00 at 8,000, 16,000, and 24,000 Hz. Recordings were manually reviewed in Kaleidoscope Pro to confirm bellow detections. Detection probability was analyzed using a binomial mixed model, and recording-effort efficiency was evaluated using Kaplan-Meier time-tofirst-detection analysis. ARUs successfully detected breeding vocalizations, supporting their feasibility for monitoring alligator breeding activity. The 16,000 Hz setting produced the highest predicted detection probability (0.61) and outperformed 8,000 Hz (0.35), while 24,000 Hz (0.51) was intermediate. Time-to-detection analysis showed that bellows were first detected as early as minute 1, but cumulative detection probability increased steadily across the 60-minute recording period, reaching 25% by minute 17, 40% by minute 37, and 50% by minute 56. Overall, results indicate that ARUs are effective tools for documenting breeding vocalizations of American alligators and that recording from 07:00 to 08:00 at 16,000 Hz provides an efficient protocol that could help standardize passive acoustic monitoring of wild populations during the breeding season. Brandon A. Gross
493: Anuran larvae possess specialized keratinized mouthparts that aid in feeding to fuel the energetically costly process of metamorphosis. Developmental deformities affecting jaw sheath and labial tooth rows have been observed in many species globally, but the exact causes of these malformations are unclear. Small variations in mouthpart morphology, such as number of labial teeth, can have significant effects on feeding biomechanics and foraging success. Chytridiomycosis infection is thought to be one major cause of tadpole mouthpart deformities as this fungal pathogen consumes keratin. Other hypothesized factors include changes in water quality parameters or exposure to environmental contaminants such as trace heavy metals and pesticides. Our study examines several populations of Rana catesbeiana and R. clamitans tadpoles in southwestern Ohio and aims to quantify the relationships among water quality parameters, environmental toxins, disease occurrence, and the prevalence of tadpole deformities. Mouthpart malformations are common at our sampling sites, with over 50% of all tadpoles sampled having aberrations in oral disk morphology. Some types of deformities, such as missing segments of labial teeth, have been detected across several localities, while others, such as aberrant keratodonts between labial tooth rows, are endemic to single ponds. Our preliminary results suggest that no single environmental factor is responsible for tadpole mouthpart deformities across sites and that malformations are being caused by a complex variety of stimuli. Zach Heiple
494: Invasive species are an ongoing concern to our natural world and pose a unique threat to aquatic ecosystems. It is increasingly more common for multiple invasive species to be present in a given habitat at the same time. Amphibians are especially vulnerable to stressors imposed by invasive species. For this study I investigated the impacts of the invasive plant species amur honeysuckle (Lonicera maackii) and tree of heaven (Alianthus altissima), as well as the invasive anuran species American bullfrog (Rana catesbeiana). These three species were chosen to analyze possible effects they may be having within aquatic ecosystems on larval amphibian life history traits, zooplankton abundance, and water chemistry. The model larval amphibian used in this experiment was the small-mouthed salamander (Ambystoma texanum). R. catesbeiana tadpoles had a significant effect on A. texanum size at metamorphosis, but not survival. In addition, R. catesbeiana tadpoles significantly decreased pH and dissolved oxygen at the experiment midpoint. The presence of both larval amphibian species resulted in significantly higher in vivo chlorophyll and abundance of copeopods, however the presence of both resulted in significantly lower abundance of cladocerns. Invasive plant species alone had no significant effects on the life history traits of either larval amphibian. However, some interactive effects were noted between R. catesbeiana tadpoles and plant species type in regard to in-vivo chlorophyll and zooplankton abundance. Understanding the impacts of multiple invasive species is important to predict the effects they may have on individual species as well as abiotic factors within the habitat. Kimberly Lavoie
495: Oviposition site selection is critical to reproductive success in amphibians because embryos and larvae develop without parental care and are highly dependent on aquatic habitat conditions. These decisions can be described within a hierarchical framework, in which females first respond to broad-scale patch characteristics (i.e., wetland size) and then to finer-scale patch-quality cues (i.e., chemical or visual) within breeding sites. Invasive plants may alter these decisions by introducing novel detrital inputs that alter habitat cues, with consequences for parental decisions and larval performance. We evaluated how wetland size, predation risk, and leaf litter identity influenced oviposition, measured as egg presence, in a factorial mesocosm experiment. Treatments varied in size, predator presence, and leaf litter treatment, including invasive Chinese tallow, native litter types, and litter-free controls. Mesocosms were surveyed throughout the breeding season to quantify oviposition. Oviposition was strongly seasonal, with mid-season peaks in predicted egg presence across treatments. At the broad scale, patch size shaped oviposition patterns, as small wetlands revealed stronger and sharper seasonal peaks than large wetlands. Within patches, predation risk acted as a primary behavioral filter, consistently reducing oviposition across the breeding season. At the finer scale, litter effects were context-dependent, varying with size, predator presence, and seasonal timing. Chinese tallow differed from controls at specific points in the breeding season, under predatorpresent conditions, by altering oviposition timing and increasing egg presence. These findings suggest that when invasive litter alters cue reliability, oviposition decisions may no longer align with offspring performance, increasing the potential for ecological traps. Caleb Z. Mullins Caleb Mullins; Christopher Schalk; Daniel Saenz; Matthew McBroom; Reuber Antoniazzi; Gabriel Andrade-Ponce;
496: Understanding movement and habitat use is essential for amphibian conservation in fragmented landscapes. The northern leopard frog (Lithobates pipiens) is at-risk across western North America, and in Canada, the endangered Rocky Mountain population persists as a small, isolated, genetically-distinct population; yet, postbreeding movement and fine-scale habitat selection remain poorly understood. We investigated post-breeding movement and habitat use by animals during the summer and fall of 2024 and 2025 using radio telemetry. Twentyseven juvenile and adult frogs equipped with transmitters revealed a wide range of movement patterns and distances travelled after breeding. Total path length (range: 13.6 m – 4,565 m, median: 596 m), total displacement (range: 12.9 m – 2,125 m, median: 414 m), and movement rate (range: 0.9 m/day – 83.0 m/day, median: 24.5 m/day) did not differ between sexes, suggesting that post-breeding movement was driven more by landscape structure and environmental conditions, rather than sex-specific behaviour. The animals selected habitat patches with cooler microclimates and higher moss cover, suggesting thermoregulation and moisture balance were important factors during the latter part of summer. Frogs also selected moderate levels of aquatic debris, which may provide visual concealment from predators. Our findings highlight the importance of structurally complex habitats and illustrate how fine-scale habitat features shape amphibian movement and habitat selection. We recommend that land managers prioritize habitat features that enhance thermal heterogeneity, maintain moss-dominated habitats, and support moderate accumulation of aquatic debris to enhance habitat suitability for at-risk amphibian populations. 497: Urbanization is rapidly reshaping thermal environments worldwide, yet its consequences for hostassociated microbiomes remain poorly understood. Elevated temperatures driven by the urban heat island effect, alongside other anthropogenic stressors, can alter gut microbial diversity with important consequences for host physiology and survival. However, background ecological contexts interact with urbanization, possibly leading to variable effects on the gut microbiome. We sampled three urban–forest populations of the crested anole (Anolis cristatellus) across three Holdridge life zones in Puerto Rico to test how urban habitats and regional climate jointly shape gut microbiome diversity and composition. We collected fecal samples from 120 individuals, sequenced the V4 region of bacterial 16S rRNA gene, and used the QIIME2 platform to characterize microbial communities. Using these data, we ask how microbiome diversity and composition are affected by (1) regional climate, (2) urbanization, and (3) their interaction. Specifically, we hypothesize that climatic variation modulates microbial responses to urbanization via differences in thermal regimes. We find that urbanization alters gut microbial composition, with population-specific responses in different climates. These findings demonstrate that gut microbiomes are sensitive to urban stressors, although downstream health and fitness consequences of these changes are unclear. More broadly, our results highlight the importance of incorporating climatic variation and ecological contexts to understand species-level patterns in gut microbiome and the extent of parallelism in response to global change. Kira Welch Kira Welch; Travis Taggart; Sara Ruane; Sean Harrington; Frank Burbrink
498: Range shifts in large marine predators like sharks can have consequences for the environment and human society, especially in nearshore nursery habitats. But current models of species distributions do not account for genetic differences due to local adaptation, even though failing to incorporate locally-adapted ecotypes may make conservation less effective. Bull sharks (Carcharhinus leucas) in the Western North Atlantic Ocean are expanding their nursery habitat poleward in response to anthropogenic warming, resulting in population-wide genetic changes over the past 30 years. Here we present evidence of local adaptation in some nurseries, suggesting that not all bull sharks will respond similarly to climate pressure. We also identify the environmental factors driving the current and future distribution of bull shark nurseries and demonstrate how habitat availability changes when ecotypes are considered. We deployed a Genetic Species Distribution Model, which identified sea surface temperature (SST) and sea surface salinity (SSS) as primary drivers of critical nursery habitat distribution. Specifically, SST was found to have influenced broad movement patterns over evolutionary time, while SSS shaped fine-scale contemporary patterning, and both model estimates changed when ecotype was considered. Taken together, our data indicated that under future climate scenarios, bull sharks are expected to retain and expand their important habitat along the U.S. Atlantic coast but lose habitat in the northeastern Gulf of Mexico. We conclude that bull sharks in the Gulf of Mexico are most at risk of climate-related disturbance and highlight key areas on which to focus future management efforts. Payton Barry
499: Evolutionary adaptation to local selection pressure can cause habitat requirements to vary between subpopulations, complicating efforts to manage species under climate change. Local adaptation is usually identified using diverse genetic loci like single nuclear polymorphisms (SNPs). But most SNPs are considered neutral, making sources of selection challenging to isolate. To understand contemporary patterns of local adaptation, we compared gene-environment associations in SNPs with functional loci subject to selection that reflect only the phenotypes that are successful under current environmental conditions. For this, we used the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) class IIβ gene, part of the adaptive immune system known to vary in response to selection. We applied a seascape genetics approach to model the relationship between environmental predictors and the presence of MHC alleles, and compared these with patterns observed with SNPs. Clustering of individuals based on shared genetic variation of the MHC revealed two non-geographic genetic clusters, unlike adaptive SNP analysis identified three distinct clusters, indicating finer-scale local adaptation. Analysis of MHC loci identified Tampa, Florida individuals as significantly divergent from all others, with site-specific alleles reflecting unique adaptation to low primary productivity. Furthermore, four broadly-distributed MHC alleles correlated with natural gradients in phosphate, temperature, and salinity, suggesting that environmental variability is shaping MHC adaptive diversity. Although gene flow is having a homogenizing effect on allele frequencies, there is strong evidence that fine-scale local adaptation is causing fine-scale evolutionary and contemporary habitat requirements to vary, even among the largest and most dispersive marine megafauna. Júlia Chaumel Cerdà
